generated_text: Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m shattered. Little Leo kept me up half the night. Teething, I think. Or just being a tiny human with no concept of sleep. Speaker_2: Oh, bless him. They're exhausting at this age, aren't they? Remember when Maisie was like that? I lived on coffee and dry shampoo for about six months. Speaker_1: I’m already mainlining the coffee. You’d think having done it with the older two would prepare you, but it doesn’t, does it? It genuinely gets *harder*. Anyway, enough about my sleep deprivation. Are you still on for Saturday? That new Italian place, Bella Notte? Speaker_2: Yes! I’ve booked a table for 8. It’ll be good to actually get out, won’t it? Just… us. Without tiny hands grabbing at everything. Speaker_1: Absolutely. I’m looking forward to it. Ben’s promised to handle bedtime, so hopefully, I won’t fall asleep face-first in my pasta. Speaking of which, what’s Mark up to these days? I haven't spoken to him properly in ages. Speaker_2: He’s… well, he’s good. Really busy at work, apparently. They're launching a new project, something to do with renewable energy. He’s been travelling a bit, too. Last week he was in Scotland. Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds interesting. He always was a clever one. Still, it's a shame he doesn’t get to see the kids as much as he’d like. Ethan was asking about him the other day. Speaker_2: I know. He feels it, you know? He feels guilty. He sends them little gifts and FaceTimes, but it’s not the same. He was saying he’s trying to block out a week in November to come home properly - help with Freya’s birthday. Speaker_1: Oh, that's lovely! What are we thinking for Freya’s birthday then? She’s turning eight, isn't she? A proper little lady now. Speaker_2: Eight! I can’t believe it. She wants a Harry Potter themed party, apparently. A full-on Hogwarts experience. Speaker_1: Oh, wow. That’s ambitious! You’ll have to get your wand-making skills up to scratch. I can maybe help with decorations? I've been doing a bit of freelance design work, so I’m fairly handy with that sort of thing. It's good money, though honestly, it's been a bit slow lately. Trying to drum up new clients is exhausting. Speaker_2: That’s fantastic, honestly. Any help with the decorations would be amazing. And maybe you could give me some advice on invites? I’m hopeless with that sort of thing. You’re so much better at the creative stuff. Speaker_1: No problem at all. Happy to. It’s just nice to use my brain for something other than baby talk and washing machine cycles, you know? Rest of the family okay? Mum and Dad been keeping well? Speaker_2: They're alright. Mum’s been badgering me to come round for Sunday lunch, of course. Said she’s making her famous roast. You going to be free? Speaker_1: I think so. Ben has a football match, but I can probably pop over afterwards. Leo might need entertaining, though. He’s a bit of a charmer, your mum adores him. Speaker_2: She does! She’s already trying to convince me to let him stay over next week. Honestly, she thinks he's the most perfect baby ever born.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the hassle of travelling in the EU now is just… exhausting. Remember when you could just *go*? Like, spontaneous weekend in Amsterdam? Those days are gone. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I’m supposed to be presenting at a conference in Berlin in October, and even just thinking about the extra admin is giving me a headache. It's not the cost, exactly, though that’s creeping up too, it's the time. The queuing. The forms. Speaker_1: Exactly! The forms! I went to Barcelona with my sister in the summer, and she’d meticulously prepped everything – passport scanned, visa stuff checked, even printed out a load of stuff just in case. She’s a planner, that one. Still took us ages to get through passport control. Speaker_2: It’s changed the whole vibe, hasn't it? It used to be so… casual. I did a backpacking trip around Europe after uni. Literally just turned up at train stations, booked hostels, figured it out as I went. Wouldn't even *think* of doing that now. Speaker_1: No way! I remember vaguely hearing stories like that. Sounds idyllic. I did a year abroad in Paris, pre-Brexit, and it was bliss. Borderless, basically. We’d hop on a train to Brussels for the day just because we felt like it. Speaker_2: Proper freedom. I tried to do a similar thing last year, got as far as Calais and then just… gave up. The queues at the ferry port were insane. Ended up driving all the way round to Dunkirk and getting the Eurotunnel. Cost me a fortune in petrol. Speaker_1: Oh, Dunkirk! That’s a detour and a half. I’ve heard stories about people getting stuck in massive traffic jams. What’s the point of a quick getaway if you spend half the time sitting in a car? Speaker_2: It’s ridiculous. And it’s not just the borders, is it? It’s the little things. Getting your phone to work, insurance, even just knowing what the rules are about driving in each country. It all adds up. Speaker_1: My mate Liam went to Italy last month. Apparently, he got a parking ticket because he didn’t realise he had to display a little disc in his windscreen showing the time. Total tourist trap. He was fuming. Speaker_2: Classic! They always get you with those little things. The ZTL zones in Italy are another nightmare. Drive into one accidentally and you’re looking at a huge fine. Speaker_1: See, I'm thinking about going to Portugal next spring. But I'm already dreading the planning. Maybe I’ll just stay in the UK and visit Scotland again. Less bother. Speaker_2: Scotland *is* nice. And no passport needed! Seriously though, it's a shame. Europe was so accessible. Hopefully, things will ease up eventually, but I'm not holding my breath. Fancy another drink? All this Brexit chat is making me thirsty. Speaker_1: Definitely. Another Pinot for me, please. And yes, Scotland is looking increasingly appealing. Maybe just embrace the staycation life for now. Speaker_2: Sounds like a plan. Cheers to less paperwork and more holiday enjoyment, even if it’s a bit closer to home. Speaker_1: Cheers to that! And to remembering the good old days of effortless European travel. Those were the days. Speaker_2: They truly were. Speaker_1: Wait, speaking of effortless travel, remember that time in Prague when we completely lost each other in that market...? Speaker_2: (laughing) Oh god, don't remind me! I spent a solid hour wandering around looking for you amongst all those wooden toys and knitted hats. Speaker_1: And you were convinced I'd been kidnapped by a puppet salesman! Speaker_2: Well, it was a very convincing puppet salesman! He had a whole menagerie of them. It was slightly terrifying. Speaker_1: (laughing) Oh, Prague. Those were good times. Simpler times.

Speaker_1: Right, so after dinner, what are we thinking for dessert? I was thinking maybe those little chocolate pots I got from the supermarket? Or would you two prefer ice cream? Understanding supply and demand, managing your resources… Speaker_2: It’s about getting all the money! Speaker_3: And making everyone else poor! Speaker_1: (laughing) Well, yes, ultimately. But it's about how you get there. And learning not to land on Park Lane with a hotel on it, obviously. That's a very expensive mistake. Speaker_2: Mummy always lands on Park Lane! Speaker_3: It's not fair! Speaker_1: It’s just bad luck! Honestly. It’s all down to the dice. But we can play a slightly shorter game tonight, maybe. Before bedtime gets too close. And maybe… maybe someone will be feeling generous with their hotels. A girl can dream… Do you want me to continue the conversation, or perhaps change the direction it's going in? Let me know! Speaker_1: Do those people have a look have they managed to change the value of their portfolio. It's just such a mess with this. Speaker_2: It's is it his brother or his uncle's. Speaker_2: When the weather is better. Speaker_1: Yeah if the weather is better or something. Speaker_2: I'd like. Speaker_2: You know. Speaker_2: Oh. Speaker_1: That's good.Homete.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the traffic was mental getting out of Durham. I thought we’d be stuck there forever. Like, *forever*. Speaker_2: Yeah, it was pretty bad. I checked the motorway cameras before we left, but it didn’t look *that* bad then. Just a bit of congestion around the A1(M) junction, you know? Speaker_1: A bit of congestion? That was an understatement. It was a solid line of red. Honestly, makes you wonder why people even bother driving when it’s like that. Speaker_2: Well, trains aren’t exactly reliable either, are they? Remember that time we tried to get back from Edinburgh and were delayed for six hours? Speaker_1: Don't even *mention* Edinburgh. I nearly lost the will to live in that station. At least in the car, you've got control, even if you’re not moving. You can blast the music and… well, complain. Speaker_2: True. Although, my control was mostly limited to muttering about the horrifying navigation choices you were making. Speaker_1: Hey! I was following the sat nav! It told me to go down that tiny little lane. Speaker_2: The one that was clearly marked “Unsuitable for HGVs”? And barely wide enough for your little Fiat? Speaker_1: It said it was the fastest route! It didn’t mention anything about agricultural vehicles. Honestly, that was terrifying. I thought we were going to end up in a field full of cows. Speaker_2: (laughs) You and a field of cows. That would have been a story. Seriously though, maybe next time we’ll stick to sticking to the main roads, even if it adds an extra twenty minutes. My blood pressure can’t handle those back lanes. Speaker_1: Fine, fine. You’re the engineer, you know about routes and stuff. Just promise me we're not going near any farms. I’ve had enough adventure for one day. Are we stopping for food soon? I'm absolutely starving. All this talk of traffic and near-death experiences has worked up an appetite. Speaker_2: I was thinking we could grab something at that service station just after Peterborough. They do a pretty decent panini, I think. And coffee, obviously. A lot of coffee. After that drive. Speaker_1: Panini sounds good. And yes, definitely coffee. A *large* coffee. Thanks for driving, by the way. I would have probably ended up driving into a ditch by now. Speaker_2: No problem. That's what boyfriends are for. Though you should really learn to navigate better. Speaker_1: Oh, hush you. Speaker_2: Just saying. Speaker_1: I'll stick to being a corpus administrator, thank you very much. My skills lie in metadata, not motorways. Speaker_2: Fair enough. Speaker_1: Speaking of metadata… did you finish that report for Professor Davies? Speaker_2: Oh great… don’t remind me. I barely started it. Speaker_1: You said that last week. Speaker_2: I know, I know! It’s just… the simulations were a nightmare to run. Kept crashing. Speaker_1: Mmhmm. Well, you have a whole car journey to think about it. And I have a panini to look forward to. Speaker_2: Excellent plan. Speaker_1: Brilliant. Speaker_2: So Peterborough, then? Speaker_1: Peterborough, it is. Speaker_2: Good. Now, if you’ll excuse me, I need to concentrate on avoiding any more unexpected farm visits.

Speaker_1: Right, well, that's the rhubarb crumble in the oven. Should be alright. Bit of ginger in it this time, you know, just to give it a little…zing. Speaker_2: Ginger, eh? Never been a huge fan, myself. Still, won't say no to a bit of crumble. More cream, I hope? Speaker_3: Of course, more cream. It wouldn’t *be* crumble without a mountain of cream. Honestly, you two. You’d think I wasn’t feeding you properly. Speaker_1: Now, now, Elsie. We appreciate it, we really do. It’s just…well, you know how we are. A bit of a sweet tooth. Did you manage to get through to the doctor’s surgery this morning? I’ve been meaning to ask. Speaker_3: Eventually. Took me nearly an hour on hold, honestly. All for a blooming appointment. And then they said the earliest they could fit me in was three weeks time! Three weeks! What’s the point of having a National Health Service if you can’t even get to see a doctor when you need to? Speaker_2: Sounds about right. It’s all gone downhill, hasn’t it? Remember Doctor Henderson? Always had time for everyone. Never rushed you. You could walk in with a sniffle and come out feeling like a new man. Speaker_1: He was a good sort. Knew everyone in the village. Now, they just seem to rotate doctors every few months. Barely remember your name, let alone your medical history. Speaker_3: This new one sounded awfully young. All bright and breezy. No sense of…well, gravity, if you know what I mean. Speaker_1: It's the modern world. Everything’s fast-paced. No time for a proper chat anymore. Speaking of which, did you hear back from that chap about the shed? The one who does the repairs? Speaker_2: He said he’d pop round Tuesday. Said he’s a bit busy with garden fences at the moment, but Tuesday should be good. It’s the felt that’s gone, you know. Leaking like a sieve when it rains. Speaker_3: Good. It’s driving me mad. Everything in the shed’s getting damp. Honestly, you'd think we lived in a rainforest sometimes. Speaker_1: Well, we are fairly close to the coast, aren't we? Always a bit of a sea breeze. Oh, I saw young Timothy from next door earlier. He's got himself a motorbike now, can you believe it? A proper roaring machine. Speaker_2: A motorbike? Goodness me. He’s barely old enough to shave. Speaker_3: I hope he’s wearing a helmet. Those youngsters think they’re invincible. Don’t they? It's a wonder more of them aren't hurt. Speaker_1: Suppose we'll find out soon enough. Though, knowing his mother, she'll be on his case about it. She's a sensible woman, Eileen. Right. Best get the cream ready. Don't want that crumble getting cold. Speaker_2: Sounds good to me. Always a winner, crumble and cream. Even with a bit of ginger in it. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Alright, alright. I'll get the cream. But don't you two expect me to eat it all myself! Speaker_1: Certainly not Elsie. We'll share. We always do. Speaker_2: Always do. Speaker_3: That’s what family’s for, isn't it? Sharing crumble…and complaining about doctors.

Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking, for the new moisturiser, we absolutely *have* to lean into the hyaluronic acid thing. Everyone’s obsessed with it. It's like the gold standard now, isn't it? Speaker_2: Yeah, definitely. But everyone's using it. It's almost…vanilla. How do we make *ours* stand out? I’m still massively hesitant about the packaging. That frosted glass just feels…expensive. Which is good, obviously, but it bumps the unit cost up so much. Speaker_1: I get you. We could look at a slightly thinner glass? Or maybe a different shape? I was looking at some square bottles, they feel a bit more modern. And we definitely need a nice label. I've been watching loads of YouTube videos on label design. It’s a minefield. Speaker_2: Label design is the worst. I spent, honestly, four hours yesterday trying to choose a font! Four hours! And I ended up going back to one I originally dismissed. It's ridiculous. Did you see Sarah at "Blooming Botanicals" on Instagram? She's doing really well. I think she's just repurposing stuff she finds, though. So, less focus on production cost, more focus on the "aesthetic." Speaker_1: Yeah, I’ve seen her. Her photos are *amazing*. But it doesn't feel…authentic, does it? Like, are the products actually that good, or is it all filters and pretty pictures? I want Honest Skincare to be genuinely good *and* look good. I’m worried about the rosehip oil sourcing, actually. I really want it to be ethically sourced, but it's adding a significant cost. Speaker_2: Okay, so ethically sourced versus price point. That’s the perennial small business struggle, isn’t it? Have you looked into suppliers in Bulgaria? I read an article saying they’re a huge producer, and the practices are generally pretty good. Might be cheaper than Chile, which is where we were initially looking. Speaker_1: That’s a good shout. I'll do some digging. Speaking of digging… Gran keeps sending me links to weird online marketplaces. She found one selling pre-owned beauty equipment! She thinks it’s a brilliant idea. Speaker_2: Oh, bless her. She’s amazing. But no, definitely not. Imagine the hygiene issues! We're trying to build a reputation for quality and trustworthiness. Pre-owned mixing vats are not the way forward. Speaker_1: Exactly! Anyway, what about the market next Saturday? Are we definitely on for a stall? I've got the banner printed, and I’m making a display stand out of some old pallets. It's…rustic. Speaker_2: Rustic is good. As long as it doesn’t look like it’s about to collapse. Yes, we're on! I’ve got the card reader sorted, and I’ve ordered a load of little sample pots. I’m thinking of doing a little “build your own face mask” station, just to get people engaged. Speaker_1: Oh, that's brilliant! People love that sort of thing. Okay, measurements… how big is your car? Because I need to figure out how much stuff I can realistically transport. Is it a hatchback, or a bigger boot? Speaker_2: It’s a…difficult question. It's a Kia Sportage. So, not enormous, but definitely more than a hatchback. I could probably fit a small wardrobe in there, if I really tried. We’ll be fine, honestly. We’re overthinking this. Speaker_1: You’re probably right. I just want it to go really well. My mum keeps asking about holiday plans. She's convinced we should all go to Cornwall together. Speaker_2: Cornwall? Oh, lord. No. That sounds like a recipe for disaster. Too many people, too much sand, too much screaming. I’m thinking maybe a weekend in the Lake District? A bit of hiking, a bit of peace and quiet. Speaker_1: That sounds

Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of things. Did you see about that MP, the one with the second home allowance? Absolutely unbelievable. Speaker_2: Oh, don't get me started. It’s the same old story, isn’t it? They think they're above it all. Makes your blood boil. Speaker_1: It really does. You work hard all your life, trying to do the right thing, and then you read about this… it’s just insulting. Speaker_2: Precisely. And the excuses they come up with! Honestly. I saw Jeremy Vine dissecting it on the telly, and even he was struggling to find any justification. Speaker_1: Jeremy Vine is good for that, isn’t he? Doesn’t pull any punches. Anyway, enough about all that doom and gloom. How are things with you? Still enjoying retirement? Speaker_2: Oh, immensely. Though it does feel a bit odd, not having the structure of the school year, you know? I miss the kids sometimes, honestly. Not the paperwork, thankfully! Speaker_1: I can imagine. It must be a big adjustment. You always were a natural with them though. Remember little Timmy Higgins? The one who used to insist on wearing a dinosaur costume to school? Speaker_2: Oh, Timmy! How could I forget? He was a character. He used to try and convince me T-Rex could write poetry. Absolutely insistent. Speaker_1: (chuckles) Oh, that's wonderful. You’ve got such patience. I always thought I’d have struggled with that. Speaker_2: It was part of the job, wasn't it? Trying to negotiate with tiny humans. Though, honestly, sometimes dealing with parents was harder. Speaker_1: Oh, don’t even mention the parents! That was often a minefield. I had one mother who insisted her son was a genius, despite him struggling to tie his shoelaces. Speaker_2: (laughing) Oh dear. They’re all at it, aren't they? It’s all about them, isn’t it? Not the child. Speaking of challenges… how’s your garden doing? Last time I was round, it was looking rather… enthusiastic. Speaker_1: Enthusiastic is one word for it! It’s gone absolutely wild. I’m losing the battle, I think. The bindweed is winning. I spend hours out there weeding and it just laughs at me. Speaker_2: You should get Derek’s son around. He's a landscaper now, apparently. Very good, apparently. Does all sorts. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s a good idea. I must remember to ask you for his number. Maybe he can tame the jungle I’ve created. Speaker_2: I’ll text it to you now, actually. One minute. There. Sent. He’s quite reasonable, too. Not one of these rip-off merchants. Speaker_1: Oh, excellent. That’s really helpful. Thank you. I’m starting to think I need professional help at this point. It's been a summer for weeds, that's for sure. Would you like me to continue the conversation further or perhaps explore a specific topic in more detail? . Speaker_2: Right that's her has done it now. Speaker_1: It's nice if you're going to leave that on. Speaker_2: That is a nice painting. Speaker_1: So you think she's doing nothing is she. Speaker_2: Nah don't think she's doing anything. Speaker_1: Oh I don't know what she. Speaker_2: You know she's really gone off.......................

Speaker_1: Honestly, the amount of food we had at Christmas was ridiculous. My mum just…keeps adding things. Like, “Oh, you haven’t had enough Brussel sprouts!” Speaker_2: (Laughing) Sounds about right. My mother-in-law is the same. It’s a competition to see who can produce the most edible mass. Speaker_3: It’s always the same, isn’t it? End up with enough food to feed a small army, and then spend Boxing Day eating leftovers for breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Speaker_4: I think we did okay. We kept it fairly streamlined. Though my aunt tried to send us a whole smoked salmon. A *whole* one. Speaker_1: No way! What did you do? Speaker_4: I politely explained that our fridge is, shall we say, not salmon-sized. She wasn’t thrilled, but she understood. Mostly. Speaker_2: Good save! It's freezing out though, isn't it? I swear the heating hasn’t been working properly all week. It’s just…lukewarm. Speaker_3: Tell me about it. I had to wear a hat while working today. A hat! In my own office. Speaker_1: You should complain! Landlords are legally obliged to make sure the heating works. Speaker_3: I’ve emailed. Several times. They just keep saying they’re “looking into it.” It's the standard response. I’m starting to suspect they just enjoy watching us shiver. Speaker_4: Reminds me of my grandad. Never fixed anything. Said it built character. Honestly, the man could barely change a lightbulb. Though he *did* have an impressive collection of tools, all perfectly organised and never used. Speaker_1: That’s classic! My dad’s the same. He has a shed full of things he's “meaning to get around to.” It’s a museum of good intentions. Speaker_2: I actually managed to fix the bathroom tap last weekend. Which felt surprisingly satisfying. Speaker_3: Ooh, go you! I’m utterly useless at DIY. I once tried to put up a shelf and ended up with it hanging at a forty-five-degree angle. It was a disaster. Speaker_4: You need a proper spirit level. Those little ones on your phone are rubbish. Speaker_1: Speaking of disasters... did anyone see Old Man Hemlock's mulberry tree finally came down in the storm? Speaker_3: Oh, no! That tree was ancient! I always loved picking mulberries from it when I was a kid. Made the best jam. Speaker_4: A real shame. Though I suspect his neighbours aren't too upset. That thing dropped mulberries all over their driveways every year. Speaker_2: Fair point! Have you guys thought about what you’re doing for New Year’s? We’re just having a quiet one at home this year. Speaker_1: We're thinking a games night. Probably Codenames or something. It’s less stressful than trying to go anywhere. Speaker_3: A good plan. I’m trying to convince my parents to learn how to play Settlers of Catan. It’s proving…challenging. Speaker_4: Tell me about it. My cousin tried to teach her grandmother Monopoly once. Ended in tears. Apparently, defrauding family members is not acceptable, even in a simulated economic environment. Speaker_1: Oh my gosh, that's amazing! Is she alright? Speaker_4: she was fuming, said she'd never trust him with her money again, even though it was a pretend game!

Speaker_1: Honestly, this cutlery is dreadful. It’s like eating with plastic spoons. Speaker_2: You always say that, love. It's perfectly functional. Speaker_3: Aye, it's alright. Not the finest silver, but it does the job. Your mother gets a new set every few years, doesn't she, and then we're all having a moan about them being too fiddly or too heavy. Speaker_4: She likes a change, she does. Always has. Though I do remember her grandmother having a truly magnificent set. Real silver, heavy as anything. You had to have muscles to lift a spoon! Speaker_5: (Chuckles) Aye, that were true. Old Bessie’s silver. Not like this modern stuff, all lightweight and flimsy. She’d polish it for hours, Bessie would. Said it was good for the soul. Speaker_1: Well, it’s not good for my soup-eating soul, that’s for sure. It’s bending already. Speaker_2: Stop attacking the cutlery, you’ll upset your mum. Speaking of which, how’s Sarah doing? Haven’t seen her in ages. Speaker_3: She’s good. Just started a new course, online I think. Something to do with digital marketing. Smart girl, that one. Always was. Speaker_4: Good for her. It’s important to keep the brain active. I’ve been trying to do those crosswords, but they’re getting harder and harder. All these obscure words… Speaker_5: Crosswords? Bah! Waste of time. Always preferred a good book. Give me a bit of Dickens any day. Speaker_1: I saw Lisa the other day, from University. She's living in London now, working as a journalist. Apparently, it’s a nightmare trying to find a flat. Speaker_2: London’s ridiculous. Don’t know how anyone affords to live there. I’m happy enough here, thank you very much. Speaker_3: It’s a good place, Chesterfield. Quiet. Everything you need is within easy reach. And your parents have a lovely house, don't they? Always immaculate. Speaker_4: Your mother does take pride in it. Though it is a bit… full. She doesn’t throw anything away. Speaker_1: That’s an understatement. It's like an antique shop in here. Still, it’s nice to be home. It feels… safe. Speaker_5: Aye, that’s what home's for. A bit of comfort. A bit of familiarity. Though I do miss the old garden. Used to grow the best tomatoes, I did. Speaker_2: You always did have a green thumb, Grandad. You should get back into it, you would enjoy it. Speaker_4: He can’t bend down that easily now, son. His knees aren’t what they used to be. Speaker_3: Well, maybe we can help him with the gardening next time we visit. I don't mind getting my hands dirty. Speaker_1: That's a lovely idea. Maybe we could all come up for a weekend next month? We could give the garden a proper overhaul. Speaker_2: That sounds good. I'll check with work. We could bring some new plants too. And maybe a better set of cutlery for your mum... just kidding! Speaker_4: (Smiling) Don't you start. Just enjoy your soup. And try not to bend the spoon. Speaker_5: Aye, enjoy your soup. And don't forget to leave room for pudding. Your mother makes a lovely apple crumble, you know.

Speaker_1: Right, so I’ve actually managed to get that report finished. Finally. Honestly, it felt like it was never going to end. Mrs. Davies kept adding little bits on, you know, “just a quick tweak here,” “could you just clarify this point?” It was relentless. Speaker_2: Mummy, can I have more peas? Speaker_1: Yes, darling, here you go. Just a little bit now. Now, where was I? Oh yes, the report. It’s with Mr. Henderson now, so hopefully, I won’t hear another word about it for a while. I’m hoping to really focus on the Peterson project next week. Speaker_2: Are we going skiing soon? Speaker_1: We are! In just over two weeks. Isn’t that exciting? We’ve got to start getting everything organized properly. Have you tried on your snow boots yet, to make sure they still fit? Speaker_2: Yes! They're a little bit tight. Speaker_1: A little bit tight? How little bit? Speaker_2: Just a little. Speaker_1: Okay, well, we’ll have to take them with us and see if we can stretch them out a bit while we’re there. Speaker_1: …and then Grandad, on my mother’s side, he was a farm labourer, down in Dorset. Proper soil under his fingernails sort of man. Apparently quite a character, always telling tall tales. Speaker_1: Oh look, a hare! Did you see that? Just darted across the field. Speaker_2: Yeah, beautiful. They’re so quick, aren’t they? Makes you wonder how they navigate all this…and those. Speaker_1: So, you’re actually going for it then? The Media Officer role at the Council? Speaker_2: Yeah, I think so. I submitted my initial application yesterday. It felt… okay. What reach did that have? Did it generate any follow-up coverage? Did it lead to increased public participation? Dig deep. They want to see you can connect your work to broader outcomes. Speaker_2: Hmm. Okay. That elections coverage… I did get a quote picked up by the regional news, and we had a noticeable spike in listeners calling in to the phone-in afterwards. I just… didn’t *write* that down. Speaker_1: See! Gold dust! That's a perfect example of impact. Even small things. They know Council jobs aren't always world-changing. It feels… formulaic. Speaker_1: It is. But it forces you to be specific. And specific is good. They want to see you can think on your feet and handle pressure. Speaker_3: (Nodding) My dad was the same. A proper handyman. Used to rebuild engines in the shed. You don’t get that anymore. Everything’s disposable. Speaker_2: My grandad was like that too. He always said, “If it’s broke, fix it. Don’t just throw it away.” He used to complain about modern life constantly. Said we'd all gone soft. Speaker_1: They weren’t wrong, you know. Still, at least we have biscuits. Anyone fancy another one? I brought the ginger nuts… they’re Arthur’s favourite, aren’t they? Speaker_3: (Smiling) You know me too well, Mary. Ginger nuts are the fuel that keeps me going. And honestly, after that talk about knee pain and steep driveways, I need a sugar boost. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Alright, alright, ginger nuts all around! Let's just hope the M6 doesn’t give *us* a sugar crash before we get to Manchester.

Speaker_2: …and honestly, I couldn’t believe it when PC Davies called this morning. He said they’d found it! Your bike! Speaker_1: No way! Seriously? Where was it? Speaker_2: Apparently, down by the Old Town, behind the fishing museum. Someone had tried to spray paint it black, but they hadn't done a very good job, thankfully. Davies recognised the serial number, which is why they knew it was yours. Speaker_1: Oh my gosh, that’s amazing! I thought I’d never see Bonnie again. I was so gutted. I mean, it wasn’t a super expensive bike, but I loved it. I used it for getting to college, remember? Speaker_2: Of course, I remember. All those mornings cycling up that hill! It's a relief it's back, honestly. It's such a pain when things get stolen. Did they catch the person who took it? Speaker_1: Not yet, apparently. They’re looking at CCTV footage from shops nearby. But Davies said the area’s been having a bit of a bike theft problem lately, loads reported in the last few weeks. Honestly, you wouldn’t believe what people get up to. Speaker_2: It’s disgusting. You see it on those Facebook neighbourhood watch groups too, don’t you? Everyone moaning about something. It's awful. Speaker_1: Yeah, it is. I was scrolling through TikTok last night, and there were loads of videos about bike security. All these clever little gadgets you can get, like alarms and GPS trackers. Speaker_2: Good idea! Maybe we should look into getting one of those. Although, it feels a bit extreme for Hastings, doesn’t it? I mean, it’s not exactly a major city. Speaker_1: I know, but it’s better to be safe than sorry, right? Especially after this. I'm going to invest in a proper heavy-duty lock as well. No more flimsy cable locks for me! Speaker_2: Sensible girl. So, are you planning on cycling to college tomorrow? Speaker_1: Definitely! I’m so excited. It’ll be so much quicker than getting the bus. Plus, it's good exercise. I’ve been feeling a bit sluggish lately, spending too much time studying. Speaking of which, how was your work today? Did Mrs. Henderson manage to get her holiday dates sorted? Speaker_2: Oh, don't even ask! She was on the phone for ages trying to re-arrange things. Apparently, the hotel has overbooked. Honestly, she's a nightmare sometimes. I brought home some leftovers from the cafe though – a tuna mayo sandwich and a flapjack. Fancy one? Speaker_1: Ooh, yes please! That sounds amazing. I skipped lunch today, I was so busy with my history essay. Thanks, Mum! And seriously, thank you so much for getting the police involved with the bike. I really appreciate it. Speaker_2: You’re very welcome, darling. That’s what Mums are for. Now, let’s get you fed, and you can tell me all about this history essay. Was it about the Tudors again? Speaker_1: You know me too well! It was about Henry VIII and his wives… again. It’s fascinating though! Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Of course it is. Speaker_1: Mmm, this sandwich is brilliant. Speaker_2: Glad you like it. Now, tell me – what did you think of Anne Boleyn? A villain, or a victim? Speaker_1: Oh, that’s a good question…

Speaker_1: Right, I’m going to try and complete this green line to Plymouth before anyone else blocks me. It’s vital. Speaker_2: Vital? It’s Ticket to Ride, Sarah, not open-heart surgery. Though I suppose strategically blocking people *is* a form of psychological warfare… Speaker_3: (Chuckles) He’s got a point. You’re taking this very seriously. I’m just enjoying the derailment potential, myself. Speaker_4: Are we having cheese and biscuits later? I had a rather large lunch, so I won’t be wanting a full meal. Just a little nibble. Speaker_5: Yes, Dai, cheese and biscuits are definitely on the cards. I picked up a lovely Mature Cheddar from that farm shop near Ross-on-Wye. It's *sharp*. Speaker_1: Oh, good. Sharp cheese is the best. Look, Rhys, don’t even *think* about trying to take that route. Speaker_2: I wasn’t! I was admiring your intensity. Honestly, you play like you’re single-handedly saving the railways. Speaking of railways… did you know the newer Hitachi trains can accelerate faster than the old Intercity 125s? Speaker_3: Can they? Really? I thought the 125s were pretty nippy. Speaker_2: They are, but the Hitachi Azumas have different traction motors. More powerful, better acceleration. Apparently, they ran tests and the difference was significant. It’s all about the torque, you see. Speaker_4: Torque? Sounds expensive. Is that why train tickets are so pricey these days? It's all the torque! Speaker_5: (Laughing) Dai, you’re terrible! It’s a bit more complicated than that, love. But yes, newer trains do cost more. Speaker_1: Actually, that's quite interesting. I always wondered why the trains to London feel so much quicker now than they used to. It's not just my imagination, then? Speaker_2: No, definitely not. It's partially the tracks being upgraded, partially the trains themselves. The newer trains can also handle steeper gradients more easily. It’s all about efficiently moving mass. It's physics, essentially. Speaker_3: You and your physics, Rhys. You’ll be explaining the Bernoulli principle next. Speaker_2: Only if someone brings up airplane wings! Just saying. Speaker_4: I remember when we used to travel up to Shrewsbury on the steam trains. Now *those* were journeys. The smell of coal smoke… the rhythmic chugging… Speaker_5: Oh yes, I remember those too. They were a bit slower, of course, but they had a certain charm. And you could wave at people from the window! Speaker_1: Right, back to strategically important routes. I *need* that connection to Bristol. Rhodes, are you looking at Bristol? Don’t you dare. Speaker_2: (Smiling innocently) Bristol? Me? I’m just admiring the scenic views of… Cardiff. Yes, Cardiff looks lovely. Speaker_3: (Groaning) Here we go… the Welsh mafia are aligning against us. Speaker_1: This is war! Speaker_4: Now, now, children. Let’s all just enjoy the game and the lovely cheese and biscuits later… Speaker_5: Exactly. And perhaps a little glass of wine? It’s a holiday, after all. Speaker_1: Fine, but I'm still blocking you, Rhodes. Just you wait. Speaker_2: Bring it on! Speaker_3: This is getting good.

Speaker_1: Right, your go. Though honestly, I’m starting to think this game is entirely luck-based. Like, seriously, how do you consistently roll a six? Speaker_2: Skill, darling, pure skill. Years of honing my dice-rolling technique. Though you’re right, it *is* a bit random, isn’t it? Still, better than Monopoly, at least. I’d rather dismantle a working television than play another round of Monopoly. Speaker_1: Oh god, don’t even mention Monopoly. It brings out the worst in people. Remember Aunt Carol last Christmas? Practically declared war over Baltic Avenue. Speaker_2: (Laughing) How could I forget? The shouting, the accusations of cheating… it was glorious. In a slightly terrifying way. Speaking of which, your parents seem remarkably calm for a Sunday afternoon. Usually, there's some sort of domestic drama unfolding. Speaker_1: They’re lulling you into a false sense of security. They're deliberately being nice because you’re here. Wait until after tea and the true chaos will begin. Probably involving a disagreement about the correct way to brew a cuppa. Speaker_2: The brewing of tea is a serious matter in these parts. I've learned that the hard way. Still, this is nice. Quiet. A bit…domestic. Reminds me of my grandparents, actually. They were big Scrabble players. Speaker_1: Oh? What was their Scrabble style like? Cutthroat, I presume? Speaker_2: Intense. My grandfather was an ex-teacher, so vocabulary was his weapon of choice. My grandmother would just try and use every single tile she had, regardless of whether it made a real word. She once tried to play "glurp." Speaker_1: (Laughing) "Glurp"? Oh, that’s brilliant! Did your grandfather let her get away with it? Speaker_2: He tried to explain the rules, patiently, for about five minutes. Then he just sighed and conceded the point. He said it was easier to let her win than argue. Describes their whole relationship, really. Speaker_1: That’s lovely. It’s funny, isn't it, how games can tell you so much about people? And about cultures. I was reading an article about drinking cultures in different countries last week. Apparently, in Japan, it’s considered incredibly rude to pour your own drink. You wait for someone else to do it for you. Speaker_2: Really? That’s fascinating. So, it's all about reciprocal obligation? I can see that. It's all very… structured. Here, it's just a free-for-all. “Get ‘em while they’re cold” is pretty much the guiding principle. Speaker_1: Exactly! And then you get the French, who apparently treat wine like it's a sacred liquid. No chugging involved. It’s all about the appreciation of the *terroir.* Speaker_2: Terroir. Of course. You can't forget the terroir. I once attempted to explain the concept of a pub crawl to a German colleague... it didn't translate well. Speaker_1: I can imagine! The idea of strategically visiting multiple establishments purely for the sake of consuming copious amounts of alcohol probably seemed incredibly barbaric to him. Speaker_2: He kept asking about the efficiency. “What is the return on investment?” he wanted to know. “What are the measurable benefits?” Bless him. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, that’s perfect. Well, I suppose we could explain the benefits of a board game victory. A surge of self-satisfaction, a temporary boost to one’s ego… Speaker_2: And the undeniable pleasure of watching you lose. Right, my turn. Prepare to be defeated.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this lasagne is divine, Kerrie. You’ve outdone yourself. Speaker_2: It is really good, isn't it? Especially after all the stress with the removal van yesterday. I thought we were going to be stuck with everything on the driveway all night. Speaker_3: Oh, don't even *start* me on removal vans. The one we used when we moved to Llanelli…absolute cowboys. Broke half my grandmother's china. Said it was ‘pre-existing damage’. Honestly! Speaker_1: Oh no! That’s awful. You’d think they’d be a bit more careful. I’m just glad ours were…competent-ish. Although they did nearly take my neighbour’s garden gnome. Speaker_2: (Laughing) A garden gnome! Imagine the outcry. How’s the new place settling in, anyway? Any disasters yet? Speaker_1: Just unpacking mountains of boxes. And the bins… the bin situation is *confusing*. Apparently, we have a blue bin for recycling, a black bin for general waste, and a green bin that’s only for garden waste *on alternate Tuesdays*. It’s a logistical nightmare. Speaker_3: Oh, the bin systems! They’re the bane of my life. Swansea is just as bad. Different coloured bins for everything, and if you put one wrong thing in the wrong bin, they won’t collect it. Honestly, it's like a test. Speaker_2: Seriously! It’s ridiculous. I’m still trying to figure out what goes where. It wouldn't hurt them to just have one bin and sort it all themselves, would it? Speaker_1: Exactly! And then there’s the white goods. The fridge in the new kitchen is…ancient. It sounds like a jet engine taking off every time it kicks in. Speaker_3: You need to get it checked. Don’t want it breaking down and ruining all your lovely food. My cousin had a fridge break down, lost a whole salmon. Tragic. Speaker_2: A whole salmon! That *is* tragic. Speaking of tragic, I bumped into Lisa from college the other day. She’s…become a solicitor. A *solicitor*! Speaker_1: Wow! Good for her. Speaker_2: I mean, good for her, but it made me question all my life choices. I’m coordinating projects, she's defending people in court! I only got a C in law. Speaker_3: Don't compare yourself to others, love. You're brilliant at what you do. And law isn't for everyone. I much prefer balancing the books, personally. Though even that's stressful with all these new tax regulations. Speaker_1: You’re right. And Lisa always was incredibly competitive. Remember how she used to cheat at Monopoly? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, I’d forgotten about that! She’d hide money in her sleeve. Absolute fiend. Still, it’s good to hear she’s doing well. Speaker_3: It is. Though it's also nice to be among friends, eating good food and not worrying about legal loopholes or rogue garden gnomes. Honestly, this lasagne is a lifesaver. It's a far cry to the casserole I made last week. It was a bit soggy. And I tried to make some lemon drizzle cake but… well, it didn’t drizzle. It just sort of…sat there. Speaker_1: (Smiling) We won’t talk about my attempt at knitting, then. It ended up looking like a mangled jellyfish. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, brilliant! We really are hopeless at crafts, aren’t we?

Speaker_1: Honestly, this traffic is mental. What’s even happening up ahead? Just… solid red. Speaker_2: Standard Saturday afternoon, darling. Everyone seems to be going somewhere at once. And it’s not even a school holiday. Though, honestly, it feels like a perpetual holiday these days with all the strikes. Speaker_1: Strikes are a nightmare. Makes everything so unpredictable. Did you have a nice week at the TLS? Anything particularly juicy come across your desk? Speaker_2: Oh, the usual academic spats and authorial egos. Honestly, sometimes I feel like a referee. Though we did get a rather delightful piece on Elizabeth Bowen… beautifully written. And the submissions are still flooding in, even though everyone keeps predicting the death of print. Speaker_1: Death of print? Come on. People still *like* holding a book, turning the pages. It’s a whole experience. Digital’s just…convenient. Speaker_2: Precisely! And let’s not forget, there’s a certain…prestige. A beautifully designed book just *feels* important. Though, the marketing team are obsessed with engagement metrics online. Always wanting me to commission more ‘listicles’ and ‘think pieces.’ Dreadful. Speaker_1: Listicles. The bane of modern existence. Speaking of things that are dreadful, that driver just cut me up. Honestly, the nerve of some people. Speaker_2: Oh, dear. Try to ignore them. Road rage won't get us to North London any faster. Remember what happened to Uncle George? Speaker_1: *(groans)* Don’t remind me. The Great A40 Incident of ‘98. Still talked about at family gatherings. Speaker_2: It’s a cautionary tale! Although, he *was* slightly justified… that other driver was going about twenty miles an hour in the fast lane. Speaker_1: Still, shouting abuse through the window? Not his finest moment. So, what are we actually getting in North London? You’ve been very mysterious about this. Speaker_2: It’s a little something for your Aunt Judith. Her birthday is next week and I found a rather lovely antique shop. They specialise in… well, let’s just say it’s something she collects. Speaker_1: Something she collects… That narrows it down to approximately three hundred things. Is it another ceramic cat? Please tell me it's not another ceramic cat. Speaker_2: *(laughs)* No, not a cat. Though she does have a fondness for them. This is… more floral. And French. She’s been talking about wanting to go back to Provence for ages. Maybe this will tide her over. Speaker_1: Provence sounds amazing. We should all go. You, me, Dad, Aunt Judith… Speaker_2: Perhaps. Though getting your father on a plane these days is like pulling teeth. And Judith would spend the entire time complaining about the lack of proper scones. Speaker_1: True. Maybe a staycation then? We could rent a cottage in Cornwall. Speaker_2: Now *that* sounds lovely. Though we might need to start planning ahead. These things don’t just magically happen, you know. Especially not when navigating British traffic. Honestly, it's barely moved another inch. Speaker_1: Oh brilliant. Just brilliant. The entertainment value of being stuck in traffic is truly limitless. Speaker_2: Look on the bright side, darling. At least we have each other’s company and a good natter. And I’m very glad you drove, you’re much calmer behind the wheel than I am. Speaker_1: Probably because I haven't had twenty years of London drivers trying to kill me.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of him. I’ve never seen anyone cling to a life raft like that. Speaker_2: You’re still on about Dave in Majorca? It was a bit choppy, give the lad a break. Speaker_3: Choppy? It was a force ten gale! He was screaming for his mum, I swear. Speaker_4: (Laughing) No way! Dave? Screaming for his mum? That doesn’t sound like the Dave I know. Speaker_5: It is entirely believable. He cries at Disney films. Speaker_1: He genuinely thought he was going to drown in about three feet of water. And the lifeguard just stood there filming it. Speaker_2: Classic. Probably thought he'd get it on TikTok. Speaking of embarrassing moments, remember that time Liam tried to serenade Sarah with a ukulele on that camping trip to the Lake District? Speaker_3: Oh god, don’t. The less said about Liam’s musical 'talent' the better. He thought he was Ed Sheeran. Speaker_4: Was it…bad? I wasn't there for that one. Speaker_5: Bad doesn’t even begin to cover it. He kept breaking the strings, and Sarah looked like she was actively plotting his demise. Speaker_1: She was making these really pointed comments about needing earplugs. It was glorious. Speaker_2: He was so insistent though, bless him. He'd learned, like, three chords. Thought he was away. Speaker_3: And then it started raining. Mid-song. The ukulele got soaked, and he just…stopped. Just stood there looking utterly defeated. Speaker_4: Oh, that *is* tragic. Though I’m picturing it and I’m laughing already. Speaker_5: It was peak Liam. Remember when we tried to take him white water rafting? He refused to let go of the instructor’s lifejacket. Speaker_1: (Snorting with laughter) He genuinely thought he’d be swept away to Spain! He kept shouting “Barcelona!” as we went down the rapids. Speaker_2: Barcelona! I've completely forgotten about that! He’s a walking disaster, that boy. A lovable disaster. Speaker_3: Honestly, planning a holiday with him is a full-time job. Constant supervision required. Speaker_4: This is why I just stick to all-inclusive resorts. Minimal risk of Liam-related incidents. Speaker_5: Sensible. Speaking of holidays, anyone got any plans for next year? I'm thinking maybe backpacking around Southeast Asia. Speaker_1: Ooh, that sounds amazing! I’m thinking maybe a city break to Amsterdam. Need some culture, you know? And waffles. Definitely waffles. Speaker_2: Amsterdam *is* good for waffles…and other things. I'm leaning towards a week in Italy, just eating my way through the country. Speaker_3: I'm saving for a deposit on a house, sadly. So city breaks are out of the question. Just a weekend in Blackpool, probably. Glamorous life, eh? Speaker_4: Blackpool could be fun! Don’t knock it. It’s got a certain…charm. And a really big tower. Speaker_5: Charm is a strong word. Speaker_1: It's certainly memorable. Right, anyone fancy another round? I’m starting to feel strangely nostalgic for Dave clinging to that life raft. Speaker_2: You're a terrible friend. Another round it is, though. Cheers to disasters and slightly questionable holiday choices! Speaker_3: Cheers! Speaker_4: Cheers! Speaker_5: Cheers!

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the silence. You wouldn’t believe the silence. Not a mechanical silence, you get enough of that in London, but a *natural* silence. Broken only by the wind, and the occasional… well, last time it was a pine marten scrabbling about. Quite close, actually. Woke me up, thinking someone was trying to get into the tent. Speaker_2: A pine marten? Goodness! You’re brave, Alistair. Wild winter camping. It sounds… intensely cold. And slightly terrifying. Speaker_1: Cold, yes, it is cold. That’s why preparation is key. Layers, proper sleeping bag, a stove for hot drinks. It’s not about suffering, it’s about being comfortable *within* the discomfort. And terrifying? Not really. It's more… humbling. You’re utterly reliant on your own skills and the weather. Makes you feel very small, and very connected, all at the same time. Speaker_3: Dad’s been trying to get me into it for years. I’ve always shied away, to be honest. Too much of a soft southerner, I suppose. Though I’ve done a bit of hill walking, obviously. Bit different lying out exposed overnight though. Speaker_1: It is different, Calum. It’s about shedding the layers of… well, everything. Modern life. All the noise and distractions. You’re forced to be present. Honestly, it's the best thing for clearing your head. Better than any therapy, if you ask me. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Now, now, Alistair. Don’t go undermining my profession! I think there are benefits to both. Though I *do* see what you mean about being present. We try to foster that in therapy, that mindful awareness. It’s just… lying in a tent, potentially freezing, seems a rather extreme method. Speaker_1: Extreme, perhaps. But effective! And the stars, Moira. You’ve never seen stars like it. Away from all the light pollution. It’s… otherworldly. I went up to Glen Affric last February, and the aurora borealis was visible. Flickering green across the loch. Spectacular. Speaker_3: Glen Affric… that does sound pretty good. Actually, I've been thinking about getting a bit more into bushcraft, you know, building shelters, foraging. Maybe a winter camping trip isn't *entirely* out of the question. Have you got a good recommendation for a lightweight stove, Dad? I've been looking at the MSR PocketRocket 2… Speaker_1: The PocketRocket is alright, efficient enough. But for winter, you want something with a bit more power. Look at the Primus OmniFuel. A bit heavier, but it’ll happily burn petrol, gas, even kerosene. You need that flexibility in colder temperatures. And don't skimp on the fuel. Speaker_2: You two and your gadgets! It sounds awfully complicated. I'm happy appreciating nature from a nice, warm pub, thank you very much. Though the aurora does sound beautiful. Perhaps a slightly less… strenuous viewing option exists? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) There are aurora forecast websites, Moira. You can track it. But you won’t get the same experience. It’s about the whole package, the isolation, the challenge… And honestly, the quiet. It changes you. Speaker_3: Yeah, it's about pushing yourself isn’t it? Though I think my first attempt will involve a slightly less ambitious location than Glen Affric… maybe somewhere nearer Aviemore. Speaker_1: sensible lad. Start small. And always tell someone where you're going. Always.

Speaker_1: Honestly though, I don't get the hype with Wes Anderson. Everyone bangs on about him, but it all feels…stylised for the sake of being stylised, y’know? Like, pretty to look at, but does anything *actually* happen? Speaker_2: I can see that. It’s very… curated, isn't it? Like a museum diorama come to life. But I think that *is* the point. It’s not about plot, it’s about the aesthetic, the world-building. It's escapism. Speaker_1: Escapism into a world where everyone speaks in a flat monotone and has commitment issues? Sounds bleak, not escapist. Give me a good gritty drama any day. Something with actual, you know, *feeling*. Speaker_2: Fair enough. What have you been reading lately? Anything gripping? I finally got around to finishing “Piranesi” – Susanna Clarke. Absolutely blew my mind. Speaker_1: Oh, I’ve *heard* about that one. It’s the one with all the statues and the tides, right? I’ve got it on my list, but I'm currently slogging through “Middlemarch". It’s…a commitment. A really, really long commitment. Speaker_2: Oh god, “Middlemarch”. That’s a proper undertaking. George Eliot’s a bit… dense, isn’t she? Lots of moralising. Speaker_1: Loads! Like, I appreciate the social commentary, but sometimes I just want someone to *shoot* someone, you know? A bit of action. Instead, it's just hours and hours of people worrying about inheritance and reputation. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Fair point. I guess it’s a different pace of storytelling. So, food-wise, what have you been up to? Any culinary masterpieces recently? I attempted to make a proper paella last weekend. It was…ambitious. Speaker_1: Ambitious and probably a disaster, let’s be honest. Paella is a nightmare to get right. I've been on a bit of a soup kick lately, actually. It’s cold, it's easy, it’s comforting. Made a really nice lentil soup the other day with chorizo. Speaker_2: Chorizo in lentil soup? That sounds amazing. I might have to steal that. I'm terrible at soup, I always end up with it being either watery or like cement. Speaker_1: The key is a good stock, honestly. And don't be afraid to blend some of it at the end to give it a bit of thickness. Makes all the difference. I got a tip from my gran, actually. She’s a soup queen. Speaker_2: Gran's always know best, don't they? Mine makes an incredible apple crumble. I've tried to replicate it for years, but it’s never quite the same. There’s always… something missing. Speaker_1: It’s the love, isn’t it? You can’t bottle gran’s love. Or her secret ingredient, probably. She's notoriously tight-lipped about it. Speaker_2: Probably a sneaky knob of butter. They always are. Speaking of sneaky ingredients...have you seen the new Martin Scorsese film? The one with DiCaprio? Speaker_1: Not yet! It's still in the cinema, yeah? I was waiting for the reviews to settle. Is it worth braving the crowds? Speaker_2: Absolutely. It's long, but it’s phenomenal. DiCaprio is on top form, obviously, and the whole thing is just…masterfully done. Definitely worth seeing on the big screen.

Speaker_1: Right, so then the wolf… he didn’t *blow* the house down, did he? He tried to trick them! He pretended to be…Grandma! Speaker_2: (Giggles) Silly wolf! Grandma doesn’t have scratchy teeth! Speaker_3: Wolves are rubbish. Lego wolves are better. They don’t try to eat you. Speaker_1: That’s very true. Lego wolves are much safer. You building anything good with your Lego today? Is that a game? Speaker_1: (Laughs) Not exactly. It's something I use for work. It helps me keep track of… well, lots of numbers and things. It’s not as fun as a spaceship, I promise. Speaking of fun, did you both enjoy Brownies tonight? Speaker_2: I learnt a new part of the Promise! The one about being truthful. Speaker_1: That’s a very important part. And then played a game where you had to say what you’d do if you found a magic lamp. I said I'd wish for a PlayStation 6! Speaker_1: A PlayStation 6! That's ambitious! They’re only on… what, a 5 now? Speaker_3: Yeah! And it’ll have even more amazing games. And faster loading times. Speaker_2: I’d wish for a pony! A sparkly pink pony! Speaker_1: A sparkly pink pony sounds amazing. Oh, look at the time. Getting late. Time to brush teeth and get ready for bed. Did either of you think of any stories tonight? Things we could read tomorrow? Speaker_3: I did! It’s about a Lego man who builds a robot army to… Speaker_1: (Smiling) We’ll hear all about it tomorrow night then. Right, teeth first. And then, no more talking about PlayStations or ponies, okay? Bedtime stories only. Speaker_2: Okay! Speaker_3: Fine. But the robot army is *really* good. Speaker_1: I’m sure it is. Now, off you go. Sweet dreams! Speaker_2 & Speaker_3: Night mummy! Speaker_1: Night loves. (A pause, then softly to herself) A typewriter… feels like another lifetime. Speaker_1: Honestly, David, you look like you’ve slept in your clothes. Not that it matters here, of course, but still! A bit of effort never hurt anyone. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, come on, Margaret. Anyway, I was reading an article the other day about deserted medieval villages. Apparently, there are hundreds of them scattered across the country. Yorkshire has quite a few. Speaker_2: Really? Speaker_2: That’s the key, isn’t it? Remembering. It gets harder, you know. Not the remembering the *herbs* part, but... everything. I keep losing my phone. Speaker_1: Happens to the best of us. All those ‘New Year, New Me’ health kicks. My Facebook feed is going to be *full* of people at the gym. Speaker_1: Oh, don't get me started on Facebook. Carol posted a picture of her avocado on toast this morning. Avocado on toast! Like that’s inspiring. Something about turning left after the third sheep and then following the lane until you see Old Man Hemmings’ scarecrow? Speaker_2: That sounds like proper Kentish directions. They haven’t updated their navigational system since 1950, have they? Speaker_3: Well, they don't have sat nav, Dad. That's the problem! I tried to be really clear. Google Maps just keeps taking you on the A20, which is a nightmare. Speaker_1: Maybe I can call your Mum and talk her through it? I'm slightly better at simplifying things. Speaker_2: Good plan. She’ll just need to know… head towards Ashford, then avoid Ashford. That’s the key. Speaker_3: Oh, and remind her to take her phone! She always forgets and then complains she can't contact anyone if she gets lost. Speaker_1: She’s so reliant on that thing. Always scrolling through Candy Crush. It's replacing actual conversation, I swear. Speaker_2: It keeps her occupied. And it’s better than her talking about her bunions for three hours. Speaking of occupied, how’s Bonnie doing? Has she been shedding much? Speaker_3: Oh, the fluff monster is in full force. I vacuumed yesterday and it looked like it hadn’t been touched five minutes later. I’m thinking of investing in one of those robotic vacuum cleaners. Speaker_1: They’re good, aren't they? A bit pricey, but worth it. You should get one, especially with Bonnie. Though, honestly, she’s a darling. Always happy to see you. Speaker_2: She is a good girl. Reminds me of Buster, our old Labrador. Though Buster was… less focused on shedding and more focused on stealing roast chicken. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Classic Buster! Oh, I almost forgot. Did you guys get a chance to try that new lavender hand cream I got you for Christmas? Speaker_1: Oh, yes! It smells divine. Thank you, darling. Speaker_2: It’s a bit floral for me, but I appreciate the thought. It’s very… soothing. Perhaps good for after gardening. Though I’m not doing any gardening until spring, frankly. Far too cold.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the new season of *Succession* is just… ruthless. I feel stressed *watching* it, let alone being in a family like that. It’s brilliantly written though, you have to admit. Speaker_2: Oh god, yeah, it's so good. But you’re right, it’s exhausting. My mum keeps saying it's a documentary, which, honestly, feels a little too close to home sometimes with my Uncle David and his… business dealings. Speaker_1: (Laughs) Oh dear. That sounds… eventful. How *is* Uncle David, actually? I haven’t seen him since Christmas. Speaker_2: He’s… David. Still ‘disrupting’ things, apparently. He’s launched another one of his schemes, this time involving ethically sourced alpaca wool. Don't ask. Mum's bracing herself for the inevitable financial fallout. But honestly, it's soul-crushing. I need a new client. Or a holiday. Or both. Speaker_2: You deserve both. They really do take the biscuit sometimes, these marketing briefs. Being a survey programmer isn’t glamorous, but at least I'm not having to write poetry about dog biscuits. Though, honestly, the questions people are asked… Sometimes I feel like *I* need therapy after reading the responses. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, tell me about it. It’s all ‘rate your satisfaction with your cable provider’ and ‘how likely are you to purchase a timeshare in the Bahamas’. The world is a strange place. Are you still thinking about doing that extra module next term? The one on behavioural economics? Speaker_2: Yeah, I think so. It feels like a good fit with the survey work, and it might open up some interesting doors afterwards. Though, the thought of more lectures… I’m already counting down the days until my thesis is finished. It feels like it’s consuming my life. Speaker_1: I can imagine. It's a huge undertaking. Listen, are you free next weekend? There's that new exhibition at the Tate Modern, the one everyone’s raving about. We could go Saturday afternoon and grab dinner afterwards? Speaker_2: Ooh, that sounds amazing! Yes, definitely. I need a cultural fix. Plus, I've been meaning to ask – how on earth are you managing financially in this city? Rent is insane! Speaker_1: (Grimaces) It’s… a struggle. I'm basically living on toast and tea most weeks. I'm trying to save for a deposit, which feels like a completely impossible dream. I’m thinking of moving back in with my parents for a bit, just to get my finances back on track. It's humiliating, but… Speaker_2: Don’t be! Lots of people are doing it. It makes perfect sense. And honestly, your mum’s cooking is legendary. It’s a win-win situation. We should brainstorm some budgeting tips later, maybe over another cup of tea? And definitely avoid talking about alpaca wool. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Absolutely. Deal. And yes, my mum's cooking is the only reason I'm even considering it. Alpaca wool is officially banned from conversation. Speaker_2: Good. Now, tell me more about this “discerning hound” brief…

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m feeling so sluggish. I really need to get back into a routine with the walking. It’s just… getting started is the hardest bit, isn’t it? Especially when it’s dark and cold. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I tried to go for a run this morning, and it was just miserable. The wind was howling. Ended up cutting it short and just walking the dog. He was much happier about that, anyway. Speaker_3: You two are braver than me. I’ve completely given up on outdoor exercise until spring. I've signed up for that online yoga thing again. It’s not the same, obviously, but it’s better than nothing. And warm. Speaker_1: Oh, is it the one with the woman who keeps talking about mindfulness? I tried that last year, and it drove me mad. All that 'being present'… I just wanted to stretch! Speaker_3: (Laughing) Yes, that's the one! She’s very… earnest. But it’s actually quite good once you get past the mindfulness bits. Ridiculous. Speaker_1: Don’t even start me on house prices. It’s completely bonkers. Remember when we thought we could afford a little place with a garden? That’s just a dream now. Speaker_2: Honestly, at this rate, we'll be renting forever. It’s just… demoralising. I’m thinking of just giving up looking for a while. It’s stressing me out for no good reason. Speaker_1: Maybe that's a good idea. It’s better to just try and enjoy where we are now, and not compare ourselves to people who've had a bit of luck. Although, I *am* craving a slightly bigger kitchen… Speaker_3: A bigger kitchen would be nice. Mine is perfectly adequate, but I’m dreaming of a proper Aga. It’s utterly impractical, I know, but a girl can dream. Speaker_2: An Aga? You’re aiming high! I’d settle for a dishwasher that actually *works*. Ours sounds like it’s about to take off every time I use it. Speaker_1: Oh, ours is on its last legs too. We’re constantly having to rearrange the plates to make sure the spray reaches everything. It’s a nightmare. Speaker_3: You know, I tried that new lemon chicken recipe I saw online last week. It was surprisingly good. Really simple, but full of flavour. I could send you the link? Speaker_1: Oh, yes please! I'm in a cooking rut at the moment. Everything tastes the same. Lemon chicken sounds amazing. Speaker_2: Sounds good to me too. Anything to escape the monotony of pasta and sauce. Although, to be fair, I'm a pretty awful cook. Lemon chicken might be a disaster in my hands. Speaker_3: Nonsense! It’s practically foolproof. And even if it is a disaster, at least it’ll be a funny story. Speaker_1: Exactly. A cooking disaster is a small price to pay for a bit of entertainment. Speaker_2: Right, well, if you’re offering a recipe, I’m game. Send it over.

Speaker_1: Right, so basically the whole department’s in meltdown because of this new archiving system. Honestly, it's a nightmare. They’ve implemented it without any proper training, and everyone's just scrambling around trying to figure it out. Speaker_2: Oh, brilliant. Sounds…fun. Is it one of those things where it’s supposed to make everything efficient, but actually just makes it slower? Speaker_1: Exactly! A thousand percent. It’s supposed to streamline things, cut down on paper, all that jazz. But it's so clunky and unintuitive. I spent three hours yesterday just trying to locate one document. Three hours! I could have written a small essay in that time. Speaker_2: Ugh. Bureaucracy at its finest. Reminds me a bit of some of the processes we have to follow on site. Endless forms for everything. It’s infuriating when you just want to *build* something. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. It’s like nobody involved has ever actually *done* the job themselves.
