Something about tax rises and cuts to…everything? It’s hard to keep track. Mum was going on about it at dinner last night, saying it’s going to ruin the country. She always does that. Speaker_1: (laughs) Mothers. Always predicting the apocalypse. I just worry about how it’s going to affect funding for things like…well, everything. The arts, education, you name it. It all seems to be on the chopping block. Speaker_2: Yeah, that’s fair. It’s a bit worrying. Speaking of things that cost money… have you seen *Wicked* yet? Speaker_1: *Wicked*? No! I’ve been wanting to for ages, but tickets are ridiculously expensive. Speaker_2: They are, aren’t they? But it was incredible. Seriously, the staging, the songs… it was just phenomenal. I went with Sarah last week. Speaker_1: Ooh, Sarah’s lucky. I’m so behind on seeing musicals. I was planning on going to see *Hamilton* when it last came to Newcastle, but then everything got cancelled with… you know. Speaker_2: Right, yeah. Everything went a bit chaotic. *Wicked* is a bit less… historically intense, I’d say. A lot of sparkle and dramatic reveals. You should definitely try to go when you can. Maybe when you're back up North visiting? Speaker_1: Definitely. I'll check ticket prices. I'm supposed to be saving for a new laptop, but… maybe a musical is a good excuse to dip into the funds. It's good for the soul, right? Speaker_2: Absolutely. Way better than spending it on more archiving software, I’d say. Is this conversation helpful? Would you like me to continue it, or perhaps generate a different one based on your specifications? Speaker_1: Definitely. I'll check ticket prices. I'm supposed to be saving for a new laptop, but… maybe a musical is a good excuse to dip into the funds. It's good for the soul, right? Speaker_2: Absolutely. Way better than spending it on more archiving software, I’d say. You deserve a treat after dealing with all that nonsense. Are you managing to switch off when you're not at work, though? It sounds exhausting. Speaker_1: Trying! It's hard when it's constantly on your mind, though. I've been trying to get back into reading, but I keep finding myself thinking about overdue documents. I might need to invest in a really good distraction. Maybe I'll finally take that pottery class I've been talking about for years. Speaker_2: Pottery! That sounds perfect. Something completely different to take your mind off things. Plus, you'd have something tangible to show for it. More than you get from archiving, anyway.

Speaker_1: Right, that’s a good covering on that fence now. Think we’re getting somewhere. It's amazing what a bit of paint does, isn’t it? Makes all the difference. Speaker_2: Aye, it does. Makes it look…finished, you know? Not like it’s been neglected for ten years, like it was. You wouldn't believe the state of some gardens I pick folks up from. Honestly. Speaker_1: People don’t prioritise, I suppose. They get caught up in…everything else. Speaking of which, have you seen what they're planning for that old dockland area? Down by the waterfront? Speaker_2: Oh, aye. More flats. Always more flats. That’s all they ever build. High rise boxes. Ridiculous. They say it's "regeneration" but it just feels like they're squeezing everyone in. No green space, no character. Speaker_1: Precisely! It's all about maximising profit margins. Remember when they talked about a community theatre there? A proper, independent theatre? Speaker_2: Aye, I do. That’d've been brilliant. I had a mate, used to be right into am-dram. Proper good he was. Played Macbeth, he did. Scary stuff. Speaker_1: Really? That’s fascinating. I’ve always been interested in acting. Never had the nerve to try myself, mind. Too self-conscious. Though, I did consider a life drawing class a few years back. Speaker_2: Life drawing? You? I can’t picture that, mate. You always struck me as more the bookish type. Speaker_1: Well, I am. But I thought it would be a good exercise in observation, in seeing the world differently. Plus, I’ve always admired good painting. Turner, obviously. But also the Pre-Raphaelites. Rossetti… Speaker_2: Rossetti…sounds proper posh. I was down the car boot sale on Sunday, trying to find a decent toolbox. Found an old record player, though. Works a treat. Cost me a tenner. Speaker_1: Bargain! I've been meaning to get a record player myself. I've got boxes of old vinyl gathering dust in the attic. You wouldn’t happen to have a spare set of those gutter brackets, would you? The ones you used on your shed? Speaker_2: Gutter brackets? Hmm. Might. I think I’ve got a couple left over. They’re a bit rusty, but they’ll do the job. Why? Your gutters playing up again? Speaker_1: A bit. There's a leak near the downpipe. It’s driving me mad. I'll try and fix it myself, but I'm no builder. I was thinking of getting someone in, but…well, you know how the budget is. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Everything’s going up. And this government…don’t get me started. They haven't got a clue, do they? Just out of touch. Speaker_1: It’s all about soundbites and spin, isn't it? No substance. What are your goals, by the way? What are you hoping to achieve in the next few years? Apart from fixing a leaky gutter, obviously. Speaker_2: (chuckles) Goals, eh? I dunno. Just want to keep working, keep the cab on the road. Maybe get a proper holiday someday. Not just a weekend in Blackpool. And get a bit more sorted, you know? The house, the garden. Proper sorted. What about you? Still aiming for that professorship? Speaker_1: That’s…the plan. Though, academia can be a bit of a slow grind. You put in the work, but recognition doesn't always come easy. It’s a bit like painting this fence, really. Slow, steady progress. And a lot of hard graft. Pass me that roller, would you? I think we need another coat.

Speaker_2: Oh look, another church. Seriously, Poland is *full* of churches. They’re beautiful, don’t get me wrong, but… another one. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) It's part of the landscape, isn't it? Historically, you know. Everything revolved around the church. And after all that’s happened with Poland, they’ve certainly clung onto their faith. It’s kind of… reassuring, in a way. Speaker_2: True. It’s just... we’ve passed like five in the last hour. Speaking of clinging onto things, have you worked out the petrol costs yet? I feel like we’re burning through diesel at an alarming rate. Speaker_1: I roughly estimated it last night. It looks like we’re each going to owe about… seventy quid, give or take. Unless we find another cheap petrol station. Polish petrol is surprisingly expensive. Speaker_2: Seventy quid… ouch. Okay. Right. Well, worth it, I suppose. This scenery is amazing. Though I’m still slightly traumatized by that guy hitchhiking with the goat. Speaker_1: (Laughing) I know! Honestly! A goat! I was half expecting him to ask for a lift *for* the goat. Is that even allowed? Speaker_2: No idea. Probably not. It was certainly a conversation starter. I wonder if he made it to Tarnow with Gertrude. Speaker_1: Gertrude? You named the goat? Speaker_2: Well, it looked like a Gertrude. A very determined Gertrude. Anyway, speaking of arriving in Tarnow, are you still up for meeting Kasia and her friends for pierogi? I texted her, and she said they've found a little place that’s supposed to be fantastic. Speaker_1: Absolutely. Pierogi are essential. I’m really looking forward to seeing Kasia again. It’s been ages. How's your friend, Liam, doing? You mentioned he was struggling a bit with things back home? Speaker_2: He’s alright, I think. Still trying to sort things out with… well, with everything. Apparently, he’s decided to have a massive clear-out. Getting rid of all his “stuff.” He says it’s liberating. Speaker_1: That sounds good. I’ve been meaning to do that for ages. This campervan life really forces you to confront just how much unnecessary stuff you accumulate. I think I need to seriously reassess my relationship with antique tea cozies. Speaker_2: (Raises an eyebrow) Tea cozies? Seriously? You have a collection of antique tea cozies? Speaker_1: (Defensive) They’re…historical artifacts! And they’re very charming. But yes, okay, probably a bit excessive when you're living in a space the size of a postage stamp. I’m thinking of donating most of them. Or maybe just keeping the really ridiculous ones. Speaker_2: Sounds like a plan. Honestly, it's funny how quickly you realise what you actually *need* when you’re travelling. Suddenly everything feels so… superfluous. Speaker_1: Exactly. Although I do miss a decent cup of tea, honestly. The Polish tea is…functional. Not exactly Earl Grey. Speaking of needing things, are we stopping for lunch soon? I'm starting to feel a bit peckish. Maybe some of those little Polish sausage rolls we saw at the roadside stall? Speaker_2: Ooh, yes! That’s an excellent idea. Sausage rolls it is. And then, Tarnow and pierogi await! I hope this fits your requirements! Let me know if you'd like me to adjust any aspect of it.

Speaker_3: Right, just off the M55 at Junction 1 then, yeah? Should be straightforward. Less traffic than usual, surprisingly. Probably everyone's at the beach. Speaker_1: Honestly, this journey feels *ages*. Are we nearly there yet? Feels like we’ve been driving for hours. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Only about twenty minutes, darling. You’re used to being whisked away in Daddy's fast car, aren’t you? This is…a more realistic pace. Speaker_1: It's just… I’m stressing about my English Lit exam tomorrow. I haven’t even finished revising *Jane Eyre*. Bronte is so… depressing. Speaker_3: *Jane Eyre*’s a classic, love. You’ll be alright. Remember I told you about my English teacher, Mr. Grimshaw? He made us all write essays about the weather. The *weather*! Said it revealed character. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Oh, that sounds delightful. And incredibly…English. Speaker_1: Seriously? The weather? That’s just…mad. I need to memorise quotes, not analyse cloud formations. Speaker_3: He was a bit of a character, Grimshaw. Always wore a tweed jacket, reeked of pipe tobacco. But he did make you *think* about things. Remember your Grandma used to say a grey sky was a good omen? Speaker_1: She was always saying something. I think she believed in fairies. Speaker_2: She had a beautiful spirit, your Grandma. So full of life. It was lovely visiting her in St Anne's, wasn’t it? Much nicer than the supermarket later. Speaker_3: Aye, it was. Though she did try to palm me off with a knitted tea cosy every time. Said it was 'good for the soul'. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, she always had a tea cosy to spare. Did you hear about the train strikes again? They’re going on for, like, forever. Speaker_3: Aye, a right mess. Trying to get down to London to see your Auntie Maureen next week will be a nightmare. Speaker_2: Perhaps we should drive. It’s a long journey, but at least we’d be in control. Speaker_1: Driving is better anyway. Though Mum warned me Preston’s a bit… rough. Speaker_3: Preston's alright. Just don’t wander down any dark alleys. It’s improved a lot in recent years. They've built a fancy new shopping centre. Though to be honest, I still prefer the market. You can get a bargain there. Speaker_2: I need to find a good greengrocer. Supermarket fruit is just…sad. It has no flavour. Speaker_1: Ooh, and I need new pens! All mine have run out of ink. And maybe some highlighters, for *Jane Eyre*. Speaker_3: We’ll get you sorted. You just focus on that exam. And try not to think about depressing novels. Think about ice cream. Speaker_1: That’s a much better plan. Chocolate flake, please. Speaker_2: We should really make a list before we go into the supermarket. We always end up buying things we don't need. Speaker_3: You're telling me! Last time we needed milk and came out with a garden gnome. Speaker_1: A garden gnome?! Why? Speaker_3: Your mother saw it and said, quote, "It needs a home." Don’t ask. Speaker_2: (Laughing) She has a weakness for garden ornaments. It's a family trait.

Speaker_2: Honestly, Mum, you scared the life out of us! Just appearing like that. We weren't expecting you until next week. Speaker_1: Oh, don't be daft, love. I saw the weather forecast – dreadful for the next few days. Thought I'd get up here while I could. Besides, I wanted to surprise young Master Theo. How's school going, lad? Speaker_3: It's alright. We're doing Shakespeare. It's… complicated. Speaker_2: Complicated is an understatement. Trying to get a fourteen-year-old interested in ‘thee’ and ‘thou’ is a full-time job. Speaker_1: Shakespeare's wonderful! I used to adore it. Although, when I was at university, we had a dreadful professor. Tried to make it all terribly serious and intellectual. It was exhausting. We used to sneak off and watch Morecambe and Wise afterwards just to recover. Now *that* was comedy. Speaker_3: Morecambe and Wise? Who are they? Speaker_2: Oh, Theo… you have a lot of catching up to do. Classic British comedy. Absolutely brilliant. We’ll have to get you some DVDs. Speaker_1: Yes, do! You need a bit of proper entertainment. This technology you youngsters are obsessed with… it’s all a bit overwhelming for me. I tried to video call Brenda last week and ended up broadcasting to the entire village. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, Mum! You and technology… It’s a disaster waiting to happen. I tried to show you how to use online banking last time and nearly had a heart attack. Speaker_1: Well, it’s complicated, isn't it? All these passwords and security questions. What if I forget my mother’s maiden name? It's been years! And all this talk about hacking… terrifying. Speaker_3: It’s not *that* scary. You just need a strong password. Speaker_1: Easy for you to say, young man. You’ve grown up with it. I was perfectly happy with a chequebook and a friendly bank manager. Anyway, I was having a clear-out and found a box of old photos. Thought I'd bring them along. We can have a good reminisce. Speaker_2: That’s lovely, Mum. Though goodness knows what horrors we’ll unearth. Remember the one of Dad with that ridiculous Hawaiian shirt? Speaker_1: Oh, dear, yes. Honestly, that shirt. He thought he looked so dashing. He did have a good heart, your father. It’s just… he struggled, you know? With his moods. It wasn’t easy for any of us. Speaker_2: It wasn't. Looking back now, it's clear he needed help. Didn’t really understand mental health back then, did we? Just told him to ‘pull himself together’. Speaker_3: Is that why he was… sad sometimes? Speaker_1: It was part of it, love. It was a long time ago. Best not to dwell on it. Let's look at the photos, shall we? Maybe we’ll find some happier memories. And then, I’m famished. Is there any of that lovely Yorkshire pudding left? Speaker_2: Yes, there is. Come on then. Let's have a look at those photos. And Theo, I promise, after pudding, we'll find you some Morecambe and Wise on YouTube. It's a cultural education, you see. Speaker_1: That’s my girl! Always thinking of culture. Now, where did I put that box…?

Speaker_1: Right, so, what do we think? Is it…is it doing alright? It felt a bit sluggish opening that tab. Speaker_2: It’s alright. Not exactly lightning, is it? What specs did you get again? You said you went for… the one with the extra ram? Speaker_1: Yeah, 16 gig. Supposed to be decent, but honestly, I’m already wondering if I should’ve splashed out on the SSD. It feels… like my old one, just slightly less terrible. Speaker_3: SSD makes a *massive* difference. Like night and day. Honestly, if you’re gonna be doing anything more than Word and emails, get one. It's worth every penny. Speaker_1: That’s what I’m thinking. I was watching a YouTube vid, this guy was saying you can clone your existing drive onto one. Is that easy enough to do? Speaker_2: Yeah, pretty straightforward. There's loads of free software out there. Macrium Reflect is good. You’ll need a SATA to USB adapter thingy to connect the new SSD, though. Speaker_1: Right, a… SATA adapter. Added to the list. Speaker_3: Nah, I've been too busy trying to get the climbing roses to actually climb. They're just flopping about like sad noodles. Speaker_1: He's insane. Knocked out three guys in the first round last week. Proper brutal. I’m thinking of trying to get back into training again. Been feeling a bit… soft. Speaker_2: Soft? But I promised myself I'd try and make that lentil soup recipe my mum sent me. It’s supposed to be super healthy. Speaker_3: Oh, the one with the seventeen different spices? Yeah, good luck with that. Sounds intense. Speaker_1: It does, doesn’t it? Alright, laptop test seems… passable. Still thinking about that SSD, though. And a new monitor. And a better chair… This could get expensive. Speaker_2: Welcome to the world of tech, mate. It never ends.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this place is lovely, isn’t it? Such a nice change from… well, everything else in Tarnow’s centre square. It was a betting shop before, wasn't it? Truly grim. Speaker_2: Yeah, a proper dive. You wouldn't have sent your nan in there. They've done a good job with it though. Really bright, and that music isn’t awful which is a bonus. Speaker_1: Exactly. It feels… hopeful. Which is weird to say about a bistro, I suppose. It feels like someone actually *invested* in something nice. I’m really hoping it does well. Speaker_2: Me too. We need more places like this. Speaking of investing in things… I've been thinking a lot about my auntie Brenda recently. Speaker_1: Oh? How’s she doing? That's awful. I was hoping she’d finally gotten a grip on that. It’s such a destructive thing. Such a… identity thing, isn't it? Like she fills a void with it. Speaker_2: Exactly! That's what I was thinking. Like, who is Brenda without the ‘thrill’ of it? It sounds so pathetic, saying it like that, but it’s true. It became *her*. And now she’s lost it and… well, she's lost herself again. Speaker_1: It's heartbreaking. I remember when she was obsessed with those fitness classes. For about six months, it was all body pump and spinach smoothies. Speaker_2: Oh, God yes! And the leggings. The endless leggings. Then she suddenly decided it was all a waste of time and started baking. A *lot* of baking. Speaker_1: And then the betting shops. It’s a cycle, isn’t it? Always searching for something to fill the space. I wonder if she ever just… wants to *be* Brenda, without needing a hobby or an obsession to define her. Speaker_2: I think she does, deep down. It's just… I don't know. It’s terrifying, isn’t it? Facing yourself, really facing yourself. It's easier to latch onto something. Speaker_1: It is. Makes you think, doesn't it? About what we all do to avoid… well, everything. I keep telling myself I'm going to start running again. I’ve had these trainers for months. They’re still in the box. Speaker_2: Classic. You and a million other people. I’m trying to be better at saying ‘no’ to things. I keep ending up agreeing to help people with stuff, and then panicking about it for a week. Speaker_1: That sounds like you! You’re a people pleaser, darling. Just like your grandma. Still, you’re doing amazing, teaching in Poland. That takes courage. And I bet you’re brilliant at it. Speaker_2: Thanks. It’s alright. It’s just… lonely sometimes. I miss having a proper friend group. And proper shops. I miss being able to just… wander around a good bookshop. Polish ones are… limited. Speaker_1: Oh, I can imagine. I’m craving a decent cheese shop, honestly. The cheese here is… functional. It’s not *inspiring*. And speaking of functional… I feel a bit weird bringing this up, but have you noticed how… unpredictable periods are getting? Speaker_2: Oh, God, don’t even get me started. It's like my body is just messing with me, taking the absolute mick. I’m convinced it’s stress. Speaker_1: That’s what I’m thinking. It’s just… everything feels a bit all over the place at the moment, doesn’t it?

Speaker_1: Right, so have you actually booked the tickets for the Steam Fair then, Grandad? Because I was looking online and it said they’re doing early bird discounts if you book before the end of the month. Speaker_2: Oh, aye, booked ‘em last week, love. Got us all in, didn’t I? Booked a disabled space for your Auntie Carol, too. She’ll need it with her hip, poor thing. They’ve got a good system there, decent facilities. Trying to get Carol’s wheelchair around those muddy fields… Nearly lost her a couple of times. Good on you for thinking ahead, Dad. Is there plenty of seating, hopefully? My back’s been playing up again. Speaker_1: Good. I was a bit worried about accessibility, to be honest. It's a huge site isn't it, and Mum was saying she doesn't want to spend the whole day standing. Speaker_2: They’ve got loads of benches dotted around and little huts selling tea and biscuits. Proper old-fashioned, it is. Reminds me of when I was a lad, going with your Grandad – *my* dad – to these sorts of things. Though it wasn’t called the Steam Fair then, it was just a local rally. They had traction engines, all gleaming and polished. Speaker_3: It sounds lovely. I do like all those old machines. It’s just getting there and getting around that’s the worry. By the way, have you seen what houses are going for around here now? Absolutely ridiculous. Speaker_1: Tell me about it! I was looking at flats in Boscombe the other day, and even tiny little one-bed places are like, £900 a month. It’s insane. Speaker_2: Bournemouth is a right little hotspot, ain’t it? Everyone’s flocking down here. Used to be a quiet seaside town, now…well, it’s just built up and pricey. When *I* first came to London, you could get a decent house for a few thousand quid. A few *thousand*! Can you imagine? Speaker_3: It’s a different world. We were talking about moving, you and me, weren’t we? Further down the coast, maybe? Somewhere a bit cheaper. Speaker_1: That’s a good idea. Somewhere with a garden, so we can have a cat. I’ve been wanting a cat forever! A little ginger one. Speaker_2: Cats are good companions. Though they shed everywhere. You wouldn’t believe the amount of cat hair your Nan used to find in the most bizarre places. She was constantly vacuuming. And then *moving* furniture around… she was always rearranging things. Speaker_3: Oh, she loved her furniture! Remember that awful floral sofa? Speaker_1: (Laughs) Oh god, yes. The one that smelled faintly of mothballs? Speaker_2: That’s the one! Reliable old thing, though. Lasted her a good twenty years, that sofa did. Which is more than you can say for most things these days. Speaking of moving things, are you still trying to get that piano to Carol’s place? Speaker_3: Yeah, still figuring that out. It’s a beast to move, isn’t it? And she lives up three flights of stairs! I’ve asked her neighbour, young Ben, if he could lend a hand, he’s quite strong. Speaker_1: Right, well, let me know if I can help. I can at least offer moral support, and maybe a cup of tea. Oh and I think Barnaby the cat is missing - have you seen him. Speaker_2: Always, love. Always happy to help. And don't you worry about the cat. Barnaby always turns up. Likely asleep in the sun somewhere.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this weather is dreadful, isn’t it? Rain, rain, rain. Reminds me of Kendal, actually. Always a bit drizzly up there. Speaker_4: Aye, it's a bit grim. Though good for the garden, I suppose. Though it’s not really a garden, is it, just a patch of… stuff. Speaker_3: Can I have another biscuit? Speaker_2: Yes, dear, but just one more. Of course, I've been reading a bit about the historical Jesus recently. Quite fascinating, actually. The layers of interpretation… it's like peeling an onion. Speaker_2: Oh, you and your theology! Anything special? Speaker_4: I thought we might go to that little artisan bakery in Thirsk. They do a brilliant sourdough. And then perhaps a quick look around the church? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You’re always one for noticing the details, aren’t you? I saw on Twitter that old Mrs. Higgins has started a pottery class. Apparently, it’s very popular. Speaker_3: Twitter? And the school uses it to send out reminders. Though sometimes it’s just people arguing. Speaker_4: It's the modern equivalent of gossiping over the garden fence, really. Speaking of, I need to start thinking about moving house again. This lease is up in six months, and everything is so expensive now. Speaker_1: Moving? Oh dear. Don't you think it's a terrible bother? All the packing and unpacking. And then getting to know a new neighbourhood. It's not worth it, not at our age. Speaker_4: I know, I know. But… we need more space. And a garden that's actually *a* garden. Perhaps somewhere closer to the Dales. Speaker_3: Can we get a dog if we move? Speaker_2: We’ll see, love. We’ll see. Let’s just focus on finishing these biscuits first. And then perhaps a lovely walk, if the rain ever stops. Oh and I think someone needs to learn some manners - elbows off the table.

Speaker_1: Right, so dentist appointment is booked for Cindy on Tuesday afternoon. Just a check-up, nothing to worry about. Speaker_2: Oh. Will it hurt? Speaker_1: No, sweetie, it shouldn’t. Three birthdays all close together. She’s turning… well, she’s a bit older than you two, but still! Speaker_3: Is she getting a Lego spaceship? Speaker_1: I highly doubt it. She’s more into… museums. And Monet. She loves Monet. You wouldn’t believe how much she knows about Impressionism. Speaker_2: What's a museum? Speaker_1: It's… a place where they keep old things. Paintings, sculptures, things like that. Remember when we went on the school trip to the Roald Dahl museum? It's a bit like that, but with different things. Speaker_3: Can we get Easter chocolate? Speaker_1: Yes, we can get Easter chocolate. But just a little bit, okay? We don’t want to ruin our appetites for dinner. And please, leave a few radishes for the salad. Honestly, you two are ravenous! Now, let's talk about this maths homework… Speaker_2: Nooooo! Speaker_3: It’s not fair! Speaker_1: (Sighs) It is fair. It's important. And it's only a few problems. Speaker_2: It’s too hard! Speaker_1: Let’s just start with the first one.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’ve been living off pesto pasta for, like, four days straight. It's a culinary low, even for me. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, you are hopeless! You were always the worst at feeding yourself properly, even at uni. Remember that time you tried to make beans on toast and set off the smoke alarm? Speaker_1: Hey! That was a momentary lapse in judgement fuelled by extreme hunger and a lack of kitchen skills. Which, admittedly, haven’t improved drastically. And you weren’t much better, constantly surviving on cereal. Speaker_2: Rude! I had a balanced diet of Fruit Loops… sometimes. But seriously, you need to expand your repertoire. I made a massive chilli last night, I could bring some round? Speaker_1: Oh my god, yes please! You are a lifesaver. I’ve been meaning to actually *cook* something, but work’s been insane. Copywriting deadlines are the bane of my existence right now. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Adult acute speech therapy is… intense. Literally spent the morning trying to help a gentleman who’d had a stroke relearn how to say ‘banana’. It’s rewarding, but draining. Speaker_1: Wow, that sounds… challenging. And heartwarming, I guess? I’m just writing slogans for shampoo. It’s not exactly changing the world. Speaker_2: Hey, someone has to make sure people know which shampoo makes their hair shiny! It all contributes. Speaking of contributing… have you started saving for a deposit on a place yet? Speaker_1: Ugh, don’t even. It feels utterly impossible. Rent in London is ridiculous, and then there’s the deposit, and stamp duty… I’ve got a spreadsheet going, but it mostly just makes me feel depressed. Speaker_2: I know, right? I’m trying to be sensible, but it's so hard. Mum keeps offering to help, but I'm stubbornly refusing. I need to do it myself. Speaker_1: Smart. It’s a whole thing with my parents, though. They're convinced I should move back to Kent. “It’s so much cheaper, darling, and you’re closer to us!” Like my entire life should revolve around their convenience. Speaker_2: Oh, god, no. Mine are the same. Constantly asking when I’m going to settle down and have kids. It's like, back off! I haven’t even figured out what I’m having for dinner, let alone the rest of my life. Speaker_1: Exactly! It's exhausting. Remember when we were kids and we swore we’d never be like them? Speaker_2: (Smiling) Oh, the grand proclamations of our teenage years. “I’m going to travel the world and become a famous artist!” Or was that just me? Speaker_1: A little bit of both, I think. I wanted to be a novelist. Now I write taglines. Progress, I guess. Hey, how’s Winston? Is he still terrorising the neighbourhood squirrels? Speaker_2: Oh, you know Winston. A tiny, fluffy tyrant. He’s fine, though. He’s actually being unusually well-behaved today. Maybe he's plotting something. Speaker_1: Definitely plotting something. Those little faces hide a lot. Speaker_2: So, chilli tomorrow then? Speaker_1: Absolutely. Rescue me from my pesto prison. Speaker_2: Consider it done. It'll be good to catch up properly, properly. Speaker_1: It really will. It feels like ages.

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the sheer audacity of it! He just rocked up with a suitcase full of francs, handed it over, and the farmer just… accepted! No solicitors, no surveys, nothing. What’s wrong with being a perfectly respectable market town? They’ve been tinkering with it for years. Remember when they widened the High Street? Ruined it completely. Took away all the character. Speaker_4: Oh, the High Street was lovely before that. Proper shops, not just charity shops and coffee chains. I did a lot of my early practice shopping there, you know. Being an NHS dentist had its perks back then. Sailing trips, for a start. Speaker_1: Sailing trips? Speaker_4: Oh yes! The dental association used to run them. Whole conferences, lectures all at sea with your oral surgeon! Can you imagine the state of things if someone had a toothache mid-Atlantic? Speaker_2: Goodness me. Sounds… memorable. Though, I suppose it was different then. More camaraderie, less litigation. Honestly, the lengths some people go to these days… I was trying to get tickets for that Hockney exhibition, completely sold out, but somehow managed to wangle a couple through a friend of a friend. Speaker_3: Ah, the old network. Still works wonders. I’m more concerned about that solar farm they approved last night. An absolute eyesore. They’ve stuck it right on the edge of town, ruining the view from the canal. Speaker_1: I know! It’s dreadful. All that countryside, wasted on a field of black panels. Though, I suppose we have to move with the times. Speaker_4: Moving with the times… that’s what they said when they started replacing all the beautiful Victorian buildings with concrete monstrosities. Progress, they called it. Made the whole town look like a Soviet housing estate. Speaker_2: It's a shame, isn't it? The architecture was so lovely. They need to do something about it. I was in Prague last year, you know. Now *that* is a city that knows how to preserve its heritage. Honestly, it's stunning. And so cheap! You can have a lovely weekend there for next to nothing. They do those bargain city breaks, don’t they? Speaker_3: Prague is beautiful. But crowded. Absolutely crammed with tourists. Still, a good option for a weekend. More pressing, though, is the jive event. Are we still on for the barn? Speaker_1: Yes! It’s booked. They’ve just finished converting it, apparently. All exposed beams and fairy lights. Perfect for a bit of swing dancing. They're using the top floor for the workshops, and the ground floor for the main dance. Speaker_4: Sounds lovely. I’m looking forward to it. Though, I haven’t jived in years. Might need a refresher course. Speaker_2: We can help with that! I used to be quite the dancer, you know. Before my knees started protesting. Speaker_3: Oh, they always protest eventually. That's just age catching up with us, I'm afraid. Still, it’ll be a good night. A good excuse to get out and about. And hopefully, a good distraction from all the doom and gloom around here.

Speaker_1: Right, so we’re agreed – short-form video is where it’s at, isn’t it? TikTok, Instagram Reels… that’s where the eyeballs are. But how do we make it *educational* without being utterly… dull? Speaker_2: Exactly! That’s the challenge. I was thinking, instead of just lecturing at a camera, we could do case studies. Like, deconstructing viral videos. Take a really popular TikTok, and break down *why* it worked. What editing techniques were used? What narrative structure? How did it tap into current trends? Speaker_1: I like that. “Moving Image Forensics,” almost. But we need a niche. Everyone’s doing ‘explainers’ now. What’s our angle? Speaker_2: Well, I’ve been thinking about my students. They struggle with visual literacy. They can *consume* endless amounts of video, but they can’t critically analyse it. They don't understand the persuasive techniques being used, or the subconscious ways images affect them. Speaker_1: So, the focus is on teaching *analysis* of visual media, rather than just *creating* it? That's clever. We're not competing with the content creators, we're equipping people to understand them. Speaker_2: Precisely. Think about it – it’s applicable to everything. Advertising, news, propaganda… understanding how images work is a crucial skill in the modern world. And we can use really accessible examples, like those ridiculous dance challenges. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Right, deconstructing the floss. I can see that. What about a platform? We could just use YouTube, but it feels…saturated. Is there a way to build a community? Speaker_2: That's what I was pondering. I’ve been playing around with Patreon. Maybe offer tiered subscriptions? Free content on YouTube to lure people in, then more in-depth analyses, downloadable resources – worksheets, analysis frameworks – behind a paywall on Patreon? Speaker_1: Hmm, Patreon is interesting. It’s relying on direct support, which is good. But it means we *have* to consistently deliver valuable content. No pressure. What about leveraging LinkedIn? Target teachers, media studies lecturers… they might be interested in using our case studies in their classrooms. Speaker_2: Oh! That’s brilliant. A B2B element as well as direct-to-consumer. We could offer licensing agreements for educational institutions. Speaker_1: Exactly. We’re solving a problem for both groups. Teachers need resources, students need skills. Building a LinkedIn presence is definitely cheaper than running Facebook ads, too. Speaker_2: And we could target specific curricula. Like, if there's a unit on persuasive techniques in GCSE media studies, we could create a series of videos specifically designed to support that. Speaker_1: Okay, okay. I’m getting excited. What do we call it? “Visual Deconstructed”? Too… academic? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Maybe. How about “Picture This”? It's a bit playful, but it gets the point across. Speaker_1: “Picture This.” I like it. Alright. First step: build a basic website, outline the first five case studies, and start filming. We've got a lot of work to do. Although being house-sitting in Australia does give us a rather pleasant backdrop while avoiding actual work. Speaker_2: You're not wrong. Although…are those kangaroos judging our brainstorming session? Speaker_1: They always are. They're very discerning critics, kangaroos. Very discerning. Speaker_2: Right then. Picture This it is. Let's get started.

Speaker_1: It’s just…remember when we went to Cornwall with Ben and Chloe, and Ben was convinced he saw a mermaid? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh god, yes! He was *so* serious. Staring out to sea with his binoculars for a solid hour. Chloe was trying to subtly steer him towards the ice cream van. Speaker_1: She knew better than to encourage it. It was freezing, honestly. Mid-September, and he was convinced a mermaid was sunbathing on the rocks. Speaker_2: He’d been reading some ridiculous folklore book beforehand, I think. Speaker_2: Precisely. I think Chloe secretly took a photo of it and threatened to use it as their Christmas card. Speaker_1: She absolutely did. Remember how cross he was when she mentioned it? He insisted it was a ‘preliminary study’. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) A preliminary study in mermaid anatomy. Classic Ben. Do you think he still believes? Speaker_1: I wouldn't be surprised. Speaker_2: You’re right. We could all do with a little more of that. It’s easy to get bogged down in…everything. Work, bills, the state of the world. A mermaid sighting, even a fabricated one, is a welcome distraction. Speaker_1: Exactly. And… it reminds me of when we were kids, spending summers at the beach. That feeling of endless possibility. That the sea held secrets. Speaker_2: Yeah. And believing anything was possible. Before reality set in. Speaker_1: (Sighs contentedly) Still…a mermaid. It's a lovely thought, isn't it? Maybe we should go back to Cornwall. Just in case. Speaker_2: Perhaps. But I’m packing the binoculars this time. Just in case *I* see something. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, you wouldn’t! Speaker_2: Don't underestimate me. I might be a scientist, but I’m not immune to a little magic. Speaker_1: I suppose not. Come on, let’s get home. It’s getting cold. And I’m suddenly craving fish and chips. Speaker_2: A fitting tribute to the mermaid hunters, I think. Let's do it. Speaker_1: Perfect. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ..........

Speaker_1: Oh my god, look at what she’s wearing! That dress is… a choice. Speaker_2: Seriously. What *is* that fabric? It looks like something my nan used to have curtains made of. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh, you’re brutal! But yes, it’s a bit much for a daytime talk show, isn’t it? It’s screaming ‘I want attention!’ Speaker_1: It's the colour too. That shade of mustard yellow... It just washes her out completely. She looks peaky. Speaker_2: You know who could pull that off? Alexa Chung. She could make a bin bag look fashionable. Speaker_3: True. Speaker_2: That’s the curse of online shopping. You never really know what you’re getting. I’m trying to be better about fast fashion though, you know? It's terrible for the environment. Speaker_3: Me too. I’ve been trying to shop my own wardrobe more, rediscover things I’d forgotten about. It’s surprisingly satisfying. Although, it also means admitting I bought some questionable things over the years… Speaker_1: Oh, we’ve all been there! Remember that phase we went through with those oversized denim jackets? Speaker_2: (Groans) Don’t remind me! I have photographic evidence somewhere, that needs to be destroyed. Speaker_3: I think I still have mine, somewhere in the attic. It’s coming back into fashion though, apparently. Don’t tell anyone I said that. Speaker_1: No way! Seriously? Maybe we should dust them off and embrace the 90s revival. It’s a pain. But a car… insurance is insane, petrol’s insane, parking’s insane…have you actually looked at the figures? Speaker_1: I’ve started to. I’ve been browsing AutoTrader, mostly just looking. I was thinking something small, economical. Maybe a little Fiat 500 or something? They seem relatively cheap to buy. Speaker_2: A Fiat 500… they’re cute, but they’re tiny. And they’re not exactly known for their reliability. Remember Sarah’s? She was constantly in the garage with it. Speaker_1: Okay, okay, point taken. I just… I feel so trapped without a car. Everyone else just *goes* places. You just drive and you’re there. I feel like I’m missing out. Speaker_2: I know, it’s frustrating. But maybe look at public transport options again? Is there a faster bus route? Or even a train line you could use for part of the journey? Speaker_1: I checked, honestly. The bus takes even longer, and the train doesn’t go anywhere near work. It’s the one major downside to living here, really. It’s lovely, but so inaccessible without a car. Speaker_2: Right. Okay. Well, if you’re serious about it, let’s sit down and really crunch the numbers. Not just the price of the car, but everything – insurance, tax, MOT, fuel, maintenance, potential repairs…it adds up quickly. Speaker_1: I know, I know. It's scary. I'm trying to start a separate savings account just for "car fund" but it feels like I'm filling a bottomless pit. Speaker_2: It's good you're thinking about saving separately. That’s smart. Maybe we could look at some second-hand options too? Something a bit older, but well-maintained? Speaker_1: That's what I was thinking. Not something brand new. Although…part of me wants something a bit…fun. Speaker_2: Fun and reliable don’t always go hand in hand, sadly. How about we cook dinner and then spend the evening looking at realistic options? I'm decent at spotting a potential money pit. Speaker_1: Deal. Pizza? I'm too overwhelmed to think about anything complicated right now. And maybe we can research how much my current bike is worth, just in case… it feels a bit sad to sell it, but needs must. Speaker_2: Pizza sounds perfect. And yeah, let’s see what the bike could fetch. One step at a time. Don't go falling in love with a red Fiat 500 just yet. Speaker_1: No promises. It’s very… appealing. Is there anything else I can help you with? Perhaps another conversation scenario? . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ............

Speaker_1: Right, now then, tea’s brewed, biscuits are out. Grandad, you want a digestive or a Rich Tea? You know you always go for a Rich Tea. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Aye, you know me too well, lass. Rich Tea it is. Though a ginger nut wouldn’t go amiss, if you're offering! Speaker_3: Don’t encourage him, love. He'll be wanting the whole tin before you know it. How’s school going, lad? Still wrestling with those A-Level equations? Speaker_2: It’s alright, Grandma. Mr. Henderson’s set us a practice paper, it’s a killer. It’s all… logarithms and stuff. I just don't *get* it. Used to just use a slide rule back in my day. No fancy dances needed. Just a bit of sliding. Speaker_2: A slide rule? What’s that even *look* like? Speaker_3: Oh, it was a long wooden thing, with bits that slid up and down. Your Grandad used one all the time when he was a shipbuilder. Speaker_4: Aye, built a fair few ships with that slide rule, I did. Though I suspect they’d be using computers now, wouldn't they? Everything’s computers these days. Speaker_1: Speaking of things these days, the washing machine’s making a right racket. I think the drum’s gone again. Honestly, it’s constantly breaking. I swear I’m funding the local repairman’s retirement. Speaker_3: Oh, those modern machines. Never as reliable as a good old twin tub. You knew where you were with a twin tub. Speaker_2: A twin tub? Was that like, two washing machines in one? Speaker_1: More like one washing machine with two sections. You washed one load, then manually transferred it to the other side for the spin. It was hard work, but they lasted forever. Speaker_4: And you didn't need a degree to work out how to use it! These new ones, you need a computer science qualification just to figure out what the buttons do. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. Anyway, I’ve booked a plumber for tomorrow. Hopefully, he can fix it without needing to replace the whole thing. That’ll be another hundred quid down the drain. Speaker_2: Did you remember to order more dog food, Mum? Barnaby’s looking a bit… peckish. He’s been staring at the biscuit tin. Speaker_1: Oh, blast! No, I completely forgot. I meant to do it this morning, but then the marking pile just… swallowed me whole. I'll order it online now. Anything else anyone needs? Speaker_3: Just a bit more tea, love. And perhaps you could tell your son to stop trying to sneak biscuits when we aren't looking! Speaker_2: (Grinning) I wasn’t! Speaker_4: (Winking at Speaker_2) Aye, right you weren't. You young ‘uns are all the same. Always sneaking biscuits. It's a national pastime, I reckon. Speaker_1: Honestly, you two are terrible influences. Now, who wants another biscuit? I might join you this time. That washing machine is stressing me out! Speaker_2: I do! Speaker_3: Me too. A ginger nut this time, if you wouldn't mind dear.

Speaker_1: Right, so pirates then. Pirates were… rather scruffy, weren’t they? Not like in the films, all lovely and clean. More… smelly. And probably quite grumpy. Speaker_2: Did they have parrots? Speaker_1: Some did! But not all. It was more of a… a fashionable thing, I think. A status symbol. Like having a really fancy hat. Speaker_3: My parrot’s called Captain! He’s a Lego one. Speaker_1: Oh, lovely! Captain the Lego Parrot. Very important. Now, we’ve got Shakespeare week next week at school, which means a *lot* of sonnets and plays. We’re trying to decide if we should go to Stratford. It’s a bit of a drive. Speaker_2: Stratford? Is that where Shakespeare lived? Speaker_1: It is! You can see his house, and the theatre where he used to put on plays. It would be a good experience, but it's a whole day. Speaker_3: Can we go to the circus instead? Speaker_1: Well, actually… that’s a really good point! There’s a circus workshop happening, and it’s in a *real* circus! With proper tents and everything. We could learn to juggle! Speaker_2: Juggling! Can I learn to juggle balls? Speaker_1: They have balls, and scarves, and… lots of things to juggle! It's on Saturday. It’s much closer than Stratford, too. We’d need to book quickly though. Speaker_3: Ooh, and can we look at the Easter pictures afterwards? The ones Grandma sent? Speaker_1: Absolutely! We can put them on the fridge. It's all very exciting. Are you both getting excited? What about some lunch? I was thinking sandwiches? Speaker_2: With pickles! Speaker_1: With pickles, of course. And maybe a little bit of magic afterwards? I’ve been practicing a card trick. Speaker_3: Can you make a card disappear? Speaker_1: I can *try*. It doesn’t always work. It's rather tricky. Oh! And I was thinking maybe we could start that stop-motion animation project we talked about. We could make little pirate adventures! Speaker_2: Using the Lego! And Captain the Parrot! Speaker_1: Exactly! A pirate Lego adventure with Captain the Parrot. Sounds like a good plan, doesn't it? Right, sandwiches first, then magic, then maybe a little bit of pirate planning. Speaker_3: And circus! Don't forget the circus! Speaker_1: Never! The circus is definitely not forgotten. Speaker_2: Can we have chocolate with our sandwiches? Speaker_1: (Laughing) We *might* be able to negotiate chocolate with our sandwiches. Let’s see how well you behave during lunchtime. Speaker_3: I’ll be very good! Speaker_2: Me too! Very, very good! Speaker_1: Excellent. Right, pickles it is then! Let’s go and get those sandwiches made. ">" Speaker_3: Yay! " ">" Speaker_2: Pirates and pickles! ">" Speaker_1: A very good combination, I’d say. A very good combination indeed. ">" Speaker_3: Do pirates eat pickles? ">" Speaker_1: They might have done! They ate lots of things to keep them going on long journeys, I expect. Pickles would have lasted a long time! ">" Speaker_2: So they were healthy pirates? ">" Speaker_1: Well… perhaps not *always*. But they needed to stay strong.

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the whole thing was utterly ridiculous. I mean, attempting to sail from Jeddah to Cyprus in a dhow? What was I *thinking*? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Sounds…ambitious, Margaret. Rather ambitious. Jeddah to Cyprus is a fair old stretch, isn’t it? Speaker_1: A fair old stretch is putting it mildly, David! It all seemed perfectly reasonable at the time, fueled by a certain amount of youthful arrogance and a few too many glasses of…well, let's just say grape juice. It wasn't *easy* to get hold of anything stronger in Saudi, you know? That’s part of the whole story. Speaker_3: You were teaching out there then, Margaret? I remember you mentioning it years ago. What was it like? Speaker_1: Chaotic. Fascinating. Oppressive. All at once. Extreme weather, very strict rules, desperately polite people…and the constant longing for a proper pint. You get used to the lack of alcohol, eventually. Although I did hear stories of various expats getting creative. Smuggling things in amongst the dates, apparently. Speaker_4: (Laughing) Dates and duty-free! A combination I haven’t heard before, Clive. Reminds me of the time a patient of mine tried to smuggle whiskey into India hidden inside medical textbooks. Didn’t end well. Customs were…thorough. Speaker_2: Speaking of alcohol, I was in Morocco once, and you could buy anything, absolutely anything, if you knew the right people. Mint tea spiked with something that tasted suspiciously like vodka was a particular favourite. Speaker_1: Oh, Morocco is wonderful. Much more relaxed than Saudi. But back to my rather unfortunate adventure…so there I am, setting sail, feeling rather pleased with myself, when I’m intercepted by the Saudi Coast Guard. Speaker_3: And…? Speaker_1: And they arrested me. Immediately. Apparently, leaving the country without proper authorization, *especially* in a vessel that wasn't exactly seaworthy, was a significant offense. They didn’t appreciate my explanation about wanting to try a Mediterranean salad. Speaker_4: (Raises an eyebrow) A Mediterranean salad? Speaker_1: It sounded more convincing at the time! Anyway, I spent three days in a rather unpleasant cell before the British Embassy intervened. They explained to the Saudis that I was a slightly eccentric English teacher and not a spy trying to destabilize the region. Speaker_2: Good grief. That’s quite a story. Speaker_3: Sounds like you’ve always had a knack for attracting attention, Margaret. Reminds me of the time I tried to sail across Windermere with a mast constructed entirely from old copies of *Dental Practice* magazine… Speaker_4: (Roaring with laughter) You did *what*?! Clive, don’t tell me that actually worked! Speaker_3: It didn’t, of course! It collapsed halfway across the lake. I spent the rest of the afternoon being rescued by a very disgruntled boat hire man. Apparently, glossy paper isn’t the ideal material for nautical engineering. Still, it made for a good story at the pub. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, you two are incorrigible. So, another glass of wine? And perhaps we can steer clear of any further stories involving questionable sailing expeditions? Speaker_2: I'll drink to that. And I still maintain that mint tea laced with… something… was the drink of champions. Speaker_4: Just promise me you won't start building boats out of dental magazines, Clive. My profession has already suffered enough. Speaker_3: (Winking) No promises.

Speaker_2: Honestly, the state of that bathroom this morning… I don’t know what goes on in there. It looked like a bomb had hit it! Speaker_1: Oh, tell me about it. I swear, teenagers operate on another plane of existence. Everything is a performance, a drama. Did you see Leo’s face when I asked if he’d remembered to flush? The outrage! Speaker_3: (Muttering) It wasn’t *my* fault the toilet roll ran out. Speaker_2: Oh, here we go. Always someone else’s fault, isn't it? It's a wonder they manage to breathe without someone else doing it *for* them. Speaker_1: Don't start, Brenda. I'm trying to remain calm. We have a school trip meeting tonight. And then, trying to get him motivated about work experience. It’s like pulling teeth. He just wants to play Fortnite all day. Speaker_2: Work experience, eh? They don't appreciate the opportunities these days. When I was his age, you were lucky to get a week down the market sweeping up. Builds character, that does. Speaker_3: Sweeping up? No thanks. I want to be an explorer. Like, discovering lost cities and stuff. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) That’s ambitious, love. Have you thought about what you'd *need* to be an explorer? Maths, geography, potentially languages... Speaker_3: I can learn all that. I’m good at geography. And I can build cool stuff, like traps. For… you know, protecting the lost cities. Speaker_2: Traps? Oh, lord. Let’s stick to the work experience for now then, shall we? I was talking to Mrs. Higgins at school, and apparently, they’re really struggling to find placements for the year tens. Speaker_1: Right, well, I've got a few contacts. Might be able to get him something with a marketing firm I do some proofing for. It’s not uncovering ancient civilizations, but it’s real world experience. Speaker_2: Good thinking. Anything is better than nothing. Though, you know what I heard? Old Man Hemmings is looking for someone to help him referee the under-10s football team. Speaker_3: Refereeing? Absolutely not! They’re all tiny terrors. And their parents are worse. Speaker_1: Probably a good point. Though, it *would* get him out the house… and away from the bathroom. Speaking of which, is anyone else wondering where all the good bath bombs disappeared to? Speaker_2: (Smiling knowingly) Oh, I saw a certain someone sneaking a few into his friend Daisy's bag yesterday. Apparently, she's the current object of affection. Speaker_3: (Turns bright red) I wasn’t sneaking! I was… sharing! Speaker_1: Sharing, were you? Sounds expensive. And speaking of expenses, I need to start thinking about our holiday. I was looking at Cornwall, but it's absolutely rammed. Speaker_2: Cornwall’s always busy. What about the Lake District? A bit more peaceful, and stunning scenery. Or even Scotland? Always a good shout. Speaker_3: Scotland! Can we go to Loch Ness and look for the monster? Speaker_1: Possibly. If you promise to behave… and start thinking about work experience. And maybe, just maybe, clean up after yourself in the bathroom. Speaker_2: And maybe offer to babysit little Charlie for us sometime? We’re desperate for a night out. Speaker_3: (Groaning) Babysitting? Seriously? Speaker_1: It builds character, darling. Remember what Brenda said?

Speaker_1: Honestly though, this bread is unreal. Like, seriously good. Speaker_2: It is lovely, isn’t it? Proper sourdough. You don’t get this in Bolton, do you? Not like this. Speaker_3: Can I have another bit? Please? Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Always, lad. You’ve already had enough, mind, don’t push your luck. You’ll be bouncing off the walls. Speaker_1: Seriously though, we need to find out where they get their flour. This changes everything. All those attempts at sourdough… wasted. Speaker_2: It’s the climate, I reckon. The air here, the quality of the grain… everything. It makes a difference. You can taste it. Speaker_3: Can we go truffle hunting tomorrow? Please, please, please? I saw a picture of a dog finding one, it was massive! Speaker_4: We’ll see, love. Depends if we can arrange it. It’s not cheap, you know. And besides, your mother’s got her heart set on that cooking class. Speaker_1: Oh, that cooking class! I’m so excited. Apparently, the chef used to work for Gordon Ramsay. Speaker_2: Gordon Ramsay, eh? He’s a shouty one. Though you have to admit, he can cook. Still, I prefer Delia Smith, myself. More… relatable. Speaker_4: Delia Smith, now there’s a name. Remember when she got onto the pitch during Norwich game? Brilliant. Speaker_3: What’s a pitch? Speaker_1: It’s like, the football field, love. Where they play football. Speaker_4: It's where grown men run around chasing a ball. Honestly, I don’t get the appeal. Though I did take young Master Thompson here to a West Ham game once. Nearly lost my voice. Speaker_2: (To Speaker_4) You took him to West Ham? You’re trying to convert him, aren’t you? Trying to turn him into a proper football supporter. Speaker_4: Someone needs to. He’s getting far too interested in… American football. All that padding and stopping and starting. It’s hardly a sport! Speaker_1: Honestly, Americans. They put cheese in everything. Speaker_3: My friend Ethan’s dad went to America. He brought back loads of candy. Speaker_2: (Sighs) Speaking of bad habits, have you managed to cut down on the cigarettes, darling? Speaker_4: (Clears throat) I’m working on it. It’s… a process. Speaker_1: It's a process that's been going on for twenty years. Speaker_4: It’s stressful work, you know? These management consultants are relentless. Always wanting reports, wanting data… It’s exhausting. Speaker_2: Stressful? Try dealing with pregnant women all day. That's stressful. One minute they’re overjoyed, the next they’re terrified. And all the paperwork! Don’t even get me started. Speaker_3: Mum, can we watch TV when we get back to the apartment? They’re showing that show about stem cells. Speaker_1: The one about… growing organs? Bit morbid for bedtime, don't you think? Speaker_4: Actually, stem cell research is fascinating. The potential benefits are enormous. Though I read an article last week about the ethical concerns… Speaker_2: Oh, don’t start on the ethics! It’ll ruin my appetite. Just let the lad watch his TV show. Speaker_1: Just don’t ask me to explain it. My biology GCSE is a distant memory. And speaking of distant memories, are you sure you remembered to pack the maps? This driving is terrifying! Narrow roads, hairpin bends… Speaker_4: Relax, darling. I'm a perfectly capable driver. And yes, I packed the maps. Though, frankly, this sat nav is doing a perfectly good job.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this canteen food is…an experience, isn’t it? I think I’ve identified at least four different shades of beige on my plate. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) It’s consistent, at least. You always know what you’re getting. And it’s cheap. Which, let’s be real, is the main draw when you’re surviving on a graduate salary. Speaker_3: True. Though I’m starting to suspect the ‘chicken’ is actually reformed potato. It has a very…structural integrity. Speaker_1: Don’t. Just…don’t. I'm trying to eat it. So, how’s that new campaign going, Ben? The one for the children’s books? Speaker_2: It’s… a challenge. We’re trying to target parents on Instagram, but the algorithm seems to hate us. Every time I think I've cracked it, engagement drops off a cliff. It's like they *want* to show people ads for teeth whitening instead of encouraging reading. Speaker_3: Instagram is a fickle beast. My nan gets targeted with ads for mobility scooters and dating apps. Simultaneously. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, bless her! That’s…a range. I’m wading through transcripts today of people describing their childhood reading experiences. It’s fascinating, actually. The way people remember details, the emotional connection… Speaker_2: Sounds a lot more fulfilling than battling algorithms, to be honest. Is it mostly positive memories? Speaker_1: Surprisingly, no. A lot of people talk about being *forced* to read certain things, or having books read *to* them in a really monotone voice. Ruined it for life, apparently. Speaker_3: My mum used to do really dramatic voices for all the characters. It was amazing. Except she always made the villain sound exactly like our headteacher. Speaker_1: (Smiling) That’s brilliant! That’s the kind of detail I’m collecting. It’s all about the nuances. What are you up to these days, Tom? Still swimming in project management? Speaker_3: Pretty much. Currently juggling three different deadlines, a temperamental printer, and a request to source seventeen copies of a book that’s been out of print for twenty years. Standard Tuesday, really. Speaker_2: seventeen copies? What on earth for? Speaker_3: Apparently, a very important academic needs them for…research purposes. He was very insistent. And slightly terrifying. Speaker_1: Oh dear. Well, at least it’s interesting? Speaker_3: That’s one word for it. It keeps me from falling into an existential crisis, I suppose. This "chicken" is actually pretty okay, you know? Maybe it *is* just chicken. Speaker_2: (Taking a bite of his food) Don't push your luck. You’ll jinx it. Speaker_1: Maybe we should just skip dessert and get a coffee. I need caffeine to power through another three hours of transcriptions. Speaker_2: Good plan. I could use a coffee break too. And a digital detox. Instagram is actively shortening my lifespan, I’m convinced. Speaker_3: I’m in. Coffee sounds excellent. And a vow to avoid thinking about spreadsheets for at least ten minutes. Speaker_1: Agreed. A spreadsheet-free zone. It’s a beautiful concept. Speaker_2: Right, mission coffee is a go! Let’s bravely venture forth. Speaker_3: Lead the way. And try not to think about reformed potato. Speaker_1: No promises. It’s haunting my thoughts already.

Speaker_2: Right, so are we definitely heading straight to Kasia’s then? No detour to that weird pottery place you found online? Speaker_1: Oh, honestly, I’m tempted, but no. We’re already running a bit late, aren't we? And Kasia’s been really good about letting us crash, I don't want to push our luck by arriving at, like, midnight. Plus, I vaguely remember reading reviews saying it’s mostly just overpriced tourist tat. Speaker_2: Good call. Tourist tat is the enemy. Are you sure you’ve got the address for Kasia’s saved? My phone signal’s being a bit patchy since we crossed the border. Speaker_1: Yes, multiple times. Not just in the phone, I’ve scribbled it down on a bit of paper too, just in case. Old-fashioned, I know, but it works. It’s… ul. Świętego Agnieszki 12, Tarnow. Does that ring any bells? Speaker_2: Sounds right. I think she mentioned something about it being near the old town square? Speaker_1: That's what I gathered. Something about a five-minute walk. Oh, and she said to look for a building with a bright blue door. Apparently, it’s very distinctive. Speaker_2: A bright blue door. Excellent. I’ll keep my eyes peeled. Are we relying on Google Maps entirely, or do you have a backup plan, like, an actual paper map? Speaker_1: (laughs) You wound me! Of course, I have a paper map. I’m not *completely* reliant on technology. It’s in the glove compartment, alongside a torch, a first-aid kit, and a questionable selection of biscuits. Speaker_2: Questionable biscuits are essential for any road trip, obviously. Just checking, are you comfortable driving on the right? You’ve been doing brilliantly so far, but I know it can take a bit of getting used to. Speaker_1: I’m managing. It’s… disconcerting, still. I keep instinctively reaching for the gear stick with my left hand! But I’m mostly staying in my lane and haven’t mounted any pavements yet, so I’m counting that as a win. Speaker_2: High praise indeed. Honestly, you're a much braver driver than I am. I’d be a wreck. Speaker_1: Oh, don't be silly. You’re a much more confident navigator – you’d have us completely lost in five minutes without you. Besides, someone has to handle the snacks. Speaker_2: True. And I take that role very seriously. Right, well, let’s see… according to Google Maps, we’re about twenty minutes away. Do you want me to put some music on? I’ve got a playlist of Polish folk music, if you’re feeling adventurous. Speaker_1: (grimaces) Oh, bless you, but perhaps not. Maybe just something… neutral? Some 80s classics? Until we’re safely delivered to Kasia’s bright blue door, at least. Speaker_2: Deal. 80s it is. Prepare for maximum cheese. Speaker_1: Bring it on. Speaker_2: Oh, actually, one more thing. Did you remember to tell your bank we're travelling abroad? I don't want our cards getting blocked halfway through the trip. Speaker_1: Oh, blast. I completely forgot. I'll do it now while I have a bit of signal. Thanks for reminding me. You really *are* the responsible one, aren’t you?

Speaker_1: Honestly, that Adidas kit they’ve done for Man U this year is… criminal. Just awful. All that red and black, it looks like someone spilled ink all over it. Speaker_2: (Eyes still mostly on the muted TV) Yeah, it’s a bit much isn’t it? They’ve gone a bit overboard. I think they’re trying too hard to be… edgy. It’s supposed to be classic, isn’t it? Man United. Speaker_1: Classic? It looks like a Valentine’s Day disaster zone. Honestly, I’d rather see them in a plain red kit. It’s always felt more *them*. It’s all about the sponsorship though, isn’t it? They’ll slap anything on a shirt if someone’s paying enough. Speaker_2: Definitely. It's all about the money. Remember when gambling sponsors were *everywhere*? It felt a bit… much. Good they’ve cracked down on that, even if it means more dodgy crypto companies are getting a look-in. Speaker_1: Oh, the betting companies were relentless. Every other advert break. Now it's all energy drinks and… well, not crypto hopefully, but something equally dubious. It's a slippery slope. I saw a rumour online about a McDonald’s sponsorship deal for a Premier League team. Speaker_2: (Laughs) McDonald’s? Seriously? Imagine the adverts. “Fuel your passion for the beautiful game with a Big Mac!” Speaker_1: I know, right? It’d be the ultimate irony. Elite athletes endorsing fast food. Though, let’s be honest, half of them are probably grabbing a McChicken on the way home from training anyway. Speaker_2: Probably. It's the convenience. And it’s cheap. Although, honestly, I haven’t been to McDonald’s in… ages. Since we moved down here, actually. There's not one near us and I'm kind of glad. Speaker_1: Me neither. It’s a guilty pleasure, isn’t it? Like, you know it’s bad for you, but sometimes you just… *need* those fries. Though, honestly, I’d take a decent chip shop over McDonald’s any day. Speaker_2: Oh, absolutely. Proper chips, with salt and vinegar. Nothing beats that. Speaking of which, do you think whoever designs those football kits even *watches* football? Speaker_1: I seriously doubt it. They’re probably sat in a boardroom somewhere, arguing about brand synergy and target demographics. They've clearly never been to a match in the rain, trying to stay warm in a flimsy plastic shirt. Speaker_2: Exactly! They wouldn't be designing something like that if they did. You need a kit that *works*. Something practical. It’s supposed to be sportswear, not a fashion statement. Speaker_1: It’s a fashion statement *and* a mobile billboard, apparently. Though, I'm still holding out hope for a throwback kit. Just a classic design, nicely done. Is that too much to ask? Speaker_2: Nope. Not at all. Just… sensible. You’d think. Speaker_1: You’d think. Right, who’s winning anyway? It's a bit hard to tell with the sound off. Speaker_2: (Glances at the screen) Looks like… yeah, Liverpool are dominating. Two-nil up, I reckon? Speaker_1: Fancy that. Still, a terrible kit doesn't change the quality of the football, does it? Speaker_2: Nope. Though it does make them look a bit… silly.

Speaker_2: Honestly, it’s infuriating. They sent me a letter, said I hadn’t declared earnings. Earnings! From where? I haven't worked a day in… well, you know. It’s just constant hassle with the Jobseekers. Speaker_1: Oh, brilliant. Sounds about right. They love doing that, don’t they? Just making life difficult. Are you going to ring them? Speaker_2: I did! Spent an hour on hold, then some kid with a really posh voice just kept repeating policy. Couldn’t explain *what* earnings they were talking about. He said “it’s all on the system,” which is just… not helpful. Speaker_1: Ugh. Classic. It’s like they deliberately train them not to actually listen. Did you mention you haven't *had* any earnings? Speaker_2: Repeatedly! He just kept saying I needed to fill out a form. A form to say I haven’t earned anything. Honestly, it's taking the mickey. Mum said she thinks I should just go down to the office, go face-to-face. Speaker_1: That might be worth it. Sometimes actually having someone look you in the eye makes them… less robotic. Though knowing you, you'd probably end up having a proper confrontation. Speaker_2: Well, someone needs to tell them it’s ridiculous! I'm barely surviving as it is. Gas and electric are through the roof, you know? Mum and Dad are helping, but… it's not right. Especially when I see what Kevin's done with his inheritance. Speaker_1: Oh, don’t even start on Kevin. Last I heard he was “investing” in NFTs. Speaker_2: NFTs! The man hasn’t had a real job in his life, suddenly he’s a financier. Spent the whole lot on pictures of monkeys, apparently. And a car. Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m still reeling from seeing Sarah with the baby. It feels… weird. Like, I *know* she wanted one for ages, and bless her, she looks absolutely exhausted, but it’s just… a shock. Speaker_1: It’s just…it’s so quiet, isn’t it? Proper quiet. Not like London quiet, where it’s just *different* noises, layered on top of each other. This is… nothing. Speaker_2: Blissful. Honestly. Speaker_1: Right, so you’re seriously thinking about getting a car then? At sixteen? Speaker_2: Yeah, well, a lot of my mates are starting to learn and… it’d be good, wouldn’t it? Cars are money pits, son. Glorious money pits, but money pits nonetheless. Speaker_2: So, like, a smaller engine would be cheaper to insure? Speaker_1: Generally, yes. Smaller engine, less powerful, statistically considered less likely to be driven recklessly. Though, honestly, insurance companies seem to base it on… well, on witchcraft and algorithms these days. They look at everything. Your postcode, your dad’s job, what A-Levels you’re taking… Speaker_2: What do my A-Levels have to do with it? Speaker_1: Apparently, it's a 'risk assessment'. They think students taking certain subjects are more likely to be involved in accidents. Honestly, it's daft. But that's how it works. Are you planning on doing Pass Plus? Speaker_2: Pass Plus? What's that? Speaker_1: It’s extra driving lessons after you’ve passed your test. Speaker_2: Right. Safety first. Speaker_1: Exactly. And honestly, before you get too carried away, get a few quotes. Online comparison sites are your friend. Just… be prepared for a shock. Don't go blaming me when your jaw hits the floor! Speaker_2: Okay, okay. I won’t. It’s just… seems like everyone's got a car except me. I’m responsible. Speaker_1: (Raises an eyebrow) We'll see about that! Now, have you finished your homework? Because responsibility also means doing your schoolwork.

Speaker_3: Oh, don't get me started. My little one put it on. It was just…loud noise and people in costumes. I haven’t the faintest idea what was going on. This is getting busy. Speaker_2: Just a bit further, love. And honestly, the supermarket prices

Speaker_1: Honestly though, I just… I can’t get my head around the idea of “shmeat.” Like, lab-grown meat. It feels so… unnatural. Speaker_2: But isn’t *all* meat unnatural in a way? Speaker_1: Right, I’m telling you, that last boss was rigged. Absolutely rigged. No way anyone beats that on their first try. Speaker_2: You’re just saying that because you died, Liam. Perhaps after the film, we can call Lesley and see if she fancy joining us for a cup of tea next week. Speaker_2: That sounds lovely. A proper catch-up. It's been too long. Speaker_1: It has, it really has. Now, are you sure you don't want another biscuit? I made a fresh batch of shortbread this morning… Speaker_2: (Laughing) Don’t tempt me! But honestly, I’m stuffed. Speaker_1: Honestly, the amount of admin I had to do for that interview yesterday… it was ridiculous. Have you seen that new magazine, *Locale*? It's all about East London, really good photography and local artist interviews. Speaker_1: No, I haven’t. I've been meaning to branch out from academic journals, though. Anything good in it? Speaker_2: Yeah, there's a piece on that vintage cinema just off Brick Lane. Speaker_1: Right, so the washing machine’s decided to give up the ghost again, hasn’t it? Honestly, I’m starting to think it’s a personal vendetta against me. Speaker_2: Oh no, not again! Although, a trip back up North wouldn't be awful. I miss a proper Sunday roast. Speaker_1: We could always convince your mum to make one when we’re down. She’s a wizard with a Yorkshire pudding. Speaker_2: True. Though she’ll insist on making us do all the washing up. It’s a trade-off. Speaker_1: Oh! I forgot to tell you, I watched that film you recommended, “Everything Everywhere All at Once.” Speaker_2: And? What did you think? It's a bit…much, isn’t it? Speaker_1: It was *wild*. Absolutely bonkers. But brilliant. I cried, I laughed, I was completely bewildered. All in the space of two hours. Definitely lived up to the hype. Speaker_2: Glad you liked it. It’s one of those films you need to watch more than once to fully appreciate, I reckon. It's got a lot going on. Speaker_1: I might do just that. Maybe while the washing machine is being…talked to. Speaker_1: Honestly, the price of houses down south is absolutely mental. Mental! You wouldn’t believe what they're asking for a shoebox in London. Speaker_2: It's just… supply and demand, isn't it? It just shows you can't trust anyone, doesn't it? Even big corporations. Speaker_2: It’s terrifying, really. The lengths they went to. And the fallout… lawsuits, recalls… and I bet the people responsible barely faced any real consequences. Speaker_2: I think some executives *did* get prosecuted, didn’t they? Though, you're right, probably not enough. It feels like the punishment never really fits the crime with these big companies. They just pay a fine and carry on. Speaker_3: Precisely. It’s just a cost of doing business. A calculated risk. That’s the problem with these massive organisations. They're too big to fail, too big to really punish. It's the same with the banks, isn’t it? Speaker_1: Absolutely. And it makes you wonder what else they’re getting away with. It’s not just cars, is it? It’s everything. Food, medicine… you name it. They’re all trying to pull the wool over our eyes. Speaker_2: You’re making me paranoid now. I’m going to start questioning everything I buy! Though… speaking of buying things, we really should think about getting a new sofa. Mine’s starting to look a bit worse for wear. Speaker_3: A new sofa? Now there's a scandal waiting to happen. Foam filled with questionable chemicals, springs made in… where are they made now? Somewhere awful, I expect. Speaker_1: (laughing) Oh, don’t start! Everything’s a conspiracy theory with you, isn’t it, David? But you’re probably right. It’s a minefield. Right, well, I’m going to put the kettle on. Anyone fancy a cup of tea?

Speaker_1: Honestly, I don’t know why I bothered writing that letter. It’s just stirred everything up again. Speaker_2: Who to, Arthur? Still to that council chap about the development? Speaker_1: Yes, yes. Pointed out again about the drainage, you know. Said it’s going to cause flooding down at the bottom of the field. They just don’t listen. It’s like talking to a brick wall. Speaker_3: Well, you always were a bit direct, weren't you, Arthur? Sometimes it’s better to… well, not ruffle feathers, shall we say. Speaker_1: Ruffle feathers?! They're building a housing estate on a floodplain! It's not ruffling feathers, it's pointing out a disaster waiting to happen! I’m just trying to be reasonable. Speaker_2: They'll say it’s all been assessed, Arthur. They always do. Professional assessments and all that. Speaker_1: Assessments done by people *they* pay! Of course it’s been assessed! You need to get out, Arthur. A bit of fresh air. It's a lovely day. Speaker_1: Fresh air won’t stop the houses causing floods, will it? I’m just… fed up. Remember Old Man Hemmings? He had a right go at them about building on that green space, and what happened? Ignored him too. Speaker_3: It's just the way things are now, I suppose. Nobody listens to older people anymore. It’s all about progress. Speaker_2: Progress that ends up with everyone’s gardens underwater. That's a peculiar sort of progress. How’s your pension looking, by the way, Mary? Any better than last month? Speaker_3: Honestly, it's a joke. Barely covering the bills. I do wish we'd saved more, but when we were younger… well, things were different. We didn’t earn much. Speaker_1: We were hoping for a bit more to help young Emily with her deposit, you know. She’s looking at places in Ipswich. Dreadful prices. Speaker_2: Ipswich is expensive now. They're building like mad there too. Heard tell of a place down near the docks, a converted warehouse. Tiny little thing, but cost a fortune. Speaker_3: They had us staying in a bed and breakfast last year when the bathroom flooded. Absolutely dreadful. Damp smell, paper-thin walls. Heard every creak and groan all night. Honestly couldn't sleep. Speaker_1: B&Bs. A sad state of affairs when that's all some people can afford. The world’s going to pot, I tell you. Going to pot. And nobody cares about the drains. Honestly, the drains! Speaker_2: Now, now Arthur. Don't get yourself all worked up again. Have another biscuit. Mary, would you like one? I think there’s a ginger snap left. Speaker_3: Oh, go on then, just the one. And Arthur, try to forget the letter for now. It won’t change anything, and it’ll only give you a headache.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the physics practical this week was a joke. Mr. Harrison just expects us to *know* stuff we haven’t even been taught yet. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I spent three hours trying to calculate the spring constant and still got it wrong. He just walked around saying "apply the principles!" Like, which principles, sir? The ones you forgot to mention? Speaker_4: Davies is alright. Though, did you see that TikTok about her? Someone claimed she accidentally called potassium “potassiumium” during a lesson. Speaker_1: No way! Is it real? Speaker_2: Apparently. It’s gone viral. There's a whole duet chain of people pretending to be her. It’s proper funny. Speaker_3: People will find anything to make fun of.
