Lots of people talking about historical sexism in science and how women are discouraged from STEM. Speaker_3: It’s that whole thing, isn’t it? Like, “oh, biology is about bodies, and women have bodies, therefore…” It's such a warped logic. Speaker_4: Exactly. And then someone tried to bring up evolution. Saying men are naturally better at scientific thinking because of… something to do with hunting and gathering or something. It was wild. Speaker_1: Oh, here we go. The caveman argument. Always a classic. Speaker_2: Ugh. It’s exhausting. Like, can’t people just accept that intelligence isn’t tied to gender? And that even *if* there were some evolutionary basis - which there isn't - it doesn't justify discrimination. Speaker_3: I think it’s just people being deliberately obtuse. Trying to find some justification for their biases. Makes you wonder why they feel the need to do that in the first place. Speaker_4: True. It’s usually projection, isn’t it? Someone feeling insecure about something. Speaking of biases, have you guys seen Liam talking to Chloe again? Speaker_1: Liam? Oh, *that's* awkward. He was going on and on about how she doesn’t get his sense of humour the other day. Speaker_2: Yeah, and then she rolled her eyes so hard I thought they were going to get stuck. It's like he’s completely oblivious to the fact she’s not interested. Speaker_3: He just doesn’t get it, does he? It’s all very… textbook toxic masculinity. Speaker_4: Exactly! He genuinely thinks rejection is a personal failing on *her* part. Honestly, it’s frustrating to watch. It’s stuff like that which fuels the whole sexism thing. Speaker_1: Right? Like, it’s not ‘she doesn’t understand me,’ it’s ‘she’s allowed to not be attracted to me’. Simple as that. Speaker_2: Preach. Anyway, anyone fancy another cake? I'm feeling a sugar rush coming on. And we really need to start thinking about that history essay. Speaker_3: Yes, please! And honestly, anything is better than thinking about Mr. Harrison's physics.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the hospital was a nightmare yesterday. The waiting room was packed, and they were running hours behind. Speaker_2: Oh, you poor love. What was the appointment for again? Just the check-up after the operation? Speaker_1: Yeah, the post-op. They wanted to see how the incision was healing, make sure there's no infection. She's always been a bit…eccentric. Still, she’s happy, and that’s all that matters. Speaker_4: Right. Now, has anyone been watching the rugby? England were awful on Saturday. Absolutely dreadful. Speaker_2: They were a bit shaky, weren't they? Too many penalties. Speaker_1: Actually, I was trying to watch it online, but the Wi-Fi kept dropping out. It’s a disaster. Trying to get someone to fix it is another thing entirely. Speaker_4: Wi-Fi, rugby... In my day, we just had a good old fashioned pint and a sing-song. Much simpler. Speaker_3: Speaking of simpler times, your Uncle George is still going on about his skiing trip. Says he’s considering going again this winter. At his age! Speaker_1: He’s a madman. Honestly. He’ll break a hip. Speaker_2: Has anyone sorted out the MOT and tyres for the car? Mine’s due next month. Speaker_1: I booked mine in for next week. The cost of tyres is ridiculous these days though, isn’t it? Speaker_4: Everything’s expensive. That’s the world we live in now. Still, got to get around, haven't we? I need to get back to the allotment, the runner beans are going wild. Speaker_3: And I need to call the hospital about my appointment. They keep changing the date. Honestly, it’s like they don’t want to see me!

Speaker_1: Right, so basically, imagine a long, long time ago…before even your Great-Grandma was born, people weren’t always treated fairly. Some people, with more power, decided they could *own* other people. Speaker_2: Own them? Like…a toy? Speaker_1: Not like a toy, sweetheart, but like…they made them work, and they didn’t let them choose where to live or who to marry, or even if they could learn to read. It was called slavery. It was terribly, terribly wrong. Speaker_3: Why did they do that? That’s mean! Speaker_1: It *was* mean. They did it because they wanted free labour – people to work for them without paying them anything. They thought they were better than other people, which, of course, wasn’t true. It mostly happened a long time ago in America, but it also happened in other parts of the world. Speaker_2: Did they get angry? Speaker_1: Oh, very angry. And brave. Many people fought against slavery, and eventually, after a long, long time, slavery was made illegal. But it caused a lot of pain and suffering for many, many years. It’s important to remember it so we don't let anything like that happen again. Speaker_3: So…like the baddies in a story? Speaker_1: In a way, yes. But it wasn't a story, it was real life, and it involved real people. Now, sometimes when countries disagree, it can lead to even worse things…like war. Speaker_2: War? Like soldiers and bangs? Speaker_1: Yes, sometimes like that. But war is much more than just soldiers and bangs. It’s when people get hurt, and families get separated, and homes get destroyed. Think about everything we have here, your toys, our comfy home, our school…war can take all of that away. Speaker_3: Is there a war now? Speaker_1: There are sadly conflicts happening in different parts of the world right now, which is very sad. That’s why it's so important to try and solve problems peacefully, by talking and understanding each other. It’s a bit like when you and your sister argue over a toy. You try to sort it out by talking, right? Speaker_2: Yeah, Mummy helps. Speaker_1: Exactly. And world leaders try to do something similar, although it's much more complicated than arguing over a toy! They’re trying to find ways to help people, and to stop the fighting. These things are all connected, you see. Speaker_1: Right, okay, dishwasher duty. Lily, can you unload the cutlery, please? Thomas, you can get the plates. Gently now, those are Mummy’s good ones. Speaker_3: Can we build his rocket train with my blocks? Speaker_1: That's a lovely idea, darling! Maybe we can look some pictures up online afterwards so you can see what it really looked like? Now, come on, let’s finish unloading this dishwasher, and then we can get building! Thomas, did you get all the bowls? Speaker_3: Almost! There’s one hiding at the back. Speaker_1: Aha! Dishwasher detectives. Good work! Now, let’s go and find that train track. Speaker_2: And then...Harry Potter! Speaker_1: And then Harry Potter, after a bit of engineering genius. Deal? Speaker_2 & Speaker_3: Deal! . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ..........

Speaker_1: Right, so I genuinely think I’m being targeted on Words With Friends. Like, someone is actively trying to ruin my life with triple word scores. So much paperwork. Proper pain in the arse. Speaker_1: Honestly, it's a minefield. I’ve found a few templates, but it’s all so confusing. And then there’s the cookies consent banner… it feels like having to ask permission to breathe. Speaker_2: It *is* a pain. I had to do it for my little bakery website. Stress baking is a real thing, you know? It helps me cope. Which reminds me, try this rosemary and sea salt focaccia when it’s ready. I've been experimenting. Speaker_4: Rosemary and sea salt, eh? Sounds good. Beats this carrot I’m currently battling. Speaker_1: So, back to the impending doom of my Words With Friends score… do you think I should just challenge someone else? Speaker_3: Maybe. Or just accept defeat with grace. That’s what I do with my niece when we play Monopoly. I let her win. Mostly. Speaker_2: You let her win? Zara would bankrupt you in five minutes flat. Speaker_3: She’s learning business skills early, alright? Besides, it’s more fun when she's happy. Anyway, I was thinking about doing another supper club next month. Should we do something Italian again? Speaker_4: Italian’s always a winner. Maybe pasta making? I’m pretty good at tossing pasta. Speaker_1: I’m terrible at cooking pasta. It always ends up either rock solid or a soggy mess. I prefer to stick to toast. Speaker_2: You and toast… it’s a lifelong romance. But seriously, Liam, how’s work? Still being swamped with clients? Speaker_1: Swamped is an understatement. Everyone wants a research grant at the same time. It’s madness. And my boss keeps asking me to take on more projects. I think she just wants to see how much I can handle before I spontaneously combust. Speaker_4: Sounds rough. At least I just make coffee. Relatively stress-free. Although, customers can be… interesting.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this canteen food is…an experience, isn’t it? I think I’ll stick to a sandwich tomorrow. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Yes, ‘experience’ is a kind word. It's...functional. They're at that age where they think they know everything. It must be difficult to keep them on task. Have you had any particularly…interesting incidents? Speaker_1: Oh, where do I begin? Speaker_2: You deserve it! I'm hoping to visit my aunt in London during half term. It's been a while since I've seen her. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s nice! London's lovely. Though, rather expensive. You'll have to try and find some good free things to do. Speaker_2: Yes, I'm planning on visiting some museums. Many are free, thankfully. Speaker_1: That's a good shout. Perhaps I will go to london with Leo sometime soon! Would be a nice day.

Speaker_1: Right, so are we definitely going to Mothercare then? ‘Cause I really wanna look at those fluffy blankets. The ones with the little… you know, the little animals on? Massive ones. Speaker_3: (chuckles) How could I forget? She used to moan for days about the mess. Used to say you were turning her house into a circus. Speaker_1: It was fun though. And remember those little plastic babies? I used to pretend they were my kids. Bit weird now, looking back. Speaker_2: You were a very nurturing child. Still are, actually. Fewer morning sickness episodes, for a start. And definitely fewer shopping trips for miniature hats. Speaker_1: It was fun though, wasn’t it? Meeting all those people. Remember Liam? He was doing a law degree and… Nevermind. Speaker_3: Liam? What about Liam? Speaker_1: Nothing, honestly. He just… experimented a bit, that’s all. Lots of people did. Don't worry about it. Oh, brilliant. This’ll add ages to the journey. Should’ve gone the other way, should’ve taken the back roads. Speaker_1: Can we just get to Mothercare? I really need to see those blankets. And maybe find a little teddy bear. It’s important to prepare, you know. For all the snuggles.

Speaker_1: Ugh, I lost *again*. This game is rigged, honestly. That level with the glowing mushrooms is impossible. Speaker_2: Now, now, darling. Nothing’s rigged. You just need to practice. Perhaps you’re rushing it a bit? Remember what you said about calming down when you're feeling stressed? Speaker_3: It’s not rigged, but it *is* designed to be frustrating. What even is that? Sounds…horrible. Like a torture device for hamsters. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) It’s a psychological concept, love. Your brother’s studying all that at uni, isn't he? Something to do with behaviour and rewards. Though I still think you just need to breathe deeply and focus. Speaker_3: It's behavioural psychology, yeah. It's horrifyingly effective, actually. That’s why games are so addictive. Anyway, how was your day, both of you? Apart from my sister’s digital suffering. Speaker_1: It was alright. History was boring, Mr. Henderson just droned on about the Tudors *again*. And then Chloe was being really annoying in maths, copying my answers. Speaker_2: Oh, that's not nice. Did you tell the teacher? Speaker_1: No, it's just…it's Chloe. She always does it. I’m starting to think she just exists to irritate me. Speaker_3: Sounds exhausting. Speaking of irritating, my lab partner completely messed up the titration today. Ruined the whole experiment. Honestly, some people shouldn’t be allowed near beakers. Speaker_2: Oh dear. That sounds stressful. Are you still thinking about going to Italy over Christmas? It sounds lovely, but it's a long way to go. Speaker_1: Italy? That sounds amazing! Can we, Mum? Please? I promise I'll be good. And I'll even try to be less grumpy. Speaker_3: It’s a bit of a trek from Frimley, granted. But it would be nice to escape the…British weather. And I’ve been reading about some really interesting science museums in Rome. Speaker_2: Well, we have to think about your Dad, darling. He doesn’t really like flying. And with work being so busy, I don’t know if he can get the time off. Speaker_1: He can work from anywhere, can't he? He always says his job is just staring at a screen. Speaker_3: Technically, yes, but it’s more complicated than that. He has meetings and stuff. It's not as glamorous as it sounds, even if he’s technically a ‘digital nomad’ now. Speaker_2: And it's expensive, going to Italy at Christmas. We need to be sensible. Perhaps we could look at somewhere closer? A nice cottage in the Lake District? Speaker_1: A cottage? With no Wi-Fi? No thanks. I need my game. And Chloe to annoy. Speaker_3: (Smiling) Always a silver lining, eh? Look, let's just hold off making plans for now. I have a mountain of work to do, and you have glowing mushrooms to conquer. We can revisit it next week. Speaker_1: Fine. But if I lose one more time…I’m throwing my phone out the window. Speaker_2: Now, now. Don’t be dramatic. Let’s all have a cup of tea. That always helps.

Speaker_1: Right, so, copper is quite easy to find in Minecraft, isn’t it? But you need loads of it to make anything decent. It’s not as good as iron, obviously. Speaker_2: Iron is *way* better. You can make swords and pickaxes and armour! And you can build a whole iron golem if you have enough! Speaker_3: And diamond is the bestest! But you have to go really, really deep to find it. Like, past where the lava is. It's scary. Speaker_1: It *is* scary. You need a good iron pickaxe, at least, to even mine diamond. Remember when we were trying to get diamond last week and you nearly fell in the lava, Leo? Speaker_3: I didn’t *nearly* fall in. I just… wobbled a bit. Speaker_2: You screamed! Loudly! Speaker_1: (chuckles) You did. Now, let’s talk fabrics. What’s your favourite fabric? I was telling Mrs. Davies about the different weaves today. Speaker_2: Is fabric like clothes? I like sparkly ones! Like my fairy dress. Speaker_1: Yes, exactly! Fabric *is* what clothes are made of. Sparkly fabrics are usually polyester, which is a plastic, actually. Not a natural fibre like cotton or wool. Speaker_3: Wool comes from sheep! We saw sheep at Farmer Giles’s farm. They were fluffy. Speaker_1: They were. And cotton comes from a plant. It’s much softer than polyester. Did you know silk comes from worms? Speaker_2: Ewww! Worms?! Speaker_1: It's true! Silkworms spin these amazing threads. It's how they make silk fabric. Speaker_3: That’s gross. I’m inventing a legend about a metal that’s stronger than diamond. It’s called… Umbralite! Speaker_1: Umbralite? That’s a good name! What does it do? Speaker_3: It can break anything! Even bedrock! And it glows in the dark. And it can make you invisible. Speaker_2: Ooh, can *I* have some Umbralite? To make a sparkly invisible dress! Speaker_3: No! It's mine! It’s a super-secret metal. Only *I* can have it. Speaker_1: Well, maybe if you share, you can both have it. Speaking of things that are good for you, did you both take your vitamins this morning? Speaker_2: I did! It was orange and fizzy. Speaker_3: I forgot. Can I take it now? Speaker_1: Yes, go on. It'll give you super-powers… maybe not as good as Umbralite, but still! Stronger bones and everything. Now, back to Minecraft. What other resources do you think are really valuable? Speaker_2: Emeralds! You can trade them for cool stuff! Speaker_3: Redstone! You can make automatic doors and traps and… everything! Speaker_1: Excellent choices, both of you. Excellent choices. Speaker_2: Can we play Minecraft now? Please? Speaker_3: Yeah! Let’s build a castle with Umbralite! Even if it’s just in our imaginations. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Okay, okay. Just let me finish washing up this bowl first. Then we can build the most amazing castle the Minecraft world has ever seen. And maybe even find some real Umbralite! Speaker_2: Yay! Speaker_3: Awesome!

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m proper stressed about this essay. Like, proper. It’s on… well, it’s on Victorian literature, but it needs a feminist perspective and I just… I don’t *do* feminist perspectives. Speaker_2: Right. That sounds rough. What’s the essay question then? Maybe I can help, even if it's just to bounce ideas off. Speaker_1: It’s about how women are portrayed in the Brontë sisters’ novels. And it’s not just “are they portrayed well,” it’s like… dissecting patriarchal structures and blah blah blah. Honestly, it feels a million miles away from just enjoying a good story. Speaker_2: Yeah, sounds a bit heavy. You always were better at the actual literature side, not all the… analysing. Remember when we did Shakespeare and you just *knew* all the lines? Haven’t heard you mention it in ages. Speaker_2: Nah, not much. Been swamped with uni work, same as you, I suppose. Plus, the string snapped a couple of weeks ago and I haven’t gotten round to replacing it. It’s just… sat there, mocking me. Speaker_1: Mocking you? That’s a bit dramatic, innit? Get a new string. You used to be obsessed. You were going to start a band! "The Rusty Sprockets" or something ridiculously named. Speaker_2: Don't remind me. That was a phase. A very, very short-lived phase. Though I do miss it sometimes. It’s just… easier to watch Netflix, you know? Speaking of which, saw that documentary about… well, you won’t believe it. About that bloke, Jimmy Savile. Speaker_1: Oh, God. Don’t. I can't even think about that. Makes my skin crawl. It’s awful, isn’t it? How people can… and get away with it for so long. Speaker_2: It’s terrifying. Makes you question everything. And then you start… overthinking about everything, worrying about who you can trust. It's no wonder people are careful around everyone these days. It's just... awful. Speaker_1: It is. Truly awful. We weren't kids ourselves when all that started coming out, were we? Still feels… wrong. Changes how you look at things, doesn't it? Honestly, I need a stronger drink. This shandy’s not cutting it. Speaker_2: Tell you what, I’ll get the next round. And maybe we can talk about something… less horrible. Like, what bands are you into at the moment? Anything new? Or are you still stuck on Arctic Monkeys? Speaker_1: Never stuck on Arctic Monkeys. Always a classic. But I’ve been listening to Yard Act a lot lately. They're proper good. You’d probably like them. Bit political, a bit shouty, but good. And I've been trying to get back into painting. It’s… therapeutic, sort of. Helps me not think about Brontë sisters and patriarchal structures. Speaker_2: Yard Act, I'll have a listen. Painting, that’s good. You were always proper talented at art. Remember that portrait you did of Old Man Hemmings? It was brilliant. Speaker_1: Ah, Old Man Hemmings. He loved that portrait! Always said it made him look younger. Bless him. Maybe I should paint your guitar. As a reminder to pick it up.

Speaker_2: Seriously though, Montenegro? That’s…random. Like, why Montenegro? Speaker_1: My Aunt Carol’s friend, Brenda, has a timeshare there. Offered it to us cheap. Apparently, it’s beautiful. Loads of mountains and beaches. Speaker_3: Sounds…okay. Is it expensive to *get* there, though? Because “cheap timeshare” doesn’t cover flights and everything else. Speaker_1: Yeah, that's the thing. It’s not exactly cheap to fly into Podgorica or whatever it’s called. But we’re looking at EasyJet, trying to find a bargain. Dad’s being optimistic, saying we can live off supermarket sandwiches for the next month to save up. Speaker_2: (grimaces) Supermarket sandwiches all month? No thanks. I’d rather just… not go. Speaker_3: You’re being dramatic. It’s just a bit of sacrifice. Although, supermarket sandwiches *are* pretty tragic. What about that Italian place on the high street? They do amazing pasta for like, six quid. Speaker_1: Six quid a meal adds up, Liv. We're trying to fund a whole trip! And I’m still stuck on this EPQ. Seriously, ‘The Ethical Implications of Fast Fashion’? What even *is* that? Mr. Davies just chucked a bunch of readings at me and said “get on with it.” Speaker_2: Sounds awful. Mine's way better – the history of skateboarding. Actual, interesting stuff. Though, finding primary sources is a pain. It’s mostly just old magazines and blurry YouTube videos. Speaker_3: I'm doing mine on the representation of female characters in Shakespeare. Which is…fine. A lot of reading, obviously. But at least it’s something I actually care about. What about you, Jamie? Are you still struggling with all your A-Levels? Speaker_1: It’s the Economics that’s killing me. Supply and demand, elasticity…it’s just endless graphs and numbers. I’m starting to think I should have dropped it and done Art instead. Speaker_2: You’d be amazing at Art. Remember that giant drawing you did of Darth Vader in Year 9? That was epic. Speaker_1: Yeah, well, Darth Vader doesn't exactly get me a place at university. Although, maybe there's a course in…Comic Book Illustration? Speaker_3: (laughs) That’s a bit of a jump from Economics, isn’t it? Have you even thought about what you want to *do* at uni? Speaker_1: Honestly? No. Not really. I'm just trying to get through the EPQ and the A-Levels first. Then I can panic about the rest. What about you two? Any ideas? Speaker_2: I’m leaning towards History. Probably at Bristol. It’s got a good reputation. And a pretty good nightlife, apparently. Speaker_3: I want to do Law. Thinking about UCL. It’s ridiculously competitive, but I've got to try. Plus, my parents are already planning the celebratory dinner. They're convinced I’m going to get in. Speaker_1: Pressure much? Speaking of parents, mine are trying to push me towards something “sensible,” like Accounting. The horror. Speaker_2: Ugh, parents. They just don’t understand. My mum keeps asking me if I've considered teaching. Like, no, Mum. Absolutely not. I’d rather juggle chainsaws. Speaker_3: (grinning) That’s a good analogy. Actually, have you ever tried juggling, Jamie? You’re pretty coordinated. Speaker_1: Once, with oranges. It ended badly. Fruit everywhere. Neighbour complained. It was a whole thing.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this kitchen is a disaster zone. Like, who leaves dirty dishes for *days*? It's grim. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I walked in earlier and nearly slipped on something… questionable. Honestly, I’m starting to think living in halls was cleaner. And that’s saying something. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) You both make it sound like a biohazard zone. It’s not *that* bad. Though I did find a rogue potato in the sink yesterday. A whole potato. Speaker_4: My nan always says you gotta clean as you go. Says it’s the key to a happy life. Speaker_1: Your nan sounds sensible. Speaker_1: Honestly, this new bus route is a joke. It’s supposed to make getting across town easier, but it just adds another twenty minutes onto everything. Speaker_2: Really? Speaker_2: (laughs) Small mercies, eh? Although, I might just stick to the bike. It's quicker, healthier, and avoids student protests. Speaker_1: Sounds like a plan. Speaker_2: Sounds like a plan. What are you up to later? Speaker_1: Not much, just a quiet night in. You? Speaker_2: Same. Might attempt a complicated recipe I found online. Probably end up ordering a takeaway though. Speaker_1: (laughs) That’s always the way. Speaker_2: Always the way. Speaker_1: Always. Speaker_2: Always. Speaker_1: Always… Speaker_2: Always. Speaker_1: Always. Speaker_2: Always. Speaker_1: Always… Speaker_2: Right, well. I best get going, I have such a lot to prepare for deadline for my next report. Speaker_1: Yes, don't stay up to late. Speaker_2: I don't think so. Speaker_1: I won't, bye. Speaker_2: Bye.

Speaker_2: Honestly, the portions at that pub were ridiculous. I felt awful afterwards. So much butter on everything. Speaker_3: You always say that, but you always finish it! Remember that lasagne in Keswick? You said you were going to leave half, and… Speaker_2: Okay, okay, I have a weakness for carbs. Sue me. How was your weekend, Mum? Did you manage to get out at all? You can’t build a house without foundations, and you can't do mathematics without knowing your times tables. It’s…logical! Speaker_2: It's amazing how passionate you still are about maths, even in retirement. Speaker_1: It was my life! Though honestly, having a bit of peace and quiet is rather lovely. Speaking of which, how's Sarah? Is she still seeing that…what was his name… the artist? Speaker_3: Ben? Yeah, they’re still going strong. He came up last week, actually. They did that hike up Scafell Pike. Speaker_2: Scafell Pike?! In February? Are they mad? Speaker_3: Apparently not. He’s pretty outdoorsy. They were all geared up, layers and everything. They had a lovely time. Mum, you wouldn’t believe the photos! Speaker_1: Honestly, these young people. No sense. Reminds me of your father. Always off climbing mountains, or sailing, or something equally reckless. Speaker_2: He always said it was about the challenge. Speaker_1: A challenge? It was about showing off! He always had to be the best at everything. Speaker_3: Well, he *was* rather competitive. Speaking of challenges, I’m trying to teach Leo some basic French. It's…a struggle. He keeps saying “Bonjour” to the dog. Speaker_2: Oh, bless him! That’s adorable. Are you using Duolingo? Speaker_3: I tried! But he just gets distracted by the little owl. It’s hopeless. I was thinking of getting a tutor, actually. Do you know anyone? Speaker_1: A tutor? For French? Goodness gracious. The English language is being ruined as it is. All this slang, all this American influence... It's appalling. Speaker_2: Oh, here we go… Speaker_3: Mum, everything’s changing. That's just life. Speaker_1: It’s a slippery slope, I tell you. A slippery slope. Now, did you get that recipe for the lemon drizzle cake I mentioned? It’s the best one, honestly. I’ll email it over tonight. Speaker_2: Yes, please! I’m hopeless at baking, but I’m willing to give it a go. Maybe it’ll distract me from the butter overload.

Speaker_1: Honestly, it’s just… endless concrete, isn’t it? I mean, it's nice to *see* the river, but they’ve just built all the way along it. It’s a shame. Speaker_2: It is a bit, yeah. Though, that’s a good view of the O2, isn’t it? Still looks a bit like a giant golf ball plopped down. Speaker_1: A very expensive golf ball. I still don’t understand why they put it *there*. We’d be stuck for hours. Though, I do sometimes envy people who can just… hop in the car and go. Remember when we tried to convince your brother to drive us to Cornwall? Speaker_1: (laughs) Oh, don't remind me! He was having *none* of it. Said his back couldn’t take it. Honestly, it’s just easier to wrestle the kids onto a train. Though, this year, even that feels… daunting. Trying to coordinate everyone’s schedules is a nightmare. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Everyone’s so busy. Are you still thinking about Brittany? I know you were looking at gîtes. Speaker_1: Yeah, Brittany's still on the cards, if I can actually book one that isn’t already snatched up. It’s just… packing for a family of five is exhausting. And then someone inevitably forgets their favourite toy and it's a full-scale meltdown. Speaker_2: (chuckles) You’re a saint, you are. Seriously. My sister went to America last year, and she was complaining about all the recipes being in cups and ounces. Said she couldn’t convert anything. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s awful! I hate American measurements. It’s so imprecise. “A dash of this, a pinch of that…” What does that even *mean*? Give me grams and millilitres any day. It's just… inherently illogical. Speaker_2: Exactly! It’s like they actively try to make it difficult. It makes you wonder, doesn’t it? Why do we cling to these arbitrary systems? Why do we define things the way we do? Speaker_1: (pauses, looking out at the river) Now you’re getting philosophical on me. Honestly, sometimes I just want a cup of tea and for everyone to be quiet for five minutes. Is that too much to ask? Speaker_2: No, not at all. A very reasonable request. Look, there’s the Cutty Sark. That’s quite something. Speaker_1: It is, isn’t it? Amazing to think of all the journeys that ship made. Makes all our holiday planning seem rather trivial, doesn’t it? Still, a little bit of sun and a good book… that’s all I really need. Speaker_2: Sounds good to me. Fancy stopping for a coffee near the market? We're almost in Greenwich now. Speaker_1: Perfect. Let’s do that. And we can avoid any more existential crises for at least another ten minutes. Speaker_2: Good plan. Speaker_1: Though, honestly, sometimes I wonder if all of this… (gestures vaguely around) …if it all really *means* anything. Speaker_2: (laughing) Here we go again… Coffee first, philosophical debates later. Deal? Speaker_1: Deal. Coffee first. Definitely coffee first.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this rain is relentless. It’s been going for days. I feel like I’m living in a perpetual grey film. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! Speaking of things I find everywhere… have you managed to get Finn properly potty-trained yet? Speaker_1: (Sighs) It's… a work in progress. We have good days and bad days. Mostly bad days, if I’m being honest. He seems to think the bathroom floor is an acceptable alternative. I’m seriously considering just sticking to nappies forever. Speaker_3: Oh, I remember those days! It's exhausting. You just feel like you're constantly cleaning up. Remember how Mum used to say it was just a phase? Speaker_2: She always did! “It’s just a phase!” That woman drives me mad sometimes. But honestly, she’s right most of the time. Still, wishing she wouldn’t offer unsolicited advice every five minutes. Speaker_1: She means well, I think. It’s just… *her* way of showing it. Oh! Did you see that new kitchen gadget advertised on TV last night? The one that makes smoothies and soups with just one button? Speaker_3: No, I missed that. Sounds a bit too good to be true, doesn’t it? Everything’s always more complicated than it looks. Speaker_2: Probably is. I’d rather just go swimming, honestly. It’s the only time I feel properly relaxed these days. Though, even the swimming pool seems to be packed with screaming kids now. You can't even enjoy a quiet length! Speaker_1: Oh, tell me about it. I tried taking Leo a couple of weeks ago, and he spent the entire time splashing everyone around him. It was less relaxing swim, and more supervised chaos! Speaker_3: Perhaps we should all go together sometime. A proper girls’ day out. And maybe leave the kids with your husbands?

Speaker_1: Right, so, genuinely, what feels… good? Not ‘should’ feel good, not what looks good on paper, but what actually excites you for the next, I don’t know, six months? Beyond just surviving this house-sitting gig, because, let's be honest, palm trees are nice, but it’s not a life plan. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) No, it’s definitely not. Okay. Well, the PGCE feels… settled. I like teaching. It’s challenging, obviously, but I genuinely enjoy it. I think… I think I'd like to look at doing some more training? Maybe a specialism? Goodness is a skill in a classroom. Is that realistically achievable alongside everything else though? Thinking about marking, planning... Speaker_2: It would be a bit of a push. But the school’s supportive. They offer funding for some courses. I’d need to look into it properly. What about you? Still obsessed with building this… empire? Speaker_1: (Laughs) Empire is a strong word. Let’s call it a moderately successful online business. Honestly? It’s plateauing. I'm getting… bored. I think I need a project, a challenge. Remember Liam and Chloe talking about expanding their marketing agency? They were sniffing around for someone with my skillset. Speaker_2: Oh, seriously? That's a tempting offer, isn’t it? Working with them would be… fun. Less solitary than what you're doing now, at least. And potentially more lucrative. But it would mean shifting everything again. Another new venture. Speaker_1: Exactly. That’s what’s holding me back. The thought of ripping everything up and starting over is exhausting. But staying where I am feels… stagnating. It’s a proper dilemma. What about… us? Longer term? We haven’t really talked about… you know. Speaker_2: (Sighs) Kids. You mean. Yes. It’s always looming, isn’t it? I… I want them. I do. But the timing never feels right. And with me being a teacher, and you flitting between projects… it feels selfish to bring someone into that. Speaker_1: Flitting is harsh! I’m a dynamic entrepreneur! (He grins, then sees her expression) Okay, okay, fair enough. Look, if I joined Liam and Chloe, it would give us some financial stability. A proper base. We could… actually plan properly. Research schools, think about childcare… Speaker_2: That's true. It would be a lot less stressful. But what if you hate it? What if the dynamic doesn't work? We’ve both seen how relationships can sour when money becomes involved. Speaker_1: We talk. That’s what we do. We talk, we compromise, we figure it out. Look, it’s not a decision for tomorrow. But it's something we need to actively consider, isn’t it? Before we get too comfortable just… existing in sunshine and borrowed houses. We need a plan, a real plan. Not just a vaguely optimistic feeling. Speaker_2: You’re right. A plan. And maybe… maybe I should book that initial consultation about the specialism course. Just to see what’s involved. Baby steps. Speaker_1: Baby steps are good. And maybe we both write down three things we genuinely want to achieve in the next six months. No pressure, just… what would make us feel genuinely fulfilled? Speaker_2: I like that. Okay. I’ll get a notepad. And maybe a glass of wine. Planning is always better with wine.

Speaker_1: Honestly though, I still can't get over how different your accent is getting, Liam. It’s like, subtly shifting every week. Speaker_2: Am I? Is it that bad? I've just been spending a lot of time with folks from Manchester, you know? It rubs off. Speaker_3: No, it's not *bad*, it's just… noticeable. You’re starting to sound like you've swallowed a tram. Speaker_4: (Laughing) A tram! That’s brilliant! Speaker_5: It’s alright, though. Still recognisably you. It’s just… less Warrington. Speaker_2: Fair enough. I'll try to tone it down. It's not deliberate, honestly. Remember when Mark tried to do a Scouse accent after that stag do in Liverpool? That was a disaster. Speaker_1: Oh god, don’t remind me. I thought I was going to have to stage an intervention. He genuinely believed he was mimicking a Liverpudlian. Speaker_3: It was like watching a car crash in slow motion. Speaking of disasters, has anyone seen Ben lately? I haven’t heard from him in ages. Speaker_4: He was talking about starting some crazy Pokémon Go challenge. Like, catching every single Pokémon in a fifty-mile radius. Think he's holed up somewhere remote, battling virtual creatures. Speaker_5: Seriously? That sounds… exhausting. Speaker_1: Classic Ben. Always with the extreme hobbies. Remember when he tried to build a fully functional replica of the Millennium Falcon out of cardboard boxes? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) And the council had to get involved because it was blocking the pavement! Good times. Say, anyone fancy popping to the shop? I'm craving chocolate. After Eights specifically. Speaker_3: Oh, go on then. You're always getting us snacks. I’ll chip in. Speaker_4: I'm good, thanks. I’m still full from that massive lunch. You know, it’s weird. I used to *love* After Eights, and now they just taste… artificial. Speaker_5: It’s an age thing. Your taste buds are evolving. Speaker_1: It’s a sign of maturity, darling. Like discerning a good Pinot Grigio from a mediocre one. Speaking of evolving, has anyone tried those new noise-cancelling headphones? Apparently, they’re amazing. Speaker_2: They’re pricey though, aren't they? I'm still rocking my ancient earbuds. Actually, I think the wire's about to snap. Speaker_3: My Fitbit keeps telling me I need to move more. It's so judgemental! I’m trying, okay Fitbit?! I walked to the bus stop. Speaker_4: (Teasingly) A whole thirty yards! Olympic effort. Honestly though, the amount of sugar and crap I’ve eaten since uni started… terrifying. Speaker_5: Don't worry about it. We’ll all die young. Speaker_1: Don’t say that! You'll give my mum a heart attack. She’s already convinced I’m going to end up living in a tent and eating squirrels. Speaker_2: Oh, right, your mum. She still thinks camping is a form of torture, doesn't she? Speaker_3: And that squirrels are just rats with fluffy tails. She's got strong opinions. Right, who's going to the shop then? I'll get the money together. And don't forget the After Eights! Or I’ll be very disappointed.

Speaker_1: Well, that was a dreadful football match wasn’t it? Absolutely dreadful. Couldn’t understand a thing the commentator was saying either, mumbling away like he had a mouthful of marbles. Speaker_2: Oh, don’t start on the football, Arthur. You say that every single week, regardless of whether you’ve actually *watched* the match! Speaker_3: It *was* a bit of a slog, Dad. Not exactly a thrilling spectacle. At least the roast was good, Mum. Honestly, your Yorkshire puddings are legendary. Speaker_4: They really are. You've outdone yourself, honestly. Best Yorkshire puddings I’ve had in ages. Speaker_2: Oh, you say that every time, you two! Just trying to be polite, are you? I’m just glad everyone’s here. It’s nice to have a proper family dinner for once. Speaker_1: Speaking of proper, have you seen what that Sunak’s up to now? Another tax hike. Honestly, it’s ridiculous. They’re bleeding us dry. Speaker_3: Dad, please, not politics at the dinner table. Let’s try and have one meal without arguing about the government. Speaker_4: Yeah, maybe we can avoid that this time? It’s nice to just… relax. Though, I did hear a rumour about potential strikes in universities if they don’t address the pay issues. It’s getting a bit tense at work. Speaker_3: Oh, you too? It's the same where I am. Everyone’s worried. We're trying to organise something, but it’s slow going. It’s the administration, you see. Always the administration. Speaker_2: University strikes? Oh dear. Sounds stressful. Are you managing alright, love? You do work so hard. Speaker_3: I’m alright, Mum. Just… a lot. Marking essays, preparing lectures, and now potentially picketing. It feels like there’s never a quiet moment. Speaker_1: Reminds me of when I used to work on the farm. Never a moment's peace! Always something needing doing. Though, mind you, at least you’ve got a pension these days. I never saved enough, always thought I’d have more time. Speaker_4: You shouldn't worry too much about that, Arthur. You always looked after us all. Besides, we're happy to help out. Speaker_2: Exactly. And we need to start planning for your birthday, Arthur. Seventy-eight, is it? What sort of fuss do you want to make? Speaker_1: Fuss? Oh, don’t make a fuss. Just a quiet evening, a nice pint, and a bit of telly. That’ll do for me. Though, I wouldn’t say no to one of your lemon drizzle cakes, Ethel. Speaker_2: Lemon drizzle it is, then! Maybe we should have a small party, though? Invite a few neighbours? Speaker_3: That sounds nice, Mum. We could decorate the garden. It’s getting warmer now, hopefully. Speaker_4: Agreed! A little garden party would be lovely. We could even get a bouncy castle… Speaker_1: (chuckles) A bouncy castle? At my age? You’re having a laugh! Speaker_2: Well, not *for* you, silly! For the grandchildren! They’d love it. Now, who’s helping me rinse up? And then we can look at some party themes… That is the end of the conversation. I hope it meets your requirements! Let me know if you’d like me to continue it.

Speaker_2: Honestly, I’m seriously considering just… chucking it all in. Speaker_1: What? Like, dropping out? Properly? Speaker_2: Yeah. I just… I don’t know what I’m doing here. Everyone else seems to have a plan, a career path, something. I’m just… existing. And accumulating debt. Speaker_1: Oh, Liv. That’s rough. But you’re good at your course, aren’t you? History of Art? You got like, a first on that essay last term. Speaker_2: Yeah, but enjoying something and being good at it are two different things, aren’t they? It's just… not sparking joy, as Marie Kondo would say. And all this reading, the essays… it feels pointless. Speaker_1: I get that. It’s hard when it doesn't feel like it’s leading anywhere. But you’ve come this far. Remember how excited you were about uni? About getting away from Liverpool? Speaker_2: I was escaping my auntie Brenda, mostly. She meant well, but she’d constantly ask me what I was going to *do* with a degree in art history. Like I needed a practical skill to justify existing. Speaker_1: Brenda sounds… Brenda. You’ve always been creative though. Remember when we were kids, and you’d make those elaborate outfits for your Barbies out of, like, curtains and tea towels? Speaker_2: Oh god, don’t remind me! Mum was furious about the curtains. She said I was ruining them. I thought I was a fashion designer! And you were always building forts. Massive ones, in the garden. You'd spend days in there. Speaker_1: It was a simpler time. No essays, no student loans. Just sticks and blankets. Speaking of simpler times, look at your shoes. Speaker_2: What about them? Speaker_1: They’re… coated. In something. Mud? Is it mud? Speaker_2: Probably. I walked across campus after it rained. It was a swamp. Speaker_1: They look like you’ve been digging for gold. You're leaving muddy footprints everywhere. Speaker_2: Dramatic much? Anyway, back to my impending life crisis… Have you ever considered dropping out? Speaker_1: Briefly. After first year, when I realised how much work a psychology degree actually involved. But my mum would have killed me. She’s always been so proud of me being at uni. Honestly, it's a bit stifling. Speaker_2: See, mine would probably just be relieved I didn’t become a performance artist or something equally unconventional. She's always wanted me to have a ‘sensible’ job. Speaker_1: Sensible is overrated. Hey, your name is interesting. Liverpool… is that where it comes from? 'Liv'? Speaker_2: Yeah! It’s short for Olivia, which is apparently derived from the olive tree. Symbolises peace and… something else boring. My nan loved Shakespeare, she picked it. Said Olivia was a beautiful name in *Twelfth Night*. Speaker_1: That's a nice story. Mine’s pretty boring. My mum just liked the sound of ‘Poppy’. Apparently, it was fashionable at the time. All the babies were called Poppy. Speaker_2: Still, it suits you. You do look like a poppy. Bright and a bit… prickly. Speaker_1: Ouch! Thanks. Look, about dropping out – maybe just, I dunno, take a break? A semester off? See how you feel then? Don’t make any rash decisions. And maybe clean your shoes. For the sake of my carpet.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this risotto is amazing. You were right to recommend this place. Though, I'm feeling slightly judged for ordering it – everyone else seems to have gone for something lighter. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, don't worry about it! It *is* proper comfort food. And honestly, you deserve a proper treat. How’s work been? Still battling spreadsheets and project deadlines? I'm so proud of him. He was so stuck in that dead-end job for so long. Is he… terrifyingly excited? Speaker_2: Terrifyingly is the word. He’s all energy and enthusiasm, bouncing off the walls. It's brilliant, but also slightly exhausting to be around! He's already talking about pitching ideas for the next 'unicorn' app. He's a bit delusional, honestly. Speaker_1: (Laughing) He always was. That’s what I love about him. Okay, this is a terrible segue, but… are you seeing anyone at the moment? You mentioned last time you were still 'exploring options'. Speaker_2: Oh god, don't even. It's been a disaster. I went on three dates last month, each more spectacularly awful than the last. One was a conspiracy theorist, one talked about his ex for the entire evening, and the third just… kept ordering more and more expensive wine and trying to impress me with his wealth. Speaker_1: Oh, *no*. That sounds truly horrific. So, you’re back to single life, then? Speaker_2: Pretty much. I'm starting to think I'm destined to be a crazy cat lady. Though, honestly, the thought is becoming increasingly appealing. Speaker_1: Don’t say that! You deserve someone amazing. Listen, I’m having a housewarming next month. It’s just a small thing, a few friends, nibbles, lots of wine. You absolutely *have* to come. It would be so good to catch up properly, outside of a frantic restaurant. Speaker_2: Oh, I’d love to! A housewarming! That's fantastic, congratulations! When is it? And more importantly, can I bring a plus one… even if that plus one is just a bottle of gin? Speaker_1: (Smiling) Of course! Bring the gin! It’s on the 18th. I’ll text you the details later. I’m so glad we finally made this happen, by the way. It feels like ages. Speaker_2: Me too. Life just gets in the way. But this… this is good. Really good. Now, tell me more about this rogue project scope – let’s commiserate properly. And maybe order another round of risotto?

Speaker_1: Right, now then, I’m having a look for that bird feeder, aren’t I? The one with the suet pellets in. Speaker_2: Mum, you bought one last week. It’s still in the garage. Speaker_1: Did I? Oh, did I now? Well, that’s a waste of money, isn't it? I could have sworn the squirrels had already demolished it. They’re crafty, those squirrels. Speaker_2: They haven’t touched it. I checked. I thought that was a good one. Speaker_1: Honestly, you lot are obsessed with food. Speaker_2: Well, it’s a good category! Everyone likes food. Speaker_3: Right, alright, my turn again. “Books”. I once did the entire plot of Hamlet using only a teapot and a biscuit! Speaker_1: (Bursting out laughing)

Speaker_1: Right, okay, so I’m going to put down a red seven. And then… oh, hang on. Rhys, you haven’t taken a card, have you? You’re just staring into space. Speaker_2: (Startled) Oh! Speaker_2: (Laughing) That's a low blow! I improved! Slightly. Speaker_4: I’ve got a red seven, but… it’s a different suit. No good, is it? Speaker_1: Nope, needs to be hearts. Right, my turn again. They’re very specific these days, aren’t they? Speaker_3: Sounds like you need a holiday just to recover from dealing with those beige-avoiding pupils. Speaker_2: You’re not wrong there. Speaker_3: Careful, I'm watching you… Speaker_4: It’s the calm before the storm. I can feel it.

Speaker_1: Honestly, *Wednesday* is just… chef’s kiss. Have you guys seen it? It’s so good. Like, properly dark and funny. Speaker_2: Ooh, I’ve heard about it! Is it on Netflix? A lot of my team are ex-apprentices, and they are solid. I mean, I went the full university route, but it’s not for everyone. Costs a fortune. Speaker_2: Speaking of costs, has anyone got any Christmas present ideas for Gran? She’s got everything. Last year I got her a foot massager and she just looked at me like I’d insulted her. Speaker_5: Ooh, tricky. Maybe a really nice photo album with family pictures? She loves looking at old photos and going on about how cute we all were. Speaker_1: Yeah, that's a good idea! Or a fancy box of biscuits. Gran loves a biscuit. Although, she *did* get a really bad cold last week… Mum was worried sick. Speaker_3: Oh no, poor Gran! Is she better now? Speaker_2: She’s on the mend, thankfully. Just a nasty bug. Mum's been forcing her to drink loads of lemon and honey. Honestly, Mum turns into a full-on nurse when anyone gets ill. I had it when I was, like, six. Speaker_1: So, Christmas plans then? Are we all doing the usual at Auntie Carol’s? I swear her turkey is always slightly dry. Speaker_3: Unfortunately, yes. Auntie Carol's turkey, Uncle Roger’s terrible jokes, the whole shebang. But it wouldn’t be Christmas without it, would it? Speaker_2: True. It's tradition. And I get to sneakily eat all the Quality Street while nobody's looking. Speaker_4: I’m in. As long as there’s a decent supply of Baileys, I’m good to go. Speaker_5: Me too! And maybe, just maybe, I'll finally convince Ben that folding jumpers is a valuable life skill.

Speaker_1: Honestly though, I don't know what’s happening with people these days. Just walking along, glued to their phones. Nearly walked straight into one earlier, you know? Outside the bakery. Speaker_2: Oh, it’s awful isn’t it? You see it *everywhere*. Like they’re living in a different world. Speaker_3: Right, and they don’t even look up! Nearly got taken out by a cyclist doing the same thing last week. Headphones in, eyes down. Reckless, that’s what it is. Speaker_1: Cyclists are the worst! I swear, they think they own the pavement. And going so fast! I nearly had a heart attack the other day, one whizzed past me on Mill Road, didn’t even ring his bell. Speaker_2: Mill Road's a nightmare. It's just constantly busy. I cycle to work sometimes, and even *I* get stressed. You're dodging pedestrians, buses, other cyclists… Speaker_3: You should get the bus, love. Safer, that is. Speaker_2: I’d love to, but the bus routes are terrible. It would take me ages, and I need to get to work for nine. Cycling is quicker, even with all the chaos. Remember when we tried to drive into town for Christmas shopping last year? Took us an hour just to find a space. Speaker_1: Hmph. Well, I still think driving is the safest option. I’ve been driving for fifty years, never had an accident. Touch wood! Speaker_2: Fifty years is a long time, Gran. Things are a bit different now, aren’t they? More traffic, more people… Speaker_3: Remember old Mr. Henderson? Used to cycle everywhere, rain or shine. Even in his eighties! Said it kept him young. Speaker_1: Oh, Henderson! A lovely man. But he was a bit of a madman, cycling in that weather. Always had a waterproof coat though, bless him. Speaker_2: Speaking of getting around, are you two still planning on coming to visit me next month? I was thinking we could walk along the river, maybe go for a picnic. Speaker_3: We are, love. Looking forward to it. As long as the weather’s decent. Speaker_1: Yes, a lovely day out. Perhaps we could take the bus, though? Just to be safe…and avoid all those cyclists! Speaker_2: That sounds good. We can look at the bus routes when I’m next over. Maybe we could even try cycling, if you're feeling brave? Speaker_3: Oh, no thank you dear. I’ll stick to walking, I think. Or maybe a nice sit down with a cup of tea. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) That sounds much more sensible, dear. That sounds perfect. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Alright, alright. Tea and cake it is. Speaker_3: Good. Speaker_1: Mmm. Now, pass me the biscuits. I hope this is what you were looking for! Let me know if you'd like any changes or additions. Speaker_1: Now, pass me the biscuits. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Alright, alright. Tea and cake it is. Speaker_3: Good. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) That sounds much more sensible, dear. That sounds perfect. Speaker_3: Oh, no thank you dear. I’ll stick to walking, I think. Or maybe a nice sit down with a cup of tea. Speaker_2: That sounds good. We can look at the bus routes when I’m next over.

Speaker_1: It’s lovely isn't it, to be back? Feels like ages since I was wandering these corridors as a student. Speaker_2: Absolutely. Though it all feels… smaller, somehow. Remember thinking everything was so grand and imposing? Speaker_3: (Chuckles) That's the trick of youth, my dear. Everything *is* smaller when you've had a few decades to grow accustomed to the real world. Though this faculty remains rather impressive. So, are you both alumni of the Law Faculty then? Speaker_1: Yes, I graduated about five years ago. I’m a Language Research Coordinator now – a bit of a mouthful, I know. It’s fascinating work though, looking at legal language across different cultures. Speaker_2: And I’m a Research Administrator. Bit more paperwork, a bit less language, but still good. Did you ever study any languages alongside law? Speaker_1: I did! Spanish, actually. Spent a year in Barcelona. Absolutely fell in love with the city. Have you been? Speaker_3: Barcelona? A beautiful city. Though I must confess, I found the Catalan independence movement a little unsettling while I was there. Fascinating linguistic situation though, isn’t it? The Basque country is even more unique. Such an isolated language family. Speaker_2: I’ve always found linguistics fascinating. It’s amazing how much law is tied up in language and interpretation. I tried Mandarin briefly, completely failed. It's just… conceptually so different. Speaker_1: Oh, Mandarin is a beast! I've dabbled a bit, but it's a whole different skillset. Have you travelled much in China? Speaker_3: I did a sabbatical in Hong Kong years ago, lecturing on comparative law. Quite an experience. Very different legal traditions, as one might imagine. Though I spent most of my time trying to avoid the humidity! Reminded me of summers in London, honestly. Speaker_2: London’s pretty humid these days, isn't it? Though not quite Hong Kong levels, I imagine. I haven’t been back to Cambridge since I graduated. I did spend a couple of years living in London after university, though. Speaker_1: It’s changed a lot even in the last few years. It's definitely… busier. Did either of you ever venture into Wales during your time here? Speaker_3: Wales? I did. Years ago. Went to watch a rugby match. Incredible atmosphere. Truly incredible. Though I confess, I didn’t quite understand all the rules. Speaker_2: (Laughs) Oh, rugby! It’s a bit of a national obsession there. My dad’s Welsh, so I was practically raised on it. Still don’t *play* it, but I can follow a game. Speaker_1: My partner’s a huge rugby fan. I’m more of a football person myself, but I appreciate the… physicality of it. Do you still follow any sport, Professor? Speaker_3: Oh, intermittently. I used to be a keen cricketer, back in the day. But these days, I’m more likely to be found poring over legal journals than watching a match. Though I do enjoy a good tennis tournament. Wimbledon, of course. It wouldn’t be British summer without it. Speaker_2: Absolutely! It’s a tradition. Well, it was lovely chatting with you both. I should probably go and find the refreshments table… all this reminiscing has made me thirsty. Speaker_1: Me too! Perhaps we can compare notes on linguistic peculiarities over a glass of something? Speaker_3: An excellent suggestion! Let’s find that refreshments table. And perhaps we can continue this discussion. I’m always happy to talk about the intricacies of language and law.

Speaker_2: Honestly though, seeing all those Ice Bucket Challenge videos pop up again on Facebook… it’s weird, isn’t it? Feels like a lifetime ago. Remember how everyone was doing it? Even Gran got involved, bless her. Speaker_1: Oh god, Gran and the ice bucket. That was… a sight. She was complaining about being cold for a week afterwards. And Uncle Barry filming it all, of course. He *loved* that. Did you see Sarah’s engagement photos? They’re all over my feed. Speaker_3: Oh, the ones in that ridiculous castle? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, Mum will try and fix everyone with pilates. It's her solution for everything! Remember when she tried to get Dad to do it for his back? He nearly strangled her. Speaker_3: She’s a force of nature, isn’t she? Speaking of forces of nature… how’s teaching going, Ben? Still battling through the grammar tenses with bewildered students? Speaker_1: It’s… a challenge. Honestly, sometimes I wonder if I made the right decision going to uni to do that. It’s not exactly a lucrative career path, eh? Plus, the paperwork. Endless forms to fill in. It feels like I spend more time doing admin than actually teaching sometimes. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Dental practices are the same. So many forms! And everyone’s got a ‘condition’ to note down. Honestly, you’d think everyone was on death’s door. Speaker_3: Sounds grim. Recruitment isn’t *that* bad. Although… trying to convince people they’re perfect for jobs they clearly aren't is a skill. I had one candidate yesterday who swore he was fluent in Mandarin. Turns out he knew how to say ‘hello’ and ‘thank you’. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Oh, brilliant. You always get those! Remember Mark from school? Said he was a black belt in karate. We found out he’d taken two lessons. Speaker_2: Oh, *Mark*. Don't even get me started on Mark. He was always exaggerating. Speaking of school…did you hear about Lisa’s little boy, Freddie? Apparently, he’s already showing signs of being a little terror. Speaker_3: No way! Lisa? A terror? I thought she was determined to be the perfect mum. All organic food and Montessori toys. Speaker_1: Apparently, he’s already staging full-blown tantrums in the supermarket. She’s losing her mind. She was talking about adoption the other day, joking, I think, but it was... intense. Speaker_2: Serious stuff. It's not easy, is it? Being parents. Especially now. The world is… a bit scary. We were talking about it the other day, me and Mark - no, not *that* Mark! - and we were wondering if we'll even *be able* to afford to have kids. Speaker_3: It is a worry. Everything's so expensive. Speaking of expensive…did you manage to get a decent price on flights for that trip to Italy you were planning? Speaker_1: I'm still looking. Prices are insane. I might have to postpone it. I was hoping to go in the spring but… maybe next year. Honestly, it's easier just to stay here, isn’t it? Bedford is… Bedford. You know what you’re getting. Speaker_2: Bedford’s not so bad. It’s home. And at least you understand the accents here. Trying to understand some people in London is a nightmare.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this coffee machine is driving me mad. It makes a perfectly good cup sometimes, and other times it just spits out lukewarm water. It's possessed, I tell you. Possessed! Speaker_2: Maybe it needs descaling? You said you hadn't done it in ages. Speaker_1: Descaling, cleaning, praying… I’ve tried it all! It's just… unreliable. Like half the politicians these days. Speaker_3: Speaking of politicians, did you see what Starmer said about… well, everything? It was predictably bland. Honestly, where are the real idealists anymore? Nobody's fighting for anything properly. Speaker_1: Oh, don’t get me started on politics. It’s just a mess. All sound and fury, signifying nothing. Though, to be fair, I’m finding it hard to care much since I retired. Less infuriating news headlines in retirement, I suppose. Speaker_2: True. Though I find myself doomscrolling far too much. It's a bad habit. Speaker_3: It is. Anyway, back to more pressing matters... have you gotten quotes yet for removing and storing some of the stuff from the attic? We really need to clear it out before winter sets in. Speaker_1: I did. It’s absolutely outrageous, the prices! One company wanted nearly four hundred pounds just to *look* at it, let alone move anything. And the storage costs... Honestly, it's cheaper to buy a new house and fill it with new stuff. Speaker_2: Four hundred pounds just to assess? That's daylight robbery! Did you try that man, Barry, from the village? He does removals on the side. Speaker_1: Yes, I did. He’s busy until October, and even then he wants more than I was hoping to pay. He said everyone is clearing out before the cold weather. Apparently, everyone's suddenly realised they've accumulated too much junk. Speaker_3: Well, we *have* accumulated a lot of junk. Let’s be honest. It’s a generational curse. Grandmother Moira was a hoarder, and it seems to be in the genes. Speaker_1: Don’t remind me. I’m still finding her teacups in the most unlikely places. And her collection of commemorative spoons. Honestly. It's madness. Speaker_2: Maybe we could have a clear-out weekend? We could all tackle it together? The more hands, the quicker it’ll be. Speaker_3: That's a good idea. Though knowing us, we'll end up reminiscing over every single item and get nothing actually *done*. Speaker_1: Probably. But it’s worth a try. At least we can make a strong cup of coffee…if this wretched machine cooperates, that is. It’s threatening to spit again. Speaker_2: Oh dear. Maybe it *is* possessed. Speaker_3: And honestly, given the state of the world, a possessed coffee machine isn’t even the strangest thing that could happen today. Rest assured it is less infuriating than the current labour leadership. Speaker_1: You aren't wrong there dear. Speaker_2: I'm going to get a another cuppa. Speaker_1: Yes dear do. Speaker_3: Good idea. Speaker_2: Back in two. Speaker_3: And have a biscuit too. Speaker_1: That's my girl. Speaker_3: That's wonderful, I'm having one too. Speaker_1: That is the spirit. Speaker_2: Okay. Speaker_1: Right.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, the thought of Christmas already fills me with dread. Not the actual day, but *getting* to the actual day. It's just… relentless, isn’t it? She’s already started hinting about wanting to carve the turkey again. Speaker_1: Oh, God, Brenda and the turkey. A horrifying image. That's exactly what I’m trying to avoid. Maybe just a small Christmas, at my place? No extended family, just close friends? Speaker_2: That sounds… sensible. Though, your father does love having everyone around. He gets so much joy from it. He secretly loves Brenda’s insistence on carving the turkey, you know. He pretends to be annoyed, but he isn’t. Speaker_1: He’s such a softie. Right. Okay. We'll have family Christmas. But I’m delegating. Seriously delegating. I can’t be responsible for *everything* again. Last year, I practically single-handedly assembled ten Lego sets. Ten! Speaker_2: (chuckles) Oh, the nephews. They are a handful. It's lovely to see their faces though, isn’t it? That pure joy. Speaker_1: It is. But my fingers were aching for a week. And speaking of aching, how is your back? Still giving you trouble? Speaker_2: It’s…manageable. I'm doing those Pilates classes, remember? Trying to. Although Mrs. Higgins keeps showing off, and it's terribly distracting. She was a ballerina, apparently. A *professional* ballerina. At seventy! Speaker_1: Good for her! It’s good to keep active. You should get Dad to join you. He’s complaining about his knees again. Speaker_2: He'd rather watch football. You know that. He's stubbornly refusing to admit he’s getting older. Keeps trying to chase after the dog. Speaker_1: (laughing) Oh, Dad. Always the sportsman. Listen, about work… I’m thinking of doing that CELTA course in January. Fully immerse myself, you know? Really boost my TEFL qualifications. Speaker_2: Oh, that’s excellent, darling! Very sensible. You’re good at that, you are. Really connecting with the students. It’s more than just teaching English, isn’t it? It’s helping them build confidence. Speaker_1: It is. And honestly, it’s more fulfilling than anything I've done. Though, the pay isn't amazing. Speaker_2: It's a start. And you enjoy it. That’s the most important thing. We can always help you out if needed. Don't be foolish and refuse. Speaker_1: I appreciate that, Mum. Honestly. And actually, speaking of help, are you and Dad free the weekend after next? I was thinking of going up to Bristol to visit Isla and Jamie, and it would be lovely if you could come with me. Speaker_2: Oh, that sounds lovely! Yes, we can do that. Just let me check with your father. He’s got that antique fair he wants to go to, but I’m sure he can reschedule. It’ll be good to see them. And it's always nice to get away from Totnes for a bit. Though, I do miss the Seven Stars.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I thought old man Hemmings was gonna have a heart attack last night. Speaker_2: What, at the pub quiz? What happened? Speaker_1: No, not at the pub quiz. At Sheila’s. He was going on *about* Geoff. Apparently, Geoff’s snoring kept him up all night. Said it sounded like a rusty engine trying to start. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh, bless him! Geoff snores worse than a badger. Did he actually complain to Geoff? Speaker_1: Apparently so. Sheila had to intervene. Said Geoff just mumbled something about needing a really strong whisky and rolled over. Hemmings was fuming. Speaker_4: Honestly, some people. It’s snoring! A bit of earplug action and job done. Speaking of Sheila, did anyone get those cream cakes from Waterfields for her birthday? Speaker_5: I did! Got a box of the little fancies. And a loaf of their sourdough. Proper good stuff, Waterfields. Speaker_1: Oh, nice one! She’ll love that. She’s obsessed with their sourdough. Says it's the only bread that doesn't give her indigestion. Speaker_2: Remember when Waterfields used to do those little sausage rolls with Richmond sausages in? Pure heaven. They stopped doing them ages ago. Tragedy. Speaker_3: Oh my god, yes! Proper Richmonds, not that cheap rubbish they use now. Honestly, it's a crime against pastry. Speaker_4: It is. It really is. Everything’s gone downhill. You can’t get a decent sausage roll anywhere anymore. Speaker_5: Speaking of things going downhill, did you see Barry yesterday? He was walking around with a… a *handkerchief*! Speaker_1: (Bursting out laughing) No way! Barry? The Barry who uses a whole roll of paper towel to wipe his nose? Speaker_2: Apparently, his mum sent him one. Said he needed to “be more of a man” and stop wasting paper. Speaker_3: Oh, his mum! She’s a character, isn’t she? Sending him a handkerchief! It’s the 21st century! Speaker_4: I bet he was mortified. Imagine Barry trying to *blow* his nose into a handkerchief. It’s a mental image I didn’t need. Speaker_5: I saw him trying to figure out how to fold it afterwards, too. Looked like he was wrestling with a small, patterned bird. Speaker_1: (Still laughing) Oh, this is brilliant. I need to tell everyone. Geoff, the rusty engine, and Barry, the handkerchief man. This is gold. Speaker_2: So, quiz tonight then? Same teams? Speaker_3: Yeah, sounds good. Just promise me we won’t get stuck on the music round again. I’m terrible with anything post-2000. Speaker_4: Deal. Though, someone needs to stop Dave from shouting out all the answers. It’s incredibly distracting. Speaker_5: I’ll try. Though knowing Dave… it's a lost cause. Speaker_1: Right, another drink then? My round. And then we can brainstorm strategies for conquering the pub quiz. And potentially, a plan to deal with old man Hemmings and his snoring grievances. Speaker_2: Sounds perfect. Speaker_3: Cheers to that! Speaker_4: Cheers! Speaker_5: Alright! Let's do it.

Speaker_1: Honestly, that was the busiest weekend ever. I feel like I haven’t stopped moving since Friday evening. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Though, mine was busy in a different way. Mostly involving stubborn sheep and fences that decided to give up their lives. Speaker_1: Oh, no! Not again with the fences? You said the last storm really did a number on them. Speaker_2: A number is putting it mildly. It was more like a total demolition. Spent most of Saturday patching things up, and then Sunday was spent checking they hadn't *immediately* fallen down again. It’s a never-ending cycle, honestly. Speaker_1: Sounds exhausting. At least mine was… social exhaustion. I went to that art exhibition with Chloe, and it was surprisingly packed. Then a birthday dinner for Liam, which went on *way* too long. Speaker_2: Liam, eh? Progress? Speaker_1: (Laughs) Don’t push it, Dad! It was just a friendly dinner. He’s good mates with Ben from work, so it was a bit of a team thing. It was nice, actually. He's got a new puppy, a little Jack Russell, absolutely adorable. Speaker_2: A puppy? You’re a sucker for a puppy, aren’t you? Speaker_1: Shut up. It was cute! Anyway, then Sunday I was helping Mum sort through old photos. That was a whole saga. Apparently, I had a phase where I only wore bright orange, and she has photographic evidence. Speaker_2: Oh, bless. Mothers and their photo albums. They’re a historical record of our shame. I remember your grandma had a photo of me in short trousers and knee socks… traumatizing. Speaker_1: (Smiling) I bet. So, what about you? Aside from battling rogue livestock, anything else happen on the farm? Any breakthroughs with the new irrigation system? Speaker_2: Not quite breakthroughs. More like minor victories. Got the pump working consistently, but the distribution is still a bit uneven. It needs another tweak, I think. I'm hoping to get a proper engineer out next week, if I can find one who isn't booked up for the next six months. Speaker_1: That sounds frustrating. It always seems to be one thing after another. Speaker_1: Right, so I was reading this paper on dialect levelling in Yorkshire, and it’s *fascinating*. It’s happened a lot in Birmingham, hasn’t it? The Brummie accent is… let’s say, less prevalent than it used to be. Probably read something in the Daily Mail. Still, means well, I suppose. You sure you’ve got all the paperwork sorted for the removal guys? Don't want any surprises. Speaker_1: Pretty sure.
