Speaker_2: Oh, that monstrosity? The floral one? Yeah, she’ll be glad to be rid of that. You feeling alright, by the way? You’ve been a bit quiet. Speaker_1: Just… a bit weird, I guess. This is the last time we’re driving this route, isn’t it? Last time we’re driving Mum back to Bedford. Feels a bit final. Speaker_2: It does. Bit sad, actually. But it’s a good thing, isn’t it? You and Chloe getting your own place. A fresh start. Though, Northamptonshire… you’re sure about that? Isn’t it a bit…quiet? Speaker_1: Chloe’s family's there, which is a big thing. And it’s affordable, which is even bigger. It’s a compromise, obviously. And it’s not *that* quiet. It’s got a cinema, apparently. Speaker_2: A cinema! Fancy that. Still, Bedford's got that little Italian place, you know, the one we always go to? Best pasta this side of Rome. Speaker_1: You’re just saying that because you have a weakness for their garlic bread. Speaker_2: It *is* exceptional garlic bread. Speaking of food, did you remember to pack any snacks? I'm starting to feel a bit peckish. Speaker_1: I grabbed a couple of biscuits. There's a bag in the glove compartment. Though, don’t eat them all. Speaker_2: Alright, alright. I don’t need to be told what to do with a biscuit. You remember that time we tried to teach your Grandma how to use Netflix? Speaker_1: (Laughs) Oh god, yes. The confusion on her face was priceless. She kept asking where the film *was*. She thought it was hiding inside the TV. Speaker_2: And then she wanted to rewind it with the remote, like a video cassette. Bless her. She still thinks the internet is something to do with spiders. Speaker_1: She's a character. I'm going to miss her terribly. You know, Chloe asked me if I regret not getting a higher-paying job so we could afford something bigger. Speaker_2: What did you tell her? Speaker_1: That doing something you enjoy is worth more than a massive mortgage. I love teaching English. It’s…rewarding. Even if it means living in Northamptonshire. Speaker_2: Good man. It’s a sensible answer. And besides, you can always commute back for garlic bread.

Speaker_1: Right, so we’re pretty much set on the menu then? Salmon en croute, obviously, because she loves it, and then that roasted vegetable medley and the dauphinoise potatoes? Speaker_2: Sounds good, Mum. Though are you sure you're not biting off a bit much with the en croute? It’s quite fiddly, isn't it? Speaker_1: Honestly, I watched a tutorial on YouTube. Apparently, the key is really cold pastry. I reckon I can manage it. Plus, it *is* her 80th. Needs to be a bit special. I’ve already ordered the salmon from Billingsgate Market, lovely bit of Scottish salmon, should be delivered Friday morning. Speaker_2: Billingsgate! Fancy. She’ll love that. She always says the supermarket salmon tastes…well, you know. Speaker_1: Exactly. Now, the seating plan. This is the tricky bit. I was thinking your Auntie Carol next to Dad, to keep her occupied. And your cousin, Emily, needs to be as far away from Uncle Barry as humanly possible. Remember last Christmas? Speaker_2: Oh god, yes. The political debate. It lasted for hours. Emily was practically in tears. Definitely good segregation there. How's Grandad doing with remembering things? Should we put him next to someone who’s good at prompting? Speaker_1: It’s…variable. Some days he’s completely lucid, other days he's asking where your father is – and your father *is* sitting opposite him! I think putting him next to me is best. I’m quite good at subtly steering conversations. And I can prompt him with names if needed. Speaker_2: Good plan. Have you got enough candles? She loves all the ambiance. Speaker_1: Loads! I went a bit overboard, actually. Got those lovely pillar candles in the cream colour, and some tealights. And those little hurricane lamps. It should look really cozy. I've also been trying to declutter the dining room. I've been attacking the cupboards, found photos from… well, ages ago. Speaker_2: Oh really? Any embarrassing ones? Speaker_1: Oh, you know the usual. Awkward school photos, questionable fashion choices. I’ve put a few out on the sideboard, hoping it'll spark some memories. Although, knowing her, she’ll probably just complain about her hair in all of them. Speaker_2: That sounds about right. Have you seen the new series of Great British Bake Off? Speaker_1: Oh, a little bit. Actually, I was thinking about trying to copy one of the cakes for her birthday next year. Not this year, too much on my plate already. But maybe next year? She’s always saying I should bake more. Speaker_2: That's a lovely idea! She'd really appreciate that. Speaking of plates, have you checked we have enough of the good ones? And the fish knives? Speaker_1: Yes, all sorted! I did a full inventory this morning. Everything is present and accounted for. Right, I think we’ve covered everything. Except…do you think we need another bottle of Prosecco? Speaker_2: Mum, it's her 80th. You can *never* have too much Prosecco. Definitely another bottle. Maybe two. Speaker_1: You are absolutely right. Two it is. Speaker_2: Excellent. She’ll be thrilled. Speaker_1: Right. Operation 80th Birthday is a go! Speaker_2: Let’s do this! Speaker_1: Right, now I need to find that recipe for the vegetable medley. It’s somewhere in this chaos…

Speaker_1: Right, so I genuinely think I’m dying. My mouth is absolutely killing me. Speaker_2: Oh no, what’s up? Did you finally get them out? Your wisdom teeth, I mean. Speaker_1: Aye, got ‘em out Tuesday. It was supposed to be straightforward, like, two little buggers. Turns out one was… impacted. And like, growing sideways. It’s proper agony. Speaker_2: Ouch! That sounds awful. Are there…holes? Like, big holes? I always worry about that. My mum’s friend had hers out and she had massive holes for ages. Speaker_1: There are holes. Not *massive* holes, thankfully, but yeah, like little caves. And the taste! Oh god, the taste is vile. Like, constantly rinsing, but it just… lingers. Speaker_2: Ugh, sounds grim. You poor thing. Are you on painkillers? Speaker_1: Yeah, loads. They make me feel like a zombie. I just wanna sleep for a week. Which, ironically, is what I need to be doing, ‘cos we’re going back to uni next week. Brilliant timing, innit? Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I’m dreading it. Especially now we’ve had a blissful week of sunshine and croissants. It’s gonna be a shock to the system going back to lectures and instant noodles. Speaker_1: Exactly! Honestly, I'm not even ready for it. I’ve barely packed. And Mum’s been on at me about moving all my stuff back, which is just…another stress. Speaker_2: Oh yeah, how’s the house move going for your parents? Is it all sorted? Speaker_1: Sort of. They’ve exchanged contracts, so it’s happening. But Dad’s panicking about everything. He keeps saying he’s gonna end up living in a tent. Dramatic, as always. Speaker_2: Bless him. He always was a worrier. My parents are pretty chilled, usually. Though Mum’s been going on about redecorating the spare room and I’m like, “Mum, I haven’t even moved back yet!” Speaker_1: They’re always like that, aren’t they? Planning your life for you. I told Mum no way was I bringing half my stuff back, I’m trying to minimise, be less of a burden. She didn’t even hear me. Speaker_2: They’re just trying to be helpful. In their own, slightly overbearing way. Hey, are you still up for going into town tomorrow? Maybe we can get some ice cream and sit by the river? Distract you from the mouth pain. Speaker_1: Oh, yeah, definitely. That sounds amazing actually. Ice cream is probably the only thing that will make me feel better. And a very gentle walk. Anything strenuous and I think I’ll cry. Speaker_2: Perfect. We'll take it easy. Anything to avoid witnessing a Doncaster-based emotional meltdown caused by impacted wisdom teeth. Speaker_1: Very funny. You’ll be singing a different tune when *you* have yours out. Speaker_2: Ha! Fair enough. Bring on the ice cream. Speaker_1: Right. Ice cream and minimal movement. Sounds like a plan. Speaker_2: And then we start mentally preparing ourselves for the inevitable… lectures. Speaker_1: Don't even. Let's just enjoy the last few days of freedom, yeah? And my painkillers. Speaker_2: Absolutely. Freedom and painkillers. A winning combination. Speaker_1: Best combination there is.

Speaker_1: Right, so for the acts of kindness, I was thinking… we could bake some cookies. But lactose-free ones, for Mrs. Peterson next door. She always says how nice it is when someone thinks of her. Speaker_2: Can we make sparkly ones? With sprinkles! Speaker_1: We can definitely do sparkly ones! And maybe some with little red envelopes tucked underneath, for Chinese New Year? Speaker_3: Ooh, like treasure! Can we use the chess pieces as money? The pawns could be one pence, and the knights could be five pence! Speaker_1: (chuckles) That’s a brilliant idea! Yes, we can use the chess pieces. We’ll need to make a little chart so we remember how much each one is worth. Speaker_2: Can I be in charge of the chart? I’m *really* good at drawing charts. Speaker_1: You absolutely can. And maybe we can write little notes to go with the cookies, wishing everyone a Happy New Year. Or a good Lunar New Year, because it's not *our* New Year just yet. Speaker_3: What's Lunar New Year? Speaker_1: It's like New Year, but it happens at a different time of the year, and lots of people in China and other countries celebrate it with fireworks and special meals and giving red envelopes full of money. Speaker_2: Can we have fireworks? Speaker_1: Not *real* fireworks, darling, that's a bit dangerous. But maybe we can find some sparkly decorations to put up? And we can watch videos of fireworks online. Speaker_3: Can we give red envelopes to Grandad and Nana too? Speaker_1: Of course! They’d love that. Although, instead of chess piece money, we’ll use real money for them. Speaking of which, I think I saw some red envelopes in the cupboard… let’s go and look. Speaker_2: While we’re looking, can we talk about dying my hair? I want it to be rainbow colours! Speaker_1: (sighs playfully) Oh, rainbow hair. We’ve discussed this. It’s a bit…permanent. Speaker_3: I think rainbow hair would be cool! Like a unicorn! Speaker_1: It would be very colourful. But maybe we could start with something a little less…intense? Perhaps just a few streaks? We could look at pictures online. Speaker_2: But rainbows are *awesome*! Speaker_1: They are awesome. We’ll think about it. First, let's find those red envelopes. And then we can brainstorm some more acts of kindness. Maybe we can help Mr. Henderson with his bins? He sometimes struggles. Speaker_3: And make him cookies too! With extra sprinkles! Speaker_1: Yes, and cookies for Mr. Henderson too. That's a lovely idea. Right, let’s go envelope hunting! Speaker_2: Chess pieces! Sparkly cookies! Rainbow hair! Chinese New Year! This is going to be the best day ever! Speaker_1: (smiling) It sounds like it will be. It sounds like it will be. Speaker_3: Can we have a lactose-free cookie too? Please? Speaker_1: Absolutely. A sparkly, lactose-free cookie for everyone. Now, let's go! Speaker_2: Yay! Speaker_3: Let's go, let's go! Speaker_1: (Laughing) Alright, alright, slow down you two! Let's find those envelopes first. . . . . . . ....

Speaker_1: So, did you see that car crash on the High Street yesterday? It was *awful*. Right outside Boots. Speaker_2: Oh, no! Really? I hadn't heard. Was anyone hurt badly? I was working late, didn't even venture out after six. Speaker_1: Apparently, yeah. Someone was trapped, the fire brigade had to come, the whole thing. I was walking back from Sarah’s and just… saw it. It made me jump. It reminded me a bit of that bit in *Alice in Wonderland* when everything gets all chaotic and confusing. Speaker_2: Oh, that's a strange comparison, but I get what you mean. A bit overwhelming, I suppose. Poor people. It’s just awful to think about, isn’t it? Were you alright after seeing it? Speaker_1: Yeah, I think so. It just… stayed with me a bit. It made me look at my little scar again. You know, the one on my knee from when I fell off my bike? Speaker_2: Oh, yes! The one you got trying to be a stunt cyclist, as I recall. It’s barely noticeable now, though. Speaker_1: I know, but it just made me think about how easily things can go wrong. And that car crash… it just felt really close. Speaker_2: Accidents happen, unfortunately. It’s good you weren't involved. Speaking of things happening, did you finish that music project for school? The one with the costumes? Speaker_1: Almost! We’re doing a song from *Wicked*, and we have to design and make costumes. Maya is doing really well with hers, it's amazing, but mine is…okay. It's just hard to find good fabric. I’ve been looking online, but everything is so expensive. Speaker_2: Oh, online is good for ideas, but you're right, pricey. Have you tried that fabric shop down by the station? Old Man Hemlock’s? He has all sorts of remnants. You might find something perfect for a bargain. Speaker_1: Oh, good idea! I forgot about him. I'll go tomorrow. What about you? How was work? Anything exciting happen? Speaker_2: Not exciting, exactly. Just the usual. Mrs. Higgins complained that I hadn't booked her a theatre ticket for *Matilda* – apparently, I promised her I would months ago. I have no recollection! Honestly. Speaker_1: Oh, typical Mrs. Higgins! She always complains about something. She’s a bit of a drama queen. Speaker_2: You’re not wrong. And then I got ten spam calls today! All about PPI claims. It's ridiculous. I swear they’re just making it up as they go along. Speaker_1: Ugh, seriously? They're annoying. I got one the other day offering me a free holiday. A *free* holiday. Yeah, right. Everything's a scam these days. I'm going to get back to my reading now, I'm nearly at the best bit. Speaker_2: Oh, what are you reading? Another fantasy novel? Speaker_1: Yep. It’s really good. It’s got magic and adventure and everything. Oh, and Mum, thanks for promising me that concert ticket for Christmas. You're the best! Speaker_2: You’re very welcome, darling. Anything for my bookworm. Now, don't let the seagulls steal your crisps when you're reading outside, alright? They're getting bolder by the day! Certainly, let me know if you'd like me to continue the conversation or explore any specific aspects in more detail.

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork they had to wade through was astonishing. They were quite panicked last night, bless them. All these solar panel applications popping up all over the place, just… blanket coverage. Speaker_2: Exactly. It's the same playbook, isn't it? They try and overwhelm, hoping people just give up. It’s what happened, in a way, with the turbines here. Initially, there was a real swell of opposition, but it just… dissipated. People got exhausted. Speaker_3: Exhausted and confused, more like. The council’s development control committee… it’s a farce. They’re not interested in preserving the landscape, or the character of the villages. They’re just ticking boxes, aren't they? Driven by targets, by the developers’ promises. Speaker_1: And the appeals! That's what really demoralises people. They fight tooth and nail, get a refusal, then the energy company just appeals and suddenly the whole thing is back on the table. It’s like fighting a hydra. Speaker_2: You have to be meticulously prepared for an appeal, though. That's what I tried to tell them last night. Photos, detailed objections, citing specific planning policies… not just “it’s ugly” which, let’s face it, it often *is*! It needs to be about demonstrable harm to the environment, to local amenities, visual impact assessments… the works. Speaker_3: It's all about the research. And that’s where these groups are usually hampered. They’re well-intentioned locals, not planning lawyers. They haven't got the time, or the resources, to really dig into it. I mean, the amount of government money that goes into *subsidising* these things rather than *researching* genuinely sustainable alternatives... it’s obscene. Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s all about quick wins. Throw some money at wind and solar, and you can say you're hitting your carbon targets. But what about energy storage? That's the real problem, isn't it? We can generate all the renewable energy in the world, but if we can’t store it efficiently, it’s useless when the wind doesn’t blow or the sun doesn’t shine. Speaker_2: And the technology isn't there yet, is it? Not on a large scale, anyway. There's a lot of talk about hydrogen, but... it's still so expensive. And the infrastructure required! Speaker_3: It’s the politics of it all, isn’t it? The planners are influenced, the energy companies have deep pockets, and the protest groups are left scrambling for scraps. It’s a rigged game. We need some genuine innovation, something that will disrupt the current model, but that needs serious investment in research, not just subsidies for existing, imperfect technologies. Speaker_1: Speaking of politics… have you both seen the latest polls for the Scottish referendum? It’s looking awfully close, isn't it? In two weeks... Speaker_2: Worryingly so. I still think it’ll be a ‘no’, but the gap is narrowing. It's all hinging on the undecideds, I suppose. Speaker_3: It’s a mess, a complete mess. Breaking up a United Kingdom… the economic consequences alone… And all the uncertainty it creates. It's… frankly, short-sighted. Though, I suppose, a bit of disruption is sometimes needed. Still, I can’t help but feel it’s a very risky gamble. Speaker_1: It certainly is. Though, in a way, fighting these turbine applications feels like a gamble too, doesn't it? You pour your heart and soul into something, and you’ve no guarantee of success. Speaker_2: True. But it's a gamble worth taking. If we don’t fight for what we believe in, what else is there?

Speaker_1: So, have you booked those driving lessons yet, love? Your mother’s been on at me about it. Saying you’re getting too old to be relying on buses. Speaker_2: Dad! I’m thirty-two, not eighty-two. And yes, I’ve booked them. Started next week, Tuesdays at 10. Hopefully, I won’t stall on the roundabout near Tesco. That place is terrifying. Speaker_3: Oh, it is a nightmare. Especially on a Saturday. Remember when your cousin, David, nearly reversed into a fruit and veg stall there? Thought your Auntie Maureen was going to have a heart attack. Speaker_1: Good heavens, yes. A right kerfuffle that was. And expensive, I seem to recall. Speaking of expensive, have you looked at car insurance quotes yet? Don't want you ending up paying more for the insurance than the car itself. Speaker_2: I have, and it's… grim. Apparently, being a London resident even though I’m visiting is pushing the price up. And the car I’m looking at, a little Fiat 500, is in insurance group… twenty-something. Speaker_3: Oh dear. A Fiat 500 is nice though. Easy to park. Your grandfather had one of those, bright red. He called her ‘Rosie’. He used to drive her everywhere. Speaker_1: He did. Even tried to take her across country lanes barely wide enough for a bicycle. Your mother nearly went spare. Anyway, back to the insurance. Have you tried comparing websites? MoneySuperMarket and the like? Speaker_2: Yep, done the comparison thing. It's still a lot. I might have to add my mum as a named driver, which feels a bit… embarrassing. Speaker_3: Nonsense, dear. It’ll bring the price down. It’s common practice. Better than driving around uninsured. We’re going to need a car for the holiday, aren’t we? Speaker_1: That's right. We’re still on for Cornwall in August, then? I've been looking at cottages online. Found one in Padstow, looks lovely. Sea view and a garden. Speaker_2: Sounds perfect! I’m really looking forward to it. Need a break from marking essays. Honestly, the things some of them write… It’s like they haven’t even *read* the texts. Speaker_3: Oh, teaching. Always a challenge. I had a right character in court yesterday. Claimed he was allergic to the legal system. Said it gave him hives. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Allergic to the legal system! You don’t hear that every day. So, what are your plans for this week then? Apart from the driving lessons, of course. Speaker_2: I’m meeting Sarah on Wednesday for coffee. And then I promised my flatmate I’d help with her flat viewing on Thursday. She's trying to find someone less… chaotic to live with. Speaker_3: Good for her. Some people are just a whirlwind of mess. And you? Anything planned, dear? Besides keeping us all in order, naturally. Speaker_1: I’m volunteering at the museum on Friday. They're cataloguing some old maps. Quite fascinating, actually. And then, hopefully, a quiet weekend. Unless your mother decides we’re having another family gathering. She’s always got something up her sleeve. Speaker_2: Oh, don't even get me started on Grandma's "gatherings." They’re usually more like interrogations disguised as afternoon tea. Speaker_3: (Smiling) She just wants to know everyone’s happy, love. It's her way of showing she cares. Now, who wants another biscuit?

Speaker_1: Honestly Dad, parking in Brighton is a nightmare. I spent twenty minutes circling yesterday just to drop off groceries. Speaker_2: Twenty minutes? In my day, you just found a space, parked, and got on with it. Never had this bother. Though, mind you, there weren’t half as many cars on the road then. Everything's different now. Speaker_1: It’s just relentless. Everyone has a car, and they’re all trying to squeeze into the same tiny spaces. Makes me almost want to get rid of mine. Speaker_2: Don’t you dare! You’ll need it to come visit your old man, won’t you? Though, I don’t see you as often as I’d like, now you’ve moved. Brighton’s a long way. Speaker_1: I know, I know. I will come more, I promise. It's just… life gets busy. And then there's this Facebook app, it's driving me mad. It keeps sending me notifications about everything. Speaker_2: Facebook? What’s that got to do with anything? You young people and your…digital contraptions. Speaker_1: Everything! It’s how everyone keeps in touch. But it’s constantly beeping and buzzing. I turned off half the notifications, but it still sends me loads. It's so distracting when I’m trying to work. Speaker_2: Switch the darn thing off then. Simple. We managed without all this technology, didn’t we? Though, I did quite enjoy the wireless back in the fifties. That was a marvel. Speaker_1: Easier said than done, Dad. It's how I get updates from uni, and keep in touch with friends. Anyway, I made a shepherd’s pie for dinner. Hope you like it. Speaker_2: Shepherd’s pie? Lovely. You always were a good cook, just like your mother. She could feed an army. Remember those Sunday dinners? Everyone crammed around the table. Speaker_1: Of course. Although, feeding kids these days is so expensive. Everything’s gone up. I heard they’re using food banks more and more. Speaker_2: It’s a disgrace, it is. Politicians promising the world and… it’s all just talk. Back in my day, a man could provide for his family on a decent wage. These days… people struggling just to get by. Speaker_1: It’s tough. Speaking of tough, how are your knees? Still giving you trouble? Speaker_2: Oh, they’re a right state. Arthritis, you know. Makes it hard to get around. And the weather’s not helping. Cold and damp. Makes the bones ache. Speaker_1: You should really try that turmeric stuff Auntie Maureen recommended. She swears by it. Says it helps with inflammation. Speaker_2: Turmeric? Sounds like something you put in a curry. Speaker_1: Well, you can, but you can also get it in capsules. It’s supposed to be really good for you. Healthy eating, that’s what it’s all about. Although I did have a biscuit with my tea earlier, don’t tell anyone. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) A biscuit won’t hurt. Although your mother always said too many sweets rotted your teeth. She was a firm believer in fresh produce. Grew all her own vegetables. Speaker_1: I remember. She was amazing. It’s a shame I don’t have her green fingers. I kill every plant I touch. Speaker_2: It’s alright, love. Not everyone can be a gardener. Just enjoy your life. And come and visit your old man more often, eh? And maybe bring another shepherd’s pie.

Speaker_2: …and then Old Man Hemmings, right, he’s the head groundskeeper, walks past and just *deadpans* “Looking a bit breezy out there, are we?” Like, mate, I'm actively battling gale-force winds to hit a tiny white ball into a slightly smaller hole. It's not a casual observation, it's a personal attack. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Hemmings sounds… delightful. Honestly, golf just seems engineered to breed passive-aggression. The whole quiet contemplation thing is a lie. It’s just frustration management with expensive clubs. Speaker_2: Exactly! And everyone pretends to be so zen about it. “Oh yes, well a slightly duffed shot is just a learning opportunity.” No, it’s a wasted five pounds and a dent to my fragile ego. Speaking of fragile egos, did you read Professor Davies' essay on *Hamlet*? Speaker_1: Oh god, the one where he tries to argue that Hamlet is actually a deeply sarcastic comedian? Speaker_2: The very one. He just kept going on about “subtextual wit” and “ironic detachment.” I'm pretty sure Hamlet's just profoundly depressed and wants everyone to die. Davies is convinced he’s the Richard Pryor of Elsinore. Speaker_1: It’s his surname, isn’t it? Davies. He *has* to find irony everywhere. My uncle’s a Davies, and the man can’t accept a genuine compliment without questioning the motivation. “Oh, you like my tie? Is this some sort of subtle dig at my financial situation?” Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Classic Davies. My grandma's a Pritchard, and they're all fiercely competitive. Even over… well, everything. Apparently, family Christmas is basically the Hunger Games with board games. Speaker_1: Sounds intense. What about nicknames? Did your family have those? We were all just called what we were called, no fun shortened versions. Speaker_2: Loads. My cousin Rhys was always “Rhino” because he was built like a tank, even as a kid. I was… annoyingly, “Little Skip” for about five years. Don't ask. Something about me skipping everywhere when I was tiny. It haunted me through secondary school. Speaker_1: “Little Skip”? Oh, brutal. I can see why you’d develop a sarcastic defence mechanism. I worked at that garden centre over the summer, remember? Speaker_2: The one near the A38? God, yes. Full of pensioners and aggressively cheerful floral displays. Speaker_1: It was soul-crushing. Mrs. Higgins, the manager, was convinced we were all secretly plotting against her. She kept asking us to write down exactly what we were doing, every fifteen minutes. “Watering the petunias. Re-stocking the compost. Suspecting Mrs. Higgins of paranoia.” Speaker_2: (Laughing) Seriously? Speaker_1: Swear to god. And she’d constantly try to “motivate” us with platitudes. “Remember, team, we're not just selling plants, we’re selling *dreams*!” I nearly lost it when she said that. I was just trying to avoid getting yelled at for mislabeling the geraniums. Speaker_2: That's... a special kind of hell. The golf feels significantly less stressful now. I might actually take up bird watching. Anything to avoid “selling dreams”. Speaker_1: Good plan. Though knowing your luck, you'd end up in a birdwatching competition with a rival birder who's secretly a former Special Forces operative. Speaker_2: (Sighs) You're probably right. I just can’t win.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this week has been *mental* at work. Like, back-to-back meetings, everything last minute. Someone pulled out of presenting at the conference, so I had to find a replacement at, like, ten o’clock on Tuesday morning. Nightmare. Speaker_2: Sounds rough, yeah. I’m just… physical work, you know? Gets tiring, but it’s not mentally draining like that. Though today, unloading that van in the rain… my back is screaming. Speaker_3: Oh, you poor thing! You need a hot bath and a serious lie-down. I had a surprisingly calm week, actually. Managed to get through all my reports without being interrupted once. Felt like a minor miracle. Although, Brenda in accounts keeps asking me about my “lifestyle choices.” Speaker_1: Oh god, Brenda. What does *that* even mean? Speaker_3: Apparently, coming in with a green smoothie every day is a “lifestyle choice.” And she made a comment about needing “proper food.” Honestly, the cheek! I just said I was trying to be healthy. Speaker_2: Proper food is a roast dinner, that's what it is. Not rabbit food. Though, I gotta admit, I've been trying to cut down on the takeaways. Bank balance is taking a beating. Speaker_1: Tell me about it! I’ve been trying this new diet, it's supposed to be amazing, but it's all kale and quinoa. I miss chips. So much. Speaker_3: Kale and quinoa? Seriously? That sounds… depressing. I’m more of a “everything in moderation” kind of gal. Although, I did start going to that yoga class with Chloe. Speaker_1: Oh, how’s that going? Is it all chanting and incense? Speaker_3: A bit, yeah. But actually, it’s pretty good. Really helps to unwind. Better than scrolling through TikTok for three hours, which is what I usually do. Speaking of Chloe, she’s still looking for a flatmate, isn’t she? Speaker_2: Yeah, I think so. She mentioned it last week. Said her last one was… interesting. Speaker_1: “Interesting” is code for chaotic, isn't it? Chloe attracts chaos. Remember when her boyfriend tried to build a hydroponic farm in her living room? Speaker_3: (laughing) Oh my god, how could I forget? It was a disaster! The whole flat smelled like wet lettuce. Speaker_2: Honestly, you guys have the best stories. My life is just… lifting things and getting wet. Although, I am thinking of finally getting that motorbike I’ve been saving for. Speaker_1: Right then, well come on through, you can see the garden properly now. Bit overgrown, mind you. Didn’t get a chance to tackle it properly this year, what with everything. Honestly! Speaker_2: Politically correct nonsense. It's the world gone mad, I tell you. Still, a bit of art is good for the soul. Always busy, aren't you? Reminds me, I need to put up that owl box. Promised young Timmy next door I'd do it for him. He’s fascinated by owls. Speaker_1: Good idea. Now, who wants a cup of tea?

Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking, for dinner, we could try that new Italian place, Bella Notte? Apparently, it’s where the old post office used to be, near the cathedral. Have you heard anything about it? Speaker_2: Bella Notte… vaguely. I think Liam mentioned it. Said it was a bit pricey, but good. Though Liam thinks anything over a tenner is ‘pricey’ these days. Still, at least Harpenden is… pretty. Sunderland’s got its charm, but it's a bit rough around the edges sometimes. You know, like driving through Hetton-le-Hole last night? The potholes… Speaker_2: (Laughs) Oh, God, yeah. It was like navigating an obstacle course. Seriously, the council needs to do something about those roads. You could lose a tyre down there. And the buses… don’t even get me started on the buses. Speaker_1: I know! Always late, always overcrowded. I swear, sometimes I think it's faster to walk. Speaking of walking, did you see the scaffolding around the cathedral? They're doing some work on the west front, I think. Speaker_2: Oh yeah, I noticed that. It looks… major. Wonder what they’re doing? Hopefully, not damaging the stonework. It's a beautiful building, even if it's not quite as grand as Durham. Speaker_1: Definitely not Durham, but it’s got a history, hasn’t it? And it looks amazing lit up at night. Anyway, back to dinner. Bella Notte or… do you fancy Indian? There’s that place on Stockton Road, ‘Spice Delight’. Speaker_2: Spice Delight… hmm. That’s a good shout. I’m leaning towards Indian, actually. My treat, by the way. I got that bonus at work, remember? Speaker_1: Oh, brilliant! You are a lifesaver. And a generous one. Okay, Spice Delight it is. Just try not to get us lost on the way, alright? You and your sat nav… it once took us to a farm in Peterlee. Speaker_2: (Protesting) Hey! That was one time! And the sat nav was being glitchy. It’s a very confusing junction, honestly. And besides, we saw some lovely cows. Speaker_1: Lovely cows… right. Just get us to the curry house, and we'll call it even. Speaker_2: Deal. Prepare for amazing food, then. And maybe slightly questionable driving. Speaker_1: (Laughing) I’ll prepare for both.

Speaker_1: …and honestly, it was insistent. Not a gentle little chirp, a full-blown announcement. I thought it was a robin at first, but it was too complex a song. Speaker_2: Oh, you and your birdsong! You're becoming quite the expert, aren't you? I just hear ‘bird’, honestly. Though, I did manage to identify a blackbird the other day. It was definitely a warbler, I reckon. A chiffchaff, maybe? I've downloaded an app now, you see. You can record it and it tells you what it is. It's utterly brilliant. Speaker_2: Goodness me. Technology. I still struggle with setting the timer on the cooker. Speaking of which, I need to get a new alarm clock. Mine’s developed a habit of going off at 3 am. Wakes the whole house, it does. Speaker_1: Oh, that's dreadful! Is it one of those digital ones with multiple alarms? Sometimes I accidentally set two, and then it's a cacophony. Speaker_2: No, it’s an old-fashioned one. With bells. I’ve changed the batteries, but it still does it. I think the mechanism's just… given up the ghost. It's a sign, isn't it? A sign I need to embrace silence. Although, that's difficult when you’ve got a cat demanding breakfast at five. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) I know the feeling. And speaking of demanding feeders… the birds are going through a fortune. I’ve filled the feeders twice this week already. The blue tits are particularly greedy. Speaker_2: They are, aren't they? Little bandits. I haven’t put much seed out recently, actually. I had a bit of a scare at the dentist last week. Speaker_1: Oh no! What happened? Speaker_2: Just a routine check-up, but he spotted a tiny erosion on one of my back teeth. Apparently, it's quite common with age… acidity. He had to do a bit of filling. Honestly, the thought of it! And I kept imagining the drill… It sent me into a bit of a state. Had a nosebleed afterwards, believe it or not. Speaker_1: Oh, you poor thing! That sounds awful. Nosebleeds are always so alarming. Speaker_2: They are. Thankfully it stopped quickly. Makes you think about looking after yourself, doesn’t it? I really should get back into the garden. It's such a mess. The weeds are taking over. Speaker_1: It’s been too wet, hasn't it? Everything’s growing like mad. I’m trying to get my roses pruned before they burst into life. It's a thankless task, though. Speaker_2: It is. My neighbour, old Mrs. Higgins, she used to have the most magnificent garden. Won prizes for it, she did. But now… well, she's not up to it anymore. Such a shame. It’s heartbreaking to see people decline like that. Speaker_1: It is. I was reading about…well, you know David’s brother, Michael… Speaker_2: Oh yes, vaguely. What about him? Speaker_1: He’s been diagnosed with throat cancer, apparently. They caught it early, which is good, but… it’s such a vicious disease. David’s terribly worried. Speaker_2: Oh, dear. How dreadful. Send David my best. It's awful when something like that happens. Makes you realise how fragile life is. We really must get together with them soon. Perhaps next week? I could make a lemon drizzle cake. Michael always loved my lemon drizzle.

Speaker_1: Honestly, it’s just… exhausting. The relentless scrolling. Everyone presenting this perfect version of their lives. It’s draining. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I deactivated my Facebook account last year. Best thing I ever did. Although, admittedly, it makes keeping up with some people… tricky. Like Auntie Mabel, she only communicates via Facebook now. Speaker_1: Oh, bless her. Mine’s my cousin, Brenda. She sends me links to conspiracy theories about 5G. Honestly, I used to just ignore them, but then she started tagging me in them publicly. So embarrassing. Speaker_2: Oh dear. It's like they forget you have a real life outside of that little blue screen. How is little Leo? Is he still a whirlwind? Speaker_1: A whirlwind is putting it mildly. He's seven now, and… well, he’s all energy. I swear he doesn’t *walk* anywhere. It's either a sprint or a jump. It's wonderful, truly. But it's also… a lot, doing it all on my own. Speaker_2: You’re brilliant, you know that. Honestly. Raising a child single-handedly, while also being a dedicated teacher… you’re a superwoman. Speaker_1: Flattery will get you everywhere! Though, sometimes I do wonder if I made the right decision, you know? Going through IVF... it was so emotionally and physically draining. Then, when it didn’t work, and I realized I wanted to be a mum *so* badly… it just felt like everything fell apart. Speaker_2: I remember. You were so strong throughout it all, though. I always admired that. Remember how we used to talk about having huge families? It's funny to think back on those naive dreams. Speaker_1: (Laughs) Oh god, yes. Fifteen kids and a pony, if I remember correctly. Life had other plans, I suppose. Speaking of plans, how's the social work going? Still battling the system? Speaker_2: Always battling the system. It's… rewarding, but utterly soul-destroying at times. The bureaucracy, the caseloads, the endless paperwork… I’m seriously considering a career change. Speaker_1: Oh really? What are you thinking of doing? You always had a creative streak. Speaker_2: I've been toying with the idea of becoming a yoga instructor. It's been such a lifeline for me, honestly. After a particularly horrible day with a case, just going to a class and stretching and breathing… it’s the only thing that keeps me sane. Plus, I’ve been documenting some of my thoughts and experiences, and a few friends have suggested I write a book. Speaker_1: That's amazing! You absolutely should! You have such a gift for storytelling, and your insights into the human condition are incredible. A book about your experiences as a social worker… it would be so powerful. Speaker_2: It's a daunting thought, though. Putting it all down on paper… it feels very exposing. Speaker_1: I can imagine. But think of the impact it could have. And honestly, you’ve already overcome so much. Writing a book is nothing compared to navigating the social care system! Speaker_2: (Laughs) You have a point. Maybe I will. I've got a quiet weekend planned next month. Perhaps I can just…start. What about you? Any secret ambitions brewing? Still dreaming of escaping to a cottage in Cornwall? Speaker_1: Always dreaming of Cornwall! But, actually, I’ve started sketching out ideas for a children’s book. It’s nothing serious yet, just a bit of fun really. Leo’s given me some… interesting suggestions. Apparently, it needs a unicorn who’s also a detective. Speaker_2: A unicorn detective? That is brilliant! See? You're a creative genius! You should definitely pursue it. We could swap manuscripts over coffee. A writers’ group of two! Speaker_1: I love that idea! And honestly, it’s just so good to catch

Speaker_1: Honestly, the traffic was dreadful getting over here. I thought I’d be stuck forever on the A38. Speaker_2: Oh, tell me about it. It's getting worse, isn't it? They say they're going to do something about the flyover near Spaghetti Junction, but I’ll believe it when I see it. Used to be able to nip across town in fifteen minutes, now it’s forty if you’re lucky. Speaker_1: It’s ridiculous. Though I suppose it’s a small price to pay for actually *living* in Birmingham. I still miss Hertfordshire sometimes, but there’s a…buzz here, isn’t there? Speaker_2: There is, aye. And people are friendlier. Hertfordshire, didn’t sound very friendly to me. All those commuter belts and fancy houses… Speaker_1: (Laughing) You’ve got me there. It’s definitely a different pace of life. So, how are you keeping, then? Still managing to get out in the garden? Speaker_2: Trying to. My knees are playing up a bit, though. Doctor says it’s just wear and tear. Apparently, decades of marking essays doesn’t do wonders for the joints. Speaker_1: Oh dear. You must have marked thousands over the years. My partner’s a teacher too, secondary school, and he’s the same. Always complaining about his back. Speaker_2: It's a demanding job, teaching. Glad I’m finished with it, to be honest. Though I do miss the kids sometimes. Especially the ones who actually *wanted* to learn. You teach languages, don’t you? Speaker_1: I do. French and Spanish, mostly. It’s lovely when you get a class that's really engaged. But you get a few who just… don’t see the point. Speaker_2: Ah, the “When am I ever going to use this?” brigade. Heard that one more times than I care to remember. My subject was history, and you’d get the same. “Why do we need to know about the Tudors?” Speaker_1: Exactly! You try explaining the importance of cultural understanding and they just glaze over. Actually, speaking of history…did you hear about that attempted robbery at the jewellery shop on the High Street? Speaker_2: No! What happened? Speaker_1: Apparently, they tried to smash the window with a hammer, but the alarm went off and they ran off empty-handed. Honestly, it's getting a bit scary around here. Speaker_2: It is. Used to be a safe area, this. Seems like there’s more trouble these days. Though, knowing Birmingham, it'll be on the news for a day and then everyone will forget about it. Speaker_1: Probably. It’s just depressing. Anyway, on a brighter note, my sister just had a baby! A little girl. Speaker_2: Oh, congratulations! That’s lovely news. What have they named her? Speaker_1: Willow. Isn’t it a sweet name? I'm going to visit next weekend. A good excuse to get out of the city, really. Speaker_2: Very nice. You should. It’s good to have family around. My son lives down in London now, doesn't see him as often as I’d like. He’s a… well, he's involved in politics now. Speaker_1: Oh really? Which party? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Best not to ask. We have different views, let’s just say. It makes family dinners…interesting. Speaker_1: (Laughing) I can imagine! Well, I should probably be going. I have a mountain of marking to do myself, sadly. Speaker_2: Alright, dear. Good to have a chat. You come again soon, won't you? Speaker_1: Absolutely. I will. It’s lovely chatting with you.

Speaker_1: Right, so who’s bringing snacks for the film tonight? I’m happy to do a supermarket run if needed. Speaker_2: Ooh, good thinking. I was planning on just bringing some biscuits, but a full supermarket haul would be much appreciated. Maybe crisps, chocolate…? Speaker_3: I can contribute some dips and, like, veggie sticks. Trying to be vaguely healthy, you know? Though I fully expect to demolish a load of chocolate later. Speaker_4: I’m happy to grab some drinks. Soft drinks, maybe some beers? Anyone got preferences? Speaker_1: Beers would be good, yeah. As long as there’s some decent non-alcoholic options too, for the designated drivers amongst us. And definitely chocolate. You can’t have a film night without chocolate. Speaker_2: Agreed. What are we even watching again? I was scrolling through Netflix earlier and got utterly lost in the options. Speaker_3: We settled on that new sci-fi thriller, “Echo Protocol,” didn’t we? The one Leo was raving about? Speaker_4: Ah, yeah, Leo said it’s brilliant. Apparently, the soundtrack is insane too. He’s a bit of a film buff. Speaker_1: Leo always has strong opinions on everything. Remember when he tried to convince us that Abba were objectively the greatest band of all time? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh god, yes! He was *so* insistent. I still think the Bee Gees are superior, sorry Leo. Speaker_3: He’s a good lad though. Always up for a debate. Speaking of music, anyone been listening to anything good lately? I’ve been stuck in a 90s Britpop phase. Speaker_4: Oh, nice! I'm revisiting some early Radiohead myself. “The Bends” still holds up incredibly well. Speaker_1: I've been listening to a lot of jungle and drum and bass recently. Bit of a throwback, but it’s perfect for getting stuff done. Although, my neighbours might disagree. Speaker_2: (Smiling) I can imagine! I've been exploring some Icelandic electronica - Sigur Rós, Björk. Very atmospheric stuff, good for winding down after work. Speaker_3: Ooh, I’ll have to check that out. I’m always looking for new music. Right, so supermarket run, drinks, dips, biscuits... are we sorted? Should we coordinate who's getting what specifically? Speaker_4: I’m happy to do the beer and soft drinks run. Let’s say I’ll grab those. Speaker_1: I'll do the main grocery shop then – crisps, chocolate, maybe some popcorn. And I can pick up some extra biscuits if needed. Speaker_2: Perfect! It’s going to be a good night. I'm already looking forward to escaping reality for a few hours. Speaker_3: Just promise me no one will try to explain the plot of “Inception” to me again. I still don’t understand it. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Don't worry, I'll shield you from Leo if he starts down that road. Speaker_1: Deal. Film night rules are in effect. Maximum enjoyment, minimum plot analysis. Speaker_2: Sounds good to me! Let's get this show on the road. Speaker_3: Let’s do it. Speaker_4: Excellent. Speaker_1: All right – supermarket, here I come! Be back shortly. Speaker_2: Text us if you need space in the car or anything. Speaker_1: Will do. See you all soon!

Speaker_1: Honestly, the gym was rammed this morning. Like, shoulder-to-shoulder rammed. Couldn't get near the squat rack. Speaker_2: Oh, no way! That’s awful. We went last year, remember? Had a decent time, despite the rain for the first three days. Speaker_3: Cornwall’s nice. A bit… predictable though, isn’t it? I’m tempted by Italy this year. Somewhere in Tuscany, maybe. Just imagine the food. Speaker_4: Tuscany sounds amazing. Proper sunshine too, hopefully. This weather we’ve been having is just… depressing. Grey, grey, grey. It’s like living in a black and white film. Speaker_1: It is grim, isn’t it? I saw a forecast saying we might get a heatwave in August, though. Fingers crossed. I'm thinking of backpacking around Southeast Asia, if I can swing it. Speaker_2: Oh, wow! That sounds incredible. Expensive though, surely? Speaker_1: Yeah, it’ll be a stretch. But I've been saving, and I'm hoping to find some cheap flights. And hostels, obviously. Not looking for luxury. Speaker_3: Smart. Hostels are the way to go. You get to meet people. Speaking of meeting people, has anyone heard anything more about that kids' camp for Leo? Speaker_4: I emailed them yesterday, still waiting for a response. Apparently, they're really popular. Hoping he can get a place. It’d be a good break for everyone. A week of peace and quiet… Speaker_2: It would be! Though, I’ll probably spend the whole week worrying about whether he’s having a good time. Mum-life, eh? Speaker_1: Tell me about it. I’m still on the fence about getting a dog. It sounds amazing, but then I remember all the responsibility… Speaker_3: Dogs are great. Just be prepared for early morning walks in the rain. And chewed-up shoes. Speaker_4: And a lot of fur. Everywhere. I’m listening to this new band, "Static Bloom", they're brilliant. Kind of indie-electronic vibe, you guys would probably like them. I’ll send you a link. Speaker_2: Ooh, nice! I’m always looking for new music. I’ve been stuck in a Taylor Swift loop lately, which is a bit embarrassing. Speaker_1: No shame in the Taylor Swift game! She writes a good song. Right, who’s up for a coffee stop? My treat. Speaker_3: Yes, please! A caffeine injection is desperately needed. Speaker_4: Sounds good to me! Let’s find somewhere decent. Speaker_2: Perfect. I could really use a latte. And maybe a biscuit.

Speaker_1: Oh, that was a dodgy tackle, wasn’t it? Right in front of the ref. Speaker_2: Absolutely. Should have been a yellow, minimum. They’re letting them get away with murder today. Honestly, it's frustrating to watch. Speaker_1: They always do this when it’s a big game. Give the benefit of the doubt. It’s ridiculous. I’ve got money on this, you know. I’m half tempted just to stay in and binge-watch something. Speaker_1: Oh come on! You’ve been cooped up working on that thesis for weeks. You need fresh air. And a proper pub meal. Speaker_2: You’re right, you’re right. I need to embrace the outdoors, even if it's just for a few hours. What films have you been wanting to see? Anything good out at the moment? Speaker_1: There’s that new sci-fi one, “Echo Bloom”. Everyone’s saying it’s visually stunning. But I'm also up for a rewatch. We haven't seen “Spirited Away” in ages. Speaker_2: “Spirited Away” is always a good shout. Classic. Okay, coast on Sunday, “Spirited Away” sometime over the weekend. Deal. Speaker_1: Deal! Right, pay attention. Looks like they're building up an attack... Oh! And he scores! About time. Speaker_2: Finally! Okay, maybe your tenner isn't lost after all. Though I still think the ref is biased. Speaker_1: Honestly, you're obsessed with the referee. Just enjoy the goal! Come on! Liverpool! Speaker_2: Easy for you to say, you’re the one with skin in the game. I'm just a neutral observer subjected to questionable officiating. Speaker_1: You choose to be a neutral observer. You secretly support Arsenal, don't you? Speaker_2: Absolutely not! Don't be ridiculous. Speaker_1: I’ve seen the evidence. The subtle sighs when they lose. The overly enthusiastic cheers when they unexpectedly win. Speaker_2: That’s just… basic empathy for the human condition. Speaker_1: Uh-huh. Sure. Speaker_2: Anyway, back to Easter. We should probably get some chocolate eggs in. For… research purposes. His birthday’s coming up soon isn’t it? Speaker_1: Oh yeah, that’s right. He's turning six. What does a six-year-old even *want* these days? Speaker_2: I have no idea. Dinosaurs? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Flattery will get you everywhere, dear. How about next Tuesday evening? After work? Speaker_1: Perfect! Thanks, love. I’m trying to cut down, anyway. It’s ridiculously expensive, and I’m coughing like an old chimney. Speaker_2: Me too. I keep saying I’ll quit, but…well, you know. Stressful job. Speaker_3: Stressful jobs! Back in my day, you just got on with it. Rested when you could, and didn’t moan. Though I suppose things are different now. Still, honestly, all that smoke isn’t doing you any good. You’ll both end up like old Mr. Peabody down the street – couldn’t walk without a oxygen tank. Speaker_1: Right, point taken. More roast, less roll-ups. And eyebrows next Tuesday. Sorted! Speaker_2: Sounds like a plan. Now, anyone fancy another coffee? I'll put the kettle on. Speaker_3: Oh, yes please, dear. Speaker_1: Right, so I think we’re officially down to two feeds a day now with Leo. It feels…strange. Like, a proper milestone, isn’t it? Speaker_2: It *is* massive! He’s doing so well, though. Seriously, he's such a good little thing. And you’re doing brilliantly, honestly. It's a huge step, taking away those extra feeds. Speaker_1: It just feels like I’ve got more time suddenly. This week’s looking busy. Your dad’s coming on Wednesday, isn’t he? Speaker_2: Yep. He wants to take Leo for a walk in the park. He’s been talking about it for ages. Speaker_1: It has been. And then I promised Auntie Carol I’d go for lunch with her on Tuesday. She’s been on at me for weeks. Speaker_2: Oh, good for you. You deserve a bit of Auntie Carol time. She'll have all the local gossip, no doubt. Speaker_1: Guaranteed! I need to book that baby sign language class, too. I keep meaning to. Speaker_2: Oh, yes! Are you still thinking of the one at the community centre? Speaker_1: Yeah, that one. It’s on Thursday mornings, apparently. I checked their website. It’s a six-week course. Speaker_2: That sounds good. It’ll be really useful, won't it? Especially when he starts getting frustrated that he can’t communicate. Speaker_1: Exactly. And I think it’s good for their brain development too, apparently. Someone at the baby group was saying it helps them with speech later on. Speaker_2: Oh, that’s interesting. I might look into that for Freya when she's a bit older. Speaker_1: I’ll let you know what it’s like. It starts next week. Oh, and I was thinking... maybe we could try and get a coffee with Emma on Sunday? I haven’t seen her since… well, before Leo was born. Speaker_2: Oh, that's a brilliant idea! She’d love to see him. Let me text her now and see if she’s free. I’m sure she’s been missing us both. Speaker_1: Perfect. Oh, Leo's got a bit of dribble going on there… excuse me a second. (Sounds of wiping baby's face) Honestly, it’s constant, isn’t it? Speaker_2: (Lightly) Completely. But look at that little smile. Worth it, right? Speaker_1: (Smiling) Always. Always worth it.

Speaker_1: It’s funny isn't it, how even a tiny rise feels like a proper hill after London. Everything’s so… flat there. Speaker_2: Absolutely. You forget what proper undulation feels like. It’s just concrete and straight lines. This is proper countryside. Everything feels… softer. Speaker_1: It’s the light too, I think. It’s different here. More expansive. London light feels… contained. Bouncing off buildings. Speaker_2: Yeah, it’s definitely the light. And the smell. You can actually *smell* things. Not just exhaust fumes and coffee. Speaker_1: Honestly. I was reading an article about how city-dwellers are losing their sense of smell. Apparently, our brains filter out the constant barrage of smells as a survival mechanism. Speaker_2: That’s depressing. So we're slowly becoming olfactory-blind? Speaker_1: Pretty much. Which is why a field of wildflowers is so overwhelming when you actually experience it. Speaker_2: It is. It just hits you. Makes you feel…reset. Look, that village over there. Little Barningham, isn't it? Speaker_1: I think so. We drove through there last autumn, remember? When we were looking at that antique shop? Speaker_2: Oh, God, yes. The one with the terrifying collection of porcelain dolls. I still have nightmares. Speaker_1: They *were* unsettling. But the shop itself was lovely. And the tea room next door was brilliant. Speaker_2: That’s true. That Victoria sponge was… legendary. It’s amazing how these tiny villages manage to sustain a tea room, isn't it? Speaker_1: Community spirit, I suppose. And tourists. We’re part of the problem, really. Descending and consuming Victoria sponge. Speaker_2: We’re contributing to the local economy! That's what you tell yourself, anyway. Look at those sheep. Just dotted all over the field. Speaker_1: So peaceful. It’s funny, isn't it? How something so…ordinary can feel so restorative. Walking. Sheep. Villages. Speaker_2: It’s the absence of… urgency, I think. In London, everything is a rush. Here, you can just *be*. Speaker_1: Exactly. No one’s aggressively checking their phone every two seconds. No one’s trying to overtake you on a country lane. Speaker_2: Though judging by that Land Rover coming towards us, some people are still trying to drive like maniacs. Speaker_1: Oh dear. They're going a bit quickly aren’t they. Perhaps they're late for their Victoria sponge. Speaker_2: Exactly. The stakes are high. Speaker_1: We *must* come back here more often. Speaker_2: Definitely. We absolutely must. Speaker_1: Before we lose our sense of smell entirely. Speaker_2: And before the porcelain dolls come for us. Speaker_1: Absolutely. Before the porcelain dolls. Speaker_2: Right... where were we? Oh yes hills. Speaker_1: Yes hills. How glorious. Speaker_2: So glorious. Speaker_1: Beautiful. Speaker_2: Yes. Speaker_1: Let’s keep walking. Speaker_2: Good idea. Speaker_1: And have a lovely day. Speaker_2: We shall do. Speaker_1: We Shall. Speaker_2: Yes. Speaker_1: Alright. Speaker_2: Yes. Speaker_1: Okay. Speaker_2: Right.

Speaker_1: …and then the ending, honestly, it just felt so… rushed. Like they’d realised they were over budget or something and just slapped something together. Speaker_2: Yeah? Speaking of fun, how’s Liam settling into the new job? He was stressing about it loads last week. Speaker_2: Actually, he’s loving it. He sent me a really long message yesterday. Apparently, he’s already working on some huge project with loads of responsibility. He’s proper thriving, which is brilliant. He was convinced they'd given him a load of grunt work to start with. No lights, no indication, just swerved right in front of us. Speaker_2: It's insane, isn't it? Like they think the roads are their personal race track. Honestly, I wouldn’t cycle in this city. Too many drivers who don’t look. Speaker_1: They’re just…arrogant. And it’s not all of them, obviously, but the ones who think the rules don’t apply to them are the worst. Especially when they’re wearing those ridiculous Lycra outfits. Speaker_2: (chuckles) Okay, that's a bit harsh! Speaker_1: No, it’s true! It’s like they’re trying to compensate for something. And they always cycle in groups, blocking the entire road. Speaker_2: Alright, alright, I get your point. They can be…frustrating. It’s just, you’ve got to share the road, right? Everyone's just trying to get where they're going. Speaker_1: Easier said than done when they’re actively trying to kill you! Honestly, if I was in charge, I'd make cyclists take mandatory lessons, like driving. And helmets, absolutely *mandatory* helmets. Speaker_2: See, now you’re getting into controversial territory. Freedom of choice and all that. Speaker_1: Freedom of choice shouldn’t involve potentially knocking someone off their motorbike! Right, I need a coffee. This cyclist rant has stressed *me* out. Speaker_2: Fair enough. There's a Costa up ahead, we can stop there. And maybe we should stick to discussing films… less chance of starting a war. Speaker_1: Good idea. Although to be fair, the cyclist was more infuriating than that film. And that's saying something. Speaker_2: (laughs) You’re incorrigible. Speaker_1: It's a gift. Speaker_2: It certainly is. Speaker_1: That is the truth. Speaker_2: Okay, Costa it is!

Speaker_1: It’s just… peaceful, isn’t it? Really properly quiet. London feels like a different planet sometimes. Speaker_2: Completely. Though I did miss the hustle a little bit yesterday, actually. Needed a bit of that energy for marking. Felt… sluggish. Speaker_1: Sluggish is a good word. I think my brain genuinely shuts down when I’m surrounded by this much green. It’s lovely, but not conducive to thinking about post-structuralism, you know? Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Though, speaking of things not conducive to thinking… did you see that article about the new agricultural subsidies? Utter chaos. Apparently, they're pushing for more cash crops, but it’s going to completely decimate the wildflower meadows. Speaker_1: Oh, I skimmed something about that. Ridiculous, isn’t it? Short-term economic gain for long-term ecological disaster. Classic. It’s always the same story. They don’t factor in the inherent *value* of biodiversity. Speaker_2: Exactly! And it's not just about aesthetics, although these poppies *are* incredible. It’s about pollination, soil health, the whole system. It’s basic economics, really. Externalities and all that. Speaker_1: You’re always bringing it back to economics. Speaker_2: Well, someone has to. You’re off chasing Derrida and Foucault, I’m grounded in reality! Although… speaking of languages, I was trying to explain ‘externalities’ to Stefan yesterday, and it just didn’t translate. He’s brilliant, but some concepts are so culturally embedded. Speaker_1: Oh, Stefan’s still struggling with the nuances of English economic terminology? Poor man. It must be exhausting. He’s fluent enough for everyday conversation, though, isn’t he? Speaker_2: Absolutely. We were talking about football last night – apparently, the local team is doing really well. He's quickly learning the required vocabulary for that at least. “Offside” and “VAR” seem to be key phrases. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Of course! That’s the priority. You know, it's funny, I was thinking about how different our research areas are. I’m dismantling the structures of language, and you're trying to understand how people *use* them to manipulate markets. Speaker_2: It’s a symbiotic relationship, really. You break things down, I try and figure out why they’re broken, and then how to fix them, or at least profit from the wreckage. Speaker_1: A very cynical view. Speaker_2: Realistic! Come on, you know it’s true. Look at that field over there. Probably earmarked for rapeseed next year, knowing our luck. Pretty, for a brief period, but ultimately… just a commodity. Speaker_1: Don’t ruin the wildflowers for me, alright? Let me enjoy the peace for five minutes. Maybe we should just promise each other to never discuss agricultural policy on a countryside walk again? Speaker_2: Deal. Unless it’s exceptionally pressing. Now, tell me about Derrida. Have you managed to wrestle with *Différance* yet? Speaker_1: (Sighs) Don’t even get me started… Speaker_2: Thought so. Speaker_1: It's beautiful out here… Speaker_2: It is. Speaker_1: Absolutely beautiful. Speaker_2: Yes. Speaker_1: Let's just walk. Speaker_2: Sounds good. Speaker_1: Just walk. Speaker_2: Okay. Speaker_1: And admire the flowers. Speaker_2: Definitely.

Speaker_1: Right, so are we still on for Saturday then? You picking me up around… one-ish? Speaker_2: Yeah, one's good. Unless something massively explodes at work, I’ll be there. What are we thinking for the football, watching it at yours? Speaker_1: Aye, at mine. Mam’s out with her friends, so we'll have the place to ourselves. She’d kill us if we watched it at hers and started shouting. She’s very proud of her living room. Speaker_2: Understandable. Your mam’s living room *is* rather… curated. Last time I was there felt like I was in a magazine shoot. Speaking of which, is it still a nightmare parking around your place? Speaker_1: Oh, it’s a disaster. It's always a disaster. Especially on match days. You'll probably have to park about a mile away and we’ll walk. I keep meaning to ask the council about a residents' permit, but I always forget. Speaker_2: Sounds fun. Good cardio at least. My car’s been making a weird noise too, by the way. I think it might be the exhaust. Sounds like a dying walrus. Speaker_1: A dying walrus? You always have the best descriptions. Should you get it checked? Before it actually dies on the A1? Speaker_2: Probably. I’ve been putting it off. It’s just… inconvenient. I’d have to book it in and take time off work. Though it’s not like anyone notices if I’m not around, really. Everyone's so busy with their projects. Speaker_1: Don't be like that. You're brilliant at what you do. They’d notice if you weren’t there to sort out their messes. Speaker_2: You’re sweet. Anyway, after the football, fancy grabbing some food? Or are you wanting a quiet night? Speaker_1: Food sounds good! There's that new Italian place that opened up near the Metro station, apparently it’s amazing. We could go there? Speaker_2: Perfect. Or we could drive out and see the Angel of the North on the way back. It’s been ages since I’ve been. Speaker_1: Ooh, aye! That'd be good. It’s always a bit bleak but impressive at the same time, isn’t it? It reminds me of being a kid. Speaker_2: Yeah, it’s a pretty iconic landmark. Have you seen that they’re building loads more flats near there now? Changing the whole landscape. Speaker_1: I have! It’s a bit depressing, to be honest. They're just cramming everything in everywhere. It feels like there’s no green space left. Although, I did see some decent flats going up near the river. Fancy swapping flats one day, escaping this student madness? Speaker_2: Maybe. Depends if my dying walrus of a car survives long enough for us to save up for a deposit. Speaking of, did you see that Wimbledon’s started? Any interest in watching any of that? Speaker_1: Not really, no. I can appreciate the skill and everything, but it just feels a bit… posh. I'd rather watch the football, to be honest. Speaker_2: Fair enough. More space for me then. I'm hoping someone can finally beat Djokovic this year. He’s unstoppable. Speaker_1: Right well, I'm gonna start thinking up some savage insults for the opposing team. Prepare yourself for a very passionate football supporter on Saturday. Speaker_2: Bring it on! I'll prepare my own arsenal of witty retorts. This is going to be a good weekend.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I can’t believe what’s happening on that celebrity trial show. It's absolute chaos! Did you see what…oh, hello dear, good morning. Lovely to see you. Coffee’s brewing, help yourself to a biscuit. Speaker_2: Morning, thank you. Oh yes, I saw a bit of it. That footballer…the one who used to be on the telly a lot? He screamed when a spider went near him! Speaker_3: (From an armchair, slightly mumbled) Screamed? Men! All show, they are. Back in my day, men were made of sterner stuff. Didn’t bother ‘em a bit, spiders. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Well, times have changed, haven't they? Though I suspect a lot of it is for the cameras, to be fair. Anyway, it's all just a bit of fun, isn't it? Though I did feel a bit sorry for the politician. He looked utterly miserable. Speaker_2: I prefer watching the wildlife programmes. David Attenborough is brilliant. I saw a program about geese migrating the other day. It's incredible, isn't it, how they know where to go? So far! Speaker_1: It is astonishing. Hundreds of miles guided by…well, nobody really knows, do they? Some sort of internal compass, I think. We had a huge flock of Canada geese land in the field behind the house last autumn. Quite a sight, though they did make a mess! Speaker_3: Mess is right! They're greedy things, geese. Come waddling along, honking and pooping everywhere. Used to have them on the allotments, they'd decimate the brassicas. Speaker_2: I saw a buzzard circling over the park yesterday. Beautiful bird. So graceful. They’ve really increased in numbers around here, haven’t they? Speaker_1: They have. It’s wonderful to see. We get kestrels occasionally, hovering over the garden. They're hoping for a vole, I imagine. It’s amazing what you notice when you just…look. Speaker_3: Vole? We used to trap voles. Nasty little things they are. Ruined my sweet peas, they did. Used to set the traps overnight. Speaker_2: It's a shame about the hedgehogs though, isn't it? I haven't seen one in months. They used to come into the garden all the time. Speaker_1: That’s worrying. Apparently, their numbers are drastically down. Loss of habitat, garden tidiness…it impacts them all. I leave a little saucer of milk out for them every night, hoping one will come along. Speaker_3: (Snorts) Milk? They don't need milk. They need bugs! Good, juicy beetles and slugs. Milk will give ‘em the tummy ache. Speaker_2: Oh, I see. Maybe I should try leaving out some cat food instead. Speaker_1: That's a good idea. They’ll happily munch on that. Back to the TV show though…did you hear about the chef? He tried to build a raft out of bamboo and it fell apart immediately! Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, dear! That sounds about right. Honestly, what are they thinking? Speaker_3: (Muttering) Wasting time, that's what they’re thinking. Should be out doing something useful. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Well, it *is* entertaining, at least. Now, shall I top up your coffee, dear? And perhaps another biscuit? Speaker_2: Yes please, that would be lovely.

Speaker_1: Honestly, this quiche is amazing. Did you make it? Speaker_2: Thanks! No, I grabbed it from that little bakery on the high street, 'Flourish'. They do the best lunchtime deals. I was desperate though, completely forgot to bring anything with me. How are you finding things now you’re back from maternity leave? Speaker_1: It's…a readjustment, massively. I underestimated how much my brain had turned to mush. Trying to remember verb conjugations after months of ‘goo goo gaas’ is surprisingly difficult. And the staff have all changed so much. Feels like starting from scratch. Speaker_2: Oh, I can imagine. It’s brutal. It took me ages to get back into the swing of things after Ruby was born. Did you have a good interview for the head of department role, by the way? Speaker_1: It was…okay. It was a lot more focused on data analysis than I expected. I felt a bit out of my depth, to be honest. They kept asking about attainment gaps and target setting. I’m good at teaching, inspiring kids, you know? This felt like a completely different job. Speaker_2: Ugh, that sounds awful. So much pressure on data these days, isn’t it? It's all numbers and very little about actual teaching. They don’t want a teacher, they want a data manager. Speaker_1: Exactly! And the person interviewing was so…intense. Kept staring at me, not really listening. I rambled a bit about creating a more inclusive learning environment, and she just raised an eyebrow and asked about spreadsheets. Speaker_2: Oh, bless you. Sounds like they already had someone in mind, honestly. Don’t beat yourself up about it. It wasn't a good fit, clearly. Honestly, sometimes I think I’d rather teach monkeys than deal with school politics. Speaker_1: Tell me about it! Although, monkeys probably wouldn’t ask you to justify every single lesson objective with quantifiable data. How’s little Leo doing, anyway? Is he sleeping through the night yet? Speaker_2: Oh, bless him. Occasionally. He had a growth spurt last week, so it’s been back to hourly wake-ups. I’m running on approximately three hours of sleep a night. I’ve started hiding chocolate in the laundry basket. Don’t judge. Speaker_1: No judgement here! I was doing the same with biscuits when Elsie was that age. It was a dark time. Oh, speaking of hiding things, have you tried that new cafe on Station Street? The one with the amazing cakes? Speaker_2: No, I haven't! Is it good? I need somewhere new to escape to when Leo finally lets me have five minutes to myself. Speaker_1: It’s ridiculously good. They do these salted caramel brownies that are basically illegal. You need to go. It’s my new self-care strategy. Forget yoga, just brownies. Speaker_2: I'm sold. Brownies are definitely superior to downward dog. I’m going to have to check it out next week. Right, more quiche? I feel like I need some serious fuel to get through the afternoon. Speaker_1:Absolutely. Help yourself. It’s the least I can do, considering I’m complaining about my awful interview. Speaker_2: Nonsense. It's good to vent! And honestly, you're a brilliant teacher. They don’t know what they’re missing. Speaker_1: You're sweet. Thanks. Speaker_2: Always. Now, tell me more about this eyebrow-raising interviewer… Speaker_1: Okay, prepare yourself.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m starting to freak out a little bit about… everything. Like, properly. Speaker_2: Everything? Big everything, or little everything? 'Cause little everything I can help with, big everything… well, that requires wine and potentially a very long rant. Speaker_1: Big everything. Like, the future. My job. Whether I'm actually doing anything meaningful. The creeping realisation that I’m officially… an adult. Speaker_2: Oh, the adulting crisis. Classic. I think we all hit that around twenty-five. It’s like suddenly you’re supposed to have a five-year plan, and all you’ve got is a vague aspiration to own a cat and not live in a shoebox. Speaker_1: Exactly! Everyone at work is all ‘promotion track’ and ‘career progression’ and I’m just… thinking about if I should finally join a pottery class. It feels so… pointless. I feel like I should be building an empire or something, not scheduling deliveries of cardboard boxes. Speaker_2: Hey, someone’s gotta schedule the boxes! It’s a vital role. Seriously. And look, I get the empire building thing, but not everyone *needs* to be a CEO. Remember Aunt Carol? She was obsessed with making artisan dog biscuits. Found her niche, absolutely thriving. Speaker_1: True. She did smell perpetually of liver. Speaker_2: A small price to pay for entrepreneurial success. But seriously, what about you? What *do* you want, aside from not cardboard boxes? Speaker_1: I don’t know! I used to think I wanted to travel, but then I realised I hate airports. And I thought maybe a different job, but everything seems… hard. And I’m good at my job, actually. It's just... not *inspiring*. Speaker_2: Okay, okay. Deep breaths. You’re allowed to want a job that doesn’t set your soul on fire. It pays the bills, right? It gives you disposable income for pottery classes and cat food. Speaker_1: That’s… a depressingly practical way of looking at it. Speaker_2: Sometimes practical is good. What about side hustles? Have you thought about something creative? You were always brilliant at drawing. Speaker_1: I haven't drawn since uni. I’m probably terrible now. And I don’t have time. I spend all my week trying to stay afloat at work, then collapse into a heap on the sofa and binge-watch terrible reality TV. Speaker_2: Okay, new plan. We're limiting reality TV. One night a week, max. And we are signing up for that life drawing class down the art centre. No excuses. Speaker_1: Life drawing? Oh god. Naked people. I’m not sure I’m ready for that level of adulting. Speaker_2: It's just figures! And a good way to reconnect with creativity. Plus, imagine the stories. Come on, it’ll be fun. We can get wine afterwards. Speaker_1: Wine *afterwards* is persuasive... alright, alright you've twisted my arm. But if I accidentally draw someone with six fingers, you're taking the blame. Speaker_2: Deal. Now, let’s talk about what we’re doing this weekend. Are you free Saturday? I was thinking we could finally visit that botanical garden. And maybe… avoid conversations about the existential dread for a few hours? Speaker_1: Sounds perfect. Botanical gardens and temporary avoidance of the future. I’m in.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m fuming with Liam. He’s been proper distant all day. Speaker_2: Oh, not again? What’s he done this time? Is he still going on about that girl from his work? Speaker_1: No, not specifically, but it's just… like he’s barely spoken to me. Just grunts and nods, you know? And he’s been on his phone *constantly*. He didn’t even notice I’d got my hair cut! Speaker_3: Ooh, that *is* bad. A haircut is a big deal. Men are clueless sometimes. Did you ask him what’s up? Speaker_1: I tried! He just said he was tired. Tired?! We’ve been sat on a beach all day, doing nothing! How can you be tired from doing nothing? Speaker_2: Boys. Honestly. It's always something. Remember when Mark pretended he had a work emergency to avoid coming to my birthday? Speaker_1: Oh god, don’t even remind me! That was awful. You were so upset. Still makes me mad for you, actually. Speaker_3: Yeah, it was rubbish. Although, looking back, he was a bit of a… well, you know. Speaker_2: A complete waste of space, yeah. You dodged a bullet with that one, babe. Speaker_1: I think I’m starting to think I need to dodge a bullet with Liam, too. It’s just… I saw him liking some girl’s photo on Instagram earlier. Not a super obvious like, just a quick double tap, but still. Speaker_2: Right, well that’s a classic move. The sneaky little double tap. Speaker_3: Ugh, the worst! Speaker_1: Right so, you were saying about the match on Saturday? Didn’t sound like a classic, from what you told me. Speaker_2: Classic? Nah, honestly, it were a right slog. Blair, ironically enough, was a bit of a football fan, wasn’t he? Speaker_2: Blair… yeah, he was always tryin' to be seen at the matches. Bit of a poseur, if you ask me. Though, to be fair, it weren’t all bad under New Labour. Things were movin', were they not? Least, that’s what they told us. Now look at ‘em, all squabblin’ and fightin'. This current lot… honestly, I wouldn’t trust ‘em to run a bath, let alone a country. Speaker_1: It's a mess, innit? I mean, the whole idea of “stakeholder capitalism” Blair was pushin'… it sounded good on paper, but it just seemed to benefit the already wealthy. And now, we’ve got this… this obsession with austerity. Talkin' about cutting public services while the fat cats are gettin' richer. It's disgusting. Speaker_2: Disgusting is the word. They’re all in it together, the lot of ‘em. And don’t even get me started on the expenses. Remember that MP who claimed for a duck house? A duck house! What kind of a country are we livin' in? I’m workin' twelve hours a day, barely makin’ ends meet, and they’re claimin' for bleedin' duck houses! Speaker_1: It was a moat, actually. A duck house *in* a moat. Details matter, you know. (smiles wryly) But the principle remains, doesn't it? A complete disconnect from reality. And this obsession with targets… remember the whole target culture they introduced? Everything had to be measured, quantified. It drove everyone mad. Speaker_2: Aye, I remember. Workin’ towards these silly targets, when all anyone wanted was to do a decent job. And then you get all the paperwork, the bureaucracy… it just stifled everything. They never understood how things actually work on the ground, did they? They were all up in their ivory towers, makin’ decisions without a clue. That’s politics for ya. Speaker_1: Suppose so. Still, gotta keep talkin’ about it, gotta hold ‘em to account. Even if it feels like shoutin’ into the void sometimes. Fancy a coffee? I think I need a bit of caffeine, after all that political angst. Speaker_2: Aye, go on then. Coffee sounds good. And maybe after that, we can have a proper moan about VAR. Now *that’s* guaranteed to ruin anyone’s afternoon.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’ve spent the entire morning wading through BNC recordings. It’s… a lot. Like, so many people saying ‘like’ every other word. It’s draining my soul. Speaker_2: Oh god, the BNC. I remember those days. Proper linguistic archaeology, innit? Though, on the topic of people saying things, LinkedIn is a whole other level of…performance. Everyone's a thought leader now.
