Speaker_1: It was nice! We went to Broadway Market. It was rammed, obviously, but we got some amazing pastries. And then just wandered around. It still feels so weird having proper weekends again, after so long working remotely. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I feel like I’ve forgotten how to ‘do’ weekends. Want to hear a ridiculous story? My aunt Carol is trying to convince me to move to Wales. She’s already found me a little cottage. Speaker_1: Wales? Proper move-to-the-country vibes? Speaker_2: Full on. Apparently, the ‘pace of life’ is much better. And she keeps talking about the stunning scenery. It’s lovely, but…it's Wales. I’d be miles from everything. Speaker_1: It's a big shift! You’re a city girl. Although... have you ever thought about just… moving *abroad*? Like, properly? Speaker_2: Oh, all the time. Spain, mostly. I've got a few friends living in Barcelona. The weather! The food! But then I get paralysed thinking about visas and learning another language. And honestly, the thought of flying terrifies me. Speaker_1: Oh, I’m the same with flying. Properly terrified. I once had a panic attack on the runway and had to practically be dragged off the plane. Speaker_2: Oh my god! That sounds awful! I just… overthink everything that could go wrong. It’s so irrational. I saw some photos of the Maldives online and was thinking ‘oooh’, but then immediately thought ‘no way’ – too much flying. Speaker_1: The Maldives would be amazing! But yeah, the flying. Maybe a really long boat trip? Although that feels even more terrifying. Speaker_2: Haha! True. It's a lose-lose situation. Have you seen Sarah’s pictures from her trip to Italy? Her pug is living its best life. Speaker_1: Oh my god, yes! Little Winston with a gelato. It’s iconic. I’m officially obsessed. I need a pug. Speaker_2: Don’t you dare. You barely have room for yourself in that flat! Although...imagine a pug wearing a tiny beret. Speaker_1: Stop! You’re making it worse. Seriously, though, that pug is winning at life. It's got a better travel schedule than I do. Speaker_2: It probably has a better skincare routine too. You know, pugs are prone to wrinkles. Anyway, enough about pampered pups. What are you thinking of making for lunch? All this talk of food is making me hungry. Speaker_1: I was thinking a quick pasta salad? Something easy. I’m still recovering from deadline stress, honestly. Speaker_2: Perfect. I’ll raid the fridge and see what we’ve got. And maybe we can avoid LinkedIn for at least another hour.

Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking, maybe a little more chilli in this? It feels a bit… tame. Speaker_2: A little more, yeah. But not *too* much, remember what happened last time? You nearly set off the smoke alarm. Honestly, you’d think you were cooking for a dragon. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Dramatic license, Mum. It needed a kick! Speaking of kicks, still thinking about getting that sleeve done? Speaker_2: Oh, the watercolour one? Maybe. Still umming and aahing. It’s a commitment, isn’t it? Plus, I’m a literary editor, I should probably project a more… subdued image. Speaker_1: Subdued? You? You dress entirely in shades of purple! A bit of ink isn’t going to ruin your gravitas. Speaker_2: Touché. It’s just… what if it clashes with my book launches? Imagine me unveiling a groundbreaking novel with a half-finished phoenix on my arm. *Doorbell rings* Speaker_1: That’ll be Sarah. Saved by the bell, eh? Saves you having to commit to dragon-level spice or permanent art. *(Speaker 1 opens the door to reveal Speaker 3)* Speaker_3: Hello, you two! Something smells amazing. Is that Thai green curry? Speaker_1: It will be. Mum was worried I was going to set the kitchen on fire. Speaker_2: A slight exaggeration. Hello, darling. Come in, come in. Did you have a nightmare on the Central Line? It was absolute chaos earlier. Speaker_3: You have *no* idea. Packed like sardines. Anyway, forget the tube, tell me about Christmas! Have you started planning yet? It’s practically November. Speaker_2: Oh, don’t even mention it. I’m supposed to be hosting this year, which means battling supermarkets and attempting to create a festive masterpiece. Honestly, I’d rather edit a manuscript written entirely in emoji. Speaker_1: Sounds stressful. You could just order everything from Deliveroo. Problem solved. Speaker_3: You and your solutions. Though, honestly, that’s not a bad idea. How’s work, by the way? Still drowning in submissions? Speaker_2: Drowning is a strong word. Submerged, perhaps. We’ve got a new intern, though. Bright as a button, but utterly clueless about the classics. I asked her if she'd read any Woolf, and she thought I meant wolf as in, the animal. Speaker_1: (Snorts with laughter) No way! Speaker_3: Oh, that’s brilliant! You’re going to have your work cut out for you. So, you’re still with the renovations, then? How’s the kitchen looking? Speaker_2: It’s… ongoing. The builders promised it would be finished by October. October has come and gone. Now they’re talking about ‘unforeseen complications’ with the plumbing. I suspect ‘unforeseen complications’ translates to ‘we underestimated the job and are now charging you extra.’ Speaker_1: Classic builders. Maybe you should get a tattoo to express your frustration. A phoenix rising from a pile of rubble, perhaps? Speaker_2: Don't encourage him. Speaker_3: Honestly, it sounds exhausting. I'm just wishing for a quiet Christmas, good food, and no plumbing disasters. Can I help with chopping anything? Speaker_1: Actually, yeah. Could you do the peppers, please? The less I'm near sharp objects, the better, given my fiery curry ambitions. Speaker_2: And maybe, just maybe, we should ditch the fancy tablecloth this year. Just in case.

Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking, because you’re a proper food writer now, or editor, whatever… could you actually give me some decent recipes? I’m getting so bored of the same four things. Bolognese, chilli, pasta with pesto… and, honestly, sometimes just toast. Speaker_2: (Stirring a pot on the hob) Toast is underrated. But yes, I can definitely help. It’s surprisingly intense, but everyone's at different levels, so no one's judging. And the instructor, Sarah, is lovely and really encouraging. I went on Tuesday, and I’m still feeling it. We can suffer together. It’ll be brilliant. Right, this smells amazing now. I’ve added a bit of chilli flake to this… hoping it's not too much. Speaker_1: Chilli flake is *always* a good idea. Unless it’s in a soufflé, possibly. Although, maybe a spicy soufflé would have been a fitting end to that whole ordeal. Speaker_2: (Grinning) You're terrible! Okay, dinner’s almost ready. So, did you ever get around to booking that trip to Portugal? You were talking about going to Lisbon… Speaker_1: I did! Flights are booked for October. Just need to sort out accommodation. I’m hoping to spend a few days wandering around, eating pastel de nata, and trying to remember how to speak Portuguese. It’s been a long time since my university days. Speaker_2: Ooh, Lisbon is incredible. You'll love it. Definitely get lost in Alfama – that's the oldest district, really charming, but a proper maze. And the food… prepare to gain about a stone in pastel de nata alone. Speaker_1: That’s a risk I’m willing to take. honestly.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the things they come up with in those essays. It’s like they haven’t even *read* the material. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Though I still maintain some of it is just… lazy. Oh! Speaking of overwhelming, have you seen Sarah’s photos from her holiday? Speaker_2: Which Sarah? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Classic Sarah. She does love a good photo op. She’s always been a bit of a… performer. Speaker_1: A performer is one word for it. It’s all very curated. And the filters! Honestly, she looks about twenty years younger. Speaker_2: She always was very conscious of her image. Remember that phase she went through with the fake tan and everything? Speaker_1: Oh god, yes! It was a disaster. She looked… orange. And she used to complain that her toenails were always getting broken. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, I’d forgotten about the toenails! She’d spend ages moaning to anyone who would listen. Apparently, it was a tragic saga. Speaker_1: Apparently! It was a daily update. You know, it’s funny. We’ve known her for years, and she’s still… Sarah. Speaker_2: Some people just don’t change. Have you heard anything from Ben lately? I haven’t seen him since the conference. He said they haven’t even attempted to define key concepts. Honestly, it sounds almost as bad as your Confucius and the French Revolution student. Would you like me to continue the conversation, or perhaps focus on a specific aspect of it? Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s like they all get the same instruction manual on how to write a deliberately confusing essay. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Maybe they do. A secret student handbook. "How to максимально irritate your lecturer." Speaker_1: Ha! Precisely. Oh, look, there's that little dumpling place we like. Fancy grabbing a quick snack before heading home? Speaker_2: That sounds perfect. I could definitely eat a dumpling or ten right now. All this talk of demanding students has made me hungry. Speaker_1: Me too. And honestly, the thought of marking is enough to send anyone running for comfort food. Speaker_2: Agreed. Dumplings it is, then. Let's escape the academic world for a while, eh? Speaker_1: Absolutely. And maybe avoid looking at social media for the rest of the evening. For the sake of my sanity.

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the whole thing was just *exhausting*. Like, pretending to be enthusiastic about sourdough starters for three hours straight. You know Brenda? Brenda from the book club? He had a whole PowerPoint presentation. Speaker_1: (Scoffs) Oh, that’s spectacular. The lengths people will go to. It’s always the ones with the PowerPoint presentations, isn't it? Extra points for a stock photo of a very happy sheep. Speaker_2: Absolutely. And he kept referencing some conspiracy theory about the government controlling the wool market. Honestly, I just wanted my coffee. It reminded me of that documentary we watched about that bloke who thought pigeons were government drones. Speaker_1: Oh, the pigeon man! He was convinced they were watching him. Slightly terrifying, actually. Makes you think, doesn’t it? You realize how easily people can get lost down those rabbit holes. Speaker_2: It does. Though, I suspect most of them just enjoy having a good story to tell. It’s cheaper than therapy. Speaking of things that are expensive, have you seen what’s happened with ticket prices for the Taylor Swift concert? Speaker_1: Don't even *start* me. I tried. I genuinely tried. My niece is obsessed. I spent two hours refreshing the page and ended up with nothing. Scalpers are charging a fortune. It’s outrageous. Speaker_2: It is. Same with Beyoncé. It’s like you need a second mortgage to go to a concert these days. Remember when tickets were, like, thirty quid? Speaker_1: Vaguely. Those were the days. Though, I suppose everything is more expensive now. Even coffee. So, how’s Sarah enjoying married life? Has she managed to convert Mark into a domestic god yet? Speaker_2: Slowly but surely. He’s attempting to learn to load the dishwasher correctly, which is a major win. And she’s officially banned him from attempting pancakes. Apparently, they ended up stuck to the ceiling last Sunday. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, Mark! He's a menace. But a lovable menace. Sounds like they’re settling in nicely though. It’s good to hear. They really suit each other. Speaker_2: They do. They really do. So, are you avoiding all films at the moment, or have you stumbled onto anything good recently? Speaker_1: I watched “Past Lives” last week. It was… incredible. Properly moving. Wrecked me, honestly, but in a good way. Have you seen it? Speaker_2: No, I haven't. I'll add it to the list. The list is getting rather long though...

Speaker_1: Dad, are we nearly there yet? Seriously, my legs are killing me. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Nearly, love, nearly. Still a good few hours to go yet, though. Cornwall's a long way from Manchester, you know. Just look at the scenery, though. Beautiful, isn’t it? All these fields, and those wind turbines spinning away. Speaker_1: They’re kind of… hypnotic. Like giant, slow-motion windmills. Do you think people used to think windmills were magic? Speaker_2: Oh, I bet they did. Everything looked magical before we understood it, didn't it? Speaking of magical, remember that time we went to Jamaica Inn? That place felt proper spooky. All dark wood and stories of smugglers. Speaker_1: Yeah! And the sheep were all black there, weren't they? That was weird. It felt like a film set. Like something out of a Sherlock Holmes story. Speaker_2: Right you are. Proper atmospheric. You know, your great-grandad used to be a telegraph operator. He could send messages in Morse code, you know. Speaker_1: Morse code? What's that? Is that like, tapping? Speaker_2: Aye, tapping. Dots and dashes. Back in the day, before texts and phones, that’s how people sent urgent messages. Think about it, a whole language based on clicks and pauses! They even had telegraphs, wires stretched across the country. Your nan used to tell me about waiting for telegrams from her brother when he was in the army. It was a big deal. Speaker_1: Wow. That’s so… slow. It would take ages to tell someone you were going to be late for dinner. Speaker_2: It did! And before that, it was letters. And before *that*… well, stories passed down through generations, like fairy tales. Do you think fairy tales started as a way of explaining things before science? Speaker_1: Maybe. Like, why the sky is blue, or where babies come from. Although, some are just really weird. Like, why does the Wicked Witch of the West melt when Dorothy throws water on her? That makes no sense. Speaker_2: (Laughs) Good question! Sometimes they don't need to make sense, do they? It’s the *feeling* of the story that matters. Look at the colours of the road! All the different shades of green and brown... reminds me of something Lewis Carroll would write about. Speaker_1: Lewis Carroll? The Alice in Wonderland guy? Speaker_2: That's the one. He was brilliant at describing details. Speaking of colours, fancy a chocolate biscuit? I’ve got a whole packet in the glove compartment. Speaker_1: YES! Snapped! Oh, and Dad? Speaker_2: Aye? Speaker_1: When we get to the beach, can we build a massive sandcastle? And can we go rock pooling? Speaker_2: Absolutely. A massive sandcastle it is. And rock pooling. And ice cream. Lots and lots of ice cream. Just gotta keep an eye on the fuel gauge. Don't want to be stranded in the middle of nowhere. How’s your book coming on? Speaker_1: Pretty good! I’m on the part where… oh, never mind, it’ll spoil it. But I think you’d like it. It's got a bit of mystery and a bit of adventure. Speaker_2: Sounds good. Right, let's see… according to the sat nav, we're coming up to Exeter soon. That means we're getting closer. And then… the caravan awaits! And hopefully, a nice, sunny beach.

Speaker_1: Honestly though, the price of a cinema ticket now is just…criminal. Ten quid for a student? It’s daylight robbery. Speaker_2: Ten quid? In my day, it was sixpence. Sixpence! And that included a bag of sweets. Real sweets, not these sugary things they have now. Proper, hard boiled ones. Speaker_3: Sixpence, wow. You’re going way back, aren’t you Grandad? Though, I do agree, it’s getting ridiculous. I saw *Dune: Part Two* last week. Good film, but…expensive. Speaker_1: *Dune?* Oh, I’ve been meaning to see that. Is it worth the tenner? Speaker_3: Yeah, definitely. Visually stunning. But prepare for a long sit. Nearly three hours. Speaker_2: Three hours! I remember when a film lasted an hour and a half, and you were grateful for it. I went to the Odeon in Sunderland, always felt a bit sticky underfoot, if I’m honest. Speaker_3: Right? Cinema floors are a hazard. Speaking of hazards, did you see the price of petrol this morning? Nearly £1.50 a litre. It’s outrageous. Speaker_1: Don’t even *start* me on petrol. It's ruining me. I'm barely using the car now, cycling everywhere, even with all the hills around here. Speaker_2: Hills? You wouldn't get hills like the Pennines around here. Used to cycle to school, I did. Timperley to Altrincham. Uphill both ways, naturally. Speaker_3: (laughing) Naturally, Grandad. It’s always uphill both ways. Speaker_1: Ha! Classic. Though this *is* hilly. I’m trying to get back into running, actually. But my stamina is…shot. How’s your swimming going, Mark? Speaker_3: Slowly. I signed up for a charity event, trying to build up to a decent distance. Nothing like a Channel swim, obviously. Speaker_2: Channel swim! When I was in the war, we used to see the boats going across. Dangerous work. Very dangerous. I was in signals, you know. Very important. Couldn't tell you what I did, naturally. Top secret. Speaker_1: Top secret, eh? Sounds exciting. I used to be really good at geography in primary school. Knew all the capitals. Still remember most of them. Speaker_3: Impressive. I was rubbish at geography. Always confusing Spain with Portugal. Speaker_2: Portugal, Spain… don’t matter to me. I preferred building things. Used to be a right dab hand with a soldering iron, back in my BT days. Proper engineering, that was. Not like this computer stuff. Speaker_1: My job is all computer stuff, actually. Corpus linguistics. Basically, I analyse huge amounts of language data. It's fascinating, honestly. Though, sometimes I wish I’d done something more…practical. Speaker_3: Practical? You’re using your brain! That’s pretty practical. I mean, my job involves making bridges not fall down. High pressure, believe me. Speaker_2: Bridges, eh? My brother built bridges. Near Manchester. Lovely chap. Always cheating at cards though. Couldn’t trust him for a minute. Speaker_1: Ha! Everyone’s got a cheat in the family. My cousin claims she always wins at Monopoly, but I suspect she hides money under the board. Speaker_3: It's always the family, isn’t it? Oh, actually, I need to call my landlord. Rent is due and I’m pretty sure he’s going to try and sneak another increase through. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s annoying. Rent here is insane, even for such a small place. It's honestly just daylight robbery.

Speaker_1: Right, so I’ve made a start on the list for moving stuff out of your spare room. It’s… extensive. Very stylish. Anyway, have you managed to sleep properly since getting back from Japan? You looked utterly wiped yesterday. Speaker_1: Honestly, no. Jet lag is brutal. I keep waking up at like, 3 am just convinced I need to be teaching a class. My brain is completely scrambled. I tried that melatonin stuff, but it just made me feel…fuzzy. Speaker_2: Oh, that's not good. Your Auntie Carol swore by chamomile tea. Said it always settled her when she used to go on those cruise holidays. Speaker_2: Oh, it’s all consuming, darling. She’s got a spreadsheet for *everything*. From the colour of the napkins to the precise angle of the fairy lights. Mark’s just trying to stay out of the way, bless him. She keeps asking me if I think teal and rose gold clash. What do you think? Speaker_1: Teal and rose gold? Uh… I honestly don't have an opinion on wedding aesthetics, Mum. They both sound… sparkly. Speaker_2: (Sighs) Men. They just don't understand the importance of these things. It’s a reflection of their future happiness, apparently. Speaking of happiness… Have you given any more thought to…well, you know. Speaker_1: (Slightly uncomfortable) To…? Speaker_1: …and honestly, the guilt is awful. I keep thinking I should have pushed her harder to go to the doctor sooner. Even though she kept saying she was fine, just tired. Speaker_2: Oh, Sarah. Speaker_1: Honestly? Exhausted. And…terrified. It feels…precarious, you know? Like everything could fall apart at any moment. It’s stupid, I know. Speaker_2: It’s not stupid at all. Speaker_4: Speaking of focus, did you see that match on Saturday? Liverpool were awful. Absolutely awful. Speaker_3: (Sighs) Don’t even get me started. It was a disaster. We’ll need to check dates, because Nana and Grandpa want to come, and Auntie Sarah… Speaker_3: Mummy, remember when Mr. Tumble said “Big hug!”? It makes me giggle. Speaker_2: I like the stories on CBeebies! The ones with the little bear! What's his name…? Bluey! Speaker_1: Bluey! Yes, you love Bluey. That's a good one. They're quite good at teaching little life lessons, aren’t they? Speaker_3: Mummy, what are we doing for World Book Day? Can I be Harry Potter? Speaker_1: We need to have a think about that, Leo. It's not for ages yet, is it? We’ll have a rummage through your books and see what inspires us. And then there's Mother’s Day next month… I'm not expecting much, honestly. Just a nice breakfast in bed would be lovely. Speaker_2: I can make you a card, Mummy! With lots of sparkly bits! Speaker_1: Oh, Elsie, that would be the *best* present ever. A sparkly card, made by my very own little artist. You two are the best. Now, let’s go and look at Lego castles online, shall we? Just to get some inspiration…and perhaps prepare my bank account for a shock. Speaker_3: Yay! Lego! Speaker_2: And sparkles! Always sparkles! Speaker_1: (Chuckling) Always sparkles. It wouldn't be a party without them, would it? Speaker_3: No way! Speaker_2: Never! Speaker_1: Right then, mission commence. Speaker_3: Can we have snacks while we look? Speaker_1: (Sighing playfully) Alright, alright. But healthy snacks! No chocolate before dinner. Speaker_2: Fine! But can we have fruit with sprinkles? Speaker_1: We'll negotiate. Now, let's see what Lego has to offer…

Speaker_1: Honestly, this weather is doing my head in. One minute it’s sunshine, the next it’s biblical rain. Makes planning anything impossible. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! I was hoping to cycle to work today, but absolutely not a chance. Completely drenched just walking to the bus stop. It’s November in England, what do you expect? Speaker_3: You’re both moaning! It’s…atmospheric. Perfect for curling up with a book. Though I will admit, the grey does get a bit much. Speaking of which, how’s the house hunt going, Ben? Any closer to escaping the North? Speaker_1: Slow. So slow. Viewings are either booked solid or the places are…well, let's just say the photos were *very* flattering. Saw one yesterday that smelled strongly of damp and had wallpaper peeling off. Speaker_2: Oh, the joys of house hunting. Remember when we were looking for this place? The one with the questionable plumbing and the garden that was mostly just weeds? Speaker_3: Good times! We got lucky with this one, though. It’s cozy, and the location’s brilliant. Though, seriously Ben, are you sure you want to move *all* the way down to Hampshire? Seems a long way from everything. Speaker_1: It’s the job, isn’t it? It's a really good opportunity and they’re offering a relocation package which helps. Honestly, I'm more worried about finding a decent internet provider down there. Apparently, it’s a broadband desert in some areas. Crucial for my work, obviously. Speaker_2: You’d think in this day and age, broadband wouldn't be an issue! It’s ridiculous. I’m still battling with BT. They keep promising to fix the signal, but it’s been “scheduled for repair” for three weeks now. Speaker_3: Don’t even get me started on tech support. Trying to explain to someone on the phone that my laptop won’t connect to the printer is a soul-crushing experience. They just read from a script. Speaker_1: Speaking of soul-crushing experiences, I braved the world of online dating again last week. Speaker_2: Oh no… how did it go? Let me guess, a lot of questionable profiles? Speaker_1: You have no idea. One woman’s profile picture was a heavily filtered selfie with a tiger. A *tiger*. And another was obsessed with crystals and claimed to communicate with dolphins. Speaker_3: (laughing) Oh, Ben! You really do attract the…interesting ones. Have you thought about giving up and embracing the hermit life? Speaker_1: Tempting. Very tempting. I might just adopt ten cats and live in a cabin in the woods. At least *they* wouldn't lie about their hobbies. Have you two been up to anything more exciting? Sarah, seen any juicy stories for the paper lately? Speaker_2: Nothing *too* juicy, unfortunately. Mostly local council meetings and school fundraising events. Though, there was a rather heated debate about the new parking restrictions. Speaker_3: I'm trying to get my Year 9s to understand the subjunctive. It’s…a challenge. They just keep looking at me with blank faces. It's like I'm speaking Klingon. Speaker_1: Sounds about right. Teenagers and grammar don’t exactly mix. Right, I’m going to refill my water. Anyone want anything? Speaker_2: I'm good, thanks. Speaker_3: Just a bit more of that salad, if you wouldn’t mind. It’s lovely!

Speaker_1: Honestly, this book was… underwhelming. All that hype for… well, for beige. It felt beige. Like a really long, beige cardigan. Speaker_2: Beige is a good word for it, actually. I kept waiting for something to *happen*. And the characters… did anyone actually *like* any of them? I found them all terribly self-absorbed. Speaker_3: I think I felt a bit sorry for the main character, actually. But yeah, the pacing was terrible. It dragged. Though, it did remind me a little of those long summer holidays we used to have as kids. Just… endless days stretching out. Speaker_1: Oh, summer holidays. That takes me back. Do you remember those little plastic ponies? The Shetties? I was obsessed. I had a whole stable of them. And I’d give them all names and stories… Speaker_2: Ooh, the Shetties! Yes! I preferred the My Little Ponies, though. The bigger ones, with the long manes you could brush. I’d spend hours doing their hair. My Nan bought me a whole set. It was proper luxury. Speaker_3: I had both, actually. My brother was really into Action Force, and I used to try and sneak their figures into my pony world. They didn’t really fit, though. It was always a bit awkward. He wasn’t keen. Speaker_1: Ha! Kids. My nephew’s all about dinosaurs at the moment. Apparently, he corrects me on the pronunciation of all their names. Apparently, I'm saying "Triceratops" wrong. Speaker_2: Oh, the tiny experts. They’re the worst! Though, I suppose it’s good they’re learning. It’s funny, isn’t it, how different things are now? I was trying to teach my niece a bit of Lincolnshire dialect the other day. She just looked at me blankly. Speaker_1: Lincolnshire dialect? What did you try and teach her? Speaker_2: Just “tha knows” and “ay up.” Simple things. But she didn’t recognise them. Apparently, all the kids at school speak with this sort of… London accent now. Even in Peterborough! Speaker_3: It’s mad, isn’t it? Everyone’s blending together. I mean, even I’ve probably lost a bit of my Essex twang over the years. Especially working in finance, you have to be… neutral, I guess. Speaker_1: Absolutely. At work, I have to consciously tone down the Boston accent sometimes. People don't always get it. They think I'm speaking with a West Country accent, which is just… wrong. It's a very distinct accent, Boston. Speaker_3: I can imagine. It's a bit the same for me. Essex gets a bit of a bad rap, doesn't it? So you end up trying to sound… less Essex. It’s exhausting. And frankly, a bit ridiculous. Speaker_2: It really is. Talking of exhausting, how’s work been, then? Still battling the spreadsheets? Speaker_1: Don't even ask. A new system's been implemented and it's a total disaster. I've spent the last three days trying to reconcile figures that simply won't reconcile. I swear, I’m going to spontaneously combust. Speaker_3: Oh no! That sounds awful. I'm actually having a relatively calm week, which is a relief. Just year-end stuff, nothing too dramatic. Though, I did have to explain to someone why "accruals" aren’t just something you pick up at the chemist’s… Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, bless them. You’ve got your work cut out for you, haven't you? Maybe we need to switch this book club to a wine club. Much less beige.

Speaker_1: So then, the satnav just completely lost it, didn’t it? Sent us down this tiny little lane, barely wide enough for the car. Speaker_2: Honestly, Mum, you two and technology. It's always an adventure. Were you near any farms or anything? You always end up near farms. Speaker_3: Oh, aye, a proper farm, pet. Sheep everywhere. And honestly, the smell! Not *unpleasant*, mind, just… agricultural. Colin was convinced one of the sheep was judging him. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) He’s always been sensitive to livestock. No, really. Once, a goose chased him around a pond for a good ten minutes. Utterly terrified. Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds brilliant! Did you get any good photos? Speaker_2: Pictures of judging sheep? Please tell me you got pictures of judging sheep. Speaker_3: I did! A right close-up. You can practically *see* the disdain in its eyes. I’ll show you later. We did manage to get to Whitby eventually, though. Beautiful place. Much nicer than getting lost in the countryside. Speaker_4: Whitby was lovely. A bit too many tourists, admittedly. Couldn’t get a decent seat on the pier to eat our fish and chips. Ended up having to take them back to the car. Speaker_1: Fish and chips in the car? Iconic. Did you at least get proper Whitby scampi? Speaker_2: That's the main question. It *has* to be Whitby scampi. Speaker_3: We did, thankfully. Massive portions. Colin nearly burst. Although, he did try to share some with a seagull… Speaker_4: A rather aggressive seagull. Nearly took his hand off. I told him, “Colin, leave the wildlife alone!” He never listens. Speaker_1: Classic Colin. Speaking of wildlife, how is Barnaby doing? Has he forgiven you for abandoning him for a week? Speaker_2: He gave us the silent treatment for a good twelve hours when we got back. Full cold shoulder. Wouldn’t even look at us. Speaker_3: Ah, cats. They hold a grudge, you know. He probably organised a feline protest while we were gone. Speaker_4: (Laughing) Probably. He’s a drama queen, that cat. We got a little souvenir for him though. A little feather toy. He perked up as soon as he saw it. Speaker_1: Good. He deserves a treat. So, what else did you get up to in Whitby? Did you go up the 199 steps? Speaker_2: Oh God, no. Not with Colin’s knees. He managed about thirty before declaring it a “health hazard.” We mostly wandered around the shops and had a few pints in a pub. Speaker_3: And people-watched. Always good entertainment, people-watching. There was this one fella, dressed as Captain Cook… Speaker_4: It was a terrible costume. Looked like he’d raided a charity shop. But he was very enthusiastic. Kept trying to pose for photos with everyone. Speaker_1: Oh my god, that sounds amazing! You two are just… a constant source of entertainment. Speaker_2: We try our best. Now, tell *us* about your weekend… any exciting pet dramas or near-death experiences involving satnavs? Speaker_3: What about the rugby, Did you watch last night? Speaker_4: The lads played alright didn't they, a bit rough though! Speaker_1: Oh honestly it was a disaster! I was hoping it would be a good night but it just was not.

Speaker_1: Right, who finished the orange juice? Seriously? I just bought a carton yesterday. Speaker_2: Not me! I had a glass with breakfast, but there was still loads left. Though, to be fair, I didn’t check *how* loads. Speaker_3: Probably Ben. He's a juice fiend, isn't he? Though, he's not here yet. Maybe he snuck in early for a fix. Speaker_1: It’s always Ben. Honestly, the man operates on 90% orange juice and 10% existential dread. Speaking of which, did you see that article about Elon Musk… honestly, the man is completely unhinged. Speaker_2: Oh, the one about the Twitter rebranding? Utter chaos. I mean, X? Really? It feels… unfinished. Like he ran out of ideas halfway through. It’s just not catchy. Speaker_3: It’s a branding nightmare. And the fact he’s actively encouraging people to call it “X” despite it sounding like a mathematical equation? It’s a disaster. I’m working on a piece about it, actually. The level of free publicity he’s getting for sheer absurdity is… impressive, I guess. Speaker_1: He's a genius at self-promotion, that’s for sure. Even when it’s spectacularly bad. I’ve been wrestling with a problem at work all week, this control system for a new bit of machinery, it’s driving me mad. Keeps throwing up errors. Speaker_2: Oh dear, that sounds stressful. What kind of machinery? Is it anything exciting? Speaker_1: Not particularly. It’s for a bottling plant. Relatively mundane, but the tolerances are super tight. One tiny miscalculation and it’ll create a cascade of broken bottles. Which, obviously, isn't ideal. Speaker_3: Sounds… messy. Are you getting support from your team? Speaker_1: They're helpful enough, but it’s one of those things where you feel like you should just *know* the answer. It's frustrating. I need to spend the afternoon properly debugging it. Maybe with copious amounts of coffee. Speaker_2: Speaking of caffeine, are we doing a grocery shop today? I'm almost out of coffee *and* tea. It’s a crisis. Also, I’m thinking of attempting that Portuguese custard tart recipe I found online. Speaker_3: Oh, yes! The *pastel de nata*? You have to. I’ve heard they’re amazing. I'll happily be a taste tester. And yes, grocery shop. I'm out of everything remotely resembling fresh produce. I’ve been surviving on biscuits for the last two days. Speaker_1: Biscuits are a perfectly acceptable diet. Don’t let anyone tell you otherwise. I can do the shop if you two want to tackle the custard tarts. Though, be warned, I will require a sample. Speaker_2: Deal! We can go later this afternoon. Anything specific you need? And are you free for that pub quiz tonight? The one at The Red Lion? Speaker_1: I think so. Though, I might need to bail if the bottling plant decides to actively sabotage me. I’ll let you know. And yes, just the usual. Milk, bread, enough coffee to fuel a small rocket. Speaker_3: Perfect. I’ll check if Ben’s free too. He's surprisingly good at obscure trivia. Although he insists on wearing a tweed jacket and a monocle, which is… a commitment. Speaker_2: A monocle! Seriously? Speaker_3: Apparently it adds to the atmosphere. Don't ask. It’s Ben.

Speaker_1: Honestly though, I still don't trust satnavs. They always try to take you down roads that are clearly not meant for cars. Speaker_2: They do, don't they? Remember when it took Dad down that farm track last summer? Thought we were going to get stuck. Speaker_3: Ha! That was brilliant. Dad was fuming. He swore he could find it quicker on a map. Speaker_4: Aye, maps were alright. Proper sense of direction you got with a map. None of this relying on a little screen telling you what to do. Though, Google Maps got me out of a right pickle in Saudi last year. Couldn’t have done it without it. Speaker_1: Saudi Arabia? What were you doing in Saudi Arabia, Reg? Speaker_4: Work, love. Bit of training with the Saudi National Guard. Hot as hell, mind you. Never known heat like it. Speaker_2: Wow. That sounds…intense. Are you going to miss it though? Moving back here full-time? Speaker_4: Not the heat, no. Though, I'll miss the lads. Good bunch. But I'm looking forward to a bit of peace and quiet, you know? Just pottering about. Maybe finally get around to decorating the spare room. Speaker_3: Decorating? You and decorating? That'll be the day. Speaker_4: (laughs) Alright, alright, I'm no DIY expert. But it needs doing. Been saying that for five years now. Speaker_1: You should get someone in. It's not worth the stress. We had that disaster with the wallpaper last year... Still finding bits of it behind the sofa. Speaker_2: Yeah, you were proper stressed, Sarah. Remember? Speaker_1: Don’t remind me! Speaking of stress, how’s the job going, Alex? Still project coordinating? Speaker_2: Yeah, still at it. It's alright. A bit chaotic at the moment, but that's just the way it is, isn’t it? Long hours. Thinking about looking for something a bit less… demanding. Speaker_3: You should, mate. Life's too short. I’m alright, though. Still doing the same. Hard work, but it pays the bills. And I get to be outside, which is a bonus. Speaker_4: Good honest work, that is. Can't knock it. Speaker_1: Have you heard from Mark recently? I haven't seen him in ages. Speaker_2: Last I heard he was backpacking through South America. Sent a postcard from Bolivia. Said he was loving it. Speaker_3: Good for him. He always did have the travel bug. Speaker_4: He's a good lad, Mark. Always up for a laugh. Right, what are we doing after this? Anyone fancy heading to The Red Lion? Last pint for Reg before he goes? Speaker_1: I'm in. Speaker_2: Sounds good to me. Speaker_3: Yeah, why not? Let’s go send Reg off in style. Though, who's driving? I'm not being the designated driver again. Speaker_1: I’ll drive. Just promise you won't ask me to follow a satnav. I hope this fits your specifications! Let me know if you'd like me to modify it in any way. I hope this fits your specifications! Let me know if you'd like me to modify it in any way. I hope this fits your specifications! Let me know if you'd like me to modify it in any way. I hope this fits your specifications! Let me know if you'd like me to modify it in any way.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I think I'm coming down with something. My throat feels a bit scratchy. It's probably this change in air, isn’t it? Stockholm air is…crisp. Speaker_2: Could be. Or you're just finally feeling the exhaustion from all the rushing around we've been doing. You’ve been pushing yourself, haven't you, trying to see everything. Speaker_3: He always does. He’s like a human hummingbird. Needs constant stimulation. Honestly, Hugh, you need to build in some downtime. You’ll burn out. Speaker_1: I’m fine, I’m fine. Just need a good night’s sleep. Though, the hotel pillows are…suboptimal. Not the fluffy cloud-like experience I was hoping for. Speaker_2: You and your pillows. Honestly. You'd think running a successful business would have allowed you to invest in decent bedding by now. Speaker_1: It's a principle! I refuse to be held hostage by a good pillow. It shouldn’t dictate my happiness. Speaker_3: (Laughing) That’s…a take. Anyway, look at this rhododendron. The colour is incredible. So much more vibrant than the ones we see back home. Speaker_2: They must do something special with the soil here. Or the water. It's amazing what a difference good garden management makes. Remember old Mrs. Higgins’ garden back in Dorchester? Utterly dreadful. Always complaining about slugs. Speaker_1: Slugs are the enemy. Absolute menace. I had a war with them in my vegetable patch last summer. Lost, utterly and completely. They won the zucchini. Speaker_3: You grow zucchini? I didn’t know you had a green thumb, Hugh. Speaker_1: Green thumb is a generous description. More like a beige thumb that occasionally flirts with green. It's mostly about sheer stubbornness, to be honest. And copious amounts of organic slug pellets. Speaker_2: Speaking of stubbornness, have you been remembering to use hand sanitiser? Everywhere we go. You’re notorious for touching everything. Speaker_1: I am not! Speaker_3: Oh yes, you are. You were stroking that statue of Carl Linnaeus like it was a beloved pet. Speaker_1: He *was* a fascinating man. Father of taxonomy, you know. And the statue was very smooth. Speaker_2: Smooth doesn't mean sterile. Germs don’t discriminate based on surface texture. Honestly, I’m carrying extra wipes. Here. (Offers wipes to Speaker_1) Use them. Just do it. Speaker_1: Alright, alright. Mother hen. (Takes wipes) Fine. But I resent the implication that I’m a walking petri dish. Speaker_3: It’s a loving implication. Seriously though, it's good you're being careful. I’ve got a meeting with a potential client next week, can’t afford to get sick. Speaker_2: And I have marking to do. Mountains of it. Year 11 essays on…Shakespeare. Joy. Speaker_1: Shakespeare. A classic. Though, honestly, sometimes I think he just made it up as he went along. Speaker_3: That's sacrilege, Hugh! Speaker_1: Just saying. It's all a bit…florid, isn’t it? All that “thee” and “thou” nonsense. Speaker_2: Well, enjoy your hand sanitiser, and try to get some rest. We're heading to the Orangery next, fancy joining us? They apparently have a fantastic collection of orchids.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the way Gran talks now, you’d never know she was born in London. It’s all… smoothed out. Like she's been practicing Received Pronunciation or something. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Don't be daft, love. Lived in Kent too long, that’s all. Picks things up, you do. Though, I s’pose when you’ve spent seventy years saying things, habits are ‘ard to break. Speaker_3: It’s funny, isn't it? I can still hear my nan’s voice clear as anything. Proper Essex. You could pinpoint Harlow just from the way she said "butter." Speaker_4: My mum’s gone the opposite way. She tries to drop all her Chatham, you know? Thinks it sounds common. It just comes out forced. Sounds… weird. Speaker_1: It does. Like she's trying too hard. Remember when she tried to say "schedule" and it came out "shed-yool"? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, that was brilliant! She went bright red. Still won’t let me live that down. Though, she had a point about Chatham accents, back in the day. Rough around the edges, some of ’em. Speaker_3: Speaking of rough around the edges… how’s Mark doing? Still… struggling? Speaker_1: It’s bad, honestly. He hit a new low last weekend. Apparently, there was an argument with Carol. Something about… well, everything, really. But mostly about him not looking for work. Speaker_4: Classic. Always the same story with him. Blames everyone else, eh? Says the jobs aren't there, but he doesn't actually *try* to find them. Speaker_2: He needs help, that lad. Real help. Not just enabling him, letting him sit around all day playing Minecraft. Speaker_1: That’s what I told Carol. I said, “He’s thirty-five, Dad! He can’t spend his life building virtual castles!” She said he finds it… therapeutic. Speaker_3: Therapeutic? It’s avoidance, plain and simple. And honestly, the amount of takeaways they get… it’s no wonder he’s put on so much weight. It's a health hazard. Speaker_4: Remember when we used to cycle everywhere as kids? Up and down those hills in Chatham? Proper fitness. Now, everyone just drives everywhere. Even to the shops. Speaker_2: We didn’t have a choice, did we? Couldn’t afford to run around in cars. Bikes were it. Good for the legs, too. I used to deliver papers on my Raleigh. Built some real stamina. Speaker_1: I’ve been trying to convince Carol to get Mark out on a bike, but she says he’s “not the outdoorsy type.” That’s code for “he’ll complain the whole time.” Speaker_3: Carol’s a good woman, but she's a bit of a pushover. She lets him get away with murder. It’s not fair on her. She deserves better. Speaker_4: And what about the kids? How are they coping with everything? Is Lucy still talking about wanting to live with me full-time? Speaker_1: She has, yeah. She said she feels… responsible for her dad, somehow. Like she has to keep him happy. It’s awful. She’s only ten. Speaker_2: That’s not right. Nobody should put that kind of pressure on a child. Have you thought about talking to a solicitor? Speaker_1: I have, but I don't even know where to start. It feels… aggressive. Like I’m trying to tear their family apart. But what about Lucy’s well-being? I just want her to be happy. Speaker_3: It's a difficult situation, love. But sometimes, the kindest thing you can do is protect them, even if it means making hard choices. Speaker_4: This mattress is killing my back, by the way. Honestly

Speaker_1: So, did you manage to grate all the cheese for the baked Alaska? It’s a surprisingly large amount, actually. Speaker_2: Yeah, Mum, it’s done. My hand’s aching though. Seriously, that was a lot of cheddar. Why does a baked Alaska need *that* much cheese? Speaker_1: Cheddar? Oh, darling. It’s not cheddar. It’s supposed to be Parmesan. You’ve grated cheddar into a baked Alaska. Speaker_2: What?! No way. Are you sure? It smelled like cheddar. I grabbed the block from the fridge… it was yellow… Speaker_1: (Sighs) Right. Well, we’ll see how it tastes. It’s probably… an interesting flavour combination. Honestly. It will be a story, at least. Remember when your aunt Mildred tried to make profiteroles and used self-raising flour? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh god, yeah! They exploded all over the kitchen. It looked like a bomb had gone off. Speaker_1: Exactly. This is a slightly less dramatic version of that. Anyway, are you excited about the Halloween party on Saturday? Speaker_2: Yeah, definitely. Ben’s going as a zombie, Liam’s being a vampire. I haven’t decided yet. Maybe a werewolf? Speaker_1: A werewolf would be good. You’d pull it off. Are you going trick-or-treating around the village, or staying local? Speaker_2: Probably local. Old Mr. Henderson gives out full-size chocolate bars, so that’s always a good start. Plus, it’s safer. There were stories last year about some older kids being a bit… rough with the younger ones. Speaker_1: It’s a shame that happens. People can be so unkind. It reminds me of something that happened when I was recruiting for the graduate scheme at work… Speaker_2: Oh, here we go. A work story. Speaker_1: It’s relevant! I promise. We had two extremely qualified candidates, both really bright. But one was… significantly older than the others. And you could tell the other interviewers were subtly, but definitely, biased against him. Treating him differently, asking different questions. It was awful. Speaker_2: That’s… not fair. Speaker_1: No, it wasn’t. I had to pull them up on it, of course. But it just highlights how ingrained some attitudes are. Even when you think people are being progressive… Speaker_2: It’s weird thinking about age, though. Like, how old is too old for… I don’t know… stuff? Speaker_1: (Slightly uncomfortable) Oh, that's a very complicated question, darling. It depends on the "stuff" doesn't it. There are legal age limits for certain things, of course. You know, the age of consent and everything. Which is really important, and we've talked about that before. But generally, it’s just about respecting people and treating them as individuals. Not judging them based on a number. Speaker_2: Right. Okay. So, back to the baked Alaska… even with cheddar? Speaker_1: (Smiling) Even with cheddar. We’ll embrace the chaos. Although, I might sneakily grate some actual Parmesan when you’re not looking. And honestly, let's just hope it doesn't taste *too* bad. Speaker_2: Deal. You grate the parmesan, I’ll start thinking about my werewolf make-up. Is there any more of that fake blood stuff? Speaker_1: Probably in the attic. I think your father stockpiled it after your first Halloween.

Speaker_1: This coffee is absolutely lovely, you’ve got a good machine here. Much better than my instant, I confess. Speaker_2: Oh, glad you like it! It was a bit of an investment, but worth it, I think. Helps get me going in the mornings, especially with marking looming. Are you alright for toast? There’s jam, marmalade… Speaker_1: Marmalade’s perfect, thank you. So, New York! You must tell me everything. I saw a tiny snippet on Instagram, of that amazing rooftop bar, but that doesn’t do it justice, does it? Speaker_2: Doesn’t even come close. Honestly, it felt like being *in* a film set. Everything’s just…bigger, bolder. The energy is incredible. We walked miles and miles, saw a show, ate far too much pizza… it was brilliant. I’m still exhausted, though. Speaker_1: Sounds exhausting and exhilarating all at once. You’ve always been a bit of a city person, haven’t you? I’m more hills and dales, personally. Though, I must admit, I did feel a pang of… something, seeing all those skyscrapers. Speaker_2: So, what’s the plan for today? I was thinking a walk along the beach? The tide’s supposed to be out this afternoon. Or we could potter around Mumbles? Speaker_1: Oh, the beach sounds lovely. I haven’t had a proper seaside walk in ages. That’d be perfect. And then maybe a pub lunch? Speaker_2: Absolutely. There’s a good one in Mumbles, overlooks the sea. We could do both, have a wander around the village afterwards. Unless you fancy something more…adventurous? Remember that conversation about flying lessons? Speaker_1: (laughs) Don’t even *start* on the flying lessons. It’s a mid-life crisis, pure and simple. Though, thinking about it... the view would be spectacular. No, no, let's stick to solid ground, thank you very much. Speaker_2: Fair enough! Though honestly, after living in Japan for so long, I'm always up for trying new things. It changes your perspective, doesn't it? Everything feels…possible. Speaker_1: It does. That’s what I loved about hearing you talk about it when we first met. It's funny, isn't it, how a place can do that to you. Though I remember when we first met, you were complaining about the tiny apartments and the constant politeness. Speaker_2: (chuckles) Oh, I was. It took some getting used to! Speaker_1: Exactly! A remix. I’m avoiding ‘fusion’ because that implies a harmonious blending, and I don't think that's what’s happening. It's more chaotic and uneven. This section here – the bit with all the footnotes – is where I lay out the theoretical framework. I’m drawing on Bourdieu, obviously, but also some work by Labov about the social stratification of language. Speaker_2: Bourdieu, naturally. Sounds… heavy. Speaker_1: It is. But it needs to be. Davies is a stickler for theory. Then this part, which is already getting way too long, is the detailed methodology. I'm planning on doing a corpus analysis of online forum posts from around Lancashire, and then some interviews with people who’ve moved away from the area over the past decade. Speaker_2: Online forums? That’s… a choice. Won't everything be riddled with intentional misspellings and slang? Speaker_1: Yeah, that's the challenge. I’m going to have to develop a pretty rigorous coding scheme to filter out the intentional noise. And then the interviews will hopefully give me some qualitative data to back up the quantitative findings. I’m hoping to find evidence of linguistic features being retained or adapted even when people aren't physically in the region. Speaker_2: Smart. So you’re looking for subtle indicators… like pronunciations slipping into standard English, or new slang being adopted from elsewhere? Speaker_1: Precisely. It's about tracing the patterns of change. And this, the bit on the pink paper, is a preliminary literature review. I realised I needed to include a section on digital dialects, like leetspeak and internet meme language. It’s relevant, even if it’s a bit tangential. Speaker_2: That’s good thinking. It shows you've considered the broader context. Honestly, it looks like you've pretty much got it nailed. Apart from the length, obviously. Speaker_1: Yeah, Davies is going to have a field day with the word count. But I’d rather submit something too long and then trim it down, than something too short and have to add content at the last minute. What about your thesis? How’s the… postcolonial critique of garden gnomes coming along? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Don’t even ask. It's a disaster. I’m starting to genuinely resent garden gnomes. And colonialism. Speaker_1: Rough. Want a coffee? We can brainstorm gnome-related issues. Maybe we can find a Bourdieu angle for your thesis too. There's gotta be one. Speaker_2: Please. A coffee and a Bourdieu-infused gnome rescue mission sounds… perfect. Speaker_1: Right, coffee it is. Just let me quickly save this… again. You never know with these things. Speaker_2: Always back it up, my friend. Always. Speaker_1: Rule number one of postgraduate life.
