Speaking of which, remember that time Liam fell asleep *standing up* at pre-drinks before Sophie’s birthday? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh my god, yes! He genuinely just…toppled. Like a tree. And he didn't even wake up! Holly had to physically hold him upright while she ordered him a Red Bull. Speaker_2: It was the funniest thing. I've got a picture somewhere, I'll send it. Hold on…*scrolling on phone*… Aha! Here. Speaker_1: (Looks at phone, bursts out laughing) Oh, bless him. He looks so peaceful, completely oblivious to the impending doom of being woken up. He was wearing that awful Hawaiian shirt too. Speaker_2: The one his gran got him? Iconique. He swore he’d burn it if he ever had to wear it again. Speaker_1: Honestly, he's such a drama queen. Have you spoken to Chloe recently? I haven’t seen her since that…incident at the quiz night. Speaker_2: Oh, god. Don’t even mention that. She's still mortified. Apparently, she's blocked Ben on everything. Speaker_1: Wow. That escalated quickly. What exactly *did* he say? I only caught the tail end of it. Something about her general knowledge being…questionable? Speaker_2: It was worse than questionable. He said she thought Marie Curie invented the microwave. And then he just kept repeating “Microwave Curie!” It was awful. Speaker_1: (Winces) Oh, cringey. Classic Ben. He doesn't realise when to stop. She's got a right to be furious. Speaker_2: Exactly! And then she tried to argue back with facts no one had ever heard of. It was a mess. It's why I avoid pub quizzes now. Too much potential for disaster. Speaker_1: Honestly, same. They’re just…stressful. Plus, the music's always terrible. Remember that time they played nothing but ABBA for two hours? Speaker_2: (Groans) Don’t remind me. I nearly walked out. I mean, I like ABBA, but there's a limit. And then *they* started a singalong. It was horrifying. Speaker_1: It was like being trapped in a Mamma Mia! musical against my will. Oh, here comes your mum. Quick, pretend we’re having a serious discussion about…economics? Speaker_2: *Sighs* Perfect. Reliable as ever. Don't look so panicked, just look studious. "Supply and demand, the cornerstone of a thriving market…" something like that. Speaker_1: (In a ridiculously formal tone) Yes, indeed. The complexities of the fiscal policy are truly fascinating, don't you agree? Speaker_2: (Joining in) Absolutely. A nuanced understanding of interest rates is crucial for…a sustainable future. Speaker_1: (Whispering under her breath) This is so ridiculous. Speaker_2: (Whispering back) Just go with it! She'll think we’re preparing for our dissertations.

Speaker_1: Right, so I’ve been through the agenda for the council planning committee meeting again. And honestly, it’s a mess. Speaker_2: A mess how? Is it the volume of applications, or is it… Councillor Davies being particularly verbose again? Speaker_1: Both, actually. But mostly the structure. It’s just all over the place. They’ve got the outline for the new housing development slotted in *after* the retrospective application for the garden shed. Speaker_2: A garden shed? Seriously? They’re dedicating committee time to a garden shed? Speaker_1: Apparently, it’s a ‘substantial structure’ that’s been erected without planning permission, and a neighbour has complained it’s blocking their light. Honestly, the drama. Speaker_2: Incredible. So, the housing development—the thing that will actually impact the entire area—is being dealt with almost as an afterthought? Speaker_1: Precisely. And they’ve scheduled the public speaking slots for the housing development *before* the presentation of the plans. Which means people will be speaking about a plan they haven’t even seen yet. Speaker_2: That’s… spectacularly bad planning, even for them. Is anyone going to point this out? Speaker_1: I’m planning to. I’ve drafted a few points, but I’m worried it’ll come across as overly critical. I don’t want to alienate anyone. Especially not Councillor Henderson. Speaker_2: Henderson’s a lost cause. He’ll support anything as long as it involves ribbon-cutting. Just be firm. Highlight the logical inconsistencies. Explain how having public speaking before the presentation undermines the whole process. Speaker_1: You're right. It’s just… I’ve been on this committee for two years now, and it’s consistently frustrating. It feels like they’re deliberately making it difficult. Speaker_2: They are. It's a combination of incompetence and a genuine desire to avoid anything resembling transparency. Remember the battle over the verge planting? Speaker_1: (Sighs) Don't remind me. Still can’t believe they approved the concrete bollards. Anyway, back to the agenda. I’m also concerned about the wording of the recommendation for the community centre refurbishment. It’s incredibly vague. Speaker_2: Vague how? Speaker_1: It just says “improvements should be made to enhance the community benefit”. No specifics about what those improvements should be, or how they’ll be funded. They’re essentially giving the contractors free rein. Speaker_2: That’s… worrying. Have you looked into the contractors at all? Speaker_1: Briefly. They’ve got a pretty patchy record, apparently. Lots of projects running over budget and behind schedule. Is it something you want to give a look at. Speaker_2: Yeah definitely. Send the file over. We should prepare together to make sure everything hits right. It’ll be helpful to have another pair of eyes on it. And honestly? Misery loves company. Especially when it’s council-related misery. Speaker_1: Good idea. I'll send it over now. Maybe we can order some takeaway and make an evening of strategic planning. Speaker_2: Brilliant. Indian? Speaker_1: Absolutely. Vindaloo it is. We'll need the fire power to get through this meeting. Speaker_2: Perfect. Then let’s tackle this mess. One garden shed and vague refurbishment proposal at a time. Speaker_1: Exactly. And try to remain calm when Councillor Davies starts droning on about the historical significance of garden gnomes. Speaker_2: No promises.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I am *starving*. I’ve been surviving on biscuits all day. And instant coffee. It’s a tragic state of affairs, really. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Sounds about right for a Monday. I managed to grab a sandwich at work, but it was… underwhelming. Turkey and cranberry, but the cranberry sauce tasted suspiciously like jam. Speaker_1: Oh, no. That’s a crime against sandwiches. What are we having then? I was thinking pasta? I could really use some carbs. Speaker_2: Pasta sounds good. Although… Mrs. Higgins was having a full-on shouting match with someone on her phone in the garden again this morning. It’s always something with her, isn’t it? Honestly, you’d think she’d run out of people to yell at. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, bless her. She’s a gift, that woman. Remember when she accused old Mr. Davies of letting his cat poo in her flowerbeds? And it turned out to be a badger? Speaker_2: Oh my god, yes! The outrage! She was furious. He was practically in tears trying to explain it wasn’t his cat. Speaking of outrage, have you seen what happened with… oh, never mind. It’s depressing news. Speaker_1: Lay it on me. I need a distraction. Is it more political nonsense? Speaker_2: Sadly, yes. Another MP caught doing something… questionable. Honestly, it’s just endless. Anyway, enough doom and gloom. Did you manage to get that dress you were looking at online? The blue one? Speaker_1: I did! It arrived this morning, and it fits perfectly. I'm planning on wearing it on Saturday. We’re going to that new cocktail bar with Chloe and Sarah, remember? Speaker_2: Oh yes! Perfect. That place looks really nice. Though I’m dreading the inevitable conversation about men. Last time we all went out, it was *all* anyone talked about. Speaker_1: (Sighs) Tell me about it. Sarah was going on about how ‘all good men are taken’ and Chloe was dissecting every single text message she’d ever received from anyone even remotely attractive. Speaker_2: It’s exhausting. Honestly, sometimes I think I’m better off just adopting seventeen cats. Although, then *I*’d be the crazy cat lady. Speaker_1: (Grinning) You’d rock the crazy cat lady look. Seriously. You’d have amazing cardigans. Have you heard from Gemma lately? From school? I was trying to find her on Instagram, but I couldn’t find an account. Speaker_2: Oh, Gemma! I think she’s living in Australia now? I saw something on Facebook a while ago, she was posting pictures of beaches and koalas. Very idyllic. Speaker_1: Wow, that’s amazing! I completely lost touch with her after uni. Should we try and organise a day out soon? Like, go to that garden centre we’ve been talking about? They’ve got that Christmas section open already, it's horrifying. Speaker_2: Yes, definitely! That sounds lovely. And we need to make a plan to actually *watch* a film. We keep meaning to, but we always end up scrolling through Netflix for an hour and then falling asleep. Did you see that new horror film everyone's talking about? Speaker_1: Oh, the one with the… creepy doll? No way. I'm a total scaredy cat. I'll pass. Pasta first, then maybe a mindless rom-com. That’s my ideal evening.

Speaker_1: Right, honestly, the state of this place. I swear, dust multiplies when you’re not looking. Speaker_2: (Without looking up from her phone) You say that every time. It’s not *that* bad. Speaker_1: Not that bad? The coffee table’s practically a geological dig site. Remember when Gran came round? She practically needed a hazmat suit. Speaker_2: Gran exaggerates. She’s lived through two World Wars, a bit of dust doesn’t phase her. Besides, I’ve been busy. I had that meeting with Mr. Davies today about the new autism assessment protocols. Speaker_1: Oh aye? How'd that go? Sounds proper head-wrecking. Speaker_2: It was…lengthy. He’s got this weird obsession with using NLP techniques. Says it can unlock hidden potential in kids with communication difficulties. Speaker_1: NLP? Seriously? Feels a bit…woo-woo, doesn’t it? Like something you’d see advertised on late-night telly with that bloke promising to make you a millionaire. Remember those adverts? Speaker_2: Exactly! It's all about ‘anchoring’ and ‘reframing’ and all this jargon. I tried to explain the neurobiological basis of dyslexia but he just kept going on about positive affirmations. Speaker_1: Blimey. Sounds like he’s been reading too many self-help books. Speaking of telly, did you see that advert for that new washing machine? The one where it’s cleaning someone’s muddy football kit? It’s amazing how they make everything look so…perfect. Speaker_2: (Finally looks up) Everything's staged, isn't it? And filters. It's all filters. I saw a TikTok the other day showing how much editing goes into those 'natural' makeup looks. It's ridiculous. Speaker_1: Don’t get me started on TikTok. It's a total time suck. I was scrolling through it for an hour yesterday. Found myself looking at videos of people organizing their spice racks. Spice racks! Speaker_2: You and your spice racks. You'd be brilliant at a car boot sale, honestly. You’d haggle the price of a rusty bucket down to a tenner. Speaker_1: I have a gift! My dad practically raised me on car boot sales. He could sniff out a bargain a mile away. Remember that time he got that antique clock for a fiver? Turned out to be worth a fortune. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh God, yes! And Mum was furious because it took up the entire hallway for weeks. She kept tripping over it. Speaker_1: Good times. I'm thinking of trying to get rid of some stuff on eBay actually. My phone’s full of photos of things I need to list. It's a proper faff though, isn’t it? All the postage and packaging… Speaker_2: It is. Online shopping's convenient, but it's created a whole new world of hassle when you want to *sell* things. And all the scams, honestly. You read about people getting robbed all the time. Speaker_1: Yeah, it’s dodgy. I saw something on the news about a spate of burglaries around here. People are getting their phones snatched right out of their hands. Mad. Speaker_2: It's scary. I've been trying to eat healthier too, you know, to combat the stress. But then I see an advert for Domino's and all good intentions fly out the window. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. I'm supposed to be cutting down on biscuits, but then I walk past the biscuit aisle in Tesco and…well, you know. It’s a vicious cycle. What are you up to this week anyway? Any big plans? Speaker_2: Just the usual really. More meetings, a supervision session, maybe try and fit in a yoga class if I can. What about you? Another week battling with unruly teenagers and their questionable grammar?

Speaker_1: Honestly, the traffic was *brutal* getting here. I left ages ago and still ended up circling the Aston Expressway for about twenty minutes. Speaker_2: Oh, tell me about it. I took a back route, hoping to avoid the worst, but even those were jammed. Birmingham seems to have permanently entered peak hour. Speaker_3: It’s just getting worse, isn’t it? They keep promising improvements, but… well, you know. Speaking of worse, has anyone tried that new Thai place near the Mailbox? I heard mixed reviews. Speaker_4: Ooh, no, not yet. Is it authentically spicy, or that watered-down ‘British Thai’ flavour? That’s the crucial question. I had a disastrous Pad Thai last month that was basically noodles in sweet tomato ketchup. Speaker_5: (Laughing) Oh, the horror! You're right to be discerning. I’ve been trying to eat more healthily lately, which is proving…challenging. I downloaded one of those meal planning apps, you know, to track calories and all that, but it’s just so dreary. Speaker_1: Which one did you get? I’ve been tempted by MyFitnessPal, but I’m worried it’ll just make me obsessed. Speaker_5: It’s called ‘PlateJoy’ or something. It’s…intense. It tells you to eat things like quinoa and kale for breakfast. Honestly, I need something more substantial to get me through the day. I’m a Yorkshire woman, I need a proper breakfast! Speaker_2: Ha! Fair enough. I’ve finally started using Spotify properly. I was so late to the party, but it’s brilliant for discovering new music. They’ve got these curated playlists that are actually really good. Speaker_3: Oh yeah, Spotify’s great. I’m still a bit old-fashioned and cling to my vinyl, though. It’s just…different, isn’t it? More tactile. Speaker_4: I get that. I've been on a documentary kick lately. Watched one about the history of journalism the other night, and it was… grim. Basically, it was a lengthy explanation of how everything’s terrible and my job is slowly disappearing. Speaker_1: Oh, *don't* say that! You're brilliant at what you do. The industry's changing, that's all. It needs good journalists like you. Speaker_5: Exactly. And there’s still a demand for good writing. I’m working on a feature about the impact of local radio on communities. It's proving harder than I thought, sifting through all the council reports! Speaker_2: Speaking of changes, any progress on the house hunt? Still looking in Harborne? Speaker_3: We had a viewing yesterday. Pretty decent place, but the garden was tiny. And apparently, the previous owner was a hoarder. It took two skips just to clear out the shed! Speaker_4: Oh, wow. That sounds… intense. You’d need hazard pay just to go in there. Speaker_1: Seriously. I'm still saving, trying to get a decent deposit together. It feels like an impossible task at the moment. The interest rates are just insane. Speaker_5: Tell me about it. We're thinking of maybe waiting another year, see if things calm down a bit. It’s just…everything feels so expensive right now. Even a simple night out is a small fortune. Speaker_2: At least we have good company and decent wine, right? Anyone fancy another glass? Speaker_3: I’m in. And maybe we should avoid discussing property prices and the impending doom of journalism for a bit. Let’s talk about something lighter. Like, um… what’s the worst film you’ve seen recently?

Speaker_1: …and honestly, finding anywhere to live was a nightmare. Everything was either a poky little flat above a shop, or a crumbling Victorian terrace that needed a fortune spent on it. We ended up renting, of course. Couldn't possibly afford to buy back then. What was it like for you, David? Coming down here as a dentist, must have been a shock from Birmingham. Speaker_4: A shock is an understatement! I remember driving down the M5, thinking, “Good Lord, what have I let myself in for?” The interview itself was… interesting. The hospital was ancient, practically falling apart. One of the senior surgeons had a pipe that he constantly relit with a lighter that smelled faintly of disinfectant! Anyway, I got the job, obviously. Then the *real* fun began – finding somewhere to live. Speaker_3: Ah, yes, the housing market of the 60s. A truly bizarre landscape. I remember when I first came to the university here, a friend and I shared a house, well, a glorified shed really, with a family of six. It had no central heating, and the bathroom was outside. Still, it was cheap. Very cheap. Speaker_2: We were lucky, I suppose. We managed to find a semi-detached house in Filton. It hadn't been modernised, to put it mildly. Avocado bathroom suite, orange shag pile… it was a sight to behold. But it was ours, eventually. And it was a good area for the kids, which was the main thing. Speaker_1: Avocado bathrooms… oh, the memories! We had one of those. It was the height of fashion, apparently. Then everything went brown in the 70s, didn't it? Remember brown Formica? Speaker_4: (Laughing) Oh, don’t even get me started on Formica! It was everywhere. The waiting room in my surgery was completely covered in the stuff. Made it look like a particularly depressing cafe. Where did you meet your wife, Arthur? Speaker_3: Now that’s a story. I met Margaret at a conference in Leeds. She was teaching English as a foreign language, and I was presenting a paper on… well, something terribly academic that nobody understood. We ended up arguing about it, naturally. And the rest, as they say, is history. What about you, Roger? Speaker_2: I met Brenda at a teacher training college in Bristol. She was training to be a primary school teacher, and I was doing my PGCE. We bonded over shared horror stories about difficult pupils and endless marking. Typical teacher romance, really. Speaker_1: Ah, teacher romances. They're the best. Mine and John's story is less glamorous. I met him at a party in Almondsbury. He was a friend of a friend, and he just happened to be the only one who would talk to me all night. He wasn’t the most handsome man, but he was a good listener. Speaker_4: Speaking of travel, I have a story about my postgraduate course. I went to Athens University to do a course on oral surgery. Spectacular place, Athens, but it was… ill-timed. The first day of the course, the military took over. Coup d’état. The whole city went into lockdown. Speaker_3: Goodness me! That sounds terrifying. Speaker_4: It was! We were all confined to our hotels. Trying to get information was impossible. And then there was the time difference to contend with! Called home to let my wife know I was alright, and ended up waking her up at three in the morning, thinking it was a perfectly reasonable hour! That whole trip was a complete disaster. But at least it gave me a good story to tell.

Speaker_1: …and then of course, the whole thing with the ceramics. Honestly, people would bring me things, dreadful things, thinking they were valuable! I had to learn very quickly how to politely tell them their grandmother’s “antique” was actually made in the 1970s. Speaker_2: Oh, you must have some stories. I imagine a lot of disappointment. It’s funny, isn’t it, what people assign value to? Sentiment, mostly I suppose. Speaker_1: Exactly! Sentiment and wishful thinking. It was a good life though, a very good life. Kept me busy. What about you, dear? Speech therapy… that must have been incredibly rewarding, but also quite draining, I should think. Speaker_2: It was. Both, actually. Massively rewarding to see a child finally communicate, to unlock that for them. But you carry their stories with you, you know? The struggles, the families... Especially the ones with acquired brain injuries. So much loss. Speaker_1: I can imagine. Losing the ability to speak… horrifying. It’s a strange thing, speech, isn't it? We take it so for granted. I often think about my own childhood, and how much I *didn't* say. My mother… well, she wasn’t one for a lot of conversation. Speaker_2: Oh? Was she a quiet woman? Speaker_1: Quiet doesn't quite cover it. More… distant. She'd had a difficult life, I think. Lost her own mother young. She threw herself into the farm, really. Just worked and worked and worked. Never much room for silliness or, well, feelings, really. We lived out near Exmoor, beautiful countryside, but awfully isolated. I used to spend hours wandering the fields, making up stories in my head. That’s probably where the art came from, I suppose. Escapism. Speaker_2: That makes sense. A way to create your own world. I grew up in Sydney, very different. Lots of noise, lots of people. My father was a shipwright, building yachts. He was a boisterous man, always laughing, always telling stories. A real character. Though, looking back, he expected a lot. I felt quite a bit of pressure to… succeed. Speaker_1: Succeed in what way? Speaker_2: Oh, he wanted me to be a doctor, or a lawyer. Something “respectable”. He wasn't terribly keen on the speech pathology, thought it was a bit…fuzzy. Not concrete enough. Typical, I suppose. But I loved it. Really loved working with people. Did you always know you wanted to be an artist? Speaker_1: Goodness, no. I dabbled. Tried secretarial work, briefly. Dreadful. Couldn't sit still. Then I started painting, just as a hobby, and people started buying my work. And then the antiques… it evolved. It all just sort of *happened*, really. I never had a grand plan. Did your father ever come around to accepting your career choice? Speaker_2: Eventually. He saw the difference I was making, I think. And he was a fair man, deep down. He just wanted me to be happy, in his own way. It took a while for him to understand that happiness didn’t necessarily look like a fancy office and a big salary. Speaker_1: It rarely does, doesn’t it? Sometimes the simplest things are the most satisfying. A good cup of tea, a beautiful sunset… and a quiet life. Speaker_2: Absolutely. And good conversation, of course. Speaker_1: Indeed. Perhaps another cup of tea? I think I’ve been rambling on enough.

Speaker_1: Right, so onions are caramelising nicely. You sure we’ve got enough balsamic? Last time felt a bit… lacking. Speaker_2: Yeah, I got a bigger bottle this time. It’s lurking somewhere in that cupboard of doom. Honestly, it's a black hole in there. I think I saw a bag of marshmallows disappear in there last month. Speaker_1: Marshmallows? What were marshmallows doing in the cupboard of doom? Speaker_2: Don’t ask. It was a late-night impulse buy. I was stressed about the bake orders and suddenly needed…fluffy sugar. I barely remember it. Did you ever end up getting that new stencil for the cake decorating? Speaker_1: Oh, yeah! It arrived yesterday. It’s the snowflake one, for Christmas stuff. It's *really* intricate. I tried it on a practice cake board, nearly had a breakdown. So fiddly. Speaker_2: Ooh, send me a picture! I need some inspo. Christmas orders are already starting to roll in. People are going mad for mince pie macarons this year. It’s ridiculous. Speaker_1: Mince pie macarons? That’s… a choice. *A knock at the door. Speaker_3 enters, carrying a large box.* Speaker_3: Alright, you two! Sorry I’m late, the delivery driver was having a “moment” with his sat nav. And look what I’ve snagged! Speaker_2: Oh my god, is that…the gingerbread house kit?! Speaker_3: The one and only! Found it in a little shop near the market. They were selling out fast, apparently. I thought we *needed* it for our Christmas tradition. Speaker_1: You are a legend. I was mentally preparing to construct one from scratch, which would have ended in disaster. Speaker_3: No way! We're aiming for a festive masterpiece, not a structural engineering failure. So, what’s for dinner? Smells amazing. Speaker_2: Caramelised onion and balsamic tart, with a side of…Christmas planning. We were just talking about the ridiculousness of mince pie macarons. Speaker_3: Oh, don’t even get me started! People request the weirdest things. I had someone ask for a cake shaped like a Brussel sprout last year. A *Brussel sprout*! Speaker_1: Seriously? Speaker_3: Dead serious. Anyway, Christmas decorations. Have you guys thought about it yet? I’m thinking maximalist this year. Fairy lights *everywhere*. Speaker_2: I'm on board with maximalist. I bought a giant inflatable snowman. It's currently taking up half my hallway. Speaker_1: An inflatable snowman? You’re really going for it, aren’t you? I think I’ll just stick to a tree and maybe some tasteful garlands. Speaker_3: Tasteful? Where’s the fun in that? We need to recreate the North Pole in here! And we absolutely *have* to make those candy cane bark things. Remember last year? Speaker_2: Oh god, the sugar rush. I was bouncing off the walls for days. Speaker_1: I think my dentist still hasn’t forgiven us. Speaking of which, maybe we should focus on the savoury tart for now before descending further into sugar-induced chaos. Speaker_3: Fair enough. But after dinner, we’re making a Christmas playlist. And brainstorming reindeer names. It’s non-negotiable. Speaker_2: Reindeer names? Speaker_3: Obviously! We need to give the inflatable snowman’s reindeer some proper identities. Speaker_1: (Sighing happily) You two are insane. But, you know what? I wouldn’t have it any other way.

Speaker_2: Honestly, Cambridge feels… smaller every time we come. Don’t you think? It's lovely, of course, but just… contained. Speaker_1: Yeah, I guess so. It’s definitely not London, that’s for sure. Feels a bit like a bubble, especially when term’s not running. More like a particularly posh village. Speaker_2: A very *expensive* posh village. Though, thinking about it… have you actually started looking at houses properly yet? Not just scrolling Rightmove on your phone, but genuinely looking at estate agents? Speaker_1: Mum, we talked about this. I’m finishing my thesis. That’s… kind of the priority. Speaker_2: I know, I know. Of course. But the thesis *will* finish eventually. And then what? You can’t just drift, darling. You need a plan. Even a vague one. Speaker_1: Vague is good. I’m good with vague. I’ve been looking, a little. Mostly at places… well, just outside Cambridge, really. Somewhere with a garden, ideally. Speaker_2: Outside Cambridge? Why? You spent three years getting a degree *in* Cambridge. Surely you want to be closer to the action. London is always an option, you know. Speaker_1: London’s… a lot. And expensive. Even more than Cambridge, I think. And I don’t know if I want to jump straight into *that*. Plus, I’d like a bit of space. Somewhere to… breathe. Speaker_2: Breathe? You sound like your father when he was having a mid-life crisis and wanted to buy a smallholding in Norfolk. Don't go buying a smallholding, please. Speaker_1: No smallholding, I promise. Just a house with a garden. Maybe a shed. For… thinking. Speaker_2: Right. Thinking in a shed. Sounds… idyllic. What about Oxford? Have you considered applying for post-doc work there? It's closer to London, better transport links. Speaker_1: Oxford… I hadn’t really. It feels a bit… competitive. And, honestly, a bit… *Oxford*. Speaker_2: (laughs) What does that even mean? Speaker_1: You know. Pretentious. Overly polished. It’s not exactly a vibe I'm going for right now. I'm not sure I have the stamina for another round of intense academic rivalry. Speaker_2: Well, you’ve certainly handled Cambridge. And, speaking of stamina, have you spoken to Aunt Carol recently? She was asking about you. Said she was worried you weren’t eating properly. Speaker_1: Oh, Carol. She always worries. I told her I was fine, just… busy. And probably surviving on instant coffee and biscuits. Speaker_2: That’s not a diet, darling. Honestly. Your grandmother would be appalled. She’d want you married off with a house and three children by now. Speaker_1: (groans) Don't even start. Speaker_2: I’m just saying. You need to think about the long term. I mean, what do *you* want? Truly want? Beyond the thesis, beyond the garden and the shed. Speaker_1: I honestly don’t know. And that’s… okay, right? It’s okay not to have it all figured out at 26? Speaker_2: It’s okay to not have it *completely* figured out, yes. But having some direction is essential. Look, I’m not trying to pressure you. I just… I want you to be happy. And I worry. It’s what mothers do. Speaker_1: I know, Mum. I appreciate it. And I’ll think about it. Seriously. Maybe after I submit, I’ll actually sit down and make a list. A vague list, of course. Speaker_2: That's all I ask. And maybe, just maybe, you should call your Aunt Carol. She just wants to know you’re looking after yourself.

Speaker_1: It’s just…it’s amazing to be back, isn’t it? It feels so different seeing it all through alumni eyes. I barely recognised the Squire Law Library after five years! Speaker_2: Completely. I feel like a visitor. Everything’s so shiny and new. I remember it being… well, a bit more worn, shall we say? Did you have Professor Armitage for Land Law? Speaker_3: (Chuckles, joining the conversation) Armitage? Oh, yes. A formidable man. Kept us all on our toes. He’d start a lecture mid-sentence, expecting us all to be perfectly up to speed with the previous week’s nuances. I’ve probably forgotten more about Land Law than either of you have learned! Speaker_1: Oh, I definitely remember him! He was…intense. I did his module on Property Rights, actually. It was fascinating, though. Though, honestly, I’m using very little of it in my current role. I’m a Language Research Coordinator now. Speaker_2: Oh, interesting! I’m an administrator in the same department. It’s a bit less academic, but still involves a lot of language work – mostly transcribing interviews and data analysis. It's a good fit. Speaker_3: Language work? Fascinating. Speaker_3: Sounds stressful. I would have just people-watched. That's my preferred Parisian activity. Cheaper, and much more comfortable. Speaker_3: They really are. And it sounds like they’re avoiding actual conversation. That never ends well. Anyway, back to you and your poor feet. Did anything *else* exciting happen? Aside from the near-death experience with the Mona Lisa crowds? Speaker_1: Well, I did manage to accidentally order a whole baguette instead of a slice… It was a surprisingly large baguette. Maybe stick to English next time, for the sake of everyone involved. Pasta then? I’ll get started. Speaker_1: Yes, please! And maybe a foot massage. Asking too much?

Speaker_1: Morning! You look… remarkably awake for a Monday. Did you have a good weekend? Speaker_2: (Laughs) Surprisingly, yeah. Actually really good. Went to Chichester with my sister. I didn’t even know she had a boyfriend! Speaker_1: Apparently, he proposed on Friday. It was all very hush-hush. She was showing it off to everyone in the coffee queue. She looked ridiculously happy. Speaker_2: Wow. That’s… a lot. I always thought she was a bit of a cynic. Good for her! Maybe I need to get out more. All my weekends lately have involved marking, or retail, or just collapsing. I’m starting to think I need a holiday. Greece maybe? Speaker_1: Greece sounds fantastic. We should all go. Although, considering my finances, instant coffee will likely be my vacation for the foreseeable future. By the way, did you ever finish that creative writing course? You mentioned wanting to write a novel. Speaker_2: I’m still chipping away at it. It's slow progress. Life gets in the way, you know? Work, family… it's hard to find the time. Plus, referencing is a nightmare. I keep getting lost in the MLA handbook. Speaker_1: Tell me about it! I'm supposed to be mentoring an undergraduate on a similar project, and I'm genuinely terrified of having to look at her bibliography. Right, I should probably head to my 9am. Don't want to be late and inflict more passive constructions on unsuspecting students. Speaker_2: Go for it! Good luck surviving the grading onslaught. And let’s grab coffee later this week – we need to dissect the Sarah engagement in detail. Speaker_1: Definitely. Sounds good. See you later!

Speaker_2: Right, so you put in… about one and a half cups of water for every cup of rice. See? Like this. Speaker_1: One and a half? That seems like a lot. Won't it be all soggy? Speaker_2: No, trust me. It absorbs it. It *needs* that much. We used to mess this up all the time when your Dad and I first moved in together. He'd just guess, and it was always either rock hard or… well, paste. Speaker_1: (chuckles) Dad and guessing. Sounds about right. So, one and a half. And then we just… boil it? Speaker_2: Boil it, then turn the heat right down, put the lid on, and let it simmer for about fifteen minutes. Don’t lift the lid! That’s the key. All the steam stays in. You lift the lid, you lose the steam, you end up with crunchy rice. Speaker_1: Right, lid on. Fifteen minutes. Got it. What about the curry sauce? Is that ready? Speaker_2: Nearly. I warmed it up, but it could do with a bit of a kick. I was thinking a finely chopped jalapeno? Speaker_1: Ooh, yeah! Good idea. They're pretty hot though, aren't they? Speaker_2: They are. That's why we only need a little bit. Though honestly, the sauce is a bit bland. I think they skimp on spices now. Remember that amazing Indian place we went to in Bristol? Speaker_1: Yeah! The one near the harbour? They did the best naan bread. Speaker_2: Exactly! And everything tasted…properly spiced. This stuff… feels like it’s got a lot of salt. I’m trying to be more aware of that kind of thing, you know? All that hidden salt and fat. Speaker_1: Yeah, Mum’s always going on about that. She used to read all the labels, checking everything. Speaker_2: It's important. It all adds up. Did you see that documentary about… oh, what was it called? About how much sugar is hidden in everything? It was horrifying. Speaker_1: No, I missed that. Was it on Netflix? Speaker_2: I think so. Anyway, back to the rice. Just keep an eye on it. Don't stir it. Honestly, it's the hardest part, resisting the urge to stir it. Speaker_1: Okay, okay. No stirring. It’s like… willpower training for cooking. Speaker_2: Precisely! Speaking of willpower, I saw Mrs. Henderson from next door at the butcher's today. She was complaining about the mince going off quickly. Apparently, it went grey yesterday. Speaker_1: Ugh. That's gross. Speaker_2: I know, right? She said it looked like it had a…a facial deformity. Speaker_1: (grimaces) Seriously? That’s a bit dramatic. Speaker_2: She *is* a bit dramatic. Still, makes you think doesn't it? About what’s actually *in* the meat. And how fresh it is. It’s made me think twice about getting it from there again. Although, their sausages are divine. Speaker_1: Yeah, the sausages are good. Did you get those vouchers for that Italian place? The ones from that magazine? Speaker_2: Oh yes! I stuck them on the fridge. Two for one on pizzas, I think. We could go next week, if you like. A reward for successfully cooking rice. Speaker_1: Sounds good! I’m starving already. And… wait, did you see that news report about the jellyfish on Bournemouth beach? Apparently, they're all stinging people. Speaker_2: Oh no! That sounds awful. Good job we’re not going there anytime soon. Right, rice. Fifteen minutes. No stirring. And try not to think about grey mince or stinging jellyfish. Just focus on dinner.

Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking, you know, about getting a telly for the room. Not a massive one, just something for… for watching stuff. Speaker_2: A telly? Seriously? You’ve been saying that for six months. You haven't even *looked* at prices. Speaker_1: I have! Sort of. I saw one in Argos, it was… fifty quid? Maybe seventy. But then I remembered I hadn’t sorted the broadband thing. Speaker_3: You need to sort that, honestly. You’re living in the Stone Age. How do you even… exist without internet? Speaker_1: I use your Wi-Fi when I’m here. And sometimes I go to the library. It’s fine. Speaker_4: It’s not fine, Liam. You’re supposed to be actively looking for work, and you need internet for that. Applications, research… everything. Speaker_1: I know, I know. It’s just… finding the money. And then actually sorting it. It’s a whole thing. Speaker_2: Have you even *applied* for any jobs this week? Honestly. Speaker_1: Don’t start, okay? I sent off two yesterday. Both at the pub. Bar work. Pretty sure I won’t hear back. Speaker_3: Pub work again? You have a degree, Liam! Speaker_1: Yeah, well, a degree in… Medieval History. Not exactly in high demand around here, is it? Speaker_4: Look, I get it’s frustrating. But you can’t just keep applying for the same thing and then being surprised when it doesn’t work. Maybe look at something completely different? Like, I’m looking at taking a course in social media marketing. Maybe something like that could open some doors. Speaker_1: Social media marketing? You? I thought you hated social media. Speaker_4: I do, mostly. But it's a skill, and it pays. And my work are actually funding it, so it’s a no-brainer. It's a bit stressful though, I'm swamped at work. Old Man Hemmings is breathing down my neck about everything. Said I wasn't “proactive” enough on my last report. Speaker_2: Hemmings is awful. He makes Mrs. Higgins from school look nice! Speaker_3: Speaking of school... How are your A-Levels going, Chloe? Are you stressing about applications yet? Speaker_2: It’s starting. I’ve got to write my personal statement. It's terrifying. Everyone says it has to be *so* perfect. Speaker_1: Just write about what you enjoy, yeah? Don't try to be someone you're not. And mention your volunteering. That always looks good. Speaker_4: He’s right. And don’t be afraid to ask for help. Your teachers are there for a reason. Though, knowing Mr. Davies, he'll probably just tell you to read more Dickens. Speaker_3: Did anyone else see that new series on Netflix? The one everyone’s talking about? Speaker_2: Which one? There's a million of them. Speaker_3: The one with the Vikings? It’s amazing! The costumes are incredible. Speaker_1: Vikings? Sounds a bit violent for me. I’m more of a… historical drama kind of guy. Something with lots of castles. And brooding lords. Speaker_4: Good luck finding that on Netflix, Liam. You’ll probably have to go back to the library. Speaker_1: Hey! I’m a man of refined tastes. And besides, I’m making shepherd’s pie. It'll be amazing. That's more culturally enriching than any Viking. I even used proper lamb, not just mince.

Speaker_1: Honestly though, I’m beat. This conference was… intense. Like, back-to-back meetings, constantly fixing things, dealing with speakers who decided they needed a completely different AV setup five minutes before they were due on stage. You know the drill. Speaker_2: Sounds stressful, love. You always take on too much, don’t ya? You've got to learn to delegate more. It’s alright saying yes to everything, but then you end up knackered like this. Are you even enjoying the job anymore? Speaker_1: I do, actually. When it’s *good* it’s really good. Meeting interesting people, seeing an event come together… it's satisfying. It's just… the sheer volume. And the people. Honestly, the egos. You wouldn’t believe. Speaker_2: Egos, eh? Always a problem. You get all sorts, don't ya? Remember old Mr. Henderson from down the road? Thought he was God's gift to gardening. Won a rosette at the village fête and acted like he'd won the Chelsea Flower Show. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, I remember! He used to lecture everyone on the proper way to prune roses. Bit of a character. But yeah, similar vibe at these conferences. These academics, they think because they’ve published a paper on, I don’t know, the socio-economic impact of garden gnomes, they’re suddenly royalty. Speaker_2: Garden gnomes! That’s a bit niche, even for academia. You need a holiday, that’s what you need. A proper one. Somewhere hot. Somewhere you can just lie by a pool and not think about logistics or AV equipment. Speaker_1: That sounds… amazing. I was thinking maybe a weekend away with the girls? Maybe Brighton? It’s not exactly the Maldives, but it’s a start. Speaker_2: Brighton’s good. Good for a laugh. Have you been keeping up with your running, by the way? You said you were trying to get back into it. Speaker_1: I try. Honestly, after work, the last thing I want to do is go for a run. I just collapse on the sofa with a glass of wine and Netflix. It's a vicious cycle. Speaker_2: Everything in moderation, eh? Although, you could try running *instead* of the wine occasionally! It’s good for the head, you know. Gets the endorphins going. Speaker_1: Easier said than done. You’ve always been good with the discipline, haven't you? Actually, how *are* you keeping? Still doing the daily walks? Speaker_2: Yeah, religiously. Keeps me sane. And it’s good to see people. Old Mrs. Peterson down the street, she’s a gossip, but she’s good company. Keeps me up to date on all the local goings-on. Apparently, young Timmy next door is getting married. Speaker_1: No way! Timmy? He’s only just left school! Time flies, doesn’t it? Honestly, it feels like yesterday we were all causing trouble in year ten. Speaker_2: Don’t remind me. Mr. Thompson nearly had a heart attack when you and Sarah Swinburne swapped the sugar and salt in the school canteen. Speaker_1: (Grinning) That was brilliant! Worth detention, definitely. Oh, hang on, I need to text Liam back. He’s asking if I want to go to that new escape room next week. Fancy joining us? It might be a good distraction from work. Speaker_2: An escape room? Sounds a bit stressful, doesn't it? Trapped in a room with a bunch of puzzles... No, I think I’ll stick with my walks and Mrs. Peterson’s gossip, thank you very much. But you go, enjoy yourself. Just try not to swap the sugar and salt *again*.

Speaker_1: Right, who’s doing the dishes? I’m not doing them again tonight. Honestly, it's like living with a pack of…well, never mind. Speaker_2: Not me. I’m revising for history. Big test tomorrow on… um… the Second World War. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Ah, the Second World War. A fascinating, albeit horrific, period. Remember, boys, history isn’t just dates and battles. It’s about understanding *why* things happened. And the consequences. Speaker_4: Can I just say, Hitler was a proper villain. Like, the worst. Speaker_1: Yes, darling, he absolutely was. A truly awful man. Now, back to the dishes. Nathan? Speaker_2: I said I’m revising! It's about the appeasement policy and the… Speaker_3: Leave him, love. He’s studying. I’ll do them. Honestly, you two, you'd think I was asking you to single-handedly build the pyramids. Speaker_1: Thank you, dear. Honestly, sometimes I wonder where they get it from. I mean, look at that beard you’re cultivating, Daniel. It’s… substantial. Speaker_3: It’s distinguished! I’m aiming for a George Clooney vibe. Besides, your mother likes it. Don’t you, darling? Speaker_1: It’s… a conversation starter. Though I do worry you look like a slightly disgruntled woodsman. Speaker_4: It looks cool, Dad. Speaker_2: Yeah, it’s alright. Though, everything you post on Instagram with it looks like a meme. Speaker_3: Everything I post? You’ve been monitoring my Instagram, have you? Speaker_2: No! I just... saw it on Lily’s feed. She follows you. Speaker_1: Oh, Lily. How *is* Lily? You haven’t mentioned her much lately. Speaker_2: She's good. We... we’re not really talking at the moment. Speaker_1: Oh. Oh dear. What happened? Speaker_2: It’s just… stuff. She’s been hanging out with Sophie a lot, and Sophie… well, Sophie thinks I’m a bit immature. Speaker_3: Sophie thinks everyone’s immature. She's fifteen. You're fourteen, right? This is all perfectly normal. Heartbreak, misunderstood feelings, questionable fashion choices… it’s all part of the teenage experience. Speaker_1: Daniel, don’t trivialize it. It's hard when a girlfriend dumps you. Even if it *is* because of Sophie. Speaker_3: I'm not trivializing it! I'm saying it’s a learning experience. It builds character. It prepares him for… well, for the nuanced world of adult relationships. Speaker_4: Did you used to get dumped a lot, Dad? Speaker_3: (Laughing) Let's just say I wasn’t always the smooth operator I am today. Your mother… she was very patient with me. She still is, thankfully. Speaker_1: Speaking of patience, have either of you remembered to book the tennis court for Saturday? I really want to have a game. Speaker_2: Oh, shoot. I completely forgot. Speaker_4: I was gonna ask you to do it, Mum. Speaker_1: Honestly! I swear, I do everything around here. Daniel? Speaker_3: I'll do it now. Leave it with me. Though, I warn you, my tennis skills are significantly more rusted than my facial hair is… substantial. Speaker_1: Just book the court. And maybe encourage Nathan to put down his history books for an hour. Fresh air wouldn't hurt him.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the sofa… it’s just *massive*. Didn’t realise how much space it would take up. Speaker_2: Did you get rid of the old one then? Or is it just… sofa city in your living room now? Speaker_1: Took it to the tip yesterday. Massive effort, that. Honestly, the queues were insane. Everyone clearly decided yesterday was ‘get rid of all your junk’ day. Speaker_3: The tip at High Lane is always rammed on a weekend. Absolute chaos. They need to sort that out. Speaker_2: It's always busy. I went a couple of weeks ago with some cardboard and had to queue for like, twenty minutes. Twenty minutes for cardboard! Speaker_1: Exactly! And then, the man unloading, he was just… grunt-y. Barely said a word. Just pointed at where to put it. Rude. Speaker_3: Oh, they can be like that. Doesn’t pay much, I suppose, dealing with other people’s rubbish all day. Still, a bit of politeness doesn't cost anything. Speaker_2: Speaking of dealing with other people’s stuff… did you hear about Sarah’s friend, Karen? Speaker_1: Oh, Karen? No, what’s happened? Her husband’s still poorly isn’t he? Speaker_2: Yeah, he’s… not great. But apparently, her washing machine broke down, and she ended up getting her mum to do all her washing. Like, *all* of it. Including… you know… things. Speaker_3: Oh, goodness me. That’s a bit much isn’t it? I mean, a few loads of normal clothes, fine. But everything? Speaker_1: Right? My mum would have a fit. She’s very particular about her washing machine. And who’s washed what in it. Speaker_2: Apparently, her mum was complaining about having to wash her son-in-law’s socks. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh, bless her. Family, eh? Always something. Remember Auntie Brenda and the Christmas pudding incident? Speaker_1: Oh god, don’t even *start* me on Auntie Brenda. She always got me those awful knitted tea cosies. Bright orange ones. Every. Single. Year. Speaker_2: My nan was the same with the scented candles. Lavender. Everywhere. You could smell it before you even got to the house. Speaker_1: It’s the thought that counts, I suppose. Though sometimes you wish people would just… ask what you want. Speaker_3: Your Grandad Harry was always good for that. He used to ask me straight: “What do you need, love? Don’t want to waste my money on something you don’t like.” Speaker_1: He was a good man, Grandad Harry. Speaker_2: So, did you see that new building they’re putting up near the train station? It's huge. What is it even going to *be*? Speaker_1: I think it's apartments. More overpriced flats. Honestly, Macclesfield doesn’t need more flats. Speaker_3: It’s ruining the character of the town, it is. All these modern buildings popping up everywhere. And the traffic! It's getting worse and worse. Speaker_2: And have you heard about the Beaver Scout Christmas party? Apparently, little Timmy swore. Right in front of Father Christmas! Speaker_1: Oh, no! Timmy? He’s normally such a quiet boy. Speaker_2: Apparently, another boy snatched his biscuit. Speaker_3: Oh, children. Always a drama. Reminds me of little Peter Davidson from primary school. Always getting into mischief. Ended up joining Network Scouts, that lad. Swore he was going to be an astronaut.

Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, the whole thing with work is just… draining. I mean, they’re calling it a “restructuring,” but we all know what that means. Speaker_2: Redundancy, love. It always means redundancy, doesn't it? Such a horrible word. Are you alright though? You sounded a bit stressed on the phone earlier. Speaker_1: Yeah, I’m okay. Just… processing. It’s not *definitely* happening yet, there’s a consultation period, but it doesn’t look good. They’re basically streamlining the project management roles. And I’ve only been there just over a year! Speaker_2: Oh, that’s awful, darling. After all the hard work you put in. You’ve always been so good at organising things. Honestly, I don't understand these companies sometimes. What are you thinking about doing? Speaker_1: Honestly? I have no idea. Start applying for everything and anything, I guess. It's just… demoralising. I was actually starting to enjoy it. Speaker_2: Well, you won’t be short of options, you’re bright and capable. You’ll find something else. So, enough about all that doom and gloom! How was your week? Did you manage to get to the gym? Speaker_1: I did! Went Tuesday and Thursday. Still feeling it, though. My legs are screaming. You should come with me sometime, it'd be good. Speaker_2: Oh, I don't know about that. I’m a bit past the energetic gym phase, I think! Though, I did walk to the shops instead of driving the other day, so I'm making *some* effort. Speaking of which, have you remembered to call Grandad? He was asking after you. Speaker_1: Oh, shoot! No, I haven’t. I meant to this morning, it completely slipped my mind. I’ll do it now, as soon as we get home. He was talking about forgetting to eat again, which is worrying. Speaker_2: He does that, doesn’t he? He gets so absorbed in his books. You need to remind him to at least have a proper lunch. And speaking of eating… I’m trying to cut down on biscuits. It’s a losing battle, I tell you. Speaker_1: I know the feeling! I’ve been craving chocolate all week. Stress-eating, clearly. What are your plans for the weekend? Anything exciting? Speaker_2: Not particularly, just a bit of gardening, maybe pop to the shops. Your Dad’s been talking non-stop about the house extension again. He’s got a whole Pinterest board dedicated to garden design now. It’s a bit obsessive! Speaker_1: Oh, good lord. He’s still on that? Is he actually going to *do* it, or is it just fantasy? Speaker_2: I honestly don’t know. He keeps changing his mind. One minute he wants a full-blown Japanese garden, the next he’s thinking a vegetable patch. He’s terrible at commitment. I might go browsing in town, need some new summer clothes now the weather’s finally picking up. Fancy coming with me? We could make a day of it. Speaker_1: That actually sounds really nice. Yes, definitely. A bit of retail therapy is *exactly* what I need. We can get lunch too, maybe somewhere with a really decadent chocolate cake… Speaker_2: Perfect. We'll make a plan then, won't we? Right, nearly there. Just past the turning for… Oh, honestly, look at that traffic!

Speaker_2: Right, nearly finished. Nearly finished. Just gotta get this… okay, there we go. Pasta’s on. You hungry? Speaker_1: Yeah, a bit. Is it just pasta again? Speaker_2: Well, what did you want? You didn’t say anything earlier. And Leo’s already eaten most of a banana, so… *(Leo, age 3, makes a happy gurgling sound and waves a piece of banana)* Speaker_1: I dunno. Something… different? Like, proper dinner? Speaker_2: *sighs* It’s pasta with tomato sauce and some bits of chicken in. It’s not exactly gruel, is it? Honestly, you’re a nightmare sometimes. Speaker_1: I didn’t ask for gruel! Speaker_2: Don't be ridiculous. Did you watch ‘Stick with Mick’ today? Speaker_1: Yeah, it was alright. He went to that… farm, didn't he? With all the sheep. Speaker_2: Good. Good for you. Keeping up with your cultural programme. Leo loves ‘Mick’. He shouts “Mick! Mick!” at the telly like he’s his best friend. Want to go swimming tomorrow? Speaker_1: Nah. Too crowded. Speaker_2: Not if we go early. We could be there for ten, before everyone else turns up. Speaker_1: Ugh. Too early. Can I just… stay in and play on the Xbox? Speaker_2: No. You need to get some fresh air. It’s the summer holidays! We need to *do* things. Your friend, Ollie, said he was going to the park with his dad. Speaker_1: Ollie’s dad is really boring. He just makes him dig holes. Speaker_2: He’s teaching him gardening! It’s good to learn things about nature. Speaking of which, I asked Mr. Doherty if you could maybe help him with his garden for a bit, earn a few quid. Speaker_1: What?! No way! I’m not weeding old man Doherty’s garden all summer. That’s… slave labour. Speaker_2: Don’t be dramatic. He said he'd pay you. It’s just a bit of tidying. Honestly, you spend too much time glued to that screen. *(Leo attempts to climb onto Speaker_2’s lap, babbling incoherently)* Speaker_2: Careful, little man! Okay, okay. What are you saying? Do you want to help mummy make dinner? See, *someone* wants to be helpful. Speaker_1: He’s three. He doesn't know any better. Speaker_2: He understands more than you give him credit for. Have you been practicing your guitar? Speaker_1: A bit. I’m trying to learn that… Japanese song. Speaker_2: Japanese? Where did you learn about Japanese songs? Speaker_1: On YouTube. It's…complicated. Lots of fast strumming. Speaker_2: Right. Well, maybe after dinner you can play me a bit. And then, we’re going to make a list of things you can do this summer. No more just sitting in your room. It's a deal? Speaker_1: Fine. But if I end up digging holes in Mr. Doherty's garden, I'm blaming you. Speaker_2: Just eat your pasta. Speaker_3: (Babbling) Mama, mama! More banana! Speaker_2: Okay, okay, Leo. One more tiny piece. And then it's dinner for you too. Honestly, you two…

Speaker_1: Right, so he’s just about to, isn’t he? This bit’s always good. The tension’s building… you reckon he actually gets away with it this time? Speaker_2: Nah, never. They *always* catch ‘em at the last minute. It's a bit predictable, innit? Still a good film though, proper classic. Reminds me of when I was a kid, always wanted to be a jewel thief, proper Ocean’s Eleven vibes. Speaker_1: (chuckles) Aye, everyone does. I wanted to be an archaeologist, digging up dinosaur bones. Then I realised it’s mostly just…dust. And paperwork. This is way more glamorous. Speaking of glamorous, have you seen that new Ridley Scott film? The one about Napoleon? Speaker_2: Heard bits and bobs. Joaquin Phoenix, yeah? Is it any good? My mam was on about it, said it’s historically inaccurate. Speaker_1: It's… a film, alright? Historically *inspired*, let’s say. Phoenix is brilliant, as always, but it’s a bit of a mess. Like, they gloss over a lot of stuff. And the battle scenes are just…loud. Reminded me of that time I went to the dentist. All drilling and shouting. Speaker_2: (laughs) That’s a mental comparison! Dentist and Napoleon’s battles. You’re alright, you. Though, yeah, a dodgy dentist is pretty terrifying. It'll ruin all other bagels for you. Speaker_

Speaker_1: Right, so this is the… the thing, isn’t it? Bit shiny. And cold. Feels proper Scandinavian this place, even the pub. Speaker_2: It *is* freezing, isn't it? Proper Nordic chill. Anyway, where’s the SIM ejection tool? Always the fussiest little thing to find. I swear they design them to deliberately get lost. Speaker_2: It’s in the little tray underneath the…blister pack stuff, I think. Here. Honestly, the packaging alone is a crime against trees. Speaker_1: Cheers. Right, SIM card in… oh, hold on. Is this… a different size SIM than the ones we usually get? It looks… smaller. Speaker_2: Nan-o-SIM, I think it’s called. They keep making them smaller and smaller. Like they’re trying to make them invisible. Good luck with your fingers, by the way. You’re gonna need them. Speaker_1: (Grunting) Right. Okay, that’s in. Now… what does this button do? Is this the power button? Or the… ejector seat button? Speaker_2: (Snorts with laughter) Definitely not the ejector seat button. It's power. Now it's asking about data privacy… terms and conditions… all the usual legal garble. Just accept it all, we haven't got all day. Speaker_2: Yeah, connect to the pub’s Wi-Fi. "PikkoMikkoGuest" I think it is. Password's on the till, if you can't find it. Then it’ll probably want you to create an account or log into an existing one. Do you want to use your Google account? Speaker_1: Let’s use Google. It’s less hassle. Although, I continually worry about how much data they collect… never mind. One battle at a time. Right… password… and… boom. There we are. Progress! Speaker_2: See? You’re a natural. Now, last bit – setting up a PIN or fingerprint access. Fingerprint is easier, don’t you think? Speaker_1: Yeah, fingerprint. Although I always feel a bit like I’m being scanned by the authorities. Speaker_2: (Smiling) It’s just your phone, Dad. Relax. Just place your finger on the sensor… there, see? Good to go. Right, all done. Now let's get yours set up. Speaker_2: Right, so Leo’s party. Are you still thinking superheroes? Speaker_1: Yeah! Definitely. It’s cool. Maybe…Spider-Man? Or Batman? Speaker_2: Mmm, those are good. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Finlay might prefer to watch from the sidelines, love. He’s still a little one. Speaking of little ones, what about birthday presents? Have you thought about what you want to get for Charlie? Speaker_1: Oh, yeah. He loves… Red Pandas, doesn't he? Speaker_2: He does! He’s absolutely obsessed. He told me yesterday they're his favourite animal in the whole world. Speaker_1: Right. Maybe a Red Panda cuddly toy? Or a book about them? Speaker_2: That’s a lovely idea. We could look online tonight. What’s *your* favourite animal then? Speaker_1: Malamooches. Speaker_2: Malamooches? What on earth are Malamooches? Speaker_1: They’re like, huge fluffy dogs. From Alaska! They pull sleds and stuff. They're really strong. I saw one on a documentary. Speaker_2: Oh, you mean Malamutes! Alaskan Malamutes. They are beautiful dogs, aren’t they? Much bigger than Poppy. Speaker_1: Yeah! Poppy’s good though. Even if she sheds everywhere. Speaker_3: (Points at Speaker_1 and babbles) Poppy! Speaker_2: He loves Poppy too. He’s always trying to pull her tail. Not allowed, of course. Anyway, back to the party. We need to decide on food. Sandwiches? Pizza? Speaker_1: Pizza! Definitely pizza. And cake. A big Superhero cake! Speaker_2: Okay, pizza and a superhero cake. Sounds good. I was thinking we might be able to fit in a trip to Granny’s during the school holidays. Are you excited about that? Speaker_1: Yeah, but it’s ages away. And I don't want to miss anything here. Speaker_2: I know, it feels like a long time. Maybe we can watch one of those Japanese films you like on the train? The one with the robot cat? Speaker_1: Ghibli? Yeah! That'd be good. But I want to play on my iPad too. Speaker_2: We'll have to ration screen time, won’t we? And maybe play some board games with Granny. Remember how much she likes Monopoly? Speaker_1: Ugh, Monopoly takes *forever*. Speaker_2: It does, doesn’t it? Oh! And you have gymnastics next week, don’t you? Are you looking forward to that? Speaker_1: It’s alright. I like the bouncing. But it’s hard. Speaker_2: It’s good exercise though, isn’t it? Speaker_1: Honestly though, Christmas at Nana’s was *always* mental. Not in a bad way, just… chaotic. Speaker_2: Chaotic is a polite word for it. It was a full-on assault on the senses. He’s the most laid-back person I know now. Speaker_3: Oh, he was a different man back then. Much more… fiery. Your Nana brought that out in him, I think. She had a way of provoking people with the most innocent-sounding questions. Speaker_4: It was a very… English Christmas, wasn’t it? All that tradition and formality. Completely different from how things are done elsewhere, I imagine. Speaker_1: Completely. I prefer a simple Christmas dinner. Though, I do remember one Christmas in Devon, we stayed at this little pub, and they did the most incredible seafood platter. That was a bit different. Speaker_1: Ugh, history was *brutal* today. Mr. Davies decided to spring a quiz on us. A quiz! On the Tudors! Speaker_2: No way! Seriously? He said he wasn’t going to do any more quizzes this term. Glitter. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Speaker_1: So, how was your week? Honestly, it feels like it’s flown by. And how’s young Thomas doing? Still causing mayhem at school? Speaker_2: Oh, don’t even start me on Thomas! Although, then what would I *do* with myself? Speaker_2: You'd be bored within a week, knowing you! You need the challenge. Though, seriously, you need to look after yourself. Even just someone to vent to. Speaker_1: Thank you, that’s very kind of you. I will. Honestly, you're a good friend. Right, changing the subject completely… I need to go to the building society tomorrow. They’ve messed up something with our savings account again. It's always something with banks, isn’t it? Speaker_2: Always. It's a nightmare. Do you want me to pop into the shops for you while I’m out? You always forget something. Speaker_1: Oh, that would be amazing, actually. Could you get some milk, and those oat biscuits Thomas likes? If he’s been a good boy, that is! Speaker_2: Ha! I’ll get them anyway. He’s a good lad, underneath all the mischief. And about cleaning, shall I do a full clean on Thursday like usual, or is there anything particular you’d like me to focus on? Speaker_1: Thursday is perfect. Honestly, just a general tidy is fine. I’m just trying to keep my head above water at the moment.

Speaker_1: Honestly, last night was *mental*. Proper rammed. You wouldn’t believe the amount of students trying to pre-drink in there before heading to the clubs. Speaker_2: Oh god, sounds chaotic. Was it a busy student night or something? I’m glad I’m just stuck with essays at the moment, sounds way more stressful than trying to understand post-structuralism.
