Speaker_1: This is actually really good. Better than I remember. Speaker_2: Told ya. Best Chinese in town, hands down. Though I still maintain Old Man Lee's used to be better…before he retired. Speaker_3: Oh, Old Man Lee's was *the* place. Remember when we were kids and we’d sneak in there after school? Speaker_4: And he’d always give us extra prawn crackers, even though Mum would kill us for having them. Good times. Speaker_1: Speaking of Mum…did anyone hear back about Auntie Carol’s funeral arrangements? Speaker_2: Yeah, Mum sent a WhatsApp. It’s next Friday, two o’clock. She wants us all there obviously. Bit grim, isn’t it? Speaker_3: Grim is an understatement. She was…a character. Always had a story, even if half of it was made up. Speaker_4: Absolutely. Remember that time she claimed she’d met Mick Jagger? Speaker_1: And she had a grainy photo as “proof.” It was clearly a cardboard cutout. Speaker_2: Classic Carol. Still, it’ll be nice to see everyone. Haven't seen cousin Dave in ages. He's still living up in Manchester, right? Speaker_3: Yeah, last I heard he was still battling with his housemates. Apparently, one of them leaves dirty dishes in the sink for *weeks*. Speaker_1: Oh, the horror! That’s a dealbreaker. Reminds me of living with Ben in uni. He thought the washing up fairy was real. Speaker_4: Haha, classic Ben. Always living in his own little world. Did you see that thing on the news about… what was it? The rising cost of… everything? Speaker_2: Yeah, depressing stuff. At this rate, we’ll all be living in cardboard boxes. Speaking of which, remember when Leo was obsessed with Bob the Builder? Speaker_3: Oh my god, yes! He’d run around with a little hard hat and shout "Can we fix it?" at everything. Speaker_1: (laughing) He even tried to ‘fix’ the garden fence with sticky tape. Speaker_4: Kids are brilliant. Hey, are any of you free to watch the cricket on Saturday? England are playing Australia. Could be a good game. Speaker_2: I might be up for that. Depending on how much gardening Mum ropes me into. Speaker_3: I’m in, definitely. Need a bit of sport in my life. Been stuck writing bids all week. It's soul destroying. Speaker_1: I'm free too. Though I wouldn't pretend to understand the intricacies of cricket. Mostly just enjoy the atmosphere and the snacks. Speaker_4: Perfect! We can order pizza, make a day of it. Anyone fancy going to see that new sci-fi film next week? The one with… the spaceships? Speaker_2: Oh, yeah, the one everyone’s raving about. I’m game. Speaker_3: Sounds good! Let’s see... I'll check my schedule and get back to you. Speaker_1: Right, more noodles then? I’m officially stuffed, but I don’t think I can resist. Hope this is to your liking! Let me know if you'd like me to adjust anything or continue the conversation. Speaker_4: And actually, speaking of things being a mess, has anyone seen my phone charger? I swear I left it in here last night, but it’s vanished. Speaker_1: Maybe it’s under the cushions? Classic charger hiding spot. Speaker_2: Or Leo’s probably nicked it to charge his tablet. He’s always scavenging for plugs. Speaker_3:Heehee. He is a little thief, isn’t he? But honestly I’m exhausted, I’m going to sneak off and watch some rubbish tv. Speaker_4: Fair enough. I'm gonna have a look for this charger again. This is really annoying, I've got a conference

Speaker_1: Honestly, Old Man Hemmings next door to Mum… he used to sunbathe in his garden wearing *nothing* but a pair of Wellington boots. Honestly! Mum was horrified, apparently, she’d draw the curtains religiously. Speaker_2: (Chuckles softly) Wellington boots, you say? Goodness me. People were different then, weren't they? Less…concerned with appearances. I remember old Mrs. Pritchard down the road in Wolverhampton. Always had a parrot on her shoulder when she went to the shops. A bright blue thing, squawking away. Caused absolute chaos in Woolworths, it did. Speaker_3: Oh, that’s brilliant! It’s the sort of thing you only read about now. Remember Auntie Mabel's obsession with rice krispy cakes? She’d eat a whole packet in one sitting, then complain she couldn't do up her shoes. Speaker_1: Oh, God, yes. And she’d always offer you one, even *after* you’d politely declined ten times. It was a compulsion. She said they were ‘good for your tummy’. Speaker_2: My sister Beatrice, now she had a peculiar habit. She collected thimbles. Hundreds of them! Filled drawers and drawers. Said each one had a story. I never understood it. She’d spend hours polishing them. Never understood where she got the time, always busy with the children. Speaker_3: It’s funny the things people latch onto, isn’t it? I’ve got a weird thing about scan-as-you-go at the supermarket. I actively avoid the self-checkouts. I feel like I'm being accused of theft every time I use one. Speaker_1: I get that. It's so impersonal. And it *always* needs assistance. Remember when we went to that new build estate near Plymouth, looking at houses? The insurance was ridiculous because of ‘potential flooding’ even though it was on a slight hill! Speaker_3: The whole thing was overpriced, anyway. And that tiny garden! I wouldn’t pay half what they were asking. Much happier with the slightly wonky fences and overgrown roses here. At least you feel like you're actually *in* a garden, not a postage stamp. Speaker_2: Gardens are important. My father, he was a keen gardener. Grew the most magnificent tomatoes. Said the secret was talking to them. I always thought he was a bit mad, but they *were* lovely tomatoes. He wouldn’t have trusted those driverless cars either, you know. Absolutely not. Said his driving was perfectly safe, thank you very much. Speaker_1: (Smiling) He probably was a very good driver, actually. Though I remember him getting completely lost in France once, convinced he could navigate by the stars. Speaker_3: Oh, that’s a wonderful story! I tried to learn French at school, but it just wouldn’t stick. All those silent letters… And then Uncle George went on that package holiday to Spain and came back complaining about the food. Said they hadn't seen a proper roast dinner in weeks. Speaker_2: (A contented sigh) It's good to reminisce, isn’t it? Brings back all sorts of memories. Though I still think Google should pay their fair share of tax. It's not right, taking advantage of the system like that. And those airfares… exorbitant! Remember when you could fly to Amsterdam for thirty pounds? Speaker_1: Those were the days. And remember when Dad used to cycle *everywhere*? Even to Exeter! Speaker_3: A man of iron! He’d have hated all this talk of electric cars, I reckon. He was a staunch petrolhead.

Speaker_1: Right, so this is the year of the dragon, apparently. Did you guys know that? Speaker_2: (Excitedly) Dragons are *amazing*! I drew one at school! It had, like, a million scales! Speaker_3: Mine had fire! Proper big flames coming out of its mouth. It was the best dragon ever. Speaker_1: Oh, fantastic! I’m glad you both enjoyed the drawing activity. We need to do more of those. It’s good to be creative. Did you learn anything else about Chinese New Year? Speaker_2: Miss Davies said it’s really lucky! And everything is red! Speaker_1: That’s right! Red symbolises good fortune and happiness. That’s why we're having noodles and spring rolls tonight – they're proper Chinese food! Though, I admit, I'm mostly making it because *someone* requested sweet and sour chicken. Speaker_3: (Grinning) It’s my favourite! Can we have extra prawns? Speaker_1: We’ll see. Let’s focus on being good first. Speaking of good, how was school today? Anything exciting happen? Speaker_2: We learned about planets! Saturn has rings made of ice! Isn't that cool? Speaker_1: That *is* cool! Which planet is your favourite? Speaker_3: I like Jupiter! It’s the biggest! And it has a giant red spot. It looks like a big eye. Speaker_1: That’s a good observation! You’re both little scientists. Now, remember we talked about practicing your instruments? How’s the piano going, Lily? Speaker_2: I learned a new song! It’s a really fast one, but I keep messing up the bit in the middle. Speaker_1: That’s okay, practice makes perfect! And you, Leo? Any progress with the drums? Are you still trying to be a rock star? Speaker_3: (Beaming) Yes! I can do a really loud roll now! It makes the windows shake. Speaker_1: (Slightly worried) Oh dear. Maybe not *too* loud a roll. We don’t want to upset the neighbours. Actually, did you remember to book Leo’s aerial hoop class for next week? Speaker_2: Oh! I forgot! Speaker_1: Right, I'll do it now. It’s getting so popular, they fill up quickly. It’s good you’re both trying different things. Keeps things interesting, doesn't it? Oh! Before I forget, did you guys watch Barbie and the Great Adventure on Saturday? Speaker_3: It was good! Barbie found a secret kingdom! Speaker_2: And she had a pet unicorn! It was *sparkly*! Speaker_1: Ah, wonderful! Glad you enjoyed it. Now, who wants to help me chop the spring onions? It’s almost time for our Chinese feast! And remember, wish for good luck…it's the year of the dragon, after all! Did you want me to continue the conversation or explore any specific aspect of it in more detail? Perhaps focus on one of the hobbies mentioned, or delve deeper into a particular topic like the Chinese New Year celebrations? . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ..........

Speaker_1: Honestly, this is…perfect. I needed this. London was just relentless for a bit there. Rain, deadlines, the general vibe… Speaker_2: Tell me about it! Though, I’m starting to miss the rain a little. This heat is…intense. I feel like I’m melting into my Aperol Spritz. Speaker_3: You two city folk. You complain about everything! It’s Rome, it’s *warm*. Embrace it! Though, yeah, it’s a bit much even for me. Still, beats Birmingham weather any day. Speaker_4: (With a broad Australian accent) Mate, you’re all soft. This is nothing. Try a summer in the Outback. You’ll be begging for a bit of drizzle, I tell ya. Speaker_1: Easy for you to say, you’re practically built for heat! Seriously though, this AirBnB was a steal. Right near the Pantheon, can’t beat the location. Speaker_2: It *is* lovely. Though, the host did warn us about the noise from the street. We’ll see how restful it actually is tonight. Speaker_3: Noise is part of the Rome experience, isn’t it? Just soak it up! So, dinner plans? I’m starving. I saw a little trattoria down the street that looked amazing. Family-run, proper Italian. Speaker_4: Sounds good to me. I’m up for anything, as long as there’s pasta involved. Honestly, I’ve already eaten my weight in carbs since we landed. Speaker_1: I’m in! I’ve been trying to brush up on my Italian, mostly just sticking to “Grazie” and “Prego” so far. It’s harder than it looks. Speaker_2: You’re doing better than me. I just point and smile a lot. It’s surprisingly effective. My Italian sounds like a strangled cat. Speaker_3: (Laughing) It’s the accent, love. No one will understand you! Although, honestly, most people here speak English anyway. Speaker_4: Yeah, and the ones who don’t are just happy you’re *trying*. Makes a big difference. Speaking of accents, I had a bloke try to tell me this morning I was actually American. Said I sounded like someone from California. Speaker_1: No way! You've got the strongest Aussie accent I’ve ever heard. Speaker_4: Tell that to the bloke! It’s the sun, I reckon. It messes with people’s ears. Speaker_2: Maybe. Though, I've noticed I'm starting to pick up little bits of Italian just from listening to people. It's like osmosis. Speaker_3: It does happen. My Nonna, she lives just outside Venice. I spent summers with her as a kid and even now, bits and pieces just come back to me. It’s weird. Speaker_1: That's lovely. I wish I'd had more opportunities to be immersed like that. My family's been in London for generations. Reliable, boring London. Speaker_2: Hey, London's great! Just…sometimes you need to escape. So, trattoria it is? Shall we head there now, or give it another half an hour? Speaker_4: Let's go! I'm already picturing the tiramisu. Speaker_3: Lead the way, then. I'm trusting you two to navigate. I have a terrible sense of direction, especially after a couple of Spritzes. Speaker_1: Don’t worry, I’ve got Google Maps. Though honestly, even *that’s* been a bit wonky here. Rome seems to actively resist being mapped. Speaker_2: That sounds about right. It’s a city that wants to be discovered, not directed. Let's go make some discoveries.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the planning for Chloe’s hen do is stressing me out. It’s just…a lot. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! Everyone has such strong opinions. I just want it to be fun for her, you know? Not a Pinterest-perfect disaster. Speaker_3: Exactly! My cousin’s hen do last year was *intense*. There were itineraries, colour schemes, choreographed dances… I nearly died of second-hand embarrassment. Speaker_4: Oh god, choreographed dances are my nightmare. Chloe would hate that. She’s more of a relaxed pub quiz and cocktails kind of girl. Speaker_1: That’s what I keep saying! But then her mum is suggesting a spa day, and her aunt wants a fancy dress theme, and… it’s endless. I’m trying to steer it towards something manageable, like maybe a crafting afternoon? Speaker_2: Ooh, a crafting afternoon! That’s a good shout! We could do flower crown making, or macramé… Or even decorate cupcakes! Speaker_3: Cupcake decorating sounds fun! I’m surprisingly good at icing, if I do say so myself. I made a three-tiered cake for my nephew’s birthday. It was…a learning experience. Speaker_4: (Laughing) A learning experience? That sounds ominous. Hopefully it didn’t end in a kitchen covered in frosting. Speaker_3: Let’s just say there was a *significant* amount of leftover icing. And a very sticky floor. Speaker_1: Okay, maybe stick to individual cupcakes then. But the crafting idea’s good! We could do everything at Rosie and Ali Bonds, right? Plenty of space. Speaker_2: Definitely! They do amazing coffee and cake there anyway. And it’s pretty central for everyone. Speaker_4: Perfect! I can take on sourcing the craft supplies. I’ve got a friend who owns a craft shop, I’m sure I can get a discount. Speaker_1: Oh, you are a lifesaver! That would be amazing. Okay, crafting at Rosie and Ali Bonds…that feels much more Chloe. Have you guys heard from Sarah lately? She was meant to be sending me a list of people who are definitely coming. Speaker_3: I think she was baking a cake yesterday, so she was probably covered in flour and ignoring her phone. That’s Sarah. Speaker_2: Classic Sarah. She gets so absorbed in baking. It’s adorable. Though I did hear she tried to make macarons and they completely collapsed. Speaker_4: Oh no! Macarons are the ultimate baking challenge. I tried once. It was a disaster. They looked like sad little pancakes. Speaker_1: Okay, we'll circle back with Sarah later. Right now, I need a caffeine boost and a slice of cake. This hen do is seriously draining my energy. Speaker_2: Agreed. Caffeine and cake are essential. And maybe a detailed list of who’s contributing what, so I don’t end up doing everything myself. Speaker_3: We've all been there! Let's divide and conquer. What needs doing? I'm happy to help with decorations, or even just making a playlist. Speaker_4: I can deal with the venue booking and the craft supplies. And I’ll pester Sarah for that guest list. Speaker_1: You guys are the best. Seriously. Chloe’s so lucky to have us. Let’s make this hen do amazing, but, you know… without the stress-induced breakdowns. (All laugh) Speaker_2: To Chloe! And to surviving hen do planning! (They raise their coffee cups)

Speaker_1: Right, so you reckon this much chilli is good for a curry for four? Seems a lot, doesn't it? Speaker_2: Nah, it's fine. You were a bit stingy last time, remember? Mum complained it wasn't spicy enough. And she *loves* spice. Speaker_1: She just likes to complain, that's her hobby. Honestly, I thought I put loads in. Still, better too much than not enough, I suppose. Are you sure we’ve got enough rice? I feel like we always run out. Speaker_2: Yeah, there's a big bag in the cupboard. I checked. You worry too much, you know? It's just rice. Speaking of running out of things, I think I’m coming down with something. Speaker_1: Oh no, what’s up? You sound a bit croaky. Speaker_2: Yeah, my throat’s killing me. And I've got a headache, and I feel all achy. I was hoping to get a decent night's sleep before teaching tomorrow, but it doesn't look like it. Speaker_1: Blast. That’s awful. You need to look after yourself. Maybe take some Lemsip? You were saying you were thinking about going to Berlin next month, right? Is that still on? Speaker_2: It is, but if I’m still feeling rough then… I don’t know. I've already booked the flights, though. And the hotel. It’s a weird little place, apparently, like a converted warehouse. Speaker_1: Oh yeah? Sounds cool. Better than another chain hotel, eh? I stayed in one in Manchester last week, absolutely soulless. Little plastic everything, all beige. Speaker_2: Beige is the enemy. That’s a good motto. This place in Berlin has exposed brick and everything. Apparently, it's right near a really good market. I’m hoping to try some proper German sausages. Speaker_1: Now you’re talking! You need to fuel up for all that sightseeing. You’ll be walking miles. You and your need to “experience the culture”. Speaker_2: Hey! It’s important! Plus, I need to practice my German. Although, I’m pretty sure I’ll just end up pointing and smiling. Speaking of fueling up, are you chopping those onions or just staring at them? Speaker_1: Chopping! Chopping! Just… contemplating their spherical perfection. They’re making my eyes water, though. It's a conspiracy, I tell you. Onions are trying to defeat humanity. Speaker_2: Dramatic much? Just wear your glasses. And maybe a gas mask. Seriously though, how did you get on with that presentation you were doing for work? You were stressing about it all last week. Speaker_1: It went okay. It was a bit nerve-wracking, but the client seemed happy. They even ordered another batch of designs. Which means more work, obviously. But hey, pays the bills, right? I'm thinking of trying to make my own bread this weekend. Speaker_2: Good on you! I've been meaning to get into baking, but I’m hopeless in the kitchen. I usually revert to beans on toast when I'm left to my own devices. Don’t tell Mum. She thinks I’m a culinary genius. Speaker_1: Your secret’s safe with me. Right, onions are done. What’s next on the list? And go easy on the chilli, yeah? Just in case Mum’s tastebuds have evolved. Speaker_2: Ha! Deal. Next is the ginger and garlic. And don’t worry, I’ll monitor the chilli situation. We don't want a repeat of the Great Curry Incident of 2022.

Speaker_1: Right, shopping list. Milk, definitely. And eggs. How many eggs do you think? A dozen? Speaker_2: A dozen's good. We'll use them for the quiche, won't we? And I fancy a victoria sponge. Oh, and apples. Braeburn, if they have them. Speaker_1: Braeburn it is. Anything else immediately springing to mind? Oh! Biscuit tin's looking rather empty. Digestives? Speaker_2: Yes, digestives. And those nice ginger snaps. You know, the ones that crumble everywhere? Speaker_1: The ones that get into the carpet for weeks! Yes, I know them well. Speaking of things that crumble… did you see Brenda’s birthday card? She put she was 65! She’s clearly lost track. She’s at least seventy, if not more. Speaker_2: Oh, Brenda. She’s always been a bit… optimistic. Remember when she insisted she was younger than me, even though we’re twins? Speaker_1: Goodness, yes! That was a stand-off. It’s ridiculous, isn’t it? The age on the card. It’s just a number, really. Speaker_2: It is. Though, I did feel a bit put out when Ethel sent me one with “70 and fabulous” on. Seventy! Still feels… a lot. Speaker_1: Oh, don't. We're getting there, aren't we? Anyway, I was thinking of getting those calendar fobs for the grandchildren. The ones with their pictures on? Speaker_2: Oh, lovely idea. They always like those. Little Leo would adore one with his dinosaur on. Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s a useful present, as well. They can put them on their keyrings. It reminds me, when I was volunteering at the school, they were doing such lovely art. All the glitter and paint. It was a complete mess, of course, but so creative. Speaker_2: They used to do that at my school. Remember making those paper chains? Always ended up covered in glue. And the smell of plasticine… Speaker_1: Oh, the plasticine! Absolutely vile smell, but we loved it. And the hockey boots! Remember being made to polish those things until you could see your face in them? Speaker_2: Horrendous. My fingers were always aching. And the smell of the leather polish! Ugh. It’s a wonder anyone took up hockey. Speaker_1: It truly is. Oh, I was reading about that chap, David, from university. He’s working at the computing museum now. Apparently, they're desperate for volunteers. Speaker_2: Really? That sounds interesting. They've a huge collection, haven't they? All those early computers… Speaker_1: Apparently, they’re getting people to help catalogue everything, and sort of… document their history. He was saying they need someone who remembers how things used to be used. You know, before everything was touch screen and cloud based. Speaker_2: Well, I certainly remember the days of floppy discs and dial-up internet! It took an age to download anything. Speaker_1: Ages! And the sheer size of the computers! I was thinking, we should donate some of our old equipment. That old Amstrad, perhaps? It still works, I think. Speaker_2: Oh, yes! The Amstrad. That thing was state-of-the-art at one point. They’d probably be thrilled to have it. That’s a good idea. Speaker_1: He said they're trying to create a real social history of computing, not just the technical side. How it impacted everyday life. You know, like how it changed the way we communicated. Speaker_2: Absolutely. It’s remarkable how quickly everything has changed. I remember when a mobile phone was the size of a brick! And cost a fortune. It is a fascinating thing to learn about.

Speaker_1: So, Old Man Hemmings next door, apparently he’s been complaining about the lights on the shed. Says they’re too bright. Speaker_2: Oh, really? He’s always moaning about something, isn’t he? Honestly, a bit of light isn’t hurting anyone. Especially not in December. Speaker_3: You'd think, wouldn't you? It’s not like you've installed a landing strip! Though knowing him, he’d probably complain about that too, if it brought more traffic. Did he actually *speak* to you, or just to…well, anyone who’d listen? Speaker_1: Spoke to Margaret, apparently. She told Brenda, who told me. So it’s gone the full Holsworthy rumour mill route. Said he couldn't sleep. Dramatic, really. Speaker_2: Men. Honestly. What did you say when you heard? Speaker_1: I just laughed. Margaret said I should probably just dim them a bit to keep the peace. Which I’ll probably do, rather than a full-blown feud with the most miserable man in Devon. Still, seems a bit much. Speaker_3: It does. Especially considering his garden looks like a jungle. You could lose a small child in there. A little shed light isn’t exactly a hazard. Speaker_2: Speaking of gardens, have you had a chance to have a proper look around yours yet? Is it…overgrown, like everyone says? Speaker_1: Overgrown is an understatement. It’s been…neglected. The previous owners clearly weren’t gardeners. It’s mostly brambles and weeds at the moment, but there are some lovely old apple trees. And a surprisingly productive rhubarb patch. Speaker_3: Oh, rhubarb! Wonderful. You’ll have to make crumble, won’t you? Speaker_1: Definitely. Though I’ll need a machete to get to it first. Seriously, I spent an hour just clearing a patch so I could see where the fence actually *was*. Speaker_2: You’ll get there. It's a project. You and I can do a gardening day together, you know. I'm fairly good at weeding. Though I wouldn't say I'm a gardener, exactly. More of a…weed assassin. Speaker_1: That would be fantastic, actually. I’m not sure I’m up to tackling it all on my own. It feels a bit daunting. It needs a proper plan. Speaker_3: Have you met the lady from number seven yet? The one with the roses? They’re absolutely stunning. She’s a proper gardening guru, apparently. Speaker_1: No, not yet. But I’ve seen her out and about. Always carrying secateurs. She looks…intense. Speaker_2: (laughing) Intense is a good word for it. But she knows everything about gardening. She’ll give you advice whether you want it or not. Speaker_1: That's good to know. I might have to seek her out, then. Though I might pack earplugs. What about the pub? Have you managed to get down to The Farmers yet? Speaker_3: We did! Last night, actually. It was buzzing. Really friendly atmosphere. And the food was excellent. Speaker_2: Oh good! I was hoping it wasn't just me imagining it was a good local. We need a good local. Speaker_1: They do a decent Sunday roast, apparently. I'm thinking of giving it a try next week. Though I’ll have to book, I suspect. It sounds popular. It’s a bit of a walk, though…

Speaker_1: Right, so I’ve been looking at getting a new graphics card, yeah? For the PC. Speaker_2: Oh aye? Which one? Don't tell me you're finally upgrading from that… fossil you’ve got. Speaker_1: Harsh, but fair. It’s seen better days. I was thinking the RTX 4070. Saw a review online, seems decent. And it’s only… well, only £550. Speaker_2: *Only* £550? You’re mental. You’ve been skint for weeks, moaning about not being able to afford a takeaway. Speaker_1: I’m prioritising! A takeaway is temporary satisfaction. A graphics card is… investment in my future! Potential stream content! Speaker_2: Potential stream content that nobody will watch because you'll be too busy complaining about lag on a £550 graphics card. Speaker_1: You’re a real ray of sunshine, you know that? Anyway, I found this website, ‘TechDealsUK’ or something. They’ve got it on offer, but the reviews are…mixed. Lots of complaints about delivery times. Speaker_2: Of course they are. It’s always the way. Everything online is either a scam or takes three weeks to arrive. Remember that phone case I ordered? Still waiting for it. Speaker_1: Oh god, yeah. The one with the glitter? That's been months now. I swear it’s circling the globe. Speaker_2: Probably. Speaking of online shopping… did you see that advert on TikTok for those weighted blankets? Apparently they're like, the best thing ever for anxiety. Speaker_1: Weighted blankets? Sounds…claustrophobic. I get anxious *thinking* about being weighed down. Speaker_2: No, it’s supposed to be comforting. Like a hug. I was thinking of getting one. Might help me actually get some sleep before these exams. Speaker_1: Fair enough. You've got proper stuff to worry about, unlike me and my…gaming ambitions. What are you watching on telly tonight? Anything good? Speaker_2: There’s that new crime drama starting, ‘Silent Shadows’ or something. Seems alright. Mum’s already claimed the living room though, she's got that baking show she’s obsessed with. Speaker_1: Oh, 'Great British Bake Off: Professionals'? She's been banging on about that for weeks. The drama! The pastries! Speaker_2: Exactly. It’s more exciting than my actual life right now. Seriously though, you should actually apply for some jobs. That online application for the supermarket was easy enough. Speaker_1: (Sighs) I did, remember? They haven’t even *looked* at my application. It’s been two weeks. They probably think a history degree is a threat to their business model. Speaker_2: Just keep applying. Something will come up. And maybe… just maybe… put the graphics card on hold for a bit? Speaker_1: Fine, fine. Maybe. But if I see another good deal… don't judge me. Speaker_2: I’ll judge you relentlessly. Now, pass me my charger. My phone’s about to die, and I need to stalk TikTok for weighted blanket recommendations. Speaker_1: Coming right up. You’re hopeless. Speaker_2: I know. That’s why I love you. Speaker_1: Smooth. Speaker_2: I practice. Now, charger, please. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Here. Take it before you start hyperventilating.

Speaker_2: So, have you managed to get any of the heating sorted then, Dad? It must be freezing in here still. Speaker_1: Oh, it’s a right palaver, I tell you. The bloke came round, said it needs a new pump. A new *pump*! Sounds expensive. He’s coming back on Tuesday, said he might be able to get one quicker if he knows I’m desperate. Desperate is an understatement! It’s like living in a fridge. Speaker_3: Oh, you poor thing. That sounds awful. Can’t you put the electric fire on in the living room, just to take the chill off? Speaker_1: I can, but it’s expensive, isn’t it? Not the way to run a house, relying on electric fires. I’m hoping this pump thing doesn’t cost the earth. It's all these old houses, you know? Built to last, they say, but everything falls apart eventually. Speaker_2: Mum, are you making lunch? I’m absolutely starving. Walking around looking at paint samples works up an appetite, you know. Speaker_3: Just finishing off some soup. Tomato and basil. It’s simple, but warming. Bit of crusty bread with it. Will that do? Speaker_2: Sounds perfect, thanks. So, Dad, you’ve been planning this coastal walk, haven't you? When are you thinking of doing it? Speaker_1: I was thinking next week, sometime. Depends on the weather, of course. And the heating! Speaker_1: Right, so I was reading this article about lab-grown meat, like, actual “shmeat” as they’re calling it, and it’s… it’s weirding me out a bit. Speaker_2: Oh, yeah? Just grown in a vat. Feels… off. Speaker_1: Exactly! And the ethical side of it feels muddled. Like, we're trying to avoid hurting animals, but isn’t there something… unsettling about creating life just to, well, consume it? Speaker_2: But isn't the current system *worse*? The conditions in factory farms are horrific. And the amount of land and water used… It's massively unsustainable. Surely, a controlled environment, even if it *is* a vat, is the lesser evil? This feels like a way for them to have their steak and eat it too, without actually confronting their consumption. Speaker_2: That’s a bit cynical, isn’t it? Some people genuinely want to reduce harm but still enjoy the taste. It could be a good compromise. I mean, I’m mostly vegetarian, but I do sometimes crave a good burger. Speaker_3: It's the whole hunting vs. abattoir thing for me. I understand people hunt to eat, there's a level of respect for the animal, it’s a quick death. Okay, moving away from existential dread, and back to actual cooking. Are you putting enough turmeric in this? It needs a kick. Speaker_2: I thought I did… it’s just a little bit. It might be a bit quicker even with the roadworks. Speaker_2: Hmm, good shout. Let's check the traffic on my phone. It looks like the A1 is backed up for miles. A19 it is. Speaker_1: Champion. Speaker_2: Alright. Let’s get some music on. Anything you fancy? Speaker_1: Nah, you pick. I’m happy with anything that isn’t country. Speaker_2: Deal. How about some Arctic Monkeys? Speaker_1: Perfect. Speaker_2: Sorted. Speaker_1: Oh, nearly forgot. Did you see the cricket scores from last night? Speaker_2: Did you see… Oh god, yes. England absolutely annihilated… never mind. Speaker_1: Right okay, so who's actually going to *do* the ordering? Because last time, Leo, you spent ten minutes debating the merits of different spring roll fillings and we ended up with nothing. I was thinking Kung Pao chicken… Speaker_2: Definitely that. And a portion of ribs. Proper ribs, not those pathetic little things some places serve. Speaker_1: (into phone) …and ribs, yes, please. Proper ribs… (to Leo and Sarah) He's giving me a weird look. Speaker_3: Just tell him we know our ribs. It's important. Speaker_1: (into phone) …yes, we *know* our ribs. Okay… and some spring rolls. Just… standard spring rolls. No lengthy debates. Speaker_2: Actually, can you ask if they do those duck spring rolls? The crispy ones? They’re amazing. The crispy kind? … Oh, you do? Fantastic… (to Leo) See? Fantastic. Speaker_3: You are *enabling* him, you know that? How long will it be? … 45 minutes? Perfect. Thank you. (hangs up) Speaker_2: Victory! Extra chips and duck spring rolls! My culinary genius has prevailed. Speaker_3: We’ll see about that when the bill comes. And just promise me you won’t try to steal all the chips again. Speaker_1: Right. Now, who’s putting on a film? Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of the NHS right now… it’s just relentless, isn’t it? I was talking to a colleague, Dr. Hayes, and she was saying the waiting lists for even basic things are just… astronomical. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I'm seeing it firsthand every day. Though, honestly, I’m starting to wonder if a sonnet about the NHS waiting times would raise more awareness than any petition. Speaker_2: (chuckles) You might be onto something there! A tragic verse, perhaps? Though I suspect even Shakespeare couldn’t cut through the red tape. It’s not just the waiting, it's the sheer *exhaustion* of the staff. Everyone's completely burnt out. Speaker_1: It's a system under immense strain. I’ve been reading about the Finnish healthcare system, you know? They seem to have a much more preventative approach. Less firefighting, more… well, actually looking after people *before* they get to crisis point. Speaker_2: Finland. Always held up as the ideal, aren’t they? Everything seems to work so well there. I wouldn’t mind a trip, just to see it in action. Though even then, I suspect it's a different cultural mindset as much as anything. Speaker_1: Absolutely. It’s not as simple as just transplanting a system. Speaking of different cultures, have you had any more trouble with the neighbours? The ones with the… enthusiastic karaoke? Speaker_2: Oh, don't even *start* me on them. It was worse last night. They were belting out some German oompah band song at two in the morning. Two! I considered calling the police, but honestly, what are they going to do? It's just… constant. Speaker_1: (wincing) Oh dear. That does sound… energetic. I recognise the feeling, though. When we first moved here, Mrs. Higgins next door decided to take up bagpipes. Bagpipes! The noise was unbelievable. It took a while, and a very carefully worded letter, to gently persuade her to limit her practicing to reasonable hours. Speaker_2: A letter? I've tried being polite. I’ve tried leaving a note. They just seem to think I'm complaining about their “enjoyment”. Honestly, sometimes I wonder if they even *have* neighbours. Speaker_1: It’s infuriating. And you have kids to think about, too. They need their sleep. Perhaps a little passive aggression is required? Like, deliberately mowing the lawn at 6 am on a Sunday? Speaker_2: (laughing) Tempting. Very tempting. But I'd probably end up in a full-blown neighbourhood feud. No, best to just document everything and try to remain… civil. Though my levels of civility are wearing thin, I can tell you that much. It's just stressful, you know? Work is stressful, the NHS is stressful, and even *home* is stressful. Speaker_1: I understand completely. It's just... life, isn't it? Throwing curveballs at every turn. At least we have a shared appreciation for a good dose of Scouse humour to get us through it all.

Speaker_1: …and then young Kevin, bless him, says to me, “Sir, is ‘ironic’ really using a word you don’t know to sound clever?” Cheeky bugger. Honestly, these students. Speaker_2: Ha! Good lad, that one. Sounds like a bright spark. They’re alright, the youngsters, if you give ‘em a chance. Though, mind, they don’t know the value of a hard day’s graft, do they? Everything’s handed to ‘em on a plate these days. Speaker_1: It’s a different world, isn’t it? Though, to be fair, finding that ‘graft’ ain’t exactly easy. I was reading about that new welfare scheme… the one where they expect folk to apply for a hundred jobs a month. Speaker_2: A hundred! What’s the point of that? You’ll spend more time filling in forms than actually *doing* a job. It’s just a way to wear people down, make ‘em give up. They want to push ‘em all onto Universal Credit, that’s what it is. Speaker_1: Seems that way, doesn't it? My wife was saying the same. She works at the Citizen's Advice Bureau, so she’s hearing it all first hand. The stories are… grim. Speaker_2: Grim, aye. Grim. Back in my day, if you wanted work, you went to the docks. Hard work, mind, but it were honest. Now… it’s all call centres and temporary contracts. And these agency fellas taking a cut of everything. Robbing buggers, the lot of ‘em. Speaker_1: Speaking of robbing… did you hear about old Mrs. Patterson down the road? Someone tried to break into her house last night. Speaker_2: No! Old Maggie? That’s terrible! Is she alright? Speaker_1: The police caught ‘em, thankfully. Apparently, a couple of lads from down the street. Said they were “looking for quick money.” The police were round all morning, forensic team and everything. Speaker_2: Always the same. Lazy buggers. Never worked a day in their lives. It’s this immigration, you know. They come over here, don't bother learning the language, just cause trouble. Speaker_1: Now, now, that’s a bit harsh, isn’t it? I’ve got several international students, lovely lads and lasses. Work hard as anything. It’s not fair to tar everyone with the same brush. Speaker_2: Oh, I don't mean *all* of ‘em. But there’s too many, that’s what I say. Too many coming over here, taking our jobs, stretching the resources. It weren't like this in my day, you know. We looked after our own. Speaker_1: Things change, don’t they? My daughter’s talking about moving to Berlin with her boyfriend. She’s a graphic designer, says there’s more opportunity there. Speaker_2: Berlin, eh? Fancy that. Still got family over there, did your mother? I remember her telling me stories about…what was his name now… her brother? Speaker_1: Uncle Klaus. Yes, she used to talk about him a lot. He was a carpenter, apparently. Lived through the war, saw some terrible things. Speaker_2: Terrible times. You hear stories, don't ya? Makes you appreciate what we’ve got, even when it's a bit rubbish. Still, better than being in a war zone, wouldn’t you say? Perhaps that lad Kevin should go and live in a warzone, then he’ll know about hard work! Ha! Speaker_1: (Chuckles) You’re a character, you are. A proper Liverpool character. I’ll tell you, sometimes I think you’re the reason I moved back here. For the stories, if nothing else.

Speaker_1: Right, so I genuinely spent half of yesterday afternoon trying to explain to my nan what a corpus actually *is*. It was… a challenge. Speaker_2: Oh god, the grandparents question. I’ve been there. Mine think I just… write dictionaries? Or something? It's close enough I suppose. Speaker_3: My mum just nods and smiles. I think she thinks it sounds important, even if she hasn’t a clue. She asked if it involved a lot of numbers. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) That's a classic. My family mostly just assume anything related to language is vaguely related to teaching English to people, which… isn’t *wrong,* exactly, but also isn't *right*. It’s a simplification. Speaker_5: I tried explaining the concept of collocation to my dad, a retired mechanic, and his eyes just glazed over. Then he asked if it was anything like ‘finding the right spanner for the job’. I gave up. Speaker_1: That’s brilliant, actually. A good analogy. Though horrifyingly inaccurate. Did anyone catch the email about the new server space? Seems a bit… limited. Speaker_2: I did. It's definitely tight. I’m already concerned about the next big data dump from the ‘Teen Talk’ project. We’re going to be scrambling for room. Speaker_3: It's always the Teen Talk data, isn't it? They just *talk* so much. Everything is documented. It’s a researcher’s dream and a server manager’s nightmare. Speaker_4: It’s amazing data though, honestly. The shifts in slang are fascinating. Have you noticed the resurgence of ‘rizz’? I saw it used in a academic paper the other day. A *serious* academic paper. Speaker_5: Oh god, 'rizz'. It makes me feel ancient. I’m pretty sure I saw someone using it unironically on LinkedIn. The world is ending. Speaker_1: LinkedIn 'rizz'? Oh no. That *is* a bad sign. Right, so, lunch plans for Friday? Thinking that new Thai place near the station? Apparently, the pad see ew is phenomenal. Speaker_2: Ooh, yes! I've heard good things. Count me in. I need a proper spice fix. Speaker_3: Sounds good to me. I’m free. Speaker_4: I'm in too. Although, fair warning, I’ll probably order everything on the menu and then complain I’m too full. It’s a habit. Speaker_5: You and me both, honestly. Pad see ew sounds amazing. Perfect end to a week of dealing with metadata. It's truly a glorious thing. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Okay, pad see ew it is. And a preemptive apology to our stomachs. Speaker_2: Excellent. We can strategise about the server space over noodles. It’ll be a productive Friday. Speaker_3: And possibly involve some slightly panicked emailing. Speaker_4: Always the panicked emailing. It’s the Corpus life. Speaker_5: Cheers to that. Cheers to panicked emailing, questionable slang, and surprisingly good Thai food. Speaker_1: Cheers! Speaker_2: Cheers! Speaker_3: Cheers! Speaker_4: Cheers! Speaker_5: Cheers!

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the recommendations algorithm on that platform is just… broken. It keeps suggesting me stuff I’ve already watched, or documentaries about competitive cheese rolling. Seriously. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Competitive cheese rolling? That’s a niche interest. Though, I did fall down a YouTube rabbit hole of extreme ironing once. Don't ask. Speaker_1: Extreme ironing? Right. That sounds… exhausting. It's just, I'm trying to broaden my horizons, you know? I want to watch something internationally acclaimed, something *subtitled*, and it just keeps offering me repeats of “Homes Under the Hammer.” Speaker_2: Subtitled, eh? Good for you. Better than anything I achieved with Mandarin. It’s funny, isn’t it? How language learning highlights cultural differences? It’s not just about the grammar, it’s about how people *think*. Speaker_1: Absolutely. It’s like, some languages even have different ways of conceptualizing time. And I've been thinking about teaching, actually. My uni department asked if I'd be interested in assisting with the first-year undergrads next semester. Speaker_2: Oh, really? That’s good, isn’t it? A bit of experience outside your PhD work. You’d be good at that. Remember how patient you were explaining statistical modelling to my aunt at Christmas? She thought a p-value was something you ordered at a pub. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) That was… a challenge. But yeah, I think I'd enjoy it. It might even make me better at explaining my own research. Which, let's be honest, is something I desperately need to work on. It all feels so… abstract sometimes. Speaker_2: I know the feeling. I spent an hour today trying to explain my work on protein folding to my mum. She just kept asking if I was finding a cure for cancer. Speaker_1: (Winces) Oh dear. The pressure! You need to give her a very carefully worded explanation. Speaker_2: I tried! Honestly, she's convinced I'm secretly working on something world-changing. I should just let her think that. It makes her proud. Actually, speaking of things academic... are you free next week? There's a talk at the Royal Geographical Society on cultural representations of the Amazon rainforest. I thought you might find it interesting. Speaker_1: Oh, that *does* sound good. Next week… let me check my schedule. I have that meeting with my supervisor on Tuesday, but everything else is pretty open. Yeah, I’m in. Send me the details. Speaker_2: Brilliant. I’ll email you the link. We could grab a bite afterwards? There’s a decent Peruvian place just around the corner. I've been meaning to try it. Speaker_1: Peruvian? Excellent. I’m always up for trying new food. Especially after that cheese rolling documentary has scarred me for life. Speaker_2: (laughing) You're welcome. And honestly, don’t dwell on the cheese rolling. It’s a small price to pay for the wonders of the internet, I suppose. Speaker_1: A very, very small price. Speaker_2: Right, well, shall we refill our coffees and prepare for another afternoon of… productive procrastination?

Speaker_1: Right, now then, have you managed to get that leak sorted in the bathroom, love? It’s been dripping for a week now, and it’s driving me round the bend. Speaker_2: Nah, not yet. I said I would, didn't I? Just haven't had the time with mock exams and everything. It's just a slow drip, isn't it? Not massively urgent. Speaker_1: Not massively urgent? It's wasting water, lad! Always fiddling with something, your Grandad was. Never a dull moment. Remember that time he tried to fix the television with a pair of pliers? Nearly blew the house up. Unless Mr. Thompson decides to give us another three hours of revision. Speaker_1: That man's a menace. I swear he thinks we live to do maths. Did you get that shopping list I left you? We're almost out of biscuits, and your Nana is arriving tomorrow. There'll be hell to pay if there aren't digestives. Speaker_3: Oh, don't worry about me. I’m not fussed about biscuits. Just happy to be here. Though a nice cup of tea would be lovely. Earl Grey if you've got it. Speaker_4: Earl Grey? Fancy. I’ll have a builder’s tea, strong as you like. And a slice of fruitcake, if there is any. Speaker_1: Footcake should be in the tin. I made it last week. Though your Grandad ate a good chunk of it while watching the cricket. Said it helped him concentrate. Speaker_4: (Winks) It does. Gives you something to chew on while you’re shouting at the telly. Speaker_2: You two are both terrible! Using the biscuit tin and cake as excuses. Speaker_1: Now, have you checked the spare room? I want to make sure Nana and Grandad are comfy. Fresh bedding, clean towels… the works. Speaker_2: Yeah, it’s all done. I even dusted. Though I think dust just reappears magically. It’s a conspiracy, I tell ya. Speaker_3: It is a conspiracy. Dust hates a clean house. It plots its return, it does. Speaker_4: (Laughing) You two are a pair. Always finding something to complain about. Speaker_1: Just making sure everything’s perfect for our visitors. They don't get out much these days. And I want them to have a lovely time. Now, does anyone want a cup of tea while I finish tidying up? Although knowing this house, it'll be messy again in five minutes. Speaker_2: I'm good, thanks. Got to revise. Speaker_3: Oh, yes please. Earl Grey, if you wouldn't mind. Speaker_4: Me too. Builder's, strong! And don't skimp on the milk. Speaker_1: Alright, alright! Coming right up. You two are demanding, you know that?

Speaker_1: Oh, look at this one! Remember Sarah’s wedding? We looked so young. And hopelessly jet-lagged, clearly. Speaker_2: (chuckles) Oh god, yes. That was…a trip. Remember that argument you had with Professor Chen about Deleuze? It went on for ages. Speaker_2: (groans) Don’t remind me. He’s brilliant, don’t get me wrong, but he’s incredibly stubborn. It was like talking to a brick wall. Still, it was a good intellectual workout. Speaker_1: It was hilarious to watch, honestly. You were so animated! Speaking of travel… I was looking at flights to Vietnam. Just daydreaming, really. Speaker_2: Vietnam? That sounds amazing! We haven't really explored Southeast Asia much. We did Thailand, but that was…well, a long time ago. Speaker_1: Exactly. I saw some photos of Ha Long Bay and I just thought…wow. Imagine kayaking through that. And the food! I’ve been craving pho for weeks. Speaker_2: (eyes lighting up) Pho…now you’re talking. Maybe when the semester finishes? We could really use a holiday that *isn’t* marking-related. Speaker_1: Definitely. Just a little adventure. Somewhere completely different. We could try and meet up with Maya and David while we’re there? Let's look into it properly tonight, yeah? Maybe start building a little itinerary? Speaker_1: Perfect. A little bit of escapism is exactly what we need. And maybe, just maybe, we can avoid any worm-dancing encounters. Speaker_2: (laughing) No promises. Ben has a habit of appearing wherever there's a party. Speaker_1: True. Oh well, we’ll cross that bridge when we come to it. For now, let's just enjoy the sunset. It's beautiful here. Speaker_2: It is. It really is. It’s funny, isn't it? Sometimes I still can’t believe we live here. China. It feels a world away from Norwich and London. Speaker_1: It does. But it’s our world now. And it’s pretty special.

Speaker_1: Honestly, my face is *killing* me. I swear, glitter is the herpes of festivals. You just get rid of it and it keeps coming back. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh my god, that's so true! Speaker_3: So dragons aren't always mean and the Green Man isn’t always angry? Speaker_1: That’s right. Sometimes things aren’t as simple as they seem. It’s all about looking at things from different points of view. Now, who wants toast? I'm making some. Speaker_2: Me! With jam! Speaker_3: And sprinkles! Can I have sprinkles? Speaker_1: Alright, alright! After hands are washed, then fairy tales. Speaker_3: I’m washing my hands now! Speaker_2: Me too! Super fast! Speaker_1: Good, good. That’s my clever pair. Now, get going. I’ll get the toaster on. Speaker_3: Mummy, can the fairy be *really* mischievous? Speaker_2: Like, really, really, really mischievous? Speaker_1: Oh, she can be *very* mischievous. You’ll see. Now wash properly, or the fairy won't visit! Speaker_2: Okay! Speaker_3: Okay! I’m washing! Speaker_1: Excellent. Right then. Toast is nearly ready and it seems a fairy tale is in high demand. It is a good thing I remembered one… Speaker_3: mummy are you making me a butterfly toast Speaker_2: Can you make me a rainbow toast Speaker_1: (chuckles) oh you two are relentless. Right. Sprinkles are on it. But this is a one time thing.

Speaker_2: So, how was the filming trip today, Lily? Did you have a good time? Speaker_3: It was REALLY good! We went to the museum, and they let us dress up as Romans! I was a centurion! And don't think about the doughnuts too much! Speaker_3: Bye, Daddy! Speaker_4: Bye! Speaker_2: Right, homework time then. Let's get started. Speaker_3: Ugh, homework. Speaker_1: So, how are things with the knee? Still giving you gip? Speaker_2: Oh, it’s a right nuisance, honestly. Best days are when it’s dry, you know? Damp gets right into it. Though, I suppose when people are struggling to make ends meet, environmental concerns tend to take a backseat. Old Man Hemmings retired from the builders, you know. All chasing the money, none wanting to do a proper job. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. My roof needs looking at, and I’m dreading the hassle. Still, at least it gives me something to put off. A woman who can tolerate a teacher’s rambling. That's a keeper. You deserve some happiness, old boy. Speaker_1: Cheers to that. Another pint? Speaker_2: Don't mind if I do. Speaker_1: I've got to say, though, that roast beef was a bit tough. Speaker_2: You never win, do you? Speaker_1: Nope. Never do. Speaker_2: When are you retiring? Speaker_1: Next year, finally. Speaker_2: About time.

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m convinced my fiddle leaf fig is actively plotting my demise. It’s just *drooping*. Despite everything. I’ve rotated it, misted it, talked to it… the whole shebang. Speaker_1: Ooh, a pasty sounds amazing right now. Especially after all this existential dread and fashion deliberation. Yes, please. Vegetable one for me, if they have it. Speaker_2: Sorted. Right, I’m off to wrestle a pasty into submission. And then we can continue to lament the state of the world…or discuss the complexities of plant parenthood. Your choice. Speaker_1: Plant parenthood, definitely. The world can wait five minutes. My fiddle leaf fig needs me. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Of course it does. Speaker_1:It is the most important thing. Speaker_1: Honestly, the students this term are… something else. I had one genuinely ask me if Plato was a real person. A *real* person! Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, you’re joking. For preschoolers! Where have all the lovely, gentle art programmes gone? Speaker_2: Lost to the algorithms, probably. Everything’s about drama and conflict now. Though to be fair, I'm pretty sure even *Blue Peter* had its fair share of near-disasters. Remember the exploding volcano kits? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, don't remind me. My mum nearly had a heart attack when I tried to make one in the kitchen. She banned all science experiments after that. Speaker_2: Sounds like my mum. She always said I was too clumsy for anything involving chemicals. More wine? Speaker_1: Definitely. This is exactly what I needed. A bit of complaining and reminiscence. Speaker_2: Agreed. A good vent, and a reminder that things were always a bit chaotic, even when we were kids. Speaker_1: Exactly. It's a comfort, in a strange way. Speaker_2: Cheers to chaos, then. Speaker_1: Cheers. Speaker_2: So, about those students... any particular standout moments of absurdity? Speaker_1: Oh, where do I even begin...? Speaker_2: Let's hear it. It'll make me feel better about my patriarchal structures accuser.

Speaker_2: …and then young Timothy, bless him, decides to paint the dog. With glitter. Honestly, glitter everywhere! Took me hours to get it out of Buster’s fur. Speaker_1: Glitter, eh? Nightmare stuff that is. Gets into everything. Reminds me of when Elsie decided to decorate the kitchen with flour. Thought she was a baker, she did. More like a blizzard, covering everything. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Sounds like you’ve had your hands full over the years, both of you. My lot are a bit more…contained. Though, I’m eternally explaining the concept of homeostasis to a fourteen-year-old who thinks it’s a trendy skincare brand. Speaker_2: Homeo-whatsit? Honestly, the things they learn in school these days! When I was at grammar school, it was all proper English and sums. No fancy science mumbo jumbo. Speaker_1: Proper sums, that’s what we needed. Not this new-fangled math, where they don't even teach you your times tables. Elsie’s granddaughter, she's struggling somethin’ awful. Said she needs a calculator just to add up ten and five. Speaker_3: It’s a shifting landscape, isn't it? They’re trying to focus on problem-solving rather than rote learning, but it feels like the foundations are missing sometimes. I’ve got a student who can explain the theory of relativity, but can’t balance a chequebook. Speaker_2: Relativity! Goodness me. All sounds awfully complicated. I remember Arthur trying to manage that hostel down by the seafront. Now *that* was complicated. Every Tom, Dick and Harry turning up needing a bed, all sorts of stories. And the state some of them left the kitchens in! Speaker_1: Hostels. Good money to be made, I suppose. My brother, Harold, he ran a little engineering workshop after the war. Always grafting, building things. He could fix anything, that man. Cars, washing machines, anything. Speaker_3: Sounds resourceful. My grandfather was similar. Had a little corner shop in Birmingham. Always working, always providing. Long hours. It was tough back then, but they were a hardworking lot. Speaker_2: Hardworking they were. My mother, she ran a little sweet shop. Remember the smell? Sugar and boiled sweets. And the abattoir down the road… not such a pleasant smell, mind you. Though, Arthur used to get his meat cheap from there. Speaker_1: Abattoirs. Always a bit grim. Old Man Hemmings had one out near Costessey. They used to say he knew every animal by name. Strange, that. Though, you needed good food back then. No fancy supermarket ready meals like you get now. Proper sausages, made with something other than sawdust, hopefully! Speaker_3: (Smiling) Quality sausages are a serious matter. Speaking of food, have you both seen the price of lamb lately? It’s astronomical! You’d think they were raising the sheep on gold leaf. Speaker_2: Don't even get me started on the price of apples! Used to be a pound a bag, now it's…well, honestly! How are people managing? Speaker_1: It’s the world we live in, I suppose. Always changing. I got a photo album here somewhere, from when Elsie and I went to Brighton… I’ll dig it out later. It'll remind us of simpler times, before all the glitter and relativity. Speaker_3: That sounds lovely, I'd really enjoy that. Speaker_2: That would be really nice, yes. It's easy to get lost in the troubles of now, isn't it? A little trip down memory lane is just what we need.

Speaker_1: So, you were a recruiter before this, right? That’s quite a jump to lecturing, isn't it? Speaker_2: Yeah, a pretty massive one, actually. Six years in recruitment. Corporate recruitment, mostly. Headhunting, the whole shebang. It paid well, honestly, but… it was draining. Soul-crushing, sometimes. Speaker_1: I can imagine. It always struck me as a very…results-oriented profession. Not much room for nuance, I’d have thought. Speaker_2: Exactly. Everything was about filling the role, hitting the targets. People were just… commodities, really. I felt awful about it, quite often. I started doing a Masters part-time, just to have something else to focus on, and that’s when I realised I wanted to be *in* academia, not just supplying it with bodies. Speaker_1: Smart move. So, what did you recruit for? Speaker_2: Mostly finance and accounting. High-end stuff. Investment bankers, CFOs… the types who think the world revolves around them. You wouldn’t believe some of the demands they had. One guy insisted his office had to face directly north for feng shui reasons. Speaker_1: (Laughs) Oh, my goodness. You're kidding! Speaker_2: I wish I were. And the egos… Don't even get me started. This job is much more rewarding, even with the marking. Speaking of which, I’m currently wrestling with assessing academic literacy on the lecturer course. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s a tricky one. How’s it going? Speaker_2: Honestly? It’s a mess. Some of them are brilliant, naturally gifted writers. But others… it’s like they’ve never written anything longer than a tweet. They just don’t understand the conventions of academic writing. Paraphrasing is a complete mystery to some of them. Speaker_1: It’s astonishing, isn't it? You’d think, being lecturers themselves, they’d have a grasp of it. Speaker_2: You’d *think*. But they’re experts in their subject matter – history, engineering, whatever – not necessarily in *how* to communicate that knowledge effectively in an academic context. I’ve had papers submitted with direct quotes used as entire paragraphs. No citation. Nothing. Speaker_1: Oh, that's… bold. Have you had to give some pretty harsh feedback? Speaker_2: (Sighs) A lot of it. And it’s hard, because you don’t want to crush their confidence. They're already feeling vulnerable putting their work out there for scrutiny. But you also can't just let poor scholarship slide. It sets a bad example for their students, doesn't it? Speaker_1: Absolutely. It's a very delicate balance. Have you tried directing them towards university writing centres or workshops? Speaker_2: Yeah, I’ve included links to all the resources available. And I’ve tried to be really explicit in the marking criteria. But I still get a lot of… well, let's just say 'creative' interpretations of what constitutes academic writing. It makes me miss the straightforwardness of a recruitment target, sometimes. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Although I suspect you wouldn't trade it back for long. Speaker_2: Definitely not. Even with the baffling academic literacy assessments. And no one's asked me to rearrange my office for feng shui yet. Speaker_1: That's a win, right there. Speaker_2: A very big win. Speaker_1: If you want to bounce some ideas around about the marking, feel free. I taught academic writing for years, although it feels like a lifetime ago.

Speaker_1: Right, so you’re saying you’ve never actually *been* to Blackpool? Speaker_2: Never. Sounds… intense. All the arcades and donkey rides and… well, everything. It’s a challenge! Speaker_2: (Feigning offense) Hey! What’s wrong with our accents? Speaker_3: (Elbowing Liam) It’s charming. Honestly. It’s just… direct. No beating around the bush. My grandma just sighs a lot. Passive-aggressive sighs of judgement. Speaker_3: Mine just comments on how much weight you’ve gained. It’s a loving gesture, apparently. Speaker_4: (Eyes widening) Oh wow. Indian grandmothers are…very different. They just want to feed you everything. Constantly. It’s a sign of affection. Speaker_1: Same! Speaker_1: (Grinning) Oh, you’re in for a treat. It’s definitely…more than digestive. It’s a whole experience. Come on then, let’s go fuel up!

Speaker_1: Honestly though, seeing that documentary about the Falklands… it’s just… bleak. All those lads, so young, sent clear across the world. Speaker_2: Yeah, it’s awful isn't it? My grandad was in the Navy, not the Falklands specifically, but he never really talked about it. Just…distant, you know? You could tell it stuck with him. Speaker_1: Exactly! Like, they’re glorified in films sometimes, all heroic and stuff, but it’s just… trauma, really. Proper trauma. Have you seen that new Top Gun film? Speaker_2: Oh, yeah! It was… fine. Visually stunning, obviously, but a bit… much? A bit like a recruitment advert dressed up as a blockbuster. Speaker_1: That’s exactly what I thought! It felt… unearned? Like, nobody’s facing actual consequences. It’s all just… stunts and swagger. Makes a mockery of the real thing, doesn't it? Speaker_2: Totally. Speaking of things that feel a bit… hollow, I’ve been trying to find a decent magazine lately. Everything’s just endless lists of things to buy. Speaker_1: Oh, tell me about it. I used to love those fashion magazines, but now it’s all influencers and fast fashion. It’s exhausting. Remember *Smash Hits*? Now *that* was a magazine. Speaker_2: *Smash Hits*! Oh my god, the posters! I used to cover my entire bedroom wall in them. Remember the free cassette tapes they’d give away? Speaker_1: Oh, the tapes! Hours of my life were spent recording over those with stuff off the radio. Speaking of old stuff, I’ve been trying to get my old computer working again. Speaker_2: Seriously? What, like a proper ancient one? Speaker_1: Pretty much. It's a dinosaur. I just want to play some of those old games again, you know? *SimCity 2000* mostly. Pure nostalgia. It’s refusing to recognise the hard drive though. Speaker_2: Ugh, computers. They’re the bane of my existence. I spent three hours on the phone with IT at work yesterday trying to get the projector working for a presentation. Three hours! Speaker_1: Oh, that’s brutal. IT people… they speak a different language, don’t they? All jargon and condescension. Speaker_2: They’re actively trying to wind me up, I swear. Anyway, have you managed to book those cinema tickets for Friday? For that new Wes Anderson film? Speaker_1: Yes! Got them for the 7:30 showing. I thought that would be a good time, give us a chance to grab some food beforehand. Speaker_2: Perfect. I’m starving just thinking about it. Maybe that new Italian place? I’ve heard good things. Speaker_1: Ooh, yes! That sounds lovely. And afterwards, maybe back to mine for a movie? I've got that box set of… oh, what's it called… that sci-fi one, with the spaceships… Speaker_2: *Battlestar Galactica*? Speaker_1: Yes! That one. We never got to finish it. Speaker_2: Excellent. It's a plan. Right, more lasagne? Speaker_1: Absolutely. Don’t mind if I do. Speaker_2: Good. It is a good plan. Speaker_1: Yeah. Speaker_2: It’ll be nice. Speaker_1: Yeah!

Speaker_1: Honestly, the state of dating apps right now is… a disaster. It’s just endless scrolling and everyone’s photos are clearly five years old. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. They think anything outside the M25 is a rural wasteland. I’m visiting my parents next month - dreading the inevitable questions about my career. "So, are you seriously still an architect? Apparently, she's a “lovely girl.” Speaker_3: (Groans) Oh no. The dentist’s daughter. That's a whole other level. Speaker_1: Right? I’m thinking of just lying and saying I’m engaged to someone incredibly unsuitable. That’ll shut them up. Speaker_2: That’s a bold move. I like it. What are you both doing next week anyway? I was thinking we could check out that new indie cinema. Speaker_3: I’m free most of next week. Sounds good! I need a film to distract me from the endless application forms.
